q: A technician is documenting the Linux boot sequence from power-on to a login prompt. Which order is correct?
explain: Firmware initializes hardware and hands off to the bootloader (GRUB2), which loads the kernel and the initramfs (temporary root filesystem with boot-critical drivers); the kernel then starts systemd as PID 1. The initramfs must come before systemd, and the kernel before both — every other order breaks the chain.

q: After editing /etc/default/grub on a RHEL 9 server (for example, to change the boot timeout), which command regenerates the bootloader configuration so the change takes effect?
explain: On RHEL-family systems, grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg rebuilds the GRUB2 configuration from /etc/default/grub and /etc/grub.d. update-grub is the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent, grub-install reinstalls the bootloader itself (not the config), and daemon-reload only affects systemd units.

q: A data center provisions bare-metal servers over the network with no local operating system installed. Which two services must the PXE infrastructure provide for these servers to boot?
options: DHCP (address plus boot-server/file info) and TFTP (bootloader and kernel files)
explain: PXE booting works in two stages: DHCP gives the client an IP address and tells it where the boot server is and which file to fetch, then TFTP serves the bootloader, kernel, and initramfs. DNS, Samba, LDAP, and NFS play no required role in the PXE boot sequence itself.

q: According to the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), system-wide configuration files belong in which directory?
explain: /etc holds host-specific system configuration (sshd_config, fstab, passwd). /var holds variable data like logs and spools, /usr holds user programs and libraries, and /proc is a virtual filesystem exposing kernel and process information — none of them store system configuration.

q: A startup wants to design custom silicon around a royalty-free, open instruction set architecture. Which architecture fits this requirement?
explain: RISC-V is an open, royalty-free ISA — anyone can implement it without licensing fees. x86_64 and x86 are proprietary (Intel/AMD), and AArch64 is ARM's licensed architecture. The XK0-006 objectives list all three server architectures: x86_64, AArch64, and RISC-V.

q: Which statement about dpkg on Debian-based systems is TRUE?
options: dpkg installs .deb files directly but does not resolve dependencies automatically — that is apt's job
dpkg automatically downloads and resolves all dependencies from configured repositories
dpkg is the low-level package tool on RPM-based distributions
explain: dpkg is the low-level Debian package tool: dpkg -i installs a local .deb but fails if dependencies are missing, while apt (the high-level frontend) resolves and fetches them. This is the classic exam trap — on Debian-family systems, dependency resolution means apt, not dpkg.

q: A new network adapter's driver module is installed but not loaded. Which command loads the module along with any modules it depends on?
explain: modprobe loads a module and automatically resolves and loads its dependencies (using data built by depmod). insmod loads a single module file with no dependency handling, lsmod only lists loaded modules, and modinfo only displays module information.

q: After adding a storage driver that is needed at boot time on a RHEL system, which command rebuilds the initramfs image to include it?
explain: dracut is the modern RHEL-family tool for generating initramfs images. mkinitrd is its legacy predecessor, update-initramfs is the Debian/Ubuntu equivalent, and grub2-mkconfig rebuilds the bootloader menu — not the initramfs.

q: You must create a GPT partition table on a 6 TB disk to use the full capacity. Which tool is purpose-built for GPT partitioning?
explain: gdisk is the GPT-aware partitioning tool; fdisk is the classic MBR-oriented tool (MBR cannot address beyond 2 TB). parted handles both, but of the choices given, gdisk is the GPT answer. mkfs and tune2fs work on filesystems, not partition tables.

q: An admin has a new partitioned disk /dev/sdb1 and wants an LVM logical volume on it. Which sequence is correct?
options: pvcreate /dev/sdb1 → vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb1 → lvcreate -L 20G -n lvdata vgdata
vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb1 → pvcreate /dev/sdb1 → lvcreate -L 20G -n lvdata vgdata
explain: LVM layers bottom-up: pvcreate initializes the physical volume, vgcreate builds the volume group from PVs, and lvcreate carves logical volumes out of the VG. You cannot create a volume group before its physical volumes exist, and lvcreate allocates from a VG — not from a raw disk.

q: The logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvvar (ext4, mounted at /var) is full. Which command extends both the logical volume AND its filesystem by 10 GB in a single step?
explain: The -r (--resizefs) flag tells lvextend to grow the filesystem along with the LV — without it, the LV grows but the filesystem stays the same size (the classic trap). -L +10G adds 10 GB; -L 10G without the plus would shrink-or-set the LV to exactly 10 GB. vgextend adds PVs to a VG, not space to an LV.

q: After extending the logical volume behind an XFS filesystem, which command grows the filesystem to use the new space?
explain: xfs_growfs grows an XFS filesystem and takes the mount point (not the device) as its argument. resize2fs is for ext2/3/4, xfs_repair fixes corruption (it does not resize), and mkfs.xfs would destroy the data. Remember: XFS can be grown but never shrunk.

q: A compliance policy states that no binaries may execute from /tmp. Which /etc/fstab mount option enforces this on the /tmp filesystem?
explain: noexec blocks execution of binaries on the mounted filesystem — the standard hardening for /tmp (and /var/tmp). nosuid blocks setuid/setgid bits, nodev blocks device files, and noatime only disables access-time updates for performance. Match the option to the goal: execution → noexec.

q: A server uses NetworkManager. Which command activates the existing connection profile named 'eth0' from the command line?
explain: nmcli is NetworkManager's CLI: 'con up' activates a connection profile (applying its IP, DNS, and routes). 'ip link set up' only raises the link layer without applying the profile, ifup is the legacy network-scripts tool, and netplan apply is Ubuntu's renderer — not NetworkManager's command.

q: On Ubuntu Server, an admin writes a new static-IP configuration in YAML. Which file location and command apply it?
options: A file under /etc/netplan/, then netplan apply
A file under /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/, then systemctl restart network
explain: Ubuntu Server uses Netplan: YAML configs live in /etc/netplan/ and netplan apply renders and activates them (netplan try is the safe test-first variant). /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts is RHEL-family, /etc/network/interfaces is legacy Debian, and resolv.conf only controls DNS resolution.

q: An admin suspects an unknown service is listening on TCP port 8080. Which modern command lists listening TCP sockets along with the owning processes?
explain: ss (part of iproute2) is the modern replacement for netstat: -t (TCP), -u (UDP), -l (listening), -n (numeric), -p (process). netstat is deprecated on Linux, lsof /etc/services reads the port-name database rather than live sockets, and nmap scans from outside without showing local process owners.

q: A script's error messages must be captured in errors.log while normal output still displays on the terminal. Which redirection does this?
explain: File descriptor 2 is standard error, so 2> redirects only errors to the file while stdout still goes to the terminal. A bare > captures stdout instead, and piping to a filename is a syntax error. (2>&1 > file would send both streams to the file — the reverse of what is wanted.)

q: From /etc/passwd, you need only the usernames — the first colon-delimited field of each line. Which command does this?
explain: cut -d: -f1 splits each line on colons and prints field 1. awk '{print $2}' splits on whitespace (wrong delimiter and wrong field here), sort only orders lines, and grep -v : would remove every line since all contain colons.

q: A user wants a custom alias available in every new interactive shell they open. Which file should define it?
explain: ~/.bashrc is read by interactive non-login shells — every new terminal. ~/.bash_profile (and ~/.profile) run only for login shells, .bash_history merely records past commands, and /etc/hosts maps hostnames to IPs. Aliases and functions belong in .bashrc.

q: Which command creates a gzipped tar archive of /etc/nginx named nginx-backup.tar.gz?
explain: c = create, z = gzip compress, f = file. -xzf would extract, -cjf creates a bzip2 (.bz2) archive, and -tzf only lists an archive's contents. Remember: c creates, x extracts, t lists — the exam loves swapping them.

q: Which command mirrors /data/ to a backup server, preserving permissions and deleting backup-side files that no longer exist in the source?
explain: -a preserves permissions/ownership/timestamps, -v is verbose, -z compresses in transit, and --delete is what makes it a true mirror by removing stale destination files. Without --delete the backup accumulates deleted files; cp cannot copy to a remote host at all, and scp lacks --delete and -a semantics.

q: Which hypervisor is built into the Linux kernel and is typically managed with libvirt and virsh?
explain: KVM turns the Linux kernel itself into a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor, with QEMU providing device emulation and libvirt/virsh/virt-manager as the management layer. VirtualBox is a hosted Type 2 hypervisor, Hyper-V is Microsoft's, and Xen is a separate standalone hypervisor — not part of the Linux kernel.

q: A VM must appear as its own host on the physical LAN, receiving an IP address from the LAN's DHCP server. Which virtual network type provides this?
explain: Bridged networking attaches the VM directly to the physical network as if it were its own machine — it gets a LAN IP from the real DHCP server. NAT hides the VM behind the host's IP, host-only/isolated keeps it off the physical LAN entirely. Match the requirement (own LAN identity) to bridged.

q: Which statement about hard links is TRUE?
options: A hard link shares the same inode as its target, cannot span filesystems, and cannot link directories
A hard link gets its own inode and can point across filesystems
Symbolic links share the target's inode, while hard links do not
explain: Hard links are additional directory entries pointing at the same inode — same data, no extra space, but confined to one filesystem and never allowed on directories. Symbolic links are separate files (own inode) holding a path, so they can cross filesystems. ln -s creates a symbolic link.

q: Which command finds files ending in .log under /var/log that were modified more than 30 days ago?
explain: find with -name matches the pattern and -mtime +30 matches modification time older than 30 days. locate queries a filename database and has no time filtering, ls -R cannot filter by age, and -atime measures access time, not modification time.

q: In /dev, how do block devices and character devices differ?
options: Block devices (e.g., /dev/sda) transfer data in buffered blocks; character devices (e.g., /dev/tty) transfer unbuffered streams
Character devices (e.g., /dev/sda) transfer data in blocks; block devices stream characters
Block devices are only for USB hardware; character devices are only for disks
There is no functional difference — the names are historical
explain: Block devices (disks like /dev/sda, /dev/nvme0n1) move data in fixed-size buffered blocks and support random access; character devices (terminals, serial ports, /dev/null) move unbuffered character streams. ls -l shows 'b' or 'c' in the first column to tell them apart.

q: Which command shows which process is using TCP port 443?
explain: lsof -i :443 lists open files (sockets) matching port 443, revealing the owning process. ps aux | grep 443 only finds processes with '443' in their command line, /proc/443 would be a PID directory (not a port), and df reports disk space.

q: Which command creates user 'deploy' with a home directory and the bash shell?
explain: -m creates the home directory (copied from /etc/skel) and -s sets the login shell. -M explicitly skips home creation (the trap), a bare useradd may not create a home depending on distro defaults, and --no-create-home does the opposite of what is wanted.

q: Why are password hashes stored in /etc/shadow rather than /etc/passwd?
options: /etc/passwd is world-readable, so hashes were moved to /etc/shadow, which only root can read
Hashes in /etc/passwd would make the file too large
explain: Historically hashes lived in world-readable /etc/passwd, letting any user copy them for offline cracking. Modern Linux keeps 'x' in passwd's password field and the real hash in /etc/shadow (mode 600/640, root-only). The roles are not reversed, and file size was never the reason.

q: An employee is terminated and their account must be locked immediately without deleting the user or their files. Which command does this?
explain: passwd -l locks the account by prefixing the hash with '!', blocking password logins while preserving the account and data. userdel removes the account entirely, changing the shell does not lock anything, and chage -m only sets the minimum days between password changes.

q: On a standard modern Linux system, regular (non-system) user accounts are typically assigned UIDs starting at which number?
explain: UID 0 is root, low UIDs (typically 1–999) are reserved for system/service accounts, and human user accounts start at 1000 on modern distributions (older RHEL used 500). Checking the UID range tells you whether an account is a user, service, or system account.

q: A process ignores SIGTERM and must be stopped immediately, with no chance to clean up. Which signal does this?
explain: SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored — the kernel terminates the process immediately. SIGTERM (15) politely asks and can be caught or ignored, SIGHUP (1) typically reloads configuration, and STOP merely suspends. Use 9 as the last resort since the process cannot flush buffers or clean up.

q: Which nice value gives a process the HIGHEST CPU priority, and who is allowed to set it?
options: -20, and only root can assign negative nice values
19, and any user can assign it
0, and only root can assign it
99, and any user can assign it
explain: Nice values run from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest); 0 is the default. Only root may set negative values (raise priority); unprivileged users may only lower their own processes' priority (raise the nice value). 99 is not a valid nice value.

q: A long-running job is in the foreground of your shell. Which keystroke suspends it, and which command then resumes it in the background?
options: Ctrl+Z to suspend, then bg to resume in the background
Ctrl+C to suspend, then bg to resume in the background
Ctrl+D to suspend, then fg to resume in the background
Ctrl+Z to suspend, then fg to resume in the background
explain: Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP, suspending the foreground job (it appears in jobs); bg then resumes it in the background. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT (kills), Ctrl+D signals end-of-input, and fg resumes in the foreground — the opposite of what is wanted.

q: Which crontab entry runs /usr/local/bin/backup.sh at 2:30 AM every day?
explain: Cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week: minute 30, hour 2, every day. Swapping the first two fields (2 30) is the classic trap — it means 2:30 only if read backwards, but cron reads minute first (2 minutes past 30:00 is invalid-ish; actually hour 30 is invalid). * * 0 restricts to Sundays.

q: On Ubuntu, which command refreshes the local package index from the configured repositories without installing anything?
explain: apt update downloads fresh package lists (the index). apt upgrade then installs newer versions of installed packages. Confusing update with upgrade is the exam's favorite apt trap: update = refresh the catalog, upgrade = install the updates.

q: Which command identifies the installed RPM package that owns the file /etc/ssh/sshd_config?
explain: rpm -qf (--query --file) maps a file path back to its owning package. -qa lists all packages (grep would rarely match a filename), -qi needs the package name first, and -e would attempt to erase — dangerous and wrong.

q: Before installing packages from a third-party repository, which step verifies the packages are authentic and untampered?
options: Import the repository's GPG key so package signatures are verified
Set gpgcheck=0 in the repo file to speed up installs
Install with --nogpgcheck to skip slow verification
Delete /etc/yum.repos.d to force a fresh download
explain: GPG signatures prove packages came from the repo owner and were not modified; importing the repo's public key enables that check. Disabling gpgcheck or using --nogpgcheck does the opposite — it blinds the system to tampered or forged packages.

q: Which single command enables the nginx service to start at boot AND starts it right now?
explain: --now combines enable (persistent across boots) with start (immediate). enable alone does not start the service now, start alone does not persist it, and chkconfig is the legacy SysV tool — not systemd.

q: An admin wants to guarantee that the apache service can NEVER start — not at boot, not manually, not even as a dependency. Which is the strongest action?
explain: mask symlinks the unit to /dev/null, making it impossible to start by any means until unmasked. disable only removes it from boot targets (it can still be started manually), stop only halts the running instance, and kill only terminates processes. mask > disable > stop in strength.

q: Which command shows only the nginx service's journal entries from today?
explain: -u filters by systemd unit and --since today bounds the time range. -f follows new entries live instead of filtering by date, dmesg shows only kernel ring-buffer messages, and /var/log/messages is the undifferentiated syslog stream, not unit-filtered.

q: In a Dockerfile, which instruction switches subsequent build steps and the container's processes to run as a non-root user?
explain: USER sets the user for following instructions and the running container — the standard way to drop root privileges. RUN useradd only creates the account without switching to it, ENTRYPOINT sets the executable, and FROM picks the base image. Running containers as non-root is a core container-hardening practice.

q: A container must share the host's network stack directly — no NAT, no network isolation. Which container network mode provides this?
explain: host mode removes network isolation: the container uses the host's interfaces and ports directly. bridge (the default) NATs container traffic behind the host, none gives the container no networking, and macvlan assigns the container its own MAC/IP on the physical network (isolated but LAN-visible).

q: A Linux server must authenticate users against Active Directory with caching for offline logins. Which daemon is the modern solution for this?
options: Winbind only, since SSSD cannot talk to AD
explain: SSSD is the modern daemon for central authentication against LDAP, Kerberos, and Active Directory, with credential caching for offline use. Winbind is the older Samba-based approach, NIS is legacy and insecure (no encryption), and xinetd is a superserver — unrelated to directory authentication.

q: Which auditd rule watches /etc/shadow for write and attribute-change attempts?
explain: -w sets a file watch, -p wa watches for writes and attribute changes (not reads), and -k adds a searchable key. -p r would log every read (noisy and wrong goal), /etc/passwd is the wrong file, and auditctl -D deletes all rules.

q: Which command joins a RHEL-family system to an Active Directory domain using realmd?
explain: realm join discovers the domain and configures SSSD/Kerberos to enroll the host. realm leave removes it, kinit only obtains a Kerberos ticket for a user (no domain join), and ldapsearch merely queries an LDAP directory.

q: Which firewalld zone silently discards all incoming packets without sending any response to the sender?
explain: drop discards packets with no reply, so scanners cannot even tell the host exists. block also denies everything but sends an ICMP reject (visible). public is the restrictive-but-functional default zone, and trusted accepts everything. drop vs. block is the exam's favorite firewalld trap.

q: Which firewall-cmd sequence permanently opens the HTTP service and applies the change?
explain: --permanent writes the rule to the persistent configuration and --reload activates it. Without --permanent the rule is runtime-only and vanishes on reload/reboot (the trap). --reload must come after the change, and raw iptables bypasses firewalld's management.

q: Which framework is the modern, unified replacement for iptables on Linux, using a single syntax for IPv4/IPv6?
explain: nftables (configured with nft) succeeds iptables in the kernel's Netfilter framework with one rule language for both IP versions. firewalld and UFW are user-friendly frontends (firewalld can use nftables underneath), and ipset is a companion tool for efficient IP-set matching — not a firewall framework itself.

q: A company hosts a web server at private IP 10.0.0.5 and must make it reachable from the internet through the firewall's public IP. Which NAT type rewrites the destination address to accomplish this?
options: PAT (Port Address Translation) for outbound sessions
explain: DNAT rewrites the destination address of inbound packets — the mechanism behind port forwarding to internal servers. SNAT/MASQUERADE rewrite the source address of outbound traffic so private hosts can reach the internet. Direction is the key: inbound to a server = DNAT, outbound from clients = SNAT.

q: Which is the safe way to edit the sudoers configuration?
options: visudo, which syntax-checks the file before saving
chmod 777 /etc/sudoers then edit with any editor
explain: visudo locks the file and validates syntax before committing — a sudoers syntax error can lock every admin out of root, so the check is critical. Direct editing risks exactly that lockout, appending blindly is equally risky, and 777 on sudoers is both insecure and will cause sudo to refuse to run.

q: A sudoers entry reads 'deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL'. What is the security concern?
options: Anyone who compromises the deploy account gets passwordless root on every host — NOPASSWD removes the last authentication barrier
There is no concern; NOPASSWD only affects the login password
NOPASSWD entries are ignored by modern sudo
The entry is invalid because ALL cannot follow NOPASSWD
explain: NOPASSWD lets the user run the listed commands as root without re-authenticating, so a compromised deploy password (or unattended session) equals instant root. The entry is valid and honored — that is precisely why the objectives flag understanding its implications.

q: Which sshd_config settings BEST harden remote administrative access?
options: PermitRootLogin no and PasswordAuthentication no (key-based auth only)
explain: Disabling direct root login forces attackers through a named account, and disabling password auth (keys only) defeats brute-force password attacks. The other options weaken security: root login enabled, empty passwords, and X11 forwarding all expand attack surface. Changing the port is obscurity, not hardening.

q: During a hardening review, which command finds all SUID binaries on the system?
explain: -perm -4000 matches the SUID bit (octal 4000). -2000 matches SGID instead (the trap), grepping ls output is unreliable, and chmod -s would strip bits blindly across the filesystem — destructive. Unnecessary SUID binaries should be removed or have the bit stripped after review.

q: A service account must never get an interactive login shell. Which command enforces this?
explain: /sbin/nologin politely refuses interactive logins (printing a message) while still allowing the account to own processes like daemons. /bin/bash grants a full shell, /bin/rbash is still a shell (restricted, but a shell), and passwd -u unlocks rather than restricts.

q: Per the XK0-006 objectives, which PAM module is associated with locking accounts after repeated failed login attempts?
explain: The objectives name pam_tally2 for failed-login accounting and lockout policy. pam_unix handles standard password authentication, pam_limits enforces resource limits, and pam_env sets environment variables. (On current RHEL-family releases the same job is done by pam_faillock, but pam_tally2 is the objectives' named module.)

q: Which technology provides full-disk (data-at-rest) encryption on Linux, as called out in the XK0-006 objectives?
explain: LUKS2 is the standard for Linux block-device/full-disk encryption (managed with cryptsetup), protecting data at rest including against physical theft. GPG encrypts individual files, while TLS and WireGuard protect data in transit — the wrong state of data for this question.

q: Which hashing approach is appropriate for verifying file integrity today?
explain: SHA-256 is a current, collision-resistant hash suitable for integrity checks (and HMAC when keyed). MD5 is broken for security use (practical collisions), DES is an obsolete cipher (not a hash), and ROT13 is not cryptography at all. The objectives explicitly call for removing weak algorithms.

q: Which tool builds a database of file hashes so unauthorized changes to system files can be detected?
explain: AIDE snapshots file hashes, permissions, and attributes, then reports deviations — classic file-integrity monitoring. rkhunter hunts rootkits specifically, nmap scans networks, and tcpdump captures packets. Match the goal (detect changed files) to AIDE.

q: Which command securely overwrites a sensitive file's contents before removing it?
explain: shred overwrites the file's blocks multiple times (-u removes it afterward); rm only unlinks the directory entry, leaving recoverable data on disk (the trap). You cannot mv to /dev/null, and touch only updates timestamps. (On journaled filesystems and SSDs, full destruction may still need crypto-erase or physical destruction.)

q: Why do the XK0-006 objectives recommend avoiding self-signed certificates?
options: Clients cannot validate them against a trusted chain, causing trust warnings and enabling man-in-the-middle attacks
They require a commercial CA to install
explain: A self-signed cert provides encryption but no third-party identity validation, so clients warn (and users click through, training bad habits) and attackers can substitute their own self-signed cert. Commercial or no-cost CAs (like Let's Encrypt) anchor trust in a verifiable chain. Encryption strength is unrelated to who signed the cert.

q: Which statement about Ansible is TRUE?
options: It is agentless — it manages nodes over SSH with no agent software installed on them
It requires a persistent agent installed on every managed node
It uses Ruby-based recipes as its primary language
It can only manage Windows hosts
explain: Ansible's agentless architecture (SSH for Linux, WinRM for Windows) is its defining trait versus agent-based tools like Puppet. Playbooks are YAML, not Ruby recipes, and its primary target is Linux/Unix infrastructure.

q: An admin needs to run a single command on 50 web servers immediately, without writing a playbook. Which Ansible approach fits?
options: An ad hoc command, e.g., ansible web -m ping
explain: Ad hoc commands execute a single module/task across an inventory pattern — ideal for one-off actions. Playbooks and roles are for repeatable, versioned automation (overkill here), the inventory alone runs nothing, and ansible-galaxy manages collections.

q: In OpenTofu, what does the state file track?
options: The mapping between the written configuration and the real-world resources actually deployed
The Git commit history of the configuration
explain: The state file is OpenTofu's memory: it records which real resources correspond to the configuration so plans and applies know what to create, change, or destroy. It is not a credential store, not version history (that is Git's job), and contains no packet data. Protect it — it may hold sensitive values.

q: Which tool automates first-boot configuration (users, keys, packages) of cloud VM images?
explain: cloud-init is the standard for customizing cloud images at first boot via user-data. Kickstart automates RHEL-family OS installations (installer-time, typically bare metal or VM installs), GRUB2 is the bootloader, and while systemd-firstboot exists, cloud-init is the objectives' named cloud tool.

q: What is the purpose of '#!/bin/bash' as the first line of a script?
options: It is the interpreter directive (shebang) telling the kernel which interpreter runs the script
It is a comment documenting the author
It sets the script's file permissions
explain: The shebang (#!) is read by the kernel's program loader to select the interpreter. Without it, the script may run under the wrong shell. It is not a mere comment — placement on line 1 is what gives it meaning — and it has nothing to do with permissions (that is chmod).

q: After running 'cp file1 file2' in a script, how do you test whether the copy succeeded?
options: echo $? — an exit code of 0 means success
echo $# — the argument count proves success
echo $$ — the PID confirms the copy
echo $! — the background job ID confirms the copy
explain: $? holds the previous command's exit status: 0 = success, nonzero = failure. $# counts positional parameters, $$ is the shell's own PID, and $! is the last backgrounded PID — none reflect the cp result. Checking $? (or testing the command directly in if) is fundamental scripting.

q: In the test '[ $a -eq $b ]', what does -eq compare?
explain: -eq, -ne, -gt, -ge, -lt, -le are integer comparisons; string comparison uses = / == / != (and =~ for regex). -e tests file existence. Mixing them — e.g., using == on numbers — is a classic scripting bug the exam probes.

q: Which syntax captures a command's output into a variable using the modern recommended form?
explain: $(...) is the modern command substitution: nestable and readable. Backticks are the legacy form (hard to nest), $ls is just a variable expansion, and (ls) runs the command in a subshell without capturing its output into the variable.

q: Given name='world' was assigned earlier, what does echo '$name' print?
explain: Single quotes suppress all expansion — the literal string $name is printed. Double quotes (echo "$name") would print world. Quoting behavior is one of the most-tested scripting fundamentals: single = literal, double = expand.

q: Which loop continues executing UNTIL its condition becomes true — the inverse of while?
explain: until runs the body while the condition is false and stops once it becomes true; while does the opposite. for iterates over a list, and case is a conditional (multi-way branch), not a loop.

q: Which command creates an isolated Python virtual environment named 'proj' using the standard library?
explain: python3 -m venv uses the stdlib venv module to build an isolated environment with its own interpreter and site-packages. pip installs packages (it does not create environments), --new-env is not a real flag, and conda is a third-party tool — not the stdlib approach the objectives name.

q: In Python, what defines a code block (e.g., the body of an if statement or function)?
explain: Python uses indentation to delimit blocks — inconsistent indentation is a syntax error. Braces belong to languages like C and JavaScript, semicolons merely separate statements on one line, and Python has no 'end' keyword. PEP 8 recommends 4 spaces per level.

q: What does 'git pull' do?
options: Fetches changes from the remote and merges them into the current branch
Pushes local commits to the remote
explain: pull = fetch + merge (the convenient combined operation). push sends local commits outward, fetch alone only downloads without merging, and clone creates a fresh local copy. Knowing pull's two halves matters when merge conflicts appear.

q: Which file tells Git to exclude local secrets (like .env) and build artifacts from commits?
explain: .gitignore lists patterns Git must never track — the standard place to exclude secrets, keys, and build output. .gitconfig stores user settings, README documents the project, and hooks run scripts (a safety net, not the exclusion mechanism).

q: A developer must build a feature without disturbing the main branch. Which workflow is correct?
options: git checkout -b feature-x, commit the work there, then merge the branch into main
Commit directly to main and hope nothing breaks
Edit files without committing until release day
explain: Feature branches isolate work: create the branch, commit there, then merge (or rebase) into main after review. Committing experiments directly to main risks everyone's builds, stash is for temporarily shelving changes (not branching), and uncommitted edits are unprotected work.

q: Per responsible-AI best practices in the XK0-006 objectives, what must an admin do before running AI-generated shell commands on a production system?
options: Human-review and test them first — never copy/paste AI output into production unreviewed
Run them immediately since AI output is always correct
Pipe them directly to bash to save time
Only check that the syntax highlighting looks right
explain: The objectives stress verifying AI output, human review, and never pasting unreviewed code — AI can produce plausible but destructive commands. Blind execution risks data loss; review plus testing in a safe environment is the required practice.

q: Which of the following should NEVER be pasted into a public large language model, per AI data-governance best practices?
options: Production credentials, API keys, or customer personal data
A generic error message with no identifying details
An anonymized code snippet with no secrets
explain: Public LLMs may retain or train on inputs, so secrets and personal data must never go in — use local/private models or redaction for sensitive work. Generic errors, man pages, and sanitized snippets are fine. Data governance means knowing where your data goes before you share it.

q: An SLO states that 99.9% of API requests must succeed each month. In SLA/SLI/SLO terms, what is the measured 'percentage of successful requests'?
options: The SLI (Service Level Indicator) — the metric being measured
The SLO (Service Level Objective) — the target itself
The SLA (Service Level Agreement) — the contract
explain: SLI = the measured indicator (actual success rate), SLO = the target for that indicator (99.9%), SLA = the contractual commitment with consequences. The exam tests the trio: indicator measures, objective targets, agreement contracts.

q: Which SNMP mechanism lets a monitored device proactively notify the management station that an event occurred, without being polled?
explain: Traps are agent-initiated asynchronous notifications (link down, threshold crossed). MIBs are the management databases describing objects, GET is the manager polling the agent, and the community string is SNMP's weak credential. Push vs. pull: traps push.

q: A server kernel-panics during boot right after last night's kernel update. What is the FIRST troubleshooting step?
options: Boot the previous known-good kernel from the GRUB menu
explain: Methodology: the most recent change (the kernel update) is the prime suspect, and GRUB keeps older kernels precisely for rollback — boot one to confirm. Reinstalling or replacing hardware before testing the obvious software change skips steps and wastes time.

q: After a failed update, the system drops to a 'grub>' rescue prompt instead of the boot menu. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: GRUB cannot find its configuration or normal module (bootloader misconfiguration)
A user cron job is malformed
The NTP service failed to sync
explain: A grub> prompt means the bootloader loaded but cannot locate grub.cfg or its modules — classic GRUB misconfiguration (wrong paths, failed update). Password expiry, cron, and NTP issues manifest long after the bootloader hands off to the kernel.

q: 'df -h' shows the filesystem only 60% full, yet writes fail with 'No space left on device'. Which command diagnoses this?
explain: Inode exhaustion: millions of small files can consume all inodes while blocks remain free, and df -i reveals it. du finds large directories (wrong symptom here), free shows memory, and deleted-but-open files are a different 'disk full' cause (that one shows 100% in df).

q: The root filesystem is at 100% usage. Which command BEST identifies the largest directories so space can be reclaimed?
explain: du summarizes disk usage per directory; sorting reveals the biggest consumers to investigate (often /var/log). df only shows filesystem-level totals, ls -lh does not recurse sizes, and blindly finding *.log misses other culprits. After locating the hog: check logrotate, truncate or archive, then fix the root cause.

q: dmesg shows 'Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (java)'. What happened?
options: The kernel's OOM killer terminated the process to protect the system from memory exhaustion
An admin manually killed the process with kill -9
The process hit a segmentation fault
explain: When RAM and swap are exhausted, the OOM killer sacrifices the highest-scoring process to keep the kernel alive — dmesg records the kill. It is not a manual kill, not a segfault (signal 11), and certainly not clean. The fix addresses memory pressure: add RAM, tune the app, or adjust overcommit policy.

q: A filesystem will not mount and the logs indicate corruption. Which tool checks and repairs it? (The filesystem is currently unmounted.)
options: fsck (e.g., fsck.ext4) on the unmounted device
explain: fsck checks and repairs filesystem inconsistencies — run on the unmounted device. mount -a will just fail again, mkfs destroys all data (never a repair step), and xfs_growfs only grows XFS. Always verify backups before repairing.

q: A server cannot ping its default gateway. What is the FIRST thing to check?
options: Physical/link status: 'ip link show' and link lights, cables, switch port
explain: Troubleshoot bottom-up: if the link is down, nothing above it (IP, gateway, DNS) can work. ip link shows link state; check cables and switch ports before touching software. DNS is irrelevant when the gateway itself is unreachable, and reinstalling/rebooting skips diagnosis.

q: curl fails on hostnames but works when given IP addresses directly. Which is the BEST first check of DNS resolution?
options: dig example.com — inspect whether the resolver returns a valid answer
explain: dig queries DNS directly and shows the full resolution path, exposing whether the resolver, the record, or the network path is at fault. /etc/hosts is checked before DNS per nsswitch, but the symptom (all names fail) points at the resolver — dig tests exactly that. Traceroute to the IP tests routing, not naming.

q: Small packets cross a VPN tunnel fine, but large file transfers stall or time out. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: MTU mismatch — large packets need fragmentation that the tunnel mishandles
explain: The size-dependent pattern is the MTU signature: small packets fit, large ones fragment or get dropped (especially with DF bit set or PMTU black holes on tunnels). DNS, DHCP, and permissions do not discriminate by packet size. Test with ping -M do -s to find the path MTU.

q: A workstation has address 169.254.10.20. What does this indicate, and what is the fix?
options: APIPA link-local address — DHCP failed; check the link and DHCP server, then renew with dhclient
A properly assigned static address — no action needed
A duplicate IP — pick a new static address
explain: 169.254.0.0/16 is the APIPA/link-local range, self-assigned only when DHCP fails — the host has no usable network config. Fix the underlying cause (cable, switch, DHCP server scope) and renew the lease. It is not a valid static assignment and has nothing to do with DNS.

q: Two hosts were accidentally given 192.168.1.50 and connectivity flaps for both. How do you confirm the duplicate IP?
options: Check the ARP/neighbor table for two different MAC addresses claiming the same IP
explain: 'ip neigh' / 'arp -a' showing the same IP mapped to two different MACs (flapping between them) confirms the conflict. A single ping cannot distinguish the owners, traceroute shows path not ownership, and resolv.conf is about DNS. Fix: assign a unique address and document the allocation.

q: An application cannot write to a directory despite 777 permissions, and the audit log shows AVC denials. What is the BEST fix?
options: Correct the SELinux context (e.g., restorecon) or set the appropriate boolean — do NOT just disable SELinux
Run setenforce 0 to turn SELinux off permanently
explain: AVC denials with permissive DAC permissions mean SELinux (MAC layer) is blocking the access — fix the type context or boolean so the policy allows it. setenforce 0 / disabling SELinux 'fixes' the symptom by removing protection (the exam's trap answer). DAC 777 was already wide open; reinstalling changes nothing.

q: A user reports 'Permission denied' on /data/report.txt. Which command traces permissions along the ENTIRE path, revealing a restrictive parent directory?
explain: namei -l resolves every path component and shows each one's permissions — the classic culprit is a parent directory lacking +x. ls -l shows only the file itself (missing the real cause), chmod guesses at a fix without diagnosing, and id shows group membership only.

q: An HTTPS service stopped working the morning after a scheduled date change on the server. What is the likely cause and how do you verify?
options: The TLS certificate expired (or is not yet valid) — check its dates with openssl s_client or the cert file
The firewall blocks port 443 — check iptables
The disk is full — check df
explain: Certificates have validity windows; a date jump can push the system outside them, breaking TLS handshakes. Verify with 'openssl s_client -connect host:443' or by inspecting the cert dates. Firewall, DNS, and disk issues do not correlate with a date change.

q: The auth log shows thousands of failed SSH logins from a single foreign IP in the last hour. What is this, and what is the BEST mitigation?
options: A brute-force attack — block the IP and harden SSH (fail2ban, key-only auth, disable root login)
A kernel bug — reboot the server
explain: High-rate failed logins from one source are brute-force password guessing. Mitigate by blocking the source, deploying fail2ban for automatic blocking, and hardening SSH (keys only, no root). Ignoring it invites eventual compromise; it is not a kernel or DNS problem.

q: 'uptime' shows a load average of 12.0 on a 4-CPU server. What does this indicate?
options: The CPUs are heavily overloaded — roughly 3x more runnable work than cores
Normal operation — load should equal the number of disks
A memory leak — load measures RAM usage
explain: Load average counts runnable/waiting processes; sustained load well above the CPU count means work is queuing for CPU time. A healthy rule of thumb: load near core count is busy, multiples of it is overloaded. Load is not a memory, disk-count, or network metric.

q: 'top' shows 45% wa (I/O wait) on a database server. Which tool BEST investigates disk I/O as the bottleneck?
explain: High %wa means CPUs are idling while waiting on disk — iostat -x shows per-device queue depth, await latency, and %util to identify the saturated device. ping tests network, lsblk shows topology, and df shows space: none measure I/O latency.

q: 'free -h' shows most RAM used and heavy swap activity, and the system is sluggish. What is the likely root cause?
options: Physical memory is exhausted — swapping is the symptom; add RAM or reduce memory pressure
The disks are failing — replace them
Swap is too large — disable swap to speed up
explain: Heavy swapping means the workload needs more RAM than exists; disk-backed swap is orders of magnitude slower, hence sluggishness. The fix is more RAM or less memory demand — not disabling swap (which would trigger the OOM killer sooner). Disks and CPU temperature do not cause swap activity.

q: One application responds slowly while everything else on the server is fine. What is the FIRST check?
options: top/htop — see whether that process is consuming CPU or memory abnormally
explain: Scope the problem first: one slow app among healthy ones points at the app itself — check its resource use, logs, and recent changes. Rebooting, reinstalling, or replacing hardware before diagnosing destroys evidence and may not help at all.

q: 'ethtool -S eth0' shows steadily rising rx_dropped counters and you suspect a duplex mismatch. Which command verifies the link's speed and duplex settings?
explain: ethtool eth0 reports negotiated speed, duplex, and link status — a half/full mismatch causes collisions, drops, and terrible throughput. Fix by setting both ends identically (prefer auto-negotiation). ping, routing tables, and socket listings cannot show link-layer negotiation.

q: A junior admin is unsure whether a server booted in UEFI mode or legacy BIOS mode. Which check definitively confirms a UEFI boot?
options: cat /proc/cpuinfo and look for a UEFI flag
fdisk -l — a GPT disk proves UEFI boot
dmesg | grep -i bios — BIOS strings prove legacy boot
ls /sys/firmware/efi — the directory exists only on a UEFI-booted system
explain: The kernel exposes /sys/firmware/efi only when the system actually booted via UEFI; its absence means legacy BIOS boot. /proc/cpuinfo describes the CPU, not the boot mode; BIOS strings appear in dmesg either way; and a GPT disk can boot in legacy mode with a BIOS boot partition, so partitioning alone proves nothing.

q: A VM will act as a router and needs IPv4 packet forwarding enabled permanently, surviving reboots. Which approach does this correctly?
options: Add ip_forward=1 to the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub
Add net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 to /etc/sysctl.conf (or /etc/sysctl.d/) and run sysctl -p
explain: Persistence requires writing the tunable to /etc/sysctl.conf or a /etc/sysctl.d/ drop-in, then applying with sysctl -p (or rebooting). Writing to /proc and sysctl -w are runtime-only and vanish on reboot — the classic trap. GRUB command-line parameters configure boot-time kernel arguments, not sysctl tunables.

q: On RHEL 9, the default Node.js module stream is version 18, but an application requires version 20. Which is the correct way to get Node.js 20?
options: dnf module list nodejs, then dnf module enable nodejs:20, then dnf install nodejs
yum install nodejs-20 — the version suffix selects the stream
dnf config-manager --add-repo nodejs20 — streams need a separate repo file
rpm -ivh nodejs-20.rpm — bypass the module system entirely
explain: RHEL AppStream ships multiple versions of software as module streams; you list them, enable the wanted stream, then install normally. A version suffix on the package name does not select streams, no extra repo file is needed, and installing a stray RPM bypasses stream management and future updates.

q: An admin inherits a SUSE Linux Enterprise Server and must refresh the repository metadata and install all available updates. Which commands fit this distribution?
explain: zypper is the SUSE-family package manager: refresh updates repo metadata, update installs newer packages. apt is Debian/Ubuntu, dnf is RHEL-family, and pacman is Arch — using the wrong family's tool is the exam's distribution trap.

q: After a suspected intrusion, an admin wants to verify that the installed openssh-server package's files match what the RPM database expects (sizes, modes, hashes). Which command does this?
explain: rpm -V (--verify) compares each installed file's size, permissions, and digest against the RPM database, flagging modifications. -qa merely lists installed packages, dnf list shows version info, and a lone md5sum has no trusted reference to compare against.

q: Yesterday's dnf update (transaction ID 42) installed a new kernel and three libraries, and now an application crashes. The admin wants to reverse that entire transaction. Which command does this?
options: dnf downgrade kernel — reverses the whole update
rpm -e kernel — removes the new kernel only
dnf clean all — clears caches and rolls back
explain: dnf history undo reverses a complete transaction — every install, upgrade, and removal it performed. dnf downgrade only lowers one package's version, rpm -e removes a single package without touching the libraries, and clean all only clears caches. For multi-package rollbacks, undo the transaction.

q: A developer needs to distribute a desktop app that runs identically on Ubuntu, Fedora, and Arch, sandboxed from the host's libraries. Which packaging approach fits?
options: Ship a native .rpm — every distro can install it
Flatpak — sandboxed, runtime-bundled apps that run across distributions
A tarball extracted into /opt — self-contained and auto-updating
pip install — the universal Linux package format
explain: Flatpak bundles the app with its runtime in a sandbox, making it distribution-independent. Native .rpm files are RHEL-family specific, a tarball in /opt has no sandboxing, dependency tracking, or update mechanism, and pip only manages Python packages.

q: Two identical 4 TB disks must hold /data with full redundancy — either disk alone must be able to serve all data. Which mdadm command creates this?
explain: RAID 1 mirrors data across disks, so either disk alone holds everything — exactly the redundancy asked for. RAID 0 stripes with no redundancy (a disk loss kills the array), RAID 5 needs at least three disks for parity, and RAID 10 needs at least four.

q: A software RAID array assembles fine when created manually with mdadm --assemble, but it is missing after every reboot. What is the durable fix?
options: Record the array in /etc/mdadm.conf (ARRAY line with UUID) so boot scripts auto-assemble it
Add the array to /etc/fstab — fstab assembles RAID devices
Run mdadm --assemble from /etc/rc.local on every boot
Store the array definition in /etc/raidtab — the modern location
explain: /etc/mdadm.conf holds ARRAY definitions (preferably by UUID) that the boot process uses to auto-assemble software RAID. /etc/fstab mounts filesystems — it cannot assemble an array that does not exist yet. /etc/raidtab is the long-obsolete location, and rc.local hacks are fragile compared to the supported config file.

q: Before a risky upgrade, an admin wants an instant, space-efficient rollback point for the btrfs root filesystem. Which command creates it?
explain: btrfs subvolume snapshot creates an instant copy-on-write snapshot sharing unchanged data blocks — fast and space-efficient. cp -a duplicates all data, LVM snapshots apply to LVM logical volumes (not btrfs subvolumes), and tar is a slow full backup, not an instant rollback point.

q: A cloud VM has no free disk partitions, but the admin must add 4 GB of swap immediately. Which sequence correctly creates a swap file?
options: dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=4096 && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile
fallocate -l 4G /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile — permissions do not matter
explain: A swap file must be allocated, locked down to mode 600 (world-readable swap is a security hole), formatted with mkswap, then activated with swapon — and added to /etc/fstab for persistence. There is no mkfs.swap command, swapon never formats, and skipping the chmod leaves swap readable by all users.

q: An /etc/fstab entry reads: /dev/sdb1  /data  ext4  defaults  0  2. What does the final field (2) control?
options: The dump backup priority for the dump utility
The order in which filesystems are mounted at boot
The fsck pass number — checked after the root filesystem during boot
How many times mount retries on failure
explain: Field 6 is the fsck pass: 0 skips checking, 1 is reserved for the root filesystem, and 2 means check after root on boot. Field 5 (the 0 here) is the dump flag — swapping the two fields is the exam trap. Neither field controls mount order or retry counts.

q: Hundreds of workstations need an NFS share available, but it should mount only the moment a user first accesses it — not at boot — and unmount when idle. Which systemd mechanism provides this?
options: A systemd automount unit (or the x-systemd.automount fstab option)
A standard fstab entry with defaults — mounts at boot
A standard fstab entry with noauto — never mounts automatically
explain: Automount units mount on first access and can idle-unmount, exactly matching on-demand semantics. defaults mounts everything at boot (slow with hundreds of shares), noauto disables automatic mounting entirely, and cron @reboot is just a delayed boot mount.

q: A server must be renamed from srv-old to srv-new permanently, effective now and after reboot. Which command does this?
explain: hostnamectl set-hostname updates /etc/hostname and the live kernel hostname — persistent and immediate. The bare hostname command and /proc writes are runtime-only and lost on reboot; /etc/hosts maps names to IPs and does not set the system's own hostname.

q: A host needs its default gateway set to 192.168.1.1 via eth0. Which command adds the correct route?
options: ip route add default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
ip addr add default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0
explain: A default route is added with 'default via <gateway>'; the first option only creates a host route to the gateway's own address, not a default. route is the deprecated net-tools syntax, and ip addr manages addresses, not routes — 'default' is meaningless to it.

q: On a NetworkManager-managed host, the admin must change the 'eth0' connection profile to the static address 10.0.0.50/24 with gateway 10.0.0.1, persistently. Which sequence does this?
options: nmcli con up eth0 — reactivating applies the desired static config
Edit /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0 — the file NetworkManager reads on all distros
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 10.0.0.50/24 ipv4.gateway 10.0.0.1 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0
ip addr add 10.0.0.50/24 dev eth0 && ip route add default via 10.0.0.1
explain: nmcli con mod edits the persistent connection profile (method manual = static), and reactivating applies it. Merely bringing the profile up changes nothing; ifcfg files are RHEL-family specific and not the tool-agnostic answer; ip addr/route changes are runtime-only and vanish on reboot.

q: On an Ubuntu 24.04 workstation, hand edits to /etc/resolv.conf keep disappearing within minutes. What is happening, and what is the proper fix?
options: /etc/resolv.conf is a symlink managed by systemd-resolved — configure DNS in /etc/systemd/resolved.conf or via netplan instead of editing the file
The file is corrupted — chattr +i it immediately to freeze the contents
DNS belongs in /etc/hosts — move the nameserver lines there
NetworkManager is broken — purge it and use static files
explain: On systemd-resolved systems /etc/resolv.conf is a stub symlink regenerated by the resolver service, so direct edits are overwritten. The durable fix is configuring the manager (resolved.conf, netplan, or NetworkManager). Freezing it with +i fights the system, /etc/hosts cannot hold resolver config, and removing NetworkManager does not address the symlink.

q: A RHEL 9 server's clock keeps drifting. Which time-synchronization service should be running, and how does the admin check its sync status?
options: ntpd — check with ntpq -p (the standard on RHEL 9)
timedatectl alone — it performs the synchronization
chronyd — check with chronyc tracking and chronyc sources
explain: RHEL 8 and later use chrony (chronyd) instead of ntpd; chronyc tracking/sources shows offset and source health. ntpd is deprecated on modern RHEL, timedatectl only configures time settings (it does not sync), and systemd-timesyncd is the Ubuntu/Debian lightweight client, not RHEL's default.

q: A server moved from Chicago to New York and must use America/New_York system-wide. Which command sets this persistently?
explain: timedatectl set-timezone updates the /etc/localtime symlink system-wide, effective for all processes. export TZ is per-session, date -s sets the clock (not the zone), and /etc/timezone is the Debian convention — on systemd systems the symlink is authoritative.

q: Before sizing a workload, an admin needs the CPU architecture, model, and core/thread counts in a readable summary. Which command provides this?
explain: lscpu parses /proc/cpuinfo into a clean summary of architecture, model, cores, threads, and caches. /etc/cpuinfo does not exist (it is /proc/cpuinfo, and raw at that), free -h reports memory, and uname -a shows kernel version with only minimal machine info.

q: A database running as user 'dbuser' needs a persistent open-files limit of 65535, including across service restarts. Where should the admin configure this?
options: ulimit -n 65535 in dbuser's ~/.bashrc — applies to every context
sysctl -w fs.file-max=65535 — sets the per-user limit
Run prlimit --nofile=65535 on the PID after each boot
explain: limits.conf (applied via PAM at session/login) is the persistent per-user mechanism. .bashrc only affects interactive shells — not systemd services. fs.file-max is the system-wide ceiling, not a per-user grant, and prlimit tweaks a live process but does not persist.

q: A latency-sensitive trading app must be pinned to CPUs 2 and 3 so other workloads never schedule there. Which command sets this CPU affinity?
options: nice -n -20 ./trading-app — highest priority keeps it on those CPUs
systemd memory limits — cgroups pin CPUs automatically
explain: taskset sets CPU affinity, restricting which cores the process may run on. nice only adjusts scheduling priority (the process still migrates), chrt sets realtime scheduling policy (not affinity), and memory cgroup limits constrain RAM, not CPU placement.

q: After adding a new disk, /dev/sdb became /dev/sdc and the fstab entry for the old /dev/sdb now mounts the wrong disk. What is the durable fix?
options: Re-cable the disks so enumeration order is restored
Reference the filesystem by UUID= (or /dev/disk/by-uuid/) in /etc/fstab
Add nofail to the fstab entry so boot continues
explain: Kernel sd-letter assignment follows enumeration order and is not stable; UUIDs (or by-uuid/by-label symlinks) identify the filesystem regardless of letter shifts. Re-cabling is fragile, nofail only hides the failure at boot, and blacklisting the disk defeats the purpose of adding it.

q: The finance team shares /shared/finance. Every new file created there must automatically be owned by group 'finance', regardless of each user's primary group. Which command enforces this?
options: chmod 777 /shared/finance — open permissions inherit the group
explain: The setgid bit on a directory makes new files and subdirectories inherit the directory's group — the standard shared-directory setup. chmod 777 only widens access, chown changes only the directory's current group, and the sticky bit (+t) restricts deletion rather than controlling group inheritance.

q: Users share /scratch, but one user keeps deleting other users' files there. Which permission change stops this while keeping the directory world-writable?
options: chmod +t /scratch — the sticky bit, shown as 't' in the mode
chmod g+s /scratch — setgid on the directory
explain: The sticky bit on a world-writable directory (like /tmp) lets anyone create files but only the owner (or root) delete or rename them. setgid controls group inheritance, 755 would block writing entirely, and +i immutable would freeze the directory so nobody could create anything.

q: With umask 027 in effect, what permissions does a newly created regular file get?
options: 644 — the same as with the default umask
600 — group and other are fully masked
explain: New files start at 666; umask 027 subtracts write for group and all access for other: 666 − 027 = 640 (rw-r-----). 644 is the result of the default umask 022. 750 applies to directories (777 − 027), since files never gain the execute bit by default.

q: User 'deploy' needs rwx on /srv/app, but the directory's group and other permissions must stay restrictive for everyone else. Which command grants this precisely?
options: chmod 777 /srv/app — then rely on the firewall
chown deploy /srv/app — ownership is the only per-user mechanism
usermod -aG appgroup deploy — group membership covers it
explain: ACLs grant fine-grained per-user permissions without altering the base owner/group/other mode. chmod 777 opens the directory to everyone, chown changes ownership (disrupting the current owner), and group membership only helps if the group already has the needed rights on the directory.

q: Every new file created inside /proj must automatically grant group 'team' read/write access. Which command sets this up for future files?
options: chmod g+s /proj — setgid propagates permissions to new files
setfacl -m g:team:rw /proj — the ACL applies to new files too
setfacl -d -m g:team:rw /proj — a default ACL inherited by new objects
explain: Default ACLs (-d) are inherited by newly created files and directories inside /proj. A regular (access) ACL only affects the directory itself, setgid inherits the group but not rw rights beyond the creator's umask, and umask in /etc/profile is system-wide, not targeted at one directory.

q: Maria is already in groups 'dev' and 'ops'. The admin must add her to 'docker' WITHOUT removing her existing memberships. Which command is safe?
explain: usermod -aG appends to the supplementary group list, preserving existing memberships. Without -a, -G replaces the entire supplementary list — silently dropping 'dev' and 'ops', the classic trap. groupadd creates groups (it does not take a user this way), and gpasswd -d removes a user from a group.

q: A contractor's engagement ends. The admin must remove the account 'temp1' along with its home directory and mail spool. Which command does this completely?
options: userdel temp1 — removes the account and all its files
passwd -l temp1 — locks it, which is equivalent to removal
rm -rf /home/temp1 — the account entry cleans itself up
explain: userdel -r removes the account entry plus the home directory and mail spool. Plain userdel leaves files orphaned on disk, passwd -l only locks the account without removing anything, and deleting /home/temp1 manually leaves the account itself (and its mail spool) behind.

q: Company policy requires new user accounts to start at UID 2000 and have passwords expire after 90 days by default. Which file defines these system-wide defaults?
options: /etc/shadow — defaults are stored per user here
/etc/group — GID ranges imply the UID policy
explain: /etc/login.defs holds the defaults useradd applies to new accounts (UID_MIN, PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_WARN_AGE, etc.). /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow store per-account data, not defaults, and /etc/group manages groups. Changing the file changes the default for every future account.

q: An admin must run a series of maintenance commands with root's full login environment (PATH, variables, working directory). Which invocation provides this?
options: su — switches user while keeping the current environment
sudo -u root command — single command with root's environment
su -c 'command' — identical to a login shell
explain: su - (dash) starts a login shell as the target user, loading root's profile, PATH, and environment. Plain su keeps the caller's environment (a common source of 'command not found' for sbin tools), sudo -u runs one command without a login shell, and su -c runs one command with the non-login environment.

q: The backup script /opt/backup.sh must run as the 'svcbackup' account, launched by an admin who should not know svcbackup's password. Which command does this?
options: su svcbackup — then enter the password when prompted
runuser -u svcbackup /opt/backup.sh — works for any admin
chmod u+s /opt/backup.sh — SUID is the safe approach
explain: sudo -u runs the command as another user according to the sudoers policy — no target password needed. su requires svcbackup's password, runuser requires the invoker to already be root, and SUID on a script is ignored by the kernel on Linux and dangerous where honored.

q: The admin must grant 'deploy' limited sudo rights without editing the main sudoers file, in a way that survives package updates. Which is the best-practice approach?
options: Append directly to /etc/sudoers — updates never touch it
chmod 4755 the allowed binaries instead of using sudo
Add the user to /etc/passwd with UID 0
Create a drop-in file in /etc/sudoers.d/ and validate with visudo -c
explain: The #includedir /etc/sudoers.d mechanism keeps custom rules modular and separate from the vendor file; visudo -c syntax-checks them. Direct sudoers edits work but are harder to audit and riskier, setuid binaries bypass sudo's logging and control, and a second UID 0 account is full root by another name.

q: The 'app' service must start only AFTER 'db' is running, and must NOT start at all if 'db' fails. Which unit directives express both requirements?
options: Wants=db.service and After=db.service — the strongest combination
Before=db.service — app starts first, which is equivalent
explain: Requires= creates the hard dependency (if db fails, app will not start) while After= only controls ordering — After alone lets app start even when db failed, the trap. Wants= is a weak dependency that tolerates db's failure, and Before= reverses the order.

q: After creating backup.timer, the admin must confirm it will actually trigger after a reboot. Which command checks this persistence?
options: systemctl status backup.service — the timer's state follows the service
systemctl is-active backup.timer — shows whether it survives reboot
systemctl list-timers — proves the timer is enabled
explain: is-enabled reports whether the unit is hooked into the boot targets — the actual persistence question. is-active shows only the current runtime state, status on the .service shows the wrong unit, and list-timers shows schedule/next-run for active timers without confirming enablement.

q: /var/log/journal has grown to 4 GB. The admin wants to trim it to 500 MB now and cap its future size. Which commands do this?
options: journalctl --vacuum-size=500M now, and set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf for the future
rm -rf /var/log/journal/* — the only way to reclaim the space
dmesg -c — clears the journal from the ring buffer
explain: journalctl --vacuum-size trims the journal to the target immediately, and SystemMaxUse in journald.conf caps future growth. Deleting files by hand works but loses everything indiscriminately, logrotate does not manage the binary journal, and dmesg -c only clears the kernel ring buffer.

q: /var/log/app.log grows without bound. The admin wants it rotated weekly, keeping 4 old copies, compressed. Which is the standard solution?
options: A cron job running mv and gzip manually each Sunday
truncate -s 0 /var/log/app.log in a weekly cron job
A logrotate config stanza with weekly, rotate 4, and compress
explain: logrotate is the standard log-rotation framework (invoked by its own cron job or timer) with exactly these directives. Hand-rolled mv scripts reinvent it poorly, journalctl only manages the systemd journal, and truncating in cron destroys log history instead of archiving it.

q: An admin must review failed SSH login attempts on both RHEL 9 and Ubuntu 24.04 hosts. Where does the authpriv facility log these on each?
options: /var/log/auth.log on both — the path is standardized
journalctl -u sshd on both — file logs are deprecated
/var/log/messages on both — auth goes to the general log
explain: rsyslog routes the authpriv facility to /var/log/secure on RHEL-family and /var/log/auth.log on Debian-family — a classic cross-distro exam trap. journalctl can show the entries too, but the question asks for the file paths, and /var/log/messages is not where auth failures land by default.

q: A developer (non-root) must build and run containers on a shared workstation, with no root-owned daemon running. Which tool fits, and why?
options: Docker — the daemon runs rootless by default
sudo docker — root privileges make it safe for shared hosts
Podman — daemonless architecture with first-class rootless containers
explain: Podman runs containers as child processes of the invoking user with no central daemon, and rootless operation is its normal mode. Docker's daemon runs as root (rootless mode exists but is not the default setup), sudo docker still routes through the root daemon, and chroot is a 1970s filesystem isolation primitive, not a container runtime.

q: A PostgreSQL container is regularly replaced with newer images, but its data directory must survive every replacement. Which storage approach guarantees this?
options: A named volume mounted at the data directory — its lifecycle is independent of any container
The container's writable layer — data stays with the image
A bind mount of /tmp/pgdata — /tmp persists across reboots
docker commit after each write — snapshots the data
explain: Named volumes are managed by the container engine and persist independently of container create/replace cycles. The writable layer is destroyed with the container, /tmp is cleared on reboot (and often tmpfs), and commit bakes data into images — an anti-pattern for databases.

q: A runaway deploy left dozens of processes named 'stuck-worker' consuming CPU. Which command terminates all of them by name in one step?
options: kill stuck-worker — kill accepts process names
pkill -f stuck — matches the name safely
explain: pkill signals processes by name directly — the purpose-built tool. kill takes only PIDs, piping pgrep into killall is redundant (that is what pkill does), and pkill -f matches against the full command line, which can over-match unrelated processes containing the substring.

q: Planned maintenance starts in 10 minutes. The admin must immediately notify every logged-in user on all terminals. Which command does this?
options: echo 'maintenance soon' > /dev/pts/* — writes to each terminal
mail -s maintenance $(who | cut -d' ' -f1) — emails them instantly
wall 'Maintenance begins in 10 minutes — save your work'
explain: wall broadcasts a message to all logged-in users' terminals immediately. Redirecting to /dev/pts/* is a fragile hack, mail is not immediate or terminal-visible, and shutdown -c cancels a pending shutdown rather than sending a standalone notice.

q: On an Ubuntu 24.04 server, the admin must allow inbound SSH and then activate host firewall protection. Which sequence does this with UFW?
options: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT — persistent across reboots
ufw allow 22/tcp — the rule takes effect immediately
explain: UFW is Ubuntu's firewall frontend, but it does nothing until enabled — the rule plus 'ufw enable' is the complete sequence. firewall-cmd is the RHEL-family tool, raw iptables rules are not persistent by default, and adding the UFW rule without enabling leaves the firewall inactive (the trap).

q: Company policy: SSH may be reached ONLY from the management subnet 10.0.0.0/24, not from the whole internet. Which firewalld configuration enforces this?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh && firewall-cmd --reload — then restrict the interface
A rich rule: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.0/24" service name="ssh" accept' && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=22/tcp — ports are more specific than services
Move eth0 to the trusted zone — trusted implies management-only
explain: Rich rules can match on source address, restricting the service to the management subnet. --add-service/--add-port open SSH to the entire zone (the trap), and the trusted zone accepts everything — the opposite of restriction.

q: A server uses nftables natively. The admin needs to see the complete live ruleset exactly as the kernel enforces it. Which command shows this?
explain: nft list ruleset dumps the live nftables ruleset from the kernel. iptables -L shows only the iptables-compat view (incomplete for native nftables), firewall-cmd shows firewalld's zone view, and /etc/nftables.conf is a file that may not reflect the currently loaded rules.

q: The admin must generate a modern, secure SSH key pair for a service account. Which command follows current best practice?
options: ssh-copy-id -t ed25519 svc@host — generates and installs in one step
explain: ed25519 keys are the modern default recommendation: strong, compact, and fast. 1024-bit RSA is below current minimum strength guidance, openssl genrsa produces PEM keys (not the OpenSSH format ssh-keygen manages), and ssh-copy-id only installs an existing public key — it generates nothing.

q: A nightly automation script must SSH using a passphrase-protected key, with no human available to type the passphrase. Which is the secure approach?
options: Remove the passphrase with ssh-keygen -p — automation needs it
Load the key into ssh-agent (ssh-add) so the decrypted key lives in memory for the session
Write the passphrase into the script next to the ssh command
Use sshpass -p with the passphrase on the command line
explain: ssh-agent holds the decrypted key in memory after one ssh-add, letting scripts authenticate without interactive prompts or stored secrets. Stripping the passphrase weakens the key permanently, embedding it in a script exposes it to anyone who reads the file, and sshpass puts the secret in the process list.

q: Key-based SSH logins fail even though the public key is correctly installed. The admin finds ~/.ssh/authorized_keys has mode 644. What is the fix, and why?
options: Restart sshd — it caches authorized_keys permissions
The key type is wrong — regenerate as RSA
644 is the required mode — the real problem is elsewhere
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and chmod 700 ~/.ssh — sshd StrictModes rejects overly permissive key files
explain: sshd's StrictModes refuses to trust authorized_keys (and the .ssh directory) unless they are writable only by the owner — 600/700. 644 lets others write the file, so a valid key could have been planted; sshd fails closed. Restarting changes nothing, and the key type is irrelevant to a permissions refusal.

q: Only the accounts 'ops' and 'deploy' may log in via SSH; all other users must be refused. Which sshd_config directive enforces exactly this?
options: AllowGroups wheel — limits SSH to the admin group
DenyUsers * — blocks every account including ops and deploy
PasswordAuthentication no — unauthenticated users cannot get in
explain: AllowUsers whitelists exactly the named accounts for SSH logins. AllowGroups filters by group (not the named-user requirement), DenyUsers * blocks everyone, and disabling password auth changes the authentication method without restricting which accounts may connect.

q: The admin wants repeat SSH password-guessers automatically blocked for a time after several failures, without writing custom scripts. Which tool provides this?
options: fail2ban with the sshd jail — scans logs and inserts temporary firewall bans
A hand-written cron job parsing /var/log/secure hourly
Moving SSH to port 2222 — attackers cannot find it
Appending attacker IPs to /etc/hosts.deny by hand
explain: fail2ban monitors log files against regex filters and dynamically firewalls offending IPs for a configurable duration — the automated solution. Hourly cron parsing is slow and fragile, a non-standard port is mere obscurity, and manual hosts.deny edits do not scale or expire.

q: Without touching the firewall, the admin must restrict the sshd daemon itself to accept connections only from 192.168.1.0/24. Which mechanism does this?
options: firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule — the firewall is the only layer
TCP wrappers: 'sshd: 192.168.1.0/24' in /etc/hosts.allow with 'ALL: ALL' in /etc/hosts.deny
sshd_config AllowUsers — filters by source network
explain: TCP wrappers (hosts.allow/hosts.deny) filter connections at the daemon level by source address — no firewall involvement. The firewall options violate the constraint, and AllowUsers filters by username, not source network.

q: The company bought a certificate from a commercial CA. The admin must generate a private key and a Certificate Signing Request to send to the CA. Which command does this?
options: ssh-keygen -t rsa -f server_key — then email the public key
explain: openssl req -new generates a CSR (and -newkey creates the private key alongside it) for submission to the CA. -x509 outputs a self-signed certificate instead of a CSR, ssh-keygen makes SSH keys (not X.509), and there is no certbot --self-signed issuance flow for commercial CAs.

q: A web server uses a Let's Encrypt certificate. The admin must ensure it renews automatically before expiry with no manual intervention. Which is the correct approach?
options: Re-run certbot certonly manually every 60 days
A cron job running certbot certonly --force-renewal daily
certbot renew via the provided systemd timer (or a twice-daily cron job) — it renews only certificates near expiry
openssl x509 -req to re-sign the existing CSR yearly
explain: certbot renew checks all certificates and renews only those within the expiry window — idempotent and safe to run frequently via the shipped timer. Manual reissuance does not scale, --force-renewal burns through rate limits, and openssl cannot renew a CA-issued certificate.

q: An admin must encrypt backup.tar with a passphrase for offsite storage. No GPG keypair exists and none should be created. Which command encrypts it symmetrically?
options: gpg -c backup.tar — symmetric encryption with a passphrase
gpg -e backup.tar — encrypts without needing any key
zip -e backup.zip backup.tar — equivalent modern cryptography
explain: gpg -c (--symmetric) encrypts with a passphrase-derived key — no keypair required. -e (--encrypt) requires a recipient's public key, --sign only adds a signature without confidentiality, and zip -e uses weak legacy crypto unsuitable for sensitive backups.

q: A web application must store user passwords. Which storage approach is appropriate?
options: A salted, deliberately slow hash (bcrypt/yescrypt/argon2 via crypt) — resistant to offline brute force
Unsalted SHA-256 — a modern hash, so it is sufficient
Base64-encoded plaintext — obfuscated from casual viewing
explain: Password storage needs a unique salt per password plus a tunable work factor so each guess is expensive — exactly what bcrypt/yescrypt/argon2 provide. Fast hashes (MD5, plain SHA-256) fall to GPU brute force in hours, and Base64 is encoding, not protection.

q: The admin must protect /etc/resolv.conf from being overwritten — even by root — until maintenance is done, then restore normal behavior. Which command applies this protection?
options: chmod 444 /etc/resolv.conf — root cannot write to read-only files
chown nobody:nogroup /etc/resolv.conf — root no longer owns it
chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf — immutable, even root must remove the flag first
explain: The immutable flag (+i) blocks all writes including by root until removed with chattr -i — the reversible protection asked for. chmod 444/000 do not stop root (root bypasses permission checks), and changing ownership likewise does not constrain root.

q: Root cannot delete /var/log/audit.log despite full permissions, and ls -l shows nothing unusual. Which command reveals the extended attributes that could explain this?
