explain: fuser -v shows the PIDs and commands accessing the mount point so they can be stopped cleanly. killall -9 kills blindly and risks data loss (the trap), lazy unmount hides the problem rather than identifying it, and df only reports disk usage.

q: After a security update, a long-running service behaves oddly, and ls -l /proc/<pid>/exe shows the path with (deleted) appended. What does this mean, and what is the fix?
options: The binary was deleted by malware; reinstall the operating system
It is a zombie process; its parent must reap it
Ignore it; (deleted) is normal for all running services
The process is still running the old, replaced binary; restart the service to load the updated one
explain: When a package update replaces a binary, already-running processes keep the old inode open, shown as (deleted) in /proc/<pid>/exe — the service is not using the security fix. Restarting loads the new binary. It is not malware or a zombie (zombies show as Z state), and ignoring it leaves the vulnerability unpatched.

q: An admin wants to stop anyone with physical access from pressing 'e' at the GRUB menu and appending init=/bin/bash to bypass authentication. Which mechanism enforces this?
options: Set a GRUB2 superuser password with grub2-setpassword
Add a password entry for the grub user in /etc/shadow
Set a BIOS/UEFI setup password only
explain: grub2-setpassword stores a PBKDF2-hashed superuser password so GRUB requires authentication before editing entries or booting non-default ones. /etc/shadow is irrelevant to the bootloader, file permissions do not apply at the pre-boot GRUB menu, and a firmware password alone does not stop editing the GRUB entry once the menu is shown.

q: A server rebooted unexpectedly overnight. The admin needs the kernel messages from the PREVIOUS boot, not the current one. Which command shows them?
explain: The -b flag selects a boot: -b (or -b 0) is the current boot and negative offsets count backward, so -b -1 is the previous boot. Bare journalctl -b and dmesg both show only the current boot, while --since yesterday spans both boots without isolating the crashed one.

q: After adding a swap entry to /etc/fstab and rebooting, the admin wants to confirm the swap space is actually ACTIVE right now. Which command shows active swap devices and their usage?
explain: swapon --show lists every currently active swap device with its size and used space. /etc/fstab shows configured entries (not runtime state — the classic config-vs-state trap), df -h excludes swap entirely, and lsblk shows the block layout without swap activation state. (free -h also displays swap totals, but swapon is the purpose-built check.)

q: The admin wants the ext4 filesystem on /dev/sdb1 to be force-checked automatically every 30 mounts. Which command sets this?
explain: tune2fs -c sets the maximum mount count between forced fsck runs. The -i flag sets a time-based interval (30 days, not 30 mounts), fsck -c performs a bad-block check rather than setting policy, and dumpe2fs only displays superblock information without changing anything.

q: SMART warnings show /dev/sdc — a physical volume in vgdata — is failing. The admin must evacuate all of its data to the remaining PVs online, with no downtime, before replacing the disk. Which command does this?
explain: pvmove migrates allocated extents off the named PV to other PVs in the volume group while everything stays online. vgrename only renames the VG, pvremove would destroy the PV metadata and strand data, and dd copies in the wrong direction onto a dying disk while filesystems are active.

q: vgdata has no free extents left. A new partition /dev/sdd1 is ready. Which sequence adds its space to the volume group?
explain: A disk must first be initialized as a physical volume with pvcreate before vgextend can add it to the VG — bottom-up layering again. lvextend grows logical volumes, not volume groups; reversing the order fails because the VG cannot absorb a non-PV; and vgcreate would try to build a second VG with a conflicting name.

q: A httpd update introduced a regression. The admin wants to revert ONLY httpd to the previous version available in the repositories, leaving every other package untouched. Which command does this?
explain: dnf downgrade installs the next-older version of the named package only. history undo reverts the entire last transaction (affecting every package it touched), erase-plus-install is needlessly destructive and loses config handling, and reinstall installs the same current version — not an older one.

q: dnf update fails because /boot is 100% full of old kernel images. Which is the safe cleanup?
options: rm /boot/vmlinuz-* to delete old kernels by hand
explain: --oldinstallonly removes old installonly packages (kernels) while keeping the two newest per installonly_limit, and it updates the bootloader and rpmdb consistently. Deleting /boot files by hand orphans rpmdb entries and can break GRUB, mkfs destroys the partition, and growing /boot treats the symptom while kernels keep accumulating.

q: Users report intermittent connectivity on eth0, and the admin suspects NIC-level errors or dropped packets. Which command shows per-interface error, drop, and overrun counters?
explain: ip -s link prints RX/TX statistics including errors, dropped, and overruns per interface — the direct evidence for faulty NICs, cables, or duplex issues. ping measures loss without counters, ss lists sockets, and traceroute maps hops. (ethtool -S shows NIC-level stats too, but ip -s link is the iproute2-native check.)

q: After disk re-cabling, fstab entries using /dev/sdX names broke. The admin needs a tree view of all block devices with their filesystem types, labels, and UUIDs to rewrite fstab. Which single command provides this?
explain: lsblk -f prints the device tree augmented with FSTYPE, LABEL, and UUID columns — precisely the identifiers needed for stable fstab entries. df -h shows only mounted filesystems without UUIDs, fdisk -l shows partitions without filesystem/UUID detail, and mount shows active mounts rather than all devices.

q: The admin suspects /data is not honoring the noexec option set in /etc/fstab, and needs to see the filesystem's LIVE mount options in a readable tree. Which command does this?
explain: findmnt displays the target, source, fstype, and live OPTIONS for a mount point in a readable tree — the direct way to confirm noexec is active. df reports usage without options, lsblk shows the block layout without mount options, and du measures directory sizes. (/proc/mounts holds the same data but findmnt is the purpose-built readable frontend.)

q: Hundreds of NFS home directories should mount only when users actually access them — not all at boot — and unmount after idle periods. Which service provides this on-demand automounting?
options: A static fstab entry per home directory
A cron job that mounts everything at 8 AM
explain: autofs mounts filesystems on first access and unmounts them after a configurable idle timeout, which is ideal for large numbers of occasionally used NFS homes. Static fstab entries mount everything at boot (slow, fragile if the server is down), cron cannot react to access patterns, and nfsstat only reports NFS statistics.

q: A build job needs 20 GB of ultra-fast temporary scratch space that never needs to survive a reboot. Which is the simplest approach?
options: Partition a disk and format it ext4
Create a 20 GB swap file and use it as scratch
explain: tmpfs is a RAM-backed filesystem — extremely fast and automatically discarded at reboot, perfect for scratch space. A swap file is for virtual memory paging, not a usable filesystem; partitioning a disk is persistent overkill for throwaway data; and /dev/null discards everything written to it.

q: After manually copying a vendor's .ko module into /lib/modules/$(uname -r)/kernel/drivers/, modprobe still reports "module not found." Which step was missed?
options: depmod -a to rebuild the module dependency database
explain: modprobe consults the modules.dep database built by depmod; a hand-copied module is invisible until depmod -a regenerates it. Rebuilding the initramfs, regenerating GRUB config, or reloading systemd units does not update the module dependency map.

q: Every kernel update breaks the vendor's out-of-tree storage driver until someone manually rebuilds it. Which framework automates rebuilding third-party modules on each kernel install?
explain: DKMS registers out-of-tree module sources and hooks into kernel installs to automatically rebuild them for each new kernel. dracut builds initramfs images, kexec boots a new kernel without a full reboot, and depmod only rebuilds the dependency map — none recompile driver sources.

q: An admin needs a single-user root shell to repair a damaged /etc/fstab, WITH filesystems mounted but WITHOUT networking started. Which systemd target provides this?
explain: rescue.target is systemd's single-user mode: filesystems mounted, minimal services, no networking, sulogin prompt. emergency.target is even more minimal (often with / mounted read-only and almost nothing started) — the classic exam distinction. multi-user and graphical are full multi-user runlevels.

q: Boot takes six minutes. systemd-analyze blame lists per-unit times, but the admin needs the actual dependency CHAIN that delayed boot completion — which units waited on which. Which command shows this?
explain: critical-chain prints the time-critical chain of units — the ordered dependency path that gated boot completion. blame lists individual unit times without showing which unit blocked which, journalctl -b -p err shows errors without timing chains, and dmesg shows kernel messages only.

q: After installing a new graphics driver, the system boots to a black screen. The admin wants to boot once with kernel mode-setting disabled to troubleshoot. Which kernel parameter, added at the GRUB edit screen, does this?
explain: nomodeset tells the kernel not to load video drivers' mode-setting code, falling back to basic BIOS video — the standard workaround for black-screen GPU driver issues. quiet only suppresses messages, rhgb enables the graphical boot splash, and single enters single-user mode without addressing the video driver.

q: A legacy runbook says "switch the server to runlevel 3." What is the correct systemd equivalent?
explain: SysV runlevel 3 maps to multi-user.target (full multi-user text mode); isolate switches immediately. graphical.target is runlevel 5, rescue.target is runlevel 1, and telinit 5 would switch to the GUI — the opposite of the runbook's intent.

q: A KVM guest named webvm must start automatically every time its host boots. Which command configures this?
explain: virsh autostart marks the domain to start with the libvirt daemon at host boot. virsh start boots it once (not persistent), enabling libvirtd starts the daemon but not individual guests, and resume only unpauses a suspended guest.

q: New LDAP users cannot log in, but local users can. Before blaming the SSSD configuration, the admin wants to verify whether the LDAP user even resolves through the name service switch. Which command tests this?
explain: getent queries every NSS source in order (files, sss, ldap), so it proves whether the directory user resolves at all. Grepping /etc/passwd only checks local files and will miss directory users by design, listing the home directory tests nothing about name resolution, and ping only verifies network reachability.

q: User maria was added to the docker group with usermod -aG docker maria, but running "groups" in her open terminal still does not list docker. What must she do for the new membership to take effect?
options: Log out and log back in, since group membership is assigned at login time
Run usermod -aG docker maria a second time
Manually edit /etc/passwd to add the group
explain: A process's group list is fixed at login, so the new membership only applies to sessions started after the change — logging out and back in is the standard fix. Rebooting is overkill, re-running usermod changes nothing (she is already a member), and /etc/passwd does not store group memberships (that is /etc/group).

q: During a compliance audit, the admin must display jdoe's complete password aging policy: last change date, expiry, warning period, and inactivity lockout. Which single command shows all of this?
explain: chage -l prints the full aging policy in human-readable form (last change, expires, warning, inactive). passwd -S shows only the account status (locked/unlocked with the hash), parsing /etc/shadow manually yields raw day-counts instead of a policy summary, and lastlog shows last login times, not aging rules.

q: Security policy requires that user ops's password expire after 90 days, with a warning starting 14 days before expiry. Which command applies exactly this?
explain: -M sets the maximum days a password stays valid and -W sets the warning window — the exact pair the policy names. The trap options swap meanings: -m is the MINIMUM days between changes, -e/-E set the ACCOUNT expiry date (a calendar date, not a password lifetime).

q: The admin suspects jsmith's account is locked but must check WITHOUT modifying anything. Which command safely shows the lock status?
explain: passwd -S reports status only (L = locked, P = usable password, NP = no password). The trap is reaching for passwd -l or usermod -L to "check" — both LOCK the account, which is a change, not a check. chage -E -1 removes account expiry rather than reporting status.

q: An admin adds "30 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/bak.sh" to /etc/cron.d/backup, but the job never runs, while identical entries in personal crontabs work. What is wrong?
options: Files in /etc/cron.d are not read by the cron daemon
Files in /etc/cron.d require a username field between the schedule and the command
The file must be named backup.cron instead of backup
The script must be listed without its path
explain: System crontabs (/etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/*) include a sixth field — the user the job runs as — which personal crontabs (crontab -e) omit. The daemon reads /etc/cron.d fine, the filename needs no special extension (only no dots, per run-parts rules), and cron requires absolute paths rather than forbidding them.

q: A workstation that is powered off every night keeps missing its 3 AM cron backup. Which facility is designed to run scheduled jobs that were missed while the machine was off?
explain: anacron runs missed periodic jobs shortly after the machine comes up, using timestamps to detect what was skipped — exactly the laptop/powered-off use case. at runs one-time jobs, @reboot runs at every boot regardless of schedule (not a daily catch-up), and OnBootSec only anchors relative to boot time.

q: The admin queued several one-time at jobs, needs to list them, and then must cancel job 12. Which command pair does this?
options: atq to list, then atrm 12 to remove
explain: atq lists the at queue and atrm deletes a queued job by number. jobs/kill manage shell jobs, not at jobs; crontab -r would delete the user's entire crontab (dangerous trap); and systemctl list-jobs shows systemd jobs, a completely different queue.

q: An admin starts a 6-hour data load with ./load.sh & over SSH, but the job dies every time the SSH session disconnects. Which invocation survives the logout?
options: setsid ./load.sh without nohup in all cases
explain: nohup makes the process ignore SIGHUP, which the kernel sends to the session's jobs on logout — & alone does not protect against that. Chaining exit after the job still delivers the hangup when the shell terminates. (setsid also detaches, but nohup is the objectives' named tool for hangup immunity.)

q: A long rsync is already running in the foreground of an SSH session that the admin must close. How can the running transfer be detached so it survives the logout?
options: Run fg and then close the terminal
Press Ctrl+Z, then run bg, then disown
Press Ctrl+C, then restart it with nohup
Run kill -9 on the rsync and start over later
explain: Ctrl+Z suspends the job, bg resumes it in the background, and disown removes it from the shell's job table so no SIGHUP reaches it on logout. Ctrl+C kills the transfer, kill -9 destroys progress, and fg keeps it attached to the dying session — the opposite of detaching.

q: An admin hand-edits /etc/systemd/system/app.service, runs systemctl restart app, but the old behavior persists. Which step was missed?
options: systemctl daemon-reload to make systemd re-read the unit files
systemctl daemon-reexec to re-execute the systemd manager
explain: systemd caches parsed unit files; daemon-reload forces it to re-read them after a hand edit, and only then does restart pick up the change. daemon-reexec restarts the manager itself (for systemd upgrades), a reboot is overkill, and reset-failed only clears the failed state counter.

q: The admin must see the EFFECTIVE nginx unit definition — the vendor unit file plus every drop-in override merged — in one view. Which command does this?
explain: systemctl cat concatenates the main unit file and all drop-ins, showing exactly what systemd parsed. Reading the vendor file directly misses /etc overrides, show prints parsed properties (not the file text), and journalctl shows logs rather than configuration.

q: A service runs a database migration script once per boot and must report as "started" only AFTER the script finishes. Which service Type fits?
explain: Type=oneshot waits for ExecStart to exit before considering the unit started, and RemainAfterExit=yes keeps it shown as active afterward — the pattern for run-once tasks. simple considers the service started the moment the process spawns, forking expects the classic double-fork daemon pattern, and idle only delays execution until other jobs dispatch.

q: A systemd timer runs a backup daily at 2 AM, but a laptop that was fully POWERED OFF at 2 AM skips the run and never catches up. Which timer option runs the missed job after the next boot?
explain: Persistent=true records the last run time on disk, so when the timer next becomes active it immediately triggers the missed elapse. OnBootSec only schedules relative to boot without catch-up semantics, AccuracySec merely widens the scheduling window, and WakeSystem=true can only wake a SUSPENDED machine — not one that was powered off.

q: The admin's laptop cannot reach db01:5432 directly. Only bastion.example.com is reachable, and the bastion CAN reach db01. Which command opens local port 5433 tunneled through the bastion to db01:5432?
explain: -L creates a LOCAL forward: connections to the laptop's port 5433 travel through the bastion to db01:5432 (db01 resolves from the bastion's side). -R reverses the direction (remote forward — the classic trap), -D opens a dynamic SOCKS proxy instead of a fixed forward, and scp has no -L forwarding flag.

q: The admin must copy backup.tgz to deploy@storage over SSH, but the storage server listens on port 2222 instead of 22. Which command is correct?
explain: scp uses capital -P for the port — the exam's favorite case-sensitivity trap, since lowercase -p means "preserve timestamps." There is no --port long flag for scp, and rsync's -P means partial/progress (its port goes via -e "ssh -p 2222").

q: Beyond disabling root login and password authentication, the admin wants sshd to allow only 3 authentication attempts per connection and to drop unauthenticated sessions after 60 seconds. Which settings do this?
explain: MaxAuthTries caps authentication attempts per connection (blunting brute force) and LoginGraceTime limits how long an unauthenticated session may linger. MaxSessions counts multiplexed sessions per connection (a different knob), ClientAliveInterval watches idle ESTABLISHED sessions, and changing the port is obscurity rather than attempt-limiting.

q: After detecting brute-force SSH attempts, the admin needs a list of FAILED login attempts with usernames, timestamps, and source IPs. Which command provides this?
explain: lastb reads /var/log/btmp, which records FAILED logins with source addresses. last reads wtmp (successful sessions), lastlog shows each user's most recent login (one line per user), and who shows who is currently logged in — none expose the failed-attempt history.

q: User svcuser runs a Podman container through a systemd user service, but the container stops every time svcuser logs out. Which command lets that user's services persist after logout?
explain: enable-linger keeps the per-user systemd manager (user@.service) running after logout, so user services survive. Enabling the user unit alone does not help if the user manager itself is torn down at logout; chage -E affects account expiry and the login shell is irrelevant to service persistence.

q: A production Java process (PID 4321, already running) is hitting "too many open files." Restarting it right now is not an option. How can the admin raise its open-file limit live?
explain: prlimit changes resource limits of an already-running process by PID. ulimit only affects the current shell and its future children, renice adjusts CPU priority (not file descriptors), and /proc/PID/limits is a read-only status view — writing to it fails.

q: An admin fixed an SELinux denial with chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/www/index.html. After the next scheduled restorecon -R /srv, the 403 errors returned. Why did the fix not survive, and what is the durable correction?
options: chcon changes are temporary and lost on relabel — use semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/www(/.*)?" then restorecon
chcon requires a reboot to take effect
The file also needs chmod 777 to be served
SELinux must be set to disabled for web content
explain: chcon writes the label directly onto the file, but the policy's file-context database still says the path should be labeled differently, so any restorecon/relabel reverts it — the exam's number-one SELinux trap. semanage fcontext updates the policy database itself, making the label survive relabels. No reboot is needed, 777 is never the fix, and disabling SELinux surrenders the protection.

q: Before debugging a suspected SELinux denial, the admin must confirm the CURRENT enforcing mode and then temporarily drop to permissive for testing — without editing config files or rebooting. Which command pair does this?
explain: getenforce reports the live mode and setenforce 0 switches to permissive immediately (until reboot or the next setenforce) — no file edits needed. /etc/selinux/config sets the boot-time default only, semanage permissive makes one DOMAIN permissive rather than the system, and /selinux/enforce is the legacy path (modern kernels use /sys/fs/selinux/enforce).

q: PostgreSQL was moved to port 5433. The firewall allows it and postgresql.conf is correct, but connections are refused and the audit log shows AVC denials naming the port. Which command resolves this?
explain: SELinux labels PORTS as well as files; postgresql_port_t covers 5432 by default, so a custom 5433 must be added with semanage port. The firewall is already open (packet filter is not the blocker), chcon labels files rather than ports, and the boolean governs outbound connections rather than the listening port label.

q: Running setsebool httpd_can_network_connect_db 1 fixed the application, but after a reboot the denial returned. What makes the boolean change survive reboots?
options: Re-running setsebool from a cron @reboot entry
explain: Without -P, setsebool changes only the runtime value, which is lost at reboot; -P writes it to the on-disk policy store. /etc/selinux/config holds the global mode and policy type (not individual booleans), a cron re-run is a fragile hack, and booleans are not files so chcon is meaningless on them.

q: On Ubuntu, an AppArmor profile is blocking a legitimate in-house application. The admin wants the application to RUN while logging what WOULD be denied, so the profile can be tuned with real data. Which command does this?
explain: aa-complain puts the profile in complain (learning) mode: actions are allowed but denials are logged, producing exactly the data needed to tune the profile. aa-enforce would keep blocking, aa-disable unloads the profile entirely (no logging baseline), and stopping AppArmor removes protection from every confined program.

q: The admin added file watches with auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p wa, but all rules vanished after a reboot. How are audit rules made persistent?
options: Write the rules in /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules and run augenrules --load
explain: auditctl manages only the RUNTIME rule set; persistent rules live in /etc/audit/rules.d/ and augenrules merges them into /etc/audit/audit.rules at boot. There is no --permanent flag for auditctl (that is a firewalld-ism — the trap), auditd.conf configures the daemon rather than the rules, and enabling the service does not save runtime rules.

q: An admin runs "iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT" but SSH stays blocked. The chain already contains an earlier "iptables -A INPUT -j DROP". What is wrong, and what is the fix?
options: The firewalld service must be restarted first
Rules are evaluated top-down and the DROP matches first — insert the ACCEPT above it with iptables -I INPUT 1 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A appends to the wrong chain; use the OUTPUT chain
The rule needs --permanent to take effect
explain: iptables uses first-match-wins, and -A appends AFTER the existing DROP, so the ACCEPT is never reached; -I inserts at a position above the DROP. The chain is correct, --permanent is a firewalld flag that iptables does not have, and no service restart reorders rules.

q: Internet clients must reach an internal web app by connecting to the firewall's port 8080, which should forward to 10.0.0.5 port 80. Which firewalld commands set this up permanently?
options: iptables -A FORWARD -j ACCEPT (firewalld will pick it up)
explain: --add-forward-port defines the port-forwarding mapping (external port, protocol, destination port and address) in the permanent config, activated by --reload. Merely opening 8080 or adding the http service does not forward anything anywhere, and hand-added iptables rules bypass firewalld's management (note: the zone also needs masquerade enabled for the forward to route).

q: The SOC wants every dropped SSH attempt logged with the prefix "SSH_DROP: " so the SIEM can parse it. Which firewalld construct supports logging with a custom prefix before dropping?
options: A rich rule combining a log action (prefix="SSH_DROP: ") with drop
explain: Rich rules support a log element with prefix and level ahead of the terminal action (accept/reject/drop), giving prefixed kernel logs for the SIEM. --add-service=ssh ALLOWS ssh rather than logging drops, auditd watches file access rather than packet filter decisions, and LogDenied is a firewalld option but without per-rule prefixes or SIEM-friendly tagging.

q: After a server rebuild (same IP, freshly generated host keys), SSH warns "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED." The rebuild was legitimate and the new fingerprint was verified out-of-band. What is the correct response?
options: ssh-keygen -R <hostname> to remove only the stale entry, then reconnect
Ignore the warning and connect anyway
explain: ssh-keygen -R removes just the offending host's old key, after which the verified new fingerprint can be accepted. Deleting all of known_hosts discards every trusted key (the lazy trap), ignoring the warning trains users to accept real man-in-the-middle attacks, and reinstalling the client changes nothing about the key mismatch.

q: The admin must verify from a client which TLS version and cipher a server ACTUALLY negotiates, and inspect the certificate chain it presents. Which command does this?
explain: openssl s_client performs a real TLS handshake and reports the negotiated protocol version, cipher suite, and full certificate chain. x509 -text only parses a LOCAL certificate file, curl -I shows HTTP headers without cipher details, and ssh -v debugs the SSH protocol, not TLS.

q: A compliance scan flags TLS 1.0 and 1.1 as enabled on a RHEL 9 server. Which is the supported SYSTEM-WIDE method to restrict the server to strong protocols and ciphers?
options: Edit every application's TLS config individually
explain: RHEL crypto policies define the system-wide TLS protocol and cipher baseline; FUTURE disables legacy protocols like TLS 1.0/1.1 for all policy-aware applications at once. Editing each app is error-prone and misses services, removing openssl breaks the system, and blocking 443 kills HTTPS instead of hardening it.

q: A provisioning script must create users with pre-hashed passwords via useradd -p, since plaintext passwords on the command line are forbidden. Which command generates a SHA-512 crypt hash suitable for this?
explain: openssl passwd -6 prompts for a password and emits a $6$ SHA-512 crypt hash in exactly the shadow-compatible format useradd -p expects. md5sum and sha256sum produce raw digests (not crypt hashes with salt and identifier), and passwd --stdin sets a live password rather than generating a hash string.

q: Compliance requires sudo to re-prompt for a password after 2 minutes of inactivity instead of the 15-minute default. Which sudoers setting enforces this?
explain: timestamp_timeout controls the credential-caching window in minutes — 2 shrinks it to two minutes. passwd_timeout is a different knob (how long sudo waits for you to TYPE the password), timestamp_timeout=0 would prompt on EVERY sudo (the over-strict trap), and there is no SUDO_TIMEOUT environment variable.

q: A monitoring agent must bind to port 443, but it must NOT run as root and SUID-root is discouraged. Which modern mechanism grants ONLY the needed privilege?
options: Running the agent as root anyway
explain: Linux capabilities grant granular privileges: cap_net_bind_service allows binding ports below 1024 without full root, stored on the binary with setcap. chmod u+s grants FULL root on execution (the dangerous trap), running as root ignores least privilege entirely, and /etc/capabilities is not a real configuration file.

q: An admin sets chmod u+s on a bash script expecting it to run as root, but it still runs as the invoking user. Why?
options: The script also needs the SGID bit set
SUID only works on files under /usr/bin
The filesystem must be remounted with the suid option
The kernel ignores the SUID bit on interpreted scripts; only compiled binaries honor it
explain: For security (race conditions between the interpreter opening the script and the kernel's privilege check), the kernel silently ignores SUID on scripts — a classic exam fact. SGID does not fix it, the path is irrelevant, and filesystems honor SUID by default; the sanctioned alternatives are sudo rules or a compiled wrapper.

q: getfacl on a file shows "user:deploy:rwx" but also "#effective:r--" and "mask::r--". The deploy user cannot write the file. What is limiting the permission?
options: The file is on a read-only filesystem
The file has the immutable attribute set
deploy is not the file owner
The ACL mask caps the maximum permission of all named user and group entries at r--
explain: The ACL mask is the ceiling for every named-user and named-group entry; getfacl even prints the #effective: line to show the reduction. The fix is setfacl -m m::rwx. A read-only filesystem or immutable flag would block the OWNER too, and named-user entries exist precisely for non-owners.

q: A PAM stack contains "auth requisite pam_deny.so" in one file and "auth required pam_unix.so" in another. What is the practical difference between requisite and required?
options: They are synonyms; the words are interchangeable
requisite applies to the account stack, required to the auth stack
required skips the remaining modules on failure
requisite fails the entire stack IMMEDIATELY on failure, while required records the failure but continues evaluating the rest of the stack before failing
explain: requisite short-circuits: the first failure aborts the stack at once (used to block obviously-bad attempts fast). required keeps evaluating subsequent modules and only fails at the end, so logging and account-info modules still run. They are not synonyms, and the stack (auth/account/password/session) is chosen by the first column, not the control flag.

q: On a system honoring /etc/securetty, which statement about root logins is TRUE?
options: It sets the root password hash
It is the sudoers include directory
Deleting it disables the root account
It lists the terminals on which root may log in via login(1); SSH root access is governed separately by sshd_config's PermitRootLogin
explain: /etc/securetty whitelists console terminals (tty1, console, etc.) for root logins through login(1). It does not store passwords, is unrelated to sudo, and deleting it does not disable root. The exam trap is conflating it with SSH: sshd never consults securetty — remote root is controlled by PermitRootLogin.

q: Servers in a remote closet keep rebooting when technicians lean on a KVM keyboard's Ctrl+Alt+Del. How can the admin disable the Ctrl+Alt+Del reboot behavior on systemd systems?
explain: On systemd, Ctrl+Alt+Del triggers the ctrl-alt-del.target unit; masking it symlinks it to /dev/null so the key combo does nothing. /etc/inittab is the legacy SysV mechanism systemd ignores, chmodding reboot breaks legitimate reboots, and kernel.panic controls reboot-after-panic behavior, not the key combo.

q: A playbook targets the entire inventory, but the admin must test it on web01 ONLY, without editing the playbook or inventory. Which flag does this?
options: Edit the inventory to comment out the other hosts
explain: --limit subsets the inventory pattern at run time, so the playbook runs against web01 only with no file changes. --tags selects tagged TASKS (not hosts), --forks only controls parallelism, and editing the inventory is exactly the file change the scenario forbids.

q: A long playbook has several tasks tagged "config". The admin wants to run ONLY those tagged tasks in a maintenance window. Which invocation does this?
explain: --tags runs only tasks carrying the named tag. --limit filters HOSTS (the trap), --skip-tags does the opposite and excludes them, and -e sets an extra variable rather than selecting tasks.

q: A single database password variable must be stored ENCRYPTED inline inside vars/main.yml (not as a separate vault file) in a shared Git repo. Which command produces the encrypted inline string?
explain: ansible-vault encrypt_string emits a !vault-tagged encrypted YAML scalar that pastes directly into a variables file — the standard pattern for one secret among plaintext vars. encrypt encrypts the WHOLE file (the trap), create makes a new fully-encrypted file, and raw gpg output is not valid Ansible vault YAML.

q: A playbook executing on web servers must generate a TLS certificate ONCE, on the Ansible control node, which holds the CA tooling. Which task keyword runs that task on a different host?
explain: delegate_to runs the task on the named host (here the control node) while the play targets the web servers, and run_once keeps it to a single execution. become only escalates privilege on the target, connection: local would misdirect every task, and delegate_facts only controls where gathered facts are stored.

q: A playbook must attempt a risky database migration, run rollback tasks IF it fails, and ALWAYS notify the monitoring system afterward. Which construct provides this try/catch/finally pattern?
options: Two separate playbooks run by a shell script
explain: block groups the attempt, rescue runs only if the block fails (the rollback), and always runs regardless — Ansible's structured error handling. ignore_errors and failed_when: false merely HIDE failures so the playbook reports success while broken (the dangerous trap), and shell-script orchestration abandons Ansible's idempotence and error model.

q: A command task returns exit code 1 when there is simply nothing to do — not an error — but Ansible marks the task failed. How should the playbook treat exit code 1 as success without masking real failures?
explain: failed_when customizes failure detection precisely: only return codes outside [0, 1] fail the task. ignore_errors: yes would also swallow genuine errors (the trap), changed_when only controls the changed/ok reporting, and warn=false merely silences deprecation warnings.

q: A playbook must deploy /files/motd to /etc/motd on all hosts, owned by root:root with mode 0644, changing the file ONLY when its content differs. Which is the correct idempotent approach?
options: ansible.builtin.copy with src, dest, owner, group, and mode (checksum-based idempotence)
explain: The copy module compares checksums and only writes (and reports changed) when content differs, while enforcing owner and mode — fully idempotent. command: cp runs every time and always reports changed (the trap), fetch copies FROM the remote host (wrong direction), and template is for variable-rendered files rather than static ones.

q: A temporary test environment built with OpenTofu must be torn down completely, removing every resource OpenTofu created. Which command does this?
explain: tofu destroy plans and applies the removal of all resources tracked in state. plan -destroy only PREVIEWS the destruction (the trap), deleting .tf files orphans real infrastructure still recorded in state, and apply would converge toward the configuration rather than tearing it down.

q: Before committing, the team wants every .tf file rewritten in the canonical style (consistent indentation and spacing). Which command does this?
explain: tofu fmt rewrites configuration files to canonical HCL formatting. validate only checks syntax and internal consistency without modifying files, plan previews changes, and init -upgrade refreshes provider plugins — none reformat code.

q: A developer wants to REVIEW upstream changes BEFORE merging them into the local branch. Which sequence does this safely?
options: git pull, then git log to review
git fetch, inspect with git log origin/main, then git merge
explain: fetch downloads remote changes WITHOUT merging, so the developer can inspect origin/main and then merge deliberately. pull merges immediately (the trap — review happens after the fact), re-cloning is wasteful, and push --dry-run tests pushing rather than reviewing incoming changes.

q: Deleting an unmerged feature branch with "git branch -d feature" is refused. What is the difference between -d and -D?
options: -d refuses to delete branches with unmerged commits (safety check); -D forces deletion, discarding those commits
explain: -d is the safe delete: it refuses when the branch contains commits not merged elsewhere. -D (--delete --force) overrides the check and the unmerged commits become unreachable. The refusal is Git protecting work — -D should follow a deliberate decision, not habit.

q: Before pushing, a developer wants a compact one-line-per-commit view of the last 5 commits. Which command does this?
explain: git log --oneline condenses each commit to one line (short hash plus subject) and -5 limits the output. status shows working-tree state, diff shows uncommitted changes, and show --stat details a single commit — none give the compact multi-commit history.

q: In a script, filename="report.txt.bak". Which parameter expansion yields "report.txt" by stripping the shortest matching .bak suffix?
explain: % trims a suffix (shortest match); %% trims the longest suffix match, so ${filename%%.*} would yield just "report" (the trap). # trims a PREFIX instead of a suffix, and string concatenation with " - .bak" is not an expansion at all.

q: A wrapper script must forward ALL of its arguments to another command, preserving arguments that contain spaces exactly. Which form is correct?
explain: "$@" expands to each positional parameter as a separately quoted word, so spaces inside arguments survive. $* joins everything into one word subject to splitting (the trap), unquoted $@ word-splits the same way, and hardcoding $1 $2 $3 breaks with any other argument count.

q: A script silently treated a misspelled variable as empty and deleted the wrong path. Which option makes referencing an unset variable an immediate error instead?
explain: set -u (nounset) aborts on expansion of unset variables, turning typos into loud failures. set -e exits on failed COMMANDS (the trap — it does not catch unset variables), set -x only traces execution, and pipefail changes pipeline exit-status semantics.

q: Every command in a long deployment script must append BOTH stdout and stderr to /var/log/deploy.log. Which single line at the top of the script accomplishes this for the whole script?
explain: exec with redirections and no command applies those redirections to the current shell itself, so every subsequent command inherits them. Editing every line is error-prone, exporting a variable name does nothing by itself, and wrapping at invocation works but is not "a line at the top of the script" as required.

q: A script must extract the "version" field from app.json for use in a variable. Which command does this robustly?
explain: jq is a real JSON parser: -r '.version' returns the raw value regardless of formatting or key order. grep/awk/cut parse text, not JSON — they break on nested objects, reordered keys, or values containing colons (the classic fragility trap).

q: Before deploying, the admin must validate that config.json is well-formed JSON and see a parse error if it is not. Which command does this?
explain: python3 -m json.tool parses and pretty-prints the file, exiting nonzero with a clear error on malformed JSON — a true validation. chmod changes executability, file guesses the type from magic bytes, and head shows one line; none parse the document.

q: A Python app must be deployed with the EXACT dependency versions recorded in requirements.txt. Which command installs them?
explain: -r installs every pinned requirement in the file, reproducing the tested environment. pip install app fetches the LATEST versions (the trap — unpinned), venv only creates the isolated environment without installing anything, and freeze GENERATES the file rather than consuming it.

q: Given name="alice" and uid=1001, which Python statement prints "User alice has UID 1001" using an f-string?
explain: The f prefix marks a format string so {name} and {uid} are interpolated. Without the f, the braces print literally (the trap); string concatenation is incomplete here; and echo with $vars is shell syntax, not Python.

q: After an overzealous /boot cleanup deleted the kernel image, the system fails with "error: file '/vmlinuz-5.14.0-362.el9.x86_64' not found" at boot. What is the correct recovery?
options: Boot a rescue/live medium, mount the system, chroot in, and reinstall the kernel package (dnf reinstall kernel), regenerating the bootloader config if needed
Run dracut -f from the GRUB command line
Copy a vmlinuz file from any other server into /boot
explain: The kernel file itself is gone, so no in-place boot is possible: offline repair via rescue media plus reinstalling the kernel package restores vmlinuz, initramfs, and modules consistently. dracut cannot run without a booted system, a foreign kernel mismatches the installed modules, and a full reinstall is overkill for one missing package.

q: On a cloud VM, top shows %st (steal time) at 40% while the guest's own workload is nearly idle. What does this indicate?
options: The VM's CPUs are 40% idle, so performance is fine
The application has a memory leak
The virtual disk is too slow
The hypervisor is not giving this VM its scheduled CPU time — the host is overcommitted or a noisy neighbor is consuming cycles
explain: Steal time is time the VM was ready to run but the hypervisor scheduled another tenant instead; high %st on an idle guest proves host-side contention, not a guest problem. It is not idle time (the trap), and neither memory nor disk explains stolen CPU. Remedies: resize, migrate hosts, or take it up with the provider.

q: iostat shows the disk saturated, and the admin must identify WHICH processes are generating the I/O in real time. Which tool does this?
explain: iotop shows per-process I/O read/write rates in a top-like live display — exactly the process-level attribution needed. top ranks by CPU/memory rather than I/O, iostat -x is per-DEVICE (it proved saturation but not the culprit), and vmstat reports system-wide aggregates.

q: free -h on a 16 GB server shows "free" at 800 MB but "available" at 12 GB. Can a new 8 GB application start safely?
options: Yes — "available" estimates memory reclaimable from caches/buffers; "free" ignores it
No — only 800 MB is actually free
explain: Linux uses spare RAM for page cache, which the kernel reclaims instantly under pressure; the "available" column estimates exactly that reclaimable memory. Reading only the "free" column is the classic misinterpretation (the trap). swapoff is unrelated and root privileges do not create memory.

q: System memory is exhausted and the OOM killer is about to select a victim. Which factor MOST influences which process it chooses?
options: The process's oom_score — driven largely by its memory footprint and tunable via oom_score_adj
The lowest PID is always killed first
Alphabetical order of the process name
explain: The OOM killer scores each process by badness (heavily weighted by RSS); oom_score_adj lets admins protect critical processes (negative) or mark sacrificial ones. PID order, nice values, and names do not decide the victim — the exam trap is assuming nice (CPU priority) governs memory-kill decisions.

q: A database server uses NVMe drives. The admin wants to check each drive's health log: temperature, media errors, and percentage used. Which command reads the NVMe health log natively?
explain: nvme smart-log queries the NVMe controller's health log directly (temperature, media/data integrity errors, percentage used). hdparm targets SATA/PATA drives (the trap), while fdisk and lsblk describe partitions and filesystems — neither reports drive health.

q: The admin wants to discover the path MTU to a remote host and see at which hop it changes. Which tool performs PMTU discovery hop by hop without requiring root?
explain: tracepath performs path-MTU discovery and reports the MTU at each hop, no root needed. A single ping -s tests one packet size only, mtr measures loss and latency rather than MTU, and dig +trace follows DNS delegation — a completely different 'trace'.

q: Users report INTERMITTENT slowness reaching a datacenter. The admin needs per-hop packet loss measured OVER TIME, not a single snapshot. Which tool fits?
options: ping against the final destination only
explain: mtr combines traceroute and ping into a continuously updating per-hop loss/latency display, which catches intermittent loss that one-shot tools miss. A single traceroute is one snapshot (the trap), ping tests only the endpoint, and dig traces DNS resolution rather than packet loss.

q: A server's NIC was replaced (new MAC address, same IP), but other hosts on the LAN still cannot reach it because their neighbor caches hold the OLD MAC. What is the fastest fix?
options: Reboot every host on the LAN
Send a gratuitous ARP from the server (arping -U -I eth0 <ip>) to update neighbors, or flush stale entries with ip neigh flush
Assign the server a different IP address
explain: A gratuitous ARP announcement pushes the new MAC into every neighbor's cache immediately; ip neigh flush clears stale entries. Rebooting the LAN is massive overkill, changing the IP dodges rather than fixes the stale cache, and the switch is not the problem — this is an ARP-cache issue, not a switching one.

q: A file has mode 777, yet a user gets "Permission denied" reading it. Listing the parent directory shows drw-r--r--. What is the cause?
options: The parent directory lacks the execute bit, so the path cannot be traversed to reach the file
The user must be root to read any file
explain: On directories, the execute bit means traverse/search: without x on EVERY component of the path, the kernel cannot reach the file no matter how permissive the file itself is — the classic layered-permissions trap. 7777 adds setuid/setgid/sticky bits irrelevantly, root is not required, and SELinux would log AVC denials rather than bare permission errors.

q: root on an NFS client cannot write to a mount even though the server exports it rw and local permissions are open. The export line is simply "/data client(rw)". Why is root denied?
options: The mount needs the suid option
The client must use NFS over UDP
root_squash (the default) maps the client's root to the anonymous nobody user, removing root's special privileges over NFS
NFS does not support the root user at all
explain: By default the server squashes client root to nobody for security, so root gets no more access than an unprivileged user — rw in the export does not override the squash. no_root_squash disables this (a security risk, not the default). NFS fully supports root clients; suid and the transport protocol are unrelated to the denial.

q: A user reports "Disk quota exceeded" when saving files, yet df shows 50 GB free on the filesystem. What is happening?
options: The filesystem is out of inodes
The user's quota limit is reached — quotas cap per-user usage independently of total filesystem free space
explain: Quotas enforce per-user (or per-group) limits that are entirely separate from filesystem capacity; hitting the quota produces this exact error while df still shows free space. df is not stale, hardware failure produces I/O errors rather than quota messages, and inode exhaustion reports "no space left," not "quota exceeded."

q: ps shows dozens of processes in "Z" state whose parent, etl-worker, is still running. What are they, and what is the correct fix?
options: They consume large amounts of RAM and must be swapped out
They are zombies — dead children the parent has not reaped; fix etl-worker to call wait(), or restart it so init adopts and reaps them
They are running normally and can be ignored
explain: A zombie is a terminated process whose exit status the parent never collected; only the parent (or init after the parent exits) can reap it, so kill -9 on a zombie does nothing (the trap). Zombies hold only a PID-table slot, not RAM. The real fix is in the parent's child-reaping logic.

q: A new admin gets "op is not in the sudoers file. This incident will be reported." when trying sudo. What is the proper fix?
options: Grant privilege properly: add op to the wheel group (usermod -aG wheel op) where %wheel is enabled in sudoers, or add a sudoers entry via visudo
chmod 777 /etc/sudoers so op can edit it
explain: Membership in the wheel group (with the %wheel rule active) is the standard path to sudo access. chmod 777 on sudoers makes sudo refuse to run and is a security hole, UID 0 creates a second root account, and deleting logs destroys the audit trail — the incident report is the system working as designed.

q: After editing httpd.conf, the admin wants to verify the configuration syntax BEFORE restarting the live web service. Which command does this safely?
options: systemctl restart httpd and watch for errors
explain: apachectl configtest (httpd -t) parses the configuration and reports syntax errors without touching the running service. Restarting to "test" risks downtime from a typo (the trap), httpd -v only prints the version, and curl tests the running server rather than the edited files.

q: Every rpm and dnf command fails with "rpmdb: damaged header" errors. Which command rebuilds the RPM database?
explain: rpm --rebuilddb reconstructs the database indices from the installed package headers. dnf clean all only clears cached downloads, deleting /var/lib/rpm DESTROYS the database (the dangerous trap), and a reboot does not repair database corruption.

q: A failed disk was physically removed. Now vgscan shows the volume group with an "[unknown]" PV and the VG refuses to activate. Which command drops the missing PV so the VG works in degraded mode?
options: pvcreate a new disk with the same name
explain: vgreduce --removemissing removes PVs that are no longer present, letting the VG activate in degraded mode (data on the missing PV is lost — mirrors/RAID are what make this survivable). Creating a same-named PV does not restore the metadata, vgremove destroys the entire VG (the catastrophic trap), and the BIOS cannot fix LVM metadata.

q: The journal shows "Found ordering cycle on multi-user.target/start" and the boot hangs. What does this mean, and what is the fix?
options: The disk is full and systemd cannot write
Add more After= dependencies to serialize startup
Two units order themselves After each other in a loop — break the cycle by removing or correcting one After=/Before= dependency
explain: An ordering cycle is a dependency loop (A After B while B After A); systemd breaks it by deleting a job, which hangs the boot. The fix is editing the units to remove the contradictory ordering — adding MORE After= lines deepens the loop (the trap). Disk space and reinstalling systemd are unrelated to dependency cycles.

q: Every SSH login prints "warning: setlocale: LC_ALL: cannot change locale" and sorting behaves oddly. The requested locale was never generated on this system. Which fixes it properly?
options: Ignore the warning; it is cosmetic
Generate the locale (localedef) and set it with localectl set-locale LANG=en_US.UTF-8
explain: The warning means the locale definition does not exist in /usr/lib/locale; localedef generates it and localectl set-locale makes it the system default. Exporting LC_ALL=C is a workaround that masks the misconfiguration (the trap), reinstalling glibc does not generate locales, and broken sorting/collation in scripts is more than cosmetic.

q: A service fails to start with "Address already in use" binding to TCP 8080. Which command identifies the process currently holding that port?
explain: ss -tlnp lists listening TCP sockets with the owning process (-p), pinpointing the conflict. ps aux | grep matches command-line text that rarely contains the port (the trap), /etc/services only maps port numbers to NAMES, and ping does not take a port. The fix is then reconfiguring or stopping the conflicting process — not blindly killing by guess.

q: After cloning a server to a new disk, it keeps booting from the old disk even though the clone is complete. efibootmgr -v shows both disks as UEFI boot entries. Which command makes the system try the new disk first?
explain: efibootmgr -o sets the UEFI BootOrder variable, controlling which entry firmware tries first. grub2-install reinstalls the bootloader (it does not reorder UEFI entries), update-grub is the Debian tool that rebuilds grub.cfg, and fdisk -l only lists partitions — none of them change the firmware boot order.

q: An admin added ipv6.disable=1 to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub and regenerated grub.cfg. How can they verify the parameter is actually in effect on the running kernel?
explain: /proc/cmdline shows the exact command line the running kernel booted with — the ground truth for whether the parameter took effect. /etc/default/grub shows configuration intent (it could be stale or misregenerated), sysctl.conf holds sysctl tunables rather than kernel parameters, and grepping dmesg for 'grub' is unreliable.

q: A new storage driver was added to the initramfs with dracut. Before rebooting, the admin wants to confirm the driver's .ko file is actually inside the new initramfs image. Which command checks this?
explain: lsinitrd lists the contents of an initramfs image, so it directly verifies the driver made it into the new image before the risky reboot. lsmod shows modules loaded in the CURRENT kernel (the new image is not booted yet), modinfo reads /lib/modules metadata rather than initramfs contents, and dmesg shows messages from the current boot.

q: A Btrfs filesystem on /data may have silent data corruption after a storage controller glitch. Which command verifies data integrity against Btrfs checksums while the filesystem stays online?
explain: btrfs scrub reads every block, verifies its checksum, and repairs from a good mirror copy when one exists — all while the filesystem stays mounted. fsck.btrfs performs only minimal checks, balance redistributes chunks across devices (no integrity verification), and defragment rewrites extents without validating their contents.

q: Before a risky database upgrade, the admin wants an instant point-in-time copy of the 500 GB logical volume vgdata/lvdb that initially consumes almost no extra space. Which command creates it?
explain: lvcreate -s creates a copy-on-write snapshot: it starts nearly empty and only stores blocks that change after the snapshot, giving an instant rollback point. Without -s, lvcreate makes a full empty volume; dd would copy all 500 GB slowly; cp on device nodes does not perform a block-level copy.

q: The ext4 filesystem on /dev/vgdata/lvapp (mounted at /app) must shrink from 100G to 60G. Which sequence does this safely?
options: resize2fs /dev/vgdata/lvapp 60G while /app is mounted, then lvreduce -L 60G /dev/vgdata/lvapp
explain: ext4 cannot shrink while mounted, so the filesystem must be unmounted, force-checked, shrunk with resize2fs FIRST, and only then may the LV be reduced — shrinking the LV first truncates live filesystem data. lvextend -r cannot shrink a mounted ext4 filesystem, resize2fs refuses online shrinking, and reducing the volume before the filesystem destroys data.

q: A RAID5 array /dev/md0 has three active devices, and a fourth disk /dev/sdd1 is ready. Which command grows the array to include the new disk without data loss?
explain: mdadm --grow reshapes a live array, restriping parity across the new device count without destroying data. --create would build a brand-new (empty) array over the disks; --assemble merely activates existing members without reshaping; formatting the disk standalone ignores the array entirely.

q: A 12 TB ext4 data disk wastes roughly 600 GB on the default 5% root-reserved blocks, which serve no purpose on a pure data volume. Which command reduces the reservation to 1% without touching the data?
explain: tune2fs -m adjusts the reserved-block percentage on an existing ext4 filesystem online with no data loss. mkfs would destroy all 12 TB of data (the dangerous trap), resize2fs has no -m option, and dumpe2fs only displays superblock information without changing anything.

q: The admin wants to label the XFS filesystem on /dev/sdb1 as datadisk so fstab can reference LABEL=datadisk. Which command sets a label on an existing XFS filesystem?
explain: xfs_admin -L writes a label into an XFS filesystem's superblock. tune2fs and e2label are ext-family tools that do not understand XFS, and xfs_growfs resizes filesystems (taking a mount point) — it has no label option. Match the tool to the filesystem type.

q: Clients get 'access denied by server' mounting the NFS share. The admin just added '/data 10.0.0.0/24(rw,sync)' to /etc/exports. What completes the fix with minimal disruption?
explain: exportfs -ra re-reads /etc/exports and applies the changes without restarting the NFS server or disturbing existing clients. A full nfs-server restart works but disrupts current mounts; mount -a processes the client's fstab (wrong side); and 777 addresses local permissions, not export-level denial — while being insecure.

q: Before troubleshooting the client, the admin wants to confirm which directories the NFS server nfs01 is actually exporting. Which command lists the server's export list?
explain: showmount -e queries the server's mount daemon and reports exactly what it exports. nfsstat -m shows the client's own mount statistics, mount | grep shows local mounts, and /etc/exports only exists on the server — useless when run on the client being debugged.

q: A CIFS share must mount at boot without embedding the password in the world-readable /etc/fstab. Which approach is correct?
options: credentials=/root/.smbcred in fstab (mode 600), with username= and password= lines inside
password=secret123 directly in the fstab options field
chmod 644 /etc/fstab so the mount helper can read it
Store the password in /etc/hosts next to the server entry
explain: A root-only (mode 600) credentials file keeps the secret out of world-readable fstab while letting the boot-time mount authenticate. Embedding the password in fstab exposes it to every local user, fstab's own permissions cannot protect inline options, and /etc/hosts is for name resolution — not secrets.

q: A new iSCSI target at 10.0.0.5 holds a LUN for this host. Which sequence discovers the target and logs into it?
options: iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p 10.0.0.5, then iscsiadm -m node -T <iqn> -p 10.0.0.5 --login
explain: Discovery (sendtargets) learns the target's IQN, then a node login establishes the iSCSI session and exposes the LUN as a local disk. Logging in without discovery has no target record to use, iSCSI is not a mountable filesystem type, and fdisk cannot reach network block targets.

q: The host needs VLAN 20 on eth0, appearing as interface eth0.20, with no reboot. Which command creates it?
options: ip link add link eth0 name eth0.20 type vlan id 20
nmcli con add type vlan eth0.20
explain: ip link add ... type vlan id 20 creates the VLAN sub-interface on the parent link; it can then be addressed and brought up. Adding an address to a nonexistent interface fails, vconfig is the deprecated legacy tool, and the nmcli syntax shown is invalid (it needs ifname/dev/id keywords).

q: Two NICs must be bonded in active-backup mode as bond0 through NetworkManager so the config survives reboots. Which command creates the bond?
options: ip link add bond0 type bond mode active-backup
nmcli con add type bond ifname bond0 mode active-backup, then enslave the NICs as bond-slaves
explain: nmcli con add type bond creates a persistent NetworkManager bond profile, with each NIC added as a bond-slave connection. ip link works but is runtime-only, modprobe merely loads the bonding module, and teamdctl manages the competing 'team' driver — not bonding.

q: An entry in /etc/hosts is being ignored and DNS answers instead. Which /etc/nsswitch.conf line restores files-first hostname resolution?
explain: nsswitch.conf controls source order: 'files dns' consults /etc/hosts before DNS. 'dns files' does the opposite, NOTFOUND=return stops resolution on a DNS negative answer before files are tried, and resolv.conf only lists DNS servers — it cannot order files versus DNS.

q: On a systemd-resolved host, /etc/resolv.conf points to the 127.0.0.53 stub. The admin needs to see which upstream DNS servers each network link actually uses. Which command shows this?
explain: resolvectl status displays systemd-resolved's per-link DNS servers, search domains, and routing. /etc/resolv.conf shows only the stub address, nmcli shows NetworkManager's configuration rather than resolved's runtime state, and dig tests resolution without revealing the upstream server list.

q: After a VM was restored from a snapshot, its clock is 40 minutes fast and chronyd will not correct such a large offset by slewing. Which command forces an immediate clock step?
explain: chronyc makestep forces chronyd to step the clock immediately regardless of offset size. tracking only reports synchronization status, disabling NTP with set-ntp false makes drift worse, and the hardware clock is equally wrong after a snapshot restore.

q: An application's /run/myapp socket directory vanishes on every reboot because /run is a tmpfs. Which mechanism recreates it early at boot with the correct owner and mode?
explain: systemd-tmpfiles reads /etc/tmpfiles.d/ early in boot and creates volatile paths with the specified ownership and mode — the designed solution for tmpfs directories. rc.local is legacy and often disabled, fstab mounts filesystems rather than creating plain directories, and @reboot cron entries run late with no ordering guarantees.

q: A buggy service occasionally consumes all CPU and RAM, starving the host. Which unit-file settings cap it at half a CPU core and 2 GB of RAM?
options: CPUQuota=50% and MemoryMax=2G in the [Service] section
Nice=19 and IOSchedulingClass=idle in the [Service] section
LimitCPU=50% and LimitMEM=2G in the [Service] section
CPUAffinity=0 and MemoryLimit=2G in the [Service] section
explain: systemd resource control uses CPUQuota= and MemoryMax= (cgroup v2) to enforce hard caps. Nice only biases scheduling without capping, LimitCPU/LimitMEM are not valid directives, and CPUAffinity merely pins CPUs while MemoryLimit is the obsolete cgroup v1 name.

q: Journal logs disappear after every reboot, complicating post-crash analysis, and /var/log/journal does not exist. Which journald.conf setting makes logs persist across boots?
explain: Storage=persistent makes journald create /var/log/journal and retain logs across reboots. volatile is the RAM-only default causing the symptom, SystemMaxUse only caps storage size, and forwarding to syslog duplicates logs elsewhere without fixing the journal itself.

q: Before deploying a new logrotate configuration for /var/log/app.log, the admin wants to verify it parses correctly and see what rotation would do — without rotating anything. Which command performs this dry run?
explain: logrotate -d is debug/dry-run mode: it parses the configuration and prints exactly what it would do without touching any logs. -f forces an immediate real rotation (the opposite of a dry run), --version only prints the version, and logrotate has no systemd service to reload — it runs from cron.

q: A KVM guest gets no network. virsh net-list --all shows the default NAT network as inactive. Which commands fix it now and keep it working across host reboots?
options: virsh net-start default && virsh net-autostart default
explain: net-start activates the virtual network immediately, and net-autostart makes libvirtd start it on every boot. Autostarting the guest does not help while its network is down, restarting libvirtd does not activate defined-but-inactive networks, and net-start alone will not survive a reboot.

q: A new daemon needs its own system group svcmon, with a GID from the system range. Which command creates it?
explain: groupadd -r creates a system group, allocating a GID from the system range (typically below 1000). Without -r it takes a regular user GID, useradd creates an entire account rather than just a group, and hand-editing /etc/group bypasses locking and syntax validation.

q: A file restored from backup is owned by root, but it must match the owner and group of its sibling config /etc/app/app.conf. Which command copies the ownership?
explain: chown --reference copies both owner and group from the reference file in one step. Hardcoding root:root moves ownership the wrong way, chmod --reference copies permission bits rather than ownership, and chgrp --reference copies only the group.

q: The script /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh needs the owner-execute bit added, without altering any other permission bits. Which command does exactly this?
explain: chmod u+x adds execute for the owner only, leaving group and other bits untouched. An absolute mode like 744 rewrites every class (potentially stripping group/other bits), while +x and a+x grant execute to everyone — broader than requested.

q: getfacl shows stale named-user ACL entries on /srv/data that no longer match policy. The admin wants every ACL removed, leaving only the base permission bits. Which command does this?
explain: setfacl -b removes all extended ACLs, keeping only the base user/group/other entries derived from the mode. -x deletes a single named entry, chmod does not strip ACLs (it may only recalculate the mask), and -m modifies entries rather than removing them.

q: With umask 022 in effect, what permissions does a newly created directory receive?
explain: Directories start at 777; umask 022 removes write for group and other, yielding 755. 644 is the FILE result under umask 022 (666 minus 022), 777 ignores the umask entirely, and 700 would require umask 077.

q: The admin wants every future useradd account to default to /bin/zsh instead of /bin/bash. Which command changes the system-wide useradd default shell?
explain: useradd -D displays and changes the defaults stored in /etc/default/useradd, including the default shell. chsh changes one existing user's shell, /etc/login.defs covers different defaults (UID ranges, password aging), and usermod has no -D defaults mode.

q: Contractor temp2 must lose ALL access, including SSH key authentication, on 2027-03-31. The admin knows passwd -l will not block key-based logins. Which command enforces the cutoff?
explain: chage -E sets account expiration; an expired account is denied everywhere, including SSH public-key authentication. passwd -l only disables password authentication (keys still work — the trap), nologin still permits some non-interactive access, and hand-editing shadow risks syntax errors and lockouts.

q: During an access review, the admin needs a quick list of recent FAILED login attempts with usernames and source IPs. Which command reads the failed-login log?
explain: lastb reads /var/log/btmp, the database of failed login attempts. last reads wtmp (successful sessions), lastlog shows each user's most recent successful login, and who shows only currently logged-in users.

q: After fixing a crashed service and starting it cleanly, systemctl status still shows the unit in a failed state from the earlier crash. Which command clears the recorded failure?
explain: systemctl reset-failed clears the failed state and restart counters for the unit. daemon-reload only re-reads unit files, mask would disable the unit entirely, and vacuuming the journal removes logs without touching unit state.

q: Before installing a vendor RPM downloaded to /tmp, the admin wants to inspect its metadata and pre-install scripts for anything suspicious. Which command queries the NOT-YET-INSTALLED package file?
explain: rpm -qip queries the info tag of a package FILE (the -p flag means 'package file' rather than the installed database). rpm -qi looks in the installed database where the package does not exist yet, dnf info needs repository metadata rather than a file, and rpm -K only verifies the signature.

q: The rarely used cups service should consume no resources until a print job actually arrives, then start automatically. Which systemd mechanism provides this on-demand behavior?
options: Enable cups.socket with the service stopped — socket activation starts it on the first connection
A cron job that starts cups every minute
explain: Socket activation lets cups.socket listen on behalf of the service; the first incoming connection triggers the service start, so it idles at zero cost otherwise. disable and mask prevent starting entirely, and cron polling is crude, delayed, and wasteful.

q: A flaky service exits with an error roughly once a day and must restart automatically, waiting 30 seconds between attempts. Which unit settings do this?
options: Restart=on-failure and RestartSec=30 in the [Service] section
explain: Restart=on-failure relaunches the service after abnormal exits, and RestartSec=30 delays each attempt. Restart=no is the default that never restarts, Type=oneshot is for run-once tasks rather than daemons, and ExecReload only handles reload requests — not crashes.

q: A service writes temporary files that must be invisible to other processes and users, and cleaned up automatically when it stops. Which hardening directive gives it a private /tmp?
explain: PrivateTmp=true mounts a private tmpfs /tmp namespace for the service, isolating its temp files and removing them when the service stops. ReadOnlyPaths=/tmp would break temp writes entirely, NoNewPrivileges blocks privilege escalation (a different goal), and ProtectHome hides home directories rather than /tmp.

q: On RHEL 9, the admin must install the entire Development Tools package group (gcc, make, and friends) in one step. Which command does this?
explain: dnf groupinstall installs a comps package group by name, pulling every member package. Installing gcc and make individually misses the rest of the group, no monolithic Development-Tools RPM exists, and modules select version streams — not package collections.

q: A recursive chmod accidentally changed permissions on hundreds of files owned by the httpd package. Which command restores the packaged default permissions?
explain: rpm --setperms resets file modes from the RPM database to their packaged values. rpm -V only reports differences without fixing them, dnf reinstall works but needlessly replaces files and can clobber configuration, and a blanket 755 breaks files that require other modes (644, 4755, and so on).

q: On Ubuntu, the admin must see which nginx version is installed, which candidate version apt would install, and whether any pinning affects it. Which command shows all three?
explain: apt-cache policy shows the installed version, the candidate version, the full version table, and pin priorities in one view. apt list and dpkg -l show only installed state, while apt-cache search finds packages without any version or pinning detail.

q: On Debian 12, which command finds which installed package owns the file /usr/bin/htop?
explain: dpkg -S searches installed packages for the owner of a path — the Debian equivalent of rpm -qf. apt-file queries all repository packages (and needs its own updated index), dpkg -L goes the other direction (package to files, needing the name first), and apt has no 'owns' subcommand.

q: A Dockerfile runs COPY . /app before RUN apt-get install ..., so every code edit re-runs the slow install step. How should the Dockerfile be reordered to fix the build cache?
options: Add more RUN layers to parallelize the build
Use ADD instead of COPY for the source tree
Move COPY . /app AFTER the install steps, copying dependency manifests first where needed
Merge everything into a single RUN instruction
explain: Docker invalidates the cache for a changed layer and every layer after it, so copying volatile source early busts the cache for the expensive install. Moving COPY after the stable install steps keeps installs cached across code edits. More layers do not help, ADD behaves the same for caching, and merging RUNs does not fix the invalidation order.

q: A Podman container named web is running. The admin needs an interactive bash shell inside it for debugging. Which command opens one?
explain: podman exec runs a new process inside the existing container, with -it making it interactive. attach hijacks the main process's stdio (and Ctrl-C can kill the container), run creates a separate new container, and containers do not run sshd unless specifically built for it.

q: The admin needs container web's full details — its IP address, mounted volumes, and environment variables — as JSON for a script. Which command outputs this?
explain: podman inspect dumps the container's complete JSON metadata, including network settings, mounts, and configuration. ps gives a one-line tabular summary, stats streams live CPU/memory usage, and top lists the processes running inside the container.

q: After adding an AD user to a new group, id username on the Linux host still shows the old groups. SSSD is caching the stale entry. Which command clears the SSSD cache?
explain: sss_cache -E invalidates cached entries so the next lookup re-queries Active Directory for fresh group membership. Restarting sssd does not purge the on-disk cache database, realm leave destroys the domain join entirely, and kinit only obtains Kerberos tickets without touching the SSSD cache.

q: During hardening, the admin must find every file with POSIX capabilities set, since capabilities like cap_setuid can be privilege-escalation paths. Which command audits this?
explain: getcap -r recursively lists every file carrying POSIX capabilities. A SUID search (-perm -4000) misses capability-based escalation entirely, ls -l does not display capabilities, and setcap assigns capabilities rather than listing them.

q: The web root moved to /srv/www. The admin fixed a denial with chcon, but the label reverted after the nightly restorecon cron job. Which approach makes the label survive relabels?
explain: semanage fcontext writes the label into the SELinux policy database, so restorecon and full relabels reapply it permanently; chcon only changes the on-disk label until the next relabel. setenforce 0 abandons mandatory access control instead of fixing the label, and chmod addresses DAC permissions — unrelated to SELinux types.

q: An admin set SELINUX=disabled in /etc/selinux/config months ago. Now setenforce 1 fails with 'SELinux is disabled'. What is required to return to enforcing mode?
options: Edit /etc/selinux/config to SELINUX=enforcing and run setenforce 1
Set SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config and reboot so the filesystem relabels on boot
explain: Once SELinux is disabled, it cannot be enabled at runtime — the kernel needs SELINUX=enforcing at boot followed by a full filesystem relabel. setenforce only toggles between enforcing and permissive while SELinux is active, and editing the config without rebooting changes nothing in the running kernel.

q: On Ubuntu, the admin must verify which AppArmor profiles are loaded and whether each is in enforce or complain mode. Which command reports this?
explain: aa-status lists loaded profiles with each one's enforce/complain state. getenforce is SELinux-only, apparmor_parser loads or replaces profiles rather than reporting status, and the systemd unit status does not break down per-profile modes.

q: For a compliance report, the admin needs a summary of all authentication events (logins, su, sudo) from the audit logs. Which command produces this summary?
explain: aureport --auth summarizes authentication-related audit events across every service. ausearch -m AVC covers SELinux denials rather than authentications, lastb only sees failed logins from btmp, and the sshd journal misses su, sudo, and console logins.

q: A new NIC eth1 landed in the public zone, but policy requires it in the internal zone permanently. Which command moves it?
options: ip link set eth1 zone internal
nmcli con mod eth1 connection.zone public
explain: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=internal --change-interface reassigns the interface's zone in the persistent configuration, activated by --reload. Without --permanent the change is runtime-only, ip has no zone concept, and the nmcli example assigns the wrong zone.

q: The admin must rate-limit new SSH connections to 5 per minute per source using nftables natively. Which rule does this?
options: nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept
nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 drop
nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 ct state new limit rate 5/minute accept
explain: The nft limit statement combined with ct state new throttles connection attempts to the specified rate. The plain accept rule has no limiting, the drop rule blocks all SSH, and mixing raw iptables syntax on an nftables-managed host creates rules outside the nft ruleset the admin manages.

q: The current iptables policy is ACCEPT on INPUT with a few allow rules — a default-allow posture. Which command switches the chain to default-deny?
explain: iptables -P sets the chain's default policy so unmatched packets are dropped. Appending DROP at the end never triggers because earlier ACCEPT rules match first, flushing removes all protections and leaves default ACCEPT wide open, and -X only deletes empty user-defined chains.
