q: Only the backup service account svcbackup must be forced to use key authentication, while other users may still use passwords. Which sshd_config approach applies this per-user override?
options: A Match User svcbackup block containing PasswordAuthentication no
explain: Match blocks apply settings conditionally by user, group, or address — the mechanism for per-user overrides. The global directive affects everyone, AllowUsers controls who may log in rather than how they authenticate, and PermitRootLogin only governs root.

q: An automation script SSHes to freshly provisioned hosts whose keys are unknown. It must accept new host keys automatically but still fail if a KNOWN host's key changes. Which option does this?
explain: accept-new auto-adds unknown host keys while still erroring on changed keys for known hosts — automation-friendly without blinding change detection. 'no' also accepts changed keys silently (the man-in-the-middle trap), 'yes' prompts and breaks automation, and /dev/null forgets everything so changes are never noticed.

q: The admin must check a certificate file's validity dates before a renewal window. Which command prints its notBefore and notAfter dates?
explain: openssl x509 -noout -dates parses the certificate and prints its validity window. The rsa subcommand inspects private keys rather than certificates, grepping a base64 PEM finds no readable dates, and s_client tests a live server instead of a file on disk.

q: The company runs an internal CA. Its root certificate was copied to /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/ on RHEL 9. Which command makes the system actually trust it?
explain: update-ca-trust extract rebuilds the consolidated system trust bundle from the source directories — copying the file alone does nothing until extraction. File permissions do not trigger a rebuild, there is no ca-trust service, and openssl rehash serves OpenSSL's legacy hashed-directory mechanism rather than the system bundle.

q: The admin must send backup.tar to the offsite team so that only the holder of the team's private key can read it. Passphrase-based encryption is not allowed. Which command does this?
explain: gpg --encrypt --recipient uses the team's public key, so only their private key can decrypt the file. --symmetric uses a shared passphrase (explicitly ruled out), --sign only proves origin without encrypting, and --export dumps the public key itself rather than the data.

q: Hardening requires that unprivileged users cannot read kernel messages, which may leak pointers useful for exploits. Which sysctl enforces this?
explain: kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 restricts dmesg to privileged users. kptr_restrict masks kernel pointers in procfs files rather than dmesg content, yama.ptrace_scope limits process debugging, and setting randomize_va_space=0 disables ASLR — the opposite of hardening.

q: An encrypted data disk must unlock at boot by prompting for its passphrase, then mount at /data. Which file configures the boot-time unlock?
options: /etc/crypttab, with an entry like: datacrypt UUID=<uuid> none
explain: /etc/crypttab maps encrypted devices for unlocking at boot, with 'none' meaning prompt for the passphrase. fstab handles the mount step after unlocking but cannot unlock LUKS, mtab is generated runtime state rather than configuration, and exports is for NFS shares.

q: The hardening checklist requires finding all world-writable regular files, excluding /tmp and /dev. Which find expression matches them?
explain: find -perm -0002 matches any file with the other-write bit set regardless of the remaining bits — the correct test for world-writable. -perm 777 matches only the exact mode (missing 666 files), -4000 matches SUID instead, and grepping ls output is fragile and slow.

q: A Linux file server shared with Windows clients needs a malware scan of /srv/share using current signatures. Which sequence does this correctly?
explain: freshclam updates the ClamAV signature database first, then clamscan -r scans recursively with current detections. Scanning with stale signatures misses new malware, rkhunter hunts Linux rootkits rather than general malware, and AIDE verifies file integrity against its own database — not malicious content.

q: An admin's playbook run keeps using /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg instead of the ./ansible.cfg in the project directory. An environment variable is set. Which variable overrides every config file location?
explain: ANSIBLE_CONFIG has the highest precedence, beating ./ansible.cfg, ~/.ansible.cfg, and /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg. ANSIBLE_INVENTORY selects the inventory rather than the config file, ANSIBLE_PLAYBOOK is not a real variable, and HOME only locates the ~/.ansible.cfg fallback.

q: Before running a newly written playbook against staging, the admin wants to validate its YAML syntax and playbook structure without contacting any hosts. Which flag does this?
explain: --syntax-check parses the playbook locally without touching any managed hosts. --check performs a dry run that still connects to hosts, --diff only changes output verbosity during a real run, and --step pauses for confirmation between real task executions.

q: A playbook task runs /usr/local/bin/healthcheck.sh via the command module. It always reports changed even when nothing changed, triggering handlers needlessly. Which task keyword fixes the idempotency report?
explain: changed_when: false tells Ansible the command never changes system state, so handlers are not needlessly notified. failed_when: false would mask real failures (dangerous), check_mode: no concerns dry-run behavior, and register only stores the result without affecting the changed status.

q: group_vars/web.yml sets ntp_server: 10.0.0.1, but host web01 needs 10.0.0.99. Without editing group_vars, where can the admin override it for web01 only?
explain: host_vars/<host>.yml overrides group_vars for that host alone — the per-host override mechanism. group_vars/all affects every host, play vars apply to all hosts in the play, and [web:vars] is group-scoped, hitting every web host rather than just web01.

q: A playbook configuring web servers must render each web server's haproxy config with the database IP, which is stored on host db01 as ansible_host. Which Jinja2 expression reads another host's variable?
explain: The hostvars magic variable exposes any host's facts and variables by inventory name. inventory_hostname is the current host's own name, groups['db'] returns a list of host names rather than their variables, and bare ansible_host resolves for the current host only.

q: A nightly CI job runs an Ansible playbook needing vault-encrypted secrets, with no human available to type the vault password. Which is the correct non-interactive approach?
options: Remove the vault encryption from the secrets
ansible-playbook --vault-password-file /etc/ansible/vault-pass site.yml, with the file readable only by root
Use --ask-vault-pass and pipe output from yes
Store the vault password in a playbook comment
explain: --vault-password-file enables automation while the password file itself is protected by strict filesystem permissions. Removing encryption or commenting the password exposes secrets in version control, and piping into an interactive prompt is fragile and unreliable.

q: A playbook must apply the hardening role in a loop over three compliance profiles chosen at runtime. Which construct handles dynamic looping over a role correctly?
explain: include_role is dynamic — evaluated at execution time — so it works with loops and conditionals. import_role is static (pre-processed when the playbook loads), the roles: keyword does not loop, and include_tasks includes task files rather than full role structure.

q: A playbook restarts the web service on 40 servers. Restarts must happen one host at a time so the site stays up. Which play keyword enforces this rolling behavior?
explain: serial controls how many hosts execute the play at once, so serial: 1 produces a strict one-at-a-time rolling update. throttle limits task concurrency per host rather than rolling across hosts, max_fail_percentage is failure tolerance, and run_once executes the task on a single host total.

q: An OpenTofu variable instance_type is set in terraform.tfvars, in TF_VAR_instance_type, and via -var='instance_type=m5.large'. Which value wins?
explain: Variable precedence is: -var CLI flags, then TF_VAR_ environment variables, then *.tfvars files, then declared defaults. The CLI flag is the most specific override, environment beats files, and files beat defaults.

q: Someone deleted a test VM directly in the cloud console. The admin wants OpenTofu to forget about it WITHOUT trying to destroy anything, since it is already gone. Which command removes it from state?
options: Delete the resource block from the .tf files
explain: tofu state rm drops the resource binding from state without touching real infrastructure. destroy calls the provider API (which errors on the missing VM), refresh-only syncs attributes but still plans recreation, and deleting the config makes plan propose destroying a resource that no longer exists.

q: An OpenTofu configuration needs the ID of the latest RHEL 9 AMI, which the cloud provider maintains and OpenTofu must never create or modify. Which block reads it?
explain: Data sources are read-only lookups of existing infrastructure. A resource block would attempt to manage (or create) the AMI, a variable requires a manually supplied value, and an output only exposes values already in state — none of them fetch the AMI ID.

q: A cloud-init user-data file contains valid YAML (users, packages, runcmd), but the VM boots with none of it applied. The file's first line is 'users:'. What is missing?
options: A .yaml file extension on the user-data
The execute bit on the user-data file
The '#cloud-config' header as the very first line
explain: cloud-init identifies the user-data format by its first line; without #cloud-config the YAML is never parsed as cloud-config directives. File extensions and execute bits are irrelevant to cloud-init, and a shebang would mark the data as a shell script — a different format entirely.

q: Before using a Kickstart file to provision 200 servers, the admin wants to catch syntax errors in it now rather than mid-install. Which tool validates the file?
explain: ksvalidator (from pykickstart) checks Kickstart syntax before deployment. shellcheck targets shell scripts, py_compile targets Python code, and anaconda has no standalone --test validation mode — each checks the wrong language for this file.

q: In a script, BACKUP_DIR may be unset or empty; the script must then use /var/backups without permanently assigning the variable. Which expansion does this?
explain: ${var:-word} substitutes the default when the variable is unset OR empty, without assigning it. ${var=word} permanently assigns (and only when unset), || tests command exit status rather than emptiness, and ${#var} expands to the string's length.

q: A script must test whether $filename is empty. Which form is safe even when the variable is unset or contains spaces?
explain: [[ ]] with a quoted variable is immune to word splitting and globbing, so empty or space-containing values test correctly. Unquoted $filename in [ ] or test breaks on spaces and emptiness, while single quotes prevent expansion entirely — testing the literal text '$filename' instead of the variable.

q: A developer committed to the wrong branch. The commit must be undone but the file changes must remain in the working tree as uncommitted edits. Which command does this?
explain: git reset HEAD~1 (default --mixed) rewinds the branch pointer one commit while leaving the changes unstaged in the working tree. revert creates a new counter-commit instead of uncommitting, --hard discards the work, and checkout HEAD~1 only detaches HEAD without moving the branch.

q: An AI assistant generated an Ansible playbook for production firewall changes. Following responsible-AI practices, what must the admin do before running it for real?
options: Run it immediately — AI output is reliably correct
Pipe it straight to the production inventory to save time
Review it manually, then run ansible-playbook --syntax-check followed by --check --diff to preview changes
Only verify that the YAML formatting looks clean
explain: AI-generated infrastructure code requires human review plus syntax validation and a check-mode dry run with diffs before touching production. Blind execution risks outages from plausible-but-wrong automation, and clean formatting says nothing about correctness or safety.

q: SSH to a server fails. From the client, the admin sees either 'Connection refused' or 'Connection timed out'. Which diagnosis is correct?
options: Refused: the host was reached but nothing listens (or a REJECT rule fired); timed out: packets were dropped/filtered or routing is broken
Refused: DNS resolution failed; timed out: the password was wrong
Both mean the sshd service is stopped
Refused: a firewall DROP rule; timed out: a firewall REJECT rule
explain: Connection refused means a TCP RST came back — the host is reachable but nothing accepts on the port, or a REJECT rule answered. A timeout means silence: DROP rules, routing failures, or a down host. DNS failures produce resolution errors rather than these messages, and the firewall mapping in the last option is backwards.

q: Every SSH login hangs about 30 seconds at 'SSH2_MSG_SERVICE_ACCEPT received' before the password prompt. Client IPs have no reverse DNS. Which server-side fix addresses this delay?
options: Set GSSAPIAuthentication no (and/or UseDNS no) in sshd_config
Open outbound port 53 on the firewall
Add every client IP to the server's /etc/hosts
explain: With GSSAPIAuthentication enabled, sshd attempts Kerberos operations that stall without working DNS/KDC, and UseDNS yes waits on reverse-DNS timeouts — disabling them removes the delay. MaxAuthTries counts attempts rather than causing delays, opening DNS treats a symptom, and per-client hosts entries do not scale.

q: Users get 'No space left on device' but df -h shows 60% free on the ext4 filesystem. Which command reveals the actually exhausted resource?
explain: df -i shows inode usage: millions of small files exhaust inodes while data blocks remain free, producing exactly this symptom. du and df -h measure blocks, and deleted-but-open files cause the opposite pattern (df full while du shows free space).

q: Mounting a CIFS share fails with 'mount error(13): Permission denied' although the credentials are correct and the server is reachable. The server recently disabled SMB1. What is the likely fix?
options: Specify vers=3.0 (or another supported dialect) in the mount options
explain: Modern servers disable old SMB dialects, so the client must request a supported one via vers=. The error comes from protocol negotiation, not local mountpoint permissions, name resolution (the server is reachable), or the firewall (traffic flows).

q: An application is slow. Overall CPU is 25% on a 4-CPU VM, yet one process seems stuck. Which command shows per-CPU utilization to check for a single-threaded bottleneck?
explain: mpstat -P ALL breaks CPU statistics down per core: one core pegged at 100% with the others idle proves a single-threaded bottleneck. uptime gives only load averages, free shows memory, and vmstat aggregates CPU without the per-core split.

q: A process vanished overnight with no application logs. The admin suspects the kernel OOM killer. Which command confirms it?
explain: The OOM killer logs 'Out of memory: Killed process <pid> (<name>)' to the kernel ring buffer, which dmesg (or journalctl -k) reveals. last tracks logins and reboots, no oom process exists to find with ps, and uptime -s only shows when the system booted.

q: Available memory shrinks steadily over days until the OOM killer strikes, recovering only after a service restart. Which approach identifies the leaking process?
options: Record ps aux --sort=-%mem output periodically and watch which process's RSS grows over time
explain: A memory leak appears as one process's RSS growing steadily across samples over time — only repeated measurements reveal the trend. A single snapshot cannot show growth, df measures disk space rather than memory, and ping tests network reachability.

q: After replacing a failed disk, lvdisplay shows the logical volumes as NOT available although the volume group exists. Which command activates them?
explain: vgchange -ay activates all logical volumes in the volume group. vgcreate would attempt to build a new group, pvscan only discovers physical volumes without activating anything, and lvremove destroys the volumes — the opposite of recovery.

q: A VM was cloned at the hypervisor level. The clone misbehaves: LVM reports duplicate PV and VG UUIDs and the wrong disks activate. Which tool regenerates the duplicate UUIDs on the clone?
explain: vgimportclone changes colliding PV and VG UUIDs so each copy of the cloned storage is uniquely identifiable. vgrename only changes the VG name without fixing UUID collisions, pvcreate would wipe the metadata, and re-cloning reproduces the same duplicates.

q: Users report a web app shows an error page. The admin needs just the HTTP status code and response headers, quickly, from the command line. Which command does this?
explain: curl -I fetches headers only, immediately revealing the HTTP status code and server headers. ping tests ICMP reachability, ssh opens a shell rather than speaking HTTP, and dig resolves DNS — none of them show HTTP responses.

q: After adding a LoadModule line to httpd.conf and restarting, a feature still does not work. The admin suspects the module never actually loaded. Which command lists the modules Apache really loaded?
explain: httpd -M dumps the modules actually loaded into the running Apache configuration, revealing typos in LoadModule lines or missing module files. httpd -v prints only the version, httpd -t tests configuration syntax without listing modules, and is-enabled reports boot persistence rather than loaded modules.

q: A local app fails with 'Can't connect to local MySQL server through socket '/var/lib/mysql/mysql.sock'' while MariaDB is running. What should the admin check first?
options: Whether the server's actual socket path (my.cnf, or mysqladmin variables) matches what the client expects
explain: The error names a specific socket path, and the classic cause is a client/server socket mismatch (for example /var/lib/mysql versus /run/mysqld). Local socket connections never traverse the firewall or use DNS, and disk space does not produce socket-path errors.

q: DNS seems broken on a host. The admin wants to see whether DNS queries actually leave the host and whether replies come back. Which command captures this live?
explain: tcpdump on port 53 shows live DNS query and response packets, proving whether traffic leaves and answers return. netstat -rn shows the static routing table, resolv.conf shows configuration rather than traffic, and ping tests ICMP — not DNS.

q: Large transfers stall while small packets flow — a suspected MTU/fragmentation issue on the path. Which ping invocation tests whether 1500-byte frames pass unfragmented?
explain: ping -M do sets the Don't Fragment bit and -s 1472 plus 28 bytes of headers totals 1500; a 'Frag needed' reply reveals the path MTU. Default pings are too small to expose the issue, -f is a flood test, and traceroute shows hops rather than MTU blackholes.

q: A host has multiple interfaces and routes. The admin must determine exactly which source IP and interface the kernel would use to reach 10.5.0.8. Which command answers this?
explain: ip route get performs the actual routing lookup for the destination, reporting the chosen interface, gateway, and source IP. Listing the route table or addresses does not resolve which entry wins, and arp shows the layer-2 neighbor cache rather than routing decisions.

q: After a kernel update, Wi-Fi broke. dmesg shows 'firmware: failed to load iwlwifi-ty-a0-gf-a0-59.ucode'. What is the fix?
options: Install or update the linux-firmware package that provides the .ucode files
explain: The driver needs its firmware blob, which ships in the linux-firmware package — the error message names the missing file. Reinstalling the kernel changes nothing about firmware files, unloading the module does not supply them, and Secure Boot is unrelated to missing firmware.

q: modprobe -r nouveau fails with 'Module nouveau is in use'. Which command shows WHAT is using it so the admin can stop the dependent first?
explain: lsmod's 'Used by' column names the modules or processes holding a reference, identifying what to stop first. modinfo shows module metadata rather than users, forced removal with rmmod -f risks a kernel crash, and dmesg does not track module reference counts.

q: dnf fails with 'repomd.xml signature could not be verified' on a repository that worked yesterday. No repo files were changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The GPG key in /etc/pki/rpm-gpg was deleted
The system clock is wrong, so the signature's validity window fails — check date and NTP sync
The repo URL now requires a proxy
The dnf metadata cache was never cleaned
explain: GPG signatures have validity periods, so a clock that jumped (dead CMOS battery, VM snapshot restore) breaks verification of an unchanged repository. Deleted keys would break every repo rather than one previously working repo, proxy problems produce connection errors rather than signature errors, and a stale cache yields checksum mismatches.

q: Every sudo invocation prints 'sudo: unable to resolve host web01: Name or service not known' but then works. What fixes the warning?
options: Add web01 to the DNS zone
Add an entry for web01 to /etc/hosts
explain: sudo resolves the hostname for logging, and the warning appears when the hostname (often set via hostnamectl) has no /etc/hosts entry — adding one silences it. Reinstalling changes nothing since sudo works, DNS is overkill for the local hostname, and disabling logging merely masks the misconfiguration.

q: A server kernel-panicked overnight and rebooted. The admin needs the memory dump for root-cause analysis. Which service and location provide it?
explain: kdump boots a capture kernel on panic and saves a full vmcore to /var/crash for analysis with the crash utility. systemd-coredump handles user-space process dumps, auditd keeps audit events, and the journal may hold the panic message — but none of them capture the kernel memory image.

q: An Ansible run fails with UNREACHABLE for all hosts after a bastion change. Playbooks and inventory are unchanged. What is the FIRST thing to verify?
options: Basic SSH connectivity to a host (ansible all -m ping) through the new bastion path
Reinstall Ansible on the control node
explain: UNREACHABLE means the transport failed, so the first step is verifying SSH itself — keys, ProxyJump/bastion config, and host keys — before blaming Ansible. Reinstalling the tool, rewriting unchanged playbooks, or clearing the temp directory cannot fix a changed network path.

q: NFS mounts hang indefinitely, and showmount -e nfs01 also hangs. The server was recently minimized and several services were disabled. Which service should the admin check first?
explain: showmount queries rpcbind on port 111 to locate mountd, so with rpcbind down both showmount and NFSv3 mounts hang. httpd and cups are unrelated to NFS, and chronyd matters for Kerberos-secured NFSv4 rather than basic mount hangs.

q: A security baseline requires Secure Boot to be enabled on every Linux server. Which command verifies the Secure Boot state from within the running OS?
explain: mokutil --sb-state queries the UEFI firmware and reports whether Secure Boot is enabled. grub2-mkconfig has no secure-boot query flag, /proc/sys/secure_boot does not exist, and efibootmgr manages boot entries and boot order, not the Secure Boot state.

q: An admin must apply UEFI firmware and NVMe firmware updates across a fleet of RHEL 9 servers without booting vendor ISOs. Which tool handles this natively?
explain: fwupdmgr is the Linux Vendor Firmware Service (LVFS) client: refresh downloads metadata and update applies firmware capsules for supported devices. dnf manages packages, not firmware capsules; flashrom is a low-level SPI flasher, not a fleet tool; and grub2-mkconfig only rebuilds the bootloader menu.

q: After installing a 10 GbE NIC, the admin must confirm which kernel driver actually bound to the PCI device. Which command shows the device together with its in-use kernel driver?
explain: lspci -k adds 'Kernel driver in use' and 'Kernel modules' lines to each PCI device listing, directly answering which driver bound. Plain lspci omits driver info, lsmod lists loaded modules without mapping them to PCI devices, and dmesg has no --show-drivers flag.

q: Before deploying KVM on a bare-metal host, the admin must verify the CPU exposes hardware virtualization extensions. Which check does this correctly?
explain: /proc/cpuinfo flags reveal CPU features: vmx means Intel VT-x and svm means AMD-V. lscpu does not print a virtualization line like that, /sys/module/kvm/version does not exist, and virsh nodeinfo cannot prove CPU extensions and requires libvirtd running.

q: vgdata has 30 GB of free extents. The admin must grow /dev/vgdata/lvapp to consume ALL remaining free space, including its ext4 filesystem, in one step. Which command does this?
explain: -l takes extents, so -l +100%FREE adds all free extents; -r grows the filesystem too. -L takes sizes, not extent percentages, so -L +100%FREE is invalid. Without the plus, -l 100%FREE would set the LV to that size (shrinking it). --use-all-space is not a real lvresize flag.

q: A cloud volume backing PV /dev/sdb was expanded from 50G to 100G at the hypervisor, but pvdisplay still shows 50G. Which command makes LVM recognize the new capacity before the LV is extended?
explain: pvresize rescans the device and grows the PV metadata to use the new space. pvcreate would destroy the existing metadata, vgextend adds new PVs rather than resizing one, and partprobe only re-reads partition tables, which does not update LVM's view of the device size.

q: After cloning a disk with dd, the original and the clone hold XFS filesystems with identical UUIDs, and the system mounts the wrong one. Which command assigns a fresh UUID to the clone's filesystem on /dev/sdc1?
explain: xfs_admin -U changes the filesystem UUID; 'generate' creates a new random one. -L sets the filesystem label, not the UUID. tune2fs only works on ext2/3/4, and xfs_growfs grows filesystems and has no -U option.

q: To keep /etc/fstab readable, the admin wants the ext4 filesystem on /dev/sdc2 to carry the label 'dbdata'. Which command applies that label to the existing filesystem?
explain: e2label is the dedicated tool for setting ext2/3/4 filesystem labels. xfs_admin is XFS-only, tune2fs -m sets the reserved-blocks percentage rather than a label, and dosfslabel is for FAT filesystems.

q: Before a maintenance window, the admin must confirm an ext4 filesystem's block size and total inode count without mounting it. Which read-only command reports superblock details?
explain: dumpe2fs -h prints the superblock (block size, inode count, mount counts) read-only. tune2fs -c sets the max mount count rather than reporting, debugfs -w opens the filesystem read-write which risks damage, and e2label only shows the label.

q: Before repartitioning /dev/sdb, the admin wants a restorable backup of its partition table. Which command saves it?
explain: sfdisk -d dumps the partition table in a format that sfdisk can later restore from. fdisk has no --dump flag, dd of sdb1 copies the first partition's data rather than the table layout, and parted has no mkbackup subcommand.

q: The admin must clone /dev/sda to an identical disk /dev/sdb, with progress shown. Which command does this correctly?
explain: if= is the input (source) and of= is the output (destination); reversing them would wipe the source disk. Cloning sda1 copies only one partition rather than the whole disk, and cp is not the block-level cloning tool and shows no progress this way.

q: /dev/md0 (RAID1) shows /dev/sdb1 as faulty, and replacement disk /dev/sdc1 is ready. Which sequence replaces the failed member without data loss?
explain: A member must be marked failed before it can be removed, then the new disk is added as a spare that rebuilds automatically. Reversing fail and remove is rejected, --create would build a fresh array and destroy data, and stop/assemble does not integrate the new disk as a rebuilding member.

q: During a RAID rebuild, the admin wants a live view of the resync progress. Which source shows it?
explain: /proc/mdstat shows the live recovery/resync bar with percentage and speed. mdadm --detail --scan prints array definitions for mdadm.conf rather than progress, /proc/partitions only lists partition sizes, and lsblk has no --resync flag.

q: A video archive on 8 TB disks must survive ANY two simultaneous disk failures while keeping usable capacity. Which RAID level fits?
explain: RAID 6 uses double distributed parity, so any two disks can fail without data loss. RAID 5 survives only one failure, RAID 1 mirrors pairs so losing both members of one mirror kills the array, and RAID 0 has no redundancy at all.

q: The monitoring system needs its own IP on the app server. Interface eth0 already gets 192.168.10.5/24 from its NetworkManager profile, and 192.168.10.6/24 must be attached as an additional address that survives reboots. Which nmcli sequence accomplishes this?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.6/24 && nmcli con up eth0
nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.6/24 && nmcli con up eth0
explain: The + prefix appends to the address list; without it, ipv4.addresses REPLACES the existing address (the trap). ip addr add is runtime-only and lost on reboot, and modifying the profile without 'con up' never applies the change to the live connection.

q: The storage network needs 9000-byte jumbo frames on eth1, surviving reboots on a NetworkManager-managed host. Which approach is correct?
options: nmcli con mod eth1 802-3-ethernet.mtu 9000 && nmcli con up eth1
explain: Setting the MTU through the NetworkManager connection profile persists across reboots. ip link, ifconfig, and the sysfs write all change only the running state and are lost at reboot, and ifconfig is deprecated on modern systems.

q: An NFS client hangs for minutes at boot when the NFS server is unreachable. Which fstab mount options let the boot continue and retry the mount in the background?
explain: bg retries the mount in the background so boot proceeds, while soft returns an error after timeo instead of hanging forever. hard retries indefinitely (the hang), _netdev only orders the mount after networking without changing retry behavior, and noauto means the share never mounts.

q: On Ubuntu, the timezone was set incorrectly during installation. Which command re-runs the package's configuration dialogs to fix it?
explain: dpkg-reconfigure re-runs a package's debconf configuration dialogs, including tzdata's timezone selection. apt reconfigure is not a real command, dpkg --configure only finishes interrupted configurations without prompting, and timedatectl has no --reconfigure flag.

q: Two Java versions are installed and /usr/bin/java must point to java-17 system-wide. Which tool manages this switch safely?
explain: update-alternatives manages the symlink farm (including slave links like javac) consistently. A manual ln -sf bypasses slave links and package tracking, --set-default is not the correct flag, and JAVA_HOME does not change what /usr/bin/java resolves to.

q: A backup script must write 'backup complete' to the system log with the tag 'nightly-backup'. Which command does this?
explain: logger sends messages to syslog with a chosen tag (-t), which is the supported scripting interface. Writing directly to /var/log/messages bypasses syslog formatting and usually fails on permissions, syslog is not a command, and journalctl reads logs rather than writing them.

q: Before installing httpd, the admin wants to see exactly which files the package would install, without installing it. Which command lists them?
explain: dnf repoquery -l queries repository metadata, so it lists package contents without installation. rpm -ql only works for already-installed packages, dnf list has no --files flag, and repoquery has no --install flag.

q: Before setting module options for the e1000e driver, the admin wants to see its tunable parameters. Which command lists them?
explain: modinfo -p displays a module's parameters and their descriptions. modprobe has no --show-params flag, lsmod takes no -p flag, and /proc/modules/e1000e does not exist (module info lives in /sys/module, not per-module proc files).

q: On an NVMe-backed database host, the admin must set the I/O scheduler to 'none' persistently via a udev rule. Which sysfs path does the rule target?
explain: The I/O scheduler for a block device is exposed at /sys/block/<device>/queue/scheduler, which udev rules can write at device-add time. The /proc/sys path does not exist, /sys/devices paths are bus-specific rather than the scheduler attribute, and sysctl cannot control I/O schedulers.

q: An admin ran 'usermod -G docker maria' to add her to the docker group. Now Maria can no longer reach dev resources she used daily. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: Without -a, -G REPLACED her supplementary groups; re-add the lost ones with usermod -aG dev,ops,docker maria
The docker group conflicts with the dev group; remove her from docker
Group changes require a reboot before they take effect
usermod -G requires -m; rerun the command with -m
explain: usermod -G without -a replaces the entire supplementary group list, silently dropping dev and ops; -aG appends instead. The groups do not conflict, no reboot is needed (only a new login session), and -m concerns home directories, not groups.

q: After 'passwd -l temp1', the terminated contractor still logs in via SSH. Why, and what is the complete fix?
options: passwd -l takes 24 hours to take effect; wait and retest
passwd -l only locks password authentication; the contractor's SSH key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys still works, so remove the key and expire the account
The account must be deleted with userdel instead of locked
sshd caches credentials; restart sshd to apply the lock
explain: passwd -l prefixes the password hash with '!', blocking password logins only; SSH public-key authentication bypasses the password entirely. There is no 24-hour delay, deletion is not required to stop access, and sshd does not cache credentials across the lock.

q: A contractor was granted sudo access but no root password. They need an interactive shell running as root with root's login environment for a maintenance task. Which command gives them this?
explain: sudo -i simulates a root login: it sets HOME, PATH, and working directory as if root logged in. sudo -s and sudo -u root bash give non-login shells that keep much of the caller's environment, and sudo su is a redundant wrapper around the same idea.

q: On a fresh RHEL 9 server, user ops is in the wheel group, but sudo still reports 'ops is not in the sudoers file'. What is the most likely cause?
options: Wheel membership requires a reboot before sudo works
ops must be added to the 'sudo' group instead
The '%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL' line is commented out in /etc/sudoers
explain: RHEL-family systems ship the wheel sudo rule commented out, so group membership alone grants nothing until it is enabled. No reboot is needed, wheel sudo is still fully supported, and the 'sudo' group is the Debian/Ubuntu convention, not RHEL's.

q: A script runs perfectly when the admin executes it, but fails from cron with 'command not found' errors. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cron runs with a minimal default PATH; the script depends on directories only in the admin's interactive PATH
Cron can execute binaries but not shell scripts
Scripts run from cron require the setuid bit
Cron jobs are forbidden from writing to /tmp
explain: Cron jobs run with a sparse environment (typically PATH=/usr/bin:/bin), so commands found via the admin's richer interactive PATH fail. Cron runs scripts fine, setuid on scripts is ignored by the kernel, and cron jobs may write to /tmp normally.

q: A backup job sometimes runs longer than its hourly schedule, and overlapping runs corrupt the backup. Which wrapper prevents a second instance from starting?
explain: flock -n takes an exclusive lock without blocking, so a second instance exits instead of overlapping. nice and ionice only adjust scheduling priority, and timeout kills a run after a duration but does nothing to prevent a concurrent second run.

q: A cache-warming script must run 15 minutes after every boot via a systemd timer. Which timer setting expresses this?
explain: OnBootSec schedules relative to system boot, which matches '15 minutes after every boot'. OnCalendar is wall-clock time, OnStartupSec is not a valid timer directive, and OnUnitActiveSec measures from when the timer unit itself last ran.

q: An application logs to the local0 syslog facility. Its messages must go to /var/log/myapp.log instead of the default syslog file. Which rsyslog rule does this?
explain: rsyslog selectors use facility.priority syntax, so local0.* matches all priorities of local0. Reversing them is invalid syntax, omitting the priority is invalid, and facility=... > is not rsyslog configuration syntax.

q: During an audit, the admin must list all members of the 'docker' group authoritatively. Which command does this?
explain: getent consults the full name-service switch, so it includes members from LDAP/SSSD as well as local files. groups shows the current user's groups, id docker describes a user named docker, and grepping /etc/group misses directory-service members entirely.

q: Before rebooting a shared server, the admin must see who is logged in and what each user is currently running. Which command shows this?
explain: w shows logged-in users, their idle times, and their current processes. whoami shows only yourself, last shows historical login records, and users lists only login names without activity details.

q: Direct SSH to db01 is blocked at the firewall; only bastion.example.com is reachable, and the bastion itself can reach db01. Which command starts an interactive SSH session on db01 through the bastion in one step?
explain: ssh -J (ProxyJump) tunnels the connection through the bastion host. -L sets up a local port forward rather than a session, -p specifies a port number not a hop, and --via is not a real ssh flag.

q: Backups must sync to the offsite host backup.example.com, but its sshd was moved to port 2022. Which rsync invocation connects over SSH on that port?
explain: rsync's -e option sets the remote shell command, so 'ssh -p 2022' directs the SSH connection to the right port. rsync has no -P or --port flag for the SSH port, and appending :2022 to the destination corrupts the remote path.

q: After removing an application with 'dnf remove', dozens of now-unused dependency packages remain. Which command removes orphaned dependencies safely?
explain: dnf autoremove removes packages that were installed as dependencies and are no longer required. dnf clean all only clears caches, --dependencies is not a dnf remove flag, and erasing every package with --nodeps would destroy the system.

q: A container exited overnight and 'podman ps' shows nothing. Which command lists it so the admin can inspect what happened?
explain: podman ps -a includes stopped containers, allowing inspection of the exited one. --exited is not a real flag, podman list is not a command, and podman images lists images rather than containers.

q: The host is sluggish and the admin suspects one container is consuming all CPU. Which command shows live per-container CPU and memory usage?
explain: podman stats streams live CPU, memory, and I/O usage per container. podman top shows processes inside one container, inspect has no --stats flag, and podman ps has no --usage flag.

q: A running container named web holds a generated config at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf that the admin must copy to the host for review. Which command does this?
explain: podman cp copies files between a container and the host filesystem directly. podman export dumps the entire filesystem as a tarball, the mount approach is convoluted, and scp cannot address a container name as an SSH host.

q: Two containers must resolve each other by name on an isolated network. Which sequence creates this?
options: podman network create appnet, then run both containers with --network appnet
podman network create appnet, then add entries to the host /etc/hosts
explain: Containers attached to the same user-defined network get automatic DNS resolution of each other's names. Host /etc/hosts edits do not propagate into containers, --network host removes isolation entirely, and --link is a legacy Docker concept.

q: Every user on the system needs APP_HOME=/opt/app in their environment at login. Which is the correct system-wide approach?
explain: Scripts in /etc/profile.d/*.sh are sourced for all login shells, making it the standard system-wide location. /root/.bashrc affects only root, /etc/hosts maps hostnames rather than setting variables, and hand-editing every home directory is unmaintainable.

q: Compliance requires /var/log/audit.log to accept new log entries but never allow modification or deletion of existing content. Which attribute enforces this?
explain: The append-only attribute (+a) permits adding data while blocking modification, truncation, or deletion. +i (immutable) would also block appends and break logging, chmod 444 does not stop root, and +A only disables atime updates.

q: A running nightly report (PID 4321) is starving the web application of CPU. The admin must lower its priority without restarting it. Which command does this?
explain: renice changes the nice value of an already-running process; +10 makes it nicer (lower priority). nice only applies at launch, -10 would raise its priority (the opposite), and ionice adjusts I/O scheduling class rather than CPU priority.

q: Internal hosts on 10.0.0.0/24 must reach the internet through the firewall's public IP, with replies routed back. Which firewalld configuration provides this outbound NAT?
explain: --add-masquerade enables MASQUERADE (dynamic source NAT) on the zone for outbound traffic. --add-forward-port is destination NAT for inbound publishing, there is no 'masquerade' service, and masquerade is not a valid rich-rule element written that way.

q: Using native nftables, the admin must allow return traffic for established connections on the input chain. Which rule does this?
options: nft add rule inet filter input state --established accept
nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept
explain: nftables matches connection tracking state with 'ct state established,related'. The first option mixes iptables syntax into nft, the third is an iptables command rather than the requested native nftables rule, and 'nft open-port' is not real syntax.

q: An admin added iptables rules that work, but they vanish on reboot. Which sequence makes them persistent on a system without firewalld?
options: iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4, with the rules restored at boot
explain: iptables-save dumps the ruleset to a file that the distribution's boot process restores (e.g., via iptables-restore). --permanent is firewalld syntax that iptables does not understand, systemctl enable iptables-restore is not a standard unit, and -j SAVE is not a real target.

q: The admin suspects a process is running in the wrong SELinux domain. Which command shows processes with their SELinux contexts?
explain: ps -Z adds the SELinux security context column to process listings. ps -x is BSD-style 'all processes' without contexts, ls -l /proc does not show contexts, and semanage has no 'process -l' subcommand.

q: The audit log shows AVC denials for a custom application. The admin wants a human-readable explanation of each denial plus a suggested fix. Which command provides this?
explain: sealert parses AVC denials and explains them in plain language with recommended actions. audit2allow generates policy modules rather than explanations, and neither semanage nor ausearch has an --explain mode for denials.

q: After tuning an AppArmor profile in complain mode using real log data, the admin must return it to enforcement. Which command does this?
explain: aa-enforce switches the named profile back to enforce mode. aa-complain moves it the other direction, --disable unloads the profile entirely, and systemctl has no --enforce flag.

q: Before adding new audit rules, the admin wants to see which watches are currently loaded. Which command lists the active rules?
explain: auditctl -l lists the currently loaded audit rules. auditctl -s shows daemon status rather than rules, aureport has no --rules option, and /proc/audit/rules does not exist.

q: After editing sshd_config, the admin wants to validate the syntax in test mode BEFORE restarting sshd. Which command checks it without affecting the running daemon?
explain: sshd -t runs in test mode: it validates the configuration and exits silently on success. sshd -T dumps the effective configuration rather than just testing, systemctl check is not a real subcommand, and ssh -t forces pseudo-terminal allocation on a client connection.

q: To prevent users from tunneling arbitrary traffic through the SSH server, which sshd_config setting disables TCP forwarding?
explain: AllowTcpForwarding controls -L, -R, and -D forwarding. PermitTunnel governs layer-3 point-to-point tunneling (a different feature), X11Forwarding only affects X11, and AllowUsers no would deny every user rather than just disabling forwarding.

q: An admin lost the .pub file for a passphrase-protected private key but must share the public key with a new server. Which command regenerates the public key from the private key?
explain: ssh-keygen -y reads the private key and prints the corresponding public key. -p changes the passphrase, -c only changes the key comment, and openssl rsa -pubout handles RSA keys, not ed25519.

q: Company policy requires rotating the passphrase on an existing SSH private key without generating a new key pair. Which command does this?
explain: ssh-keygen -p changes the passphrase protecting the private key in place, keeping the key pair itself. -y prints the public key, passwd only manages login passwords, and ssh-add has no -p flag.

q: A teammate needs the admin's GPG public key to verify signed releases. Which command exports it in ASCII-armored form?
explain: gpg --armor --export outputs the public key in ASCII-armored text suitable for sharing. --export-secret-keys would leak the private key (the dangerous trap), --decrypt operates on encrypted data, and --import reads keys in rather than exporting them.

q: After deploying a TLS private key with mode 644, the security scan flags it. What is the correct remediation?
options: chmod 600 on the private key so only root can read it
Keep 644; the scanner is a false positive
Move the key to /tmp for safety
Encrypt the key with a second certificate
explain: A world-readable private key lets any local user impersonate the service, so it must be restricted to 600 (root-only). Dismissing the finding leaves the exposure, /tmp is world-accessible and worse, and layering another certificate does not fix the permissions problem.

q: Policy forbids reusing any of the last 5 passwords. Which PAM configuration enforces password history?
explain: pam_pwhistory with remember=5 stores old hashes and rejects reuse, and it belongs in the password stack. pam_unix does not implement history, the auth stack handles authentication rather than password changes, and pam_tally2 handles failed-login lockout.

q: Only members of the wheel group may use 'su' to become root. Which PAM configuration enforces this?
options: Add a '# wheel only' comment to /etc/pam.d/su
explain: pam_wheel in the auth stack of /etc/pam.d/su denies su to anyone outside wheel; use_uid checks the invoking user. pam_unix has no wheel_only option, the account stack is the wrong phase for this control, and a comment changes nothing.

q: A junior admin must edit /etc/hosts with elevated privileges. Which is the safest method?
explain: sudoedit copies the file to a temp location edited as the unprivileged user, then installs it as root, so no root-owned editor process ever runs. sudo vim runs a full editor as root where shell escapes yield a root shell, su -c has the same flaw, and the chmod dance briefly exposes the file to everyone.

q: After granting a binary a capability with setcap, which command verifies the capability is actually set on the file?
explain: getcap reads and displays file capabilities. ls -l does not show capabilities, capsh has no --show-file flag, and getfacl shows POSIX ACLs, which are a separate mechanism.

q: Hardening requires address space layout randomization (ASLR) fully enabled. Which sysctl setting enforces this persistently?
explain: kernel.randomize_va_space=2 enables full ASLR; writing it under /etc/sysctl.d/ makes it persistent. The other three are not real sysctl tunables on modern kernels (exec-shield was a legacy RHEL patch).

q: An admin needs the exact parameters of the ansible.builtin.copy module without opening a browser. Which command shows its documentation?
explain: ansible-doc renders module documentation from the installed collections. ansible --help shows CLI options rather than module docs, there is no ansible-copy man page, and ansible-galaxy manages roles and collections rather than displaying docs.

q: A playbook only restarts services and never uses host facts, but fact-gathering adds 30 seconds per host. How should the play be optimized?
options: Set facts: no under [defaults] in ansible.cfg
Delete the setup module file from the Python packages
Set gather_facts: false at the play level
explain: gather_facts: false disables the implicit setup task for that play. facts: no is not a valid ansible.cfg setting, --skip-facts is not a real flag, and deleting the setup module would break Ansible itself.

q: During a --check run, the admin wants to see the exact line-level changes a template task WOULD make. Which flag adds this detail?
explain: --diff shows unified diffs of file changes alongside --check's dry run, so the admin can review exactly what would change before approving the run. --verbose-diff, --dry-run, and --list-changes are not real ansible-playbook flags.

q: A playbook must capture the output of 'systemctl is-active nginx' and display it for the operator. Which task pattern does this?
options: Use the command module with output: display
Register the command result with register, then display it with the debug module
Set display_output: true on the task
explain: register stores the module result in a variable, and the debug module prints it; this is the standard capture-and-show pattern. The command module has no output: display parameter, /dev/console redirection bypasses Ansible's output handling, and display_output is not a real task keyword.

q: The team must change the password protecting all Ansible Vault-encrypted files after a staff departure. Which command rotates the vault password?
options: Decrypt and re-encrypt every file by hand
explain: ansible-vault rekey re-encrypts files with a new password in one operation. passwd and change-key are not ansible-vault subcommands, and manual decrypt/re-encrypt is error-prone and unnecessary.

q: An inventory needs a 'datacenter' group containing the existing 'web' and 'db' groups. Which inventory syntax expresses this?
explain: The :children suffix defines nested groups, so web and db become members of datacenter. :parents is not valid, a plain header would make web and db hosts rather than groups, and :vars defines group variables.

q: A variable ntp_server must apply to EVERY host in the inventory, without editing individual files. Where should it be defined?
explain: group_vars/all applies to the implicit 'all' group, covering every host. host_vars/all.yml is not a standard location, 'default' is not a special group name, and inventory/all.yml is not read as a variables file.

q: A playbook connects via ansible_host=10.0.0.5 (a NAT address) but must write the host's real inventory name into a config file. Which variable holds the inventory name?
explain: inventory_hostname is the name exactly as written in the inventory, independent of connection details. ansible_host is the connection address (the NAT IP here), and ansible_inventory and host_name are not real magic variables.

q: A database migration task in a playbook targeting 10 app servers must execute exactly once, not once per host. Which task keyword ensures this?
explain: run_once: true runs the task on a single host only. once: true is not a real keyword, delegate_to: all is invalid, and serial is a play-level keyword, not a task keyword.

q: Before 'tofu plan', the team wants a fast syntax and consistency check of the .tf files without contacting any cloud API. Which command does this?
explain: tofu validate checks configuration syntax and internal consistency without API access. check-syntax and -dry-run are not real, and fmt -check only verifies formatting, not validity.

q: A database created manually in the cloud console must now be managed by the existing OpenTofu configuration without recreating it. Which command brings it under management?
options: Paste the resource into terraform.tfstate by hand
explain: tofu import binds an existing real-world resource to a configuration address. adopt and --import are not real, and hand-editing the state file risks corruption and is not supported.

q: A VM is corrupted but its configuration is unchanged, so 'tofu plan' proposes nothing. Which command forces OpenTofu to recreate that one resource?
explain: -replace marks the resource for recreation on the next apply. -force is not a real flag, recreate is not a subcommand, and taint was removed from OpenTofu in favor of -replace, so it no longer works.

q: A VM booted but none of the cloud-init user-data (users, packages) was applied. Where should the admin look FIRST to diagnose why?
explain: cloud-init writes its detailed run log to /var/log/cloud-init.log and command output to /var/log/cloud-init-output.log. There is no /var/log/user-data.log, no user-data systemd unit, and no debug log at that /etc path.

q: A deployment script fails at an unknown line. The admin wants each command printed to stderr as it executes, to trace the failure. Which option enables this?
explain: set -x traces execution by printing each command (after expansion) before running it. set -v prints lines as read before expansion, set -t exits after one command, and set -e exits on error without tracing.

q: In a script, 'mysqldump mydb | gzip > backup.sql.gz' succeeds even when mysqldump fails, producing an empty backup. Which option makes the pipeline report mysqldump's failure?
explain: set -o pipefail makes a pipeline return the rightmost nonzero exit status, so mysqldump's failure is caught. set -e alone does not catch mid-pipeline failures (the classic trap), set -u errors on unset variables, and noclobber only prevents overwriting files with >.

q: Inside a bash function, the author used 'exit 1' on error, which kills the entire deployment script instead of just the function. Which statement returns control to the caller with a failure status?
options: Keep exit 1; it is already correct
explain: return exits only the function, passing the status to the caller. break and continue control loops rather than functions, and exit terminates the whole shell, which is exactly the bug being fixed.

q: Before committing, a developer wants to review exactly what is staged versus the last commit. Which command shows this?
explain: git diff --staged (synonym --cached) diffs the index against HEAD, showing what the commit would contain. Plain git diff shows unstaged working-tree changes, git status has no --show-diff flag, and git log -p shows the previous commit's diff rather than the staged changes.

q: After a kernel update, boot panics with 'VFS: Unable to mount root fs on unknown-block'. The previous kernel boots fine. What is the most likely cause?
options: The root password expired during the update
/etc/fstab has the wrong filesystem type for /boot
The new initramfs lacks the storage controller driver for the root disk
explain: The new kernel cannot see the root disk because its driver is missing from the new initramfs; rebuilding it (dracut) or booting the old kernel confirms this. Password expiry, GRUB timeout, and the /boot fstab entry cannot produce a VFS root-mount panic.

q: 'ip link show eth0' reports state DOWN with NO-CARRIER, though the interface is administratively up. What does this indicate?
options: No physical link is detected; check the cable, switch port, and NIC
The DHCP server is not responding
Another host is using the same IP address
The routing table has no default route
explain: NO-CARRIER is a layer-1 signal: the NIC detects no physical link. DHCP, duplicate IPs, and missing routes are higher-layer issues that would still show a carrier; with no carrier, start at the cable and switch port.

q: Users can reach 'db01.corp.example.com' but 'db01' alone fails to resolve. IP connectivity is fine. What is the most likely cause?
options: The search domain is missing from the resolver configuration
nsswitch.conf is missing the dns entry
explain: Short names are expanded using the search/domain list, so a missing search domain breaks 'db01' while the FQDN still resolves, proving DNS itself works. A down server or missing nsswitch dns entry would break the FQDN too, and /etc/hosts is not consulted for this lookup path.

q: A host pings everything on its local subnet but cannot reach anything beyond it. 'ip route show' lists only the link-scoped route. What is missing?
options: An ARP entry for the gateway
explain: Without a default route the kernel has no path for off-subnet destinations, while on-link traffic works via the connected route. DNS does not affect pings by IP, the mask is implicit in the link route, and ARP entries populate automatically once a gateway route exists.

q: traceroute to a remote host shows valid hops 1-3, then '* * *' for every remaining hop, yet the application works. What does this most likely mean?
options: A firewall beyond hop 3 filters the probe packets while passing real traffic
explain: Stars mean the probes got no reply, which firewalls commonly cause by dropping ICMP/UDP traceroute packets while forwarding TCP application traffic normally. The working application proves the path and remote host are up, and the local gateway answered hops 1-3.

q: The admin must quickly test whether TCP port 5432 is reachable on db01 from this host. Which command performs a fast port check without sending application data?
explain: nc -zv attempts the TCP connection and reports success or failure verbosely without exchanging data. ping does not accept ports, telnet has no --port-test flag, and curl has no --ping flag.

q: To determine whether a wrong DNS answer comes from the local resolver or upstream, the admin queries 8.8.8.8 directly for the same name. Which command does this?
explain: dig @server directs the query to that specific resolver, isolating upstream behavior from the local resolver. --server is not dig syntax, nslookup has no -s flag, and host has no --resolver flag.

q: Mounting an NFS share fails with 'Protocol not supported'. The server is old and only speaks NFSv3. Which mount option is the likely fix?
explain: Modern clients default to NFSv4.x, so forcing -o vers=3 matches the old server. vers=4.2 is the failing default, proto=udpv3 is not a real option, and nfsvers=auto is not valid mount syntax.

q: On a UEFI-booted RHEL 9 server, the admin ran 'grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg', but boot menu changes never appear. What went wrong?
options: grub2-mkconfig requires a --uefi flag on UEFI systems
The changes need systemctl daemon-reload first
UEFI systems do not use grub.cfg at all
On UEFI systems GRUB reads /boot/efi/EFI/redhat/grub.cfg; the BIOS-path file is ignored
explain: UEFI-booted RHEL reads its GRUB config from the EFI system partition path, so regenerating the BIOS path (/boot/grub2/grub.cfg) has no effect. There is no --uefi flag, daemon-reload only affects systemd units, and UEFI RHEL does use grub.cfg, just at the EFI path.

q: After fixing /etc/fstab from the emergency shell, the admin wants to continue booting normally without rebooting. Which command resumes the normal boot?
explain: systemctl default starts the default target, continuing the boot from the emergency shell. Rebooting is unnecessary once fstab is fixed, init 3 would only reach multi-user rather than the default target, and exit may simply drop back to the emergency shell.

q: Before repairing a suspect unmounted XFS filesystem, the admin wants a non-destructive scan showing what WOULD be fixed. Which command does this?
explain: xfs_repair -n runs in no-modify mode, reporting problems without changing anything. --dry-run is not an xfs_repair flag, xfs_check is deprecated and removed, and -f is not the check-only flag.

q: Users reported slowness between 2:00 PM and 2:30 PM yesterday. Which journalctl invocation shows only that window's messages?
explain: journalctl accepts --since and --until with natural time expressions to bound the output window. --from/--to, bare time ranges on -b, and --window are not real journalctl options.

q: SSH authentication fails with no clear error. The admin wants verbose client-side debugging of the handshake and authentication methods attempted. Which flag provides this?
explain: ssh -v enables verbose mode showing key exchange, offered keys, and auth attempts (up to -vvv for more detail). --debug is not an ssh flag, -d is not debug, and -t forces pseudo-terminal allocation.

q: A server crashes randomly with no pattern in the logs, and the admin suspects faulty RAM. Which is the appropriate next diagnostic?
options: Run fsck on the RAM disk
Boot memtest86+ from the GRUB menu and run a full memory test
explain: memtest86+ exercises RAM outside the OS and catches faulty modules that cause random crashes. fsck checks filesystems rather than memory, more swap does not test RAM, and reinstalling the kernel will not fix bad hardware.

q: SMART data is inconclusive but the admin suspects failing sectors on /dev/sdb. Which command performs a read-only scan for bad blocks?
explain: badblocks -sv performs a read-only scan with progress output. -w is the destructive write test that would destroy data (the trap), fsck -b selects an alternate superblock rather than scanning, and dd has no --scan flag.

q: A container keeps exiting with code 137 and no application errors. Which check confirms the kernel OOM killer is responsible?
explain: The OOMKilled field in the container state records whether the kernel OOM killer terminated it; exit code 137 (128+9, SIGKILL) is the hint. Application logs will not show a kernel kill, --oom is not a stats flag, and dmesg names processes rather than container names.

q: The admin needs a top-like view of resource usage grouped by systemd service/cgroup rather than individual processes. Which tool provides this?
explain: systemd-cgtop aggregates CPU, memory, and I/O by control group, which maps to services, making it easy to spot which service is consuming resources. systemctl top, cgtop --systemd, and ps --cgroup-top are not real commands.

q: 'systemctl status app' shows 'activating (auto-restart)' cycling every 30 seconds. Which combination diagnoses the crash loop?
options: systemctl mask app to stop the loop permanently
kill -9 the app processes to break the cycle
Check journalctl -u app for the crash, fix the root cause; the loop is driven by the unit's Restart= setting
Raise RestartSec to make the failures less visible
explain: The journal reveals why the process exits; Restart= in the unit file is what keeps relaunching it, so the fix is the root cause, not the loop. Masking or killing only suppresses the symptom, and raising RestartSec merely slows a still-broken cycle.

q: After adding a virtual host, Apache serves the wrong site. The admin wants to see how Apache parsed all vhost definitions and which one is the default. Which command shows this?
explain: httpd -S dumps the parsed virtual host configuration, including the default vhost for each address. -M lists loaded modules, -D DUMP_VHOSTS_EXTRA is not real syntax, and configtest has no --vhosts flag.

q: After editing nginx configuration across several included files, the admin wants to see the entire effective configuration as nginx parsed it. Which command dumps this?
explain: nginx -T tests the syntax and then dumps the full merged configuration to stdout. nginx -t only tests without dumping, -s sends signals like reload or quit, and --show-config is not a real flag.

q: A monitoring script must quickly check whether PostgreSQL is accepting connections, without running a query. Which command does this?
explain: pg_isready attempts a connection and reports the server's readiness state, which is exactly what monitoring needs. psql has no --ping flag, pg_ctl manages local clusters rather than probing remote ones, and postgres has no --check flag.

q: After editing named.conf, the admin wants to validate BIND's configuration syntax before reloading the DNS server. Which command checks it?
explain: named-checkconf parses named.conf and reports syntax errors before they can break the running server. named -t sets a chroot directory rather than testing, rndc checkconf is not a real subcommand, and named-checkzone validates zone files, not the main configuration file.

q: kdump.service is enabled and active, but after a test panic no vmcore appears in /var/crash. The admin checks /proc/cmdline and finds no crashkernel parameter in the boot command line. What is the missing piece?
options: Reinstall the kexec-tools package; the capture kernel binaries are missing
Add crashkernel=auto to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX in /etc/default/grub, regenerate grub.cfg, and reboot
Increase the size of /var/crash so the dump fits
Set kernel.panic=10 in /etc/sysctl.d/ so the system reboots faster after a panic
explain: kdump cannot capture anything without memory reserved for its capture kernel, and that reservation comes only from the crashkernel= kernel parameter — enabling the service alone is not enough. Reinstalling kexec-tools changes nothing about the reservation; /var/crash size is irrelevant when no capture kernel ever boots; kernel.panic=10 merely auto-reboots and discards the very state a dump would preserve.

q: A 1 GB cloud VM with no disk-based swap keeps triggering the OOM killer during package updates, and the provider bills for every gigabyte of attached disk. The admin wants swap space that lives in compressed RAM instead of on disk. Which sequence creates it?
options: Set vm.swappiness=100 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-swap.conf and run sysctl --system
Add zswap.enabled=1 to the kernel command line and reboot
explain: The zram module creates a compressed block device in RAM; sizing it, formatting it with mkswap, and enabling it with swapon yields swap with no disk involved. A swapfile consumes billable disk; vm.swappiness=100 only makes the kernel swap more aggressively and creates no swap space at all; zswap is a compressed cache in front of an existing disk-backed swap device, so without one it provides nothing.

q: A file server with 64 GB of RAM is swapping heavily even though 40 GB sits in page cache, and application latency has spiked. The admin wants the kernel to strongly prefer keeping application memory over cache, persistently across reboots. Which change does this?
options: Set vm.swappiness=10 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-tuning.conf and apply it with sysctl --system
Set vm.swappiness=100 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-tuning.conf and apply it with sysctl --system
Run swapoff -a to disable swapping immediately
explain: vm.swappiness controls how eagerly the kernel swaps anonymous memory versus dropping caches; lowering it to 10 keeps application pages resident, and the sysctl.d drop-in plus sysctl --system makes it persistent. A value of 100 does the opposite and increases swapping; swapoff -a is a runtime-only hammer that also removes the safety net entirely; vfs_cache_pressure tunes dentry and inode reclaim, not the swap-versus-cache balance.

q: A database vendor's tuning guide recommends backing the shared buffer pool with 2 MB hugepages to cut TLB misses, requiring 1024 of them reserved at boot on every database host. Which persistent configuration reserves them?
options: Add transparent_hugepage=always to the kernel command line
Set vm.nr_hugepages=1024 with sysctl -w for immediate effect only
Set vm.nr_hugepages=1024 in /etc/sysctl.d/99-hugepages.conf and apply it with sysctl --system
Raise the memlock limit for the database user in /etc/security/limits.conf
explain: vm.nr_hugepages statically reserves that many hugepages from boot, and the sysctl.d file makes it persistent across reboots. Transparent hugepages are a separate automatic mechanism, not the explicit static pool the vendor asked for; sysctl -w alone is lost on reboot; raising the memlock ceiling only permits a user to lock memory and reserves no hugepages at all.

q: An admin must assign the static IPv6 address 2001:db8::10/64 with gateway 2001:db8::1 to the NetworkManager connection profile 'eth0', surviving reboots. Which nmcli sequence is correct?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses 2001:db8::10/64 ipv6.gateway 2001:db8::1 ipv6.method manual && nmcli con up eth0
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses 2001:db8::10/64 ipv6.method auto && nmcli con up eth0
ip -6 addr add 2001:db8::10/64 dev eth0 && ip -6 route add default via 2001:db8::1
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 2001:db8::10/64 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0
explain: Static IPv6 through NetworkManager requires setting ipv6.addresses and ipv6.gateway with ipv6.method manual, then reactivating the profile. Method auto ignores the static address and uses SLAAC or DHCPv6 instead; the ip -6 commands work immediately but vanish on reboot because they bypass NetworkManager; the ipv4.* properties cannot hold an IPv6 address at all.

q: Site standards forbid the bonding driver, but a server still needs active-backup link redundancy through the newer teaming driver, configured persistently with NetworkManager. Which command creates it?
options: nmcli con add type bond con-name team0 ifname team0 mode active-backup
ip link add team0 type team
nmcli con add type team con-name team0 ifname team0 config '{"runner": {"name": "activebackup"}}'
explain: nmcli con add type team creates a persistent teaming connection, and the JSON config selects the activebackup runner. Type bond uses the forbidden bonding driver; teamdctl only controls an already-existing teamd instance at runtime and creates nothing; ip link add builds a team interface that disappears on reboot because it is not stored in any NetworkManager profile.

q: A KVM guest must be bridged directly onto the physical LAN through a new bridge br0 that enslaves eth0, and the configuration must survive reboots via NetworkManager. Which sequence does this?
options: ip link add br0 type bridge && ip link set eth0 master br0
nmcli con add type bridge-slave ifname eth0 master br0 without creating the bridge first
nmcli con add type bridge con-name br0 ifname br0 && nmcli con add type bridge-slave con-name br0-port1 ifname eth0 master br0
Attach the guest to the default NAT network and add a static route on the LAN router
explain: NetworkManager needs a bridge connection profile first, then a bridge-slave profile enslaving eth0 to it; both persist across reboots. The ip link commands build the same topology but only until the next reboot; a slave profile alone fails because there is no master bridge to join; the NAT network keeps the guest off the LAN behind NAT, which is the opposite of bridged.

q: Users report clock-related authentication flakiness, and the admin suspects chronyd is not actually syncing. Which command shows each configured NTP source with its reachability and offset, so the admin can see whether any source is usable?
explain: chronyc sources -v lists every configured source with stratum, polling interval, reachability, and last offset — exactly the per-source health view needed. chronyc tracking summarizes the system clock itself (stratum, RMS offset) but not individual sources; timedatectl only reports whether NTP synchronization is active; ntpq talks to the legacy ntpd daemon, not chronyd.

q: A RHEL 9 server's physical console must use the German keyboard layout for all future logins. Which command sets this persistently?
explain: localectl set-keymap writes the console keymap to /etc/vconsole.conf, making it persistent for the virtual console. loadkeys changes only the current session and is lost on reboot; set-locale changes language and formatting variables, not the keyboard layout; dpkg-reconfigure keyboard-configuration is the Debian-family tool and does not exist on RHEL.

q: An openSUSE Tumbleweed workstation (a rolling-release distribution) has not been updated in months. Which command correctly performs the update, given how rolling releases must be upgraded?
explain: On rolling-release openSUSE Tumbleweed, zypper dup (distribution upgrade) is the supported update path because it resolves the large dependency shifts a rolling snapshot brings, including vendor changes. zypper update only updates within the current snapshot and can leave a Tumbleweed system in a broken mixed state; zypper patch applies official maintenance patches, which do not exist for Tumbleweed; install-new-recommends only adds recommended packages.

q: Before installing packages from a new vendor repository, the admin must import the vendor's GPG public key into the RPM database so package signatures can be verified. Which command does this?
explain: rpm --import loads the key into the RPM database that dnf and rpm consult when checking package signatures. gpg --import loads it into a user's personal GPG keyring, which the package tools never read; rpm -K verifies a package file's signature but imports nothing; --add-repo registers the repository without trusting its key, so installs would still fail signature checks.

q: /boot keeps filling with old kernels on a RHEL 9 server. The admin wants dnf to automatically keep only the three most recent kernels on every future update, without manual cleanup. Which persistent setting does this?
options: A weekly cron job running package-cleanup --oldkernels --count=3
Manually erasing old kernels with rpm -e after each update
explain: installonly_limit in /etc/dnf/dnf.conf tells dnf how many installonly packages (kernels) to retain, pruning older ones automatically on every transaction. /etc/sysctl.conf holds kernel tunables, not dnf settings; a cron job running package-cleanup is a fragile external workaround rather than the built-in mechanism; manually erasing kernels after each update is error-prone and defeats the purpose of automation.

q: A kernel regression appeared after last night's update, and the admin wants the previous known-good kernel to boot by default until the vendor ships a fix. Which is the supported persistent way to set it on RHEL 9?
options: Edit /boot/grub2/grub.cfg and move the old kernel's menuentry to the top
Set GRUB_DEFAULT=0 in /etc/default/grub without regenerating the configuration
explain: grubby --set-default updates the bootloader environment to make the specified kernel the default, which survives grub.cfg regenerations. Hand-editing grub.cfg is overwritten the next time grub2-mkconfig runs; changing GRUB_DEFAULT without regenerating grub.cfg has no effect at all; grub2-install reinstalls bootloader binaries to the disk and does not change which kernel boots by default.

q: After encrypting the root volume with LUKS and adding it to /etc/crypttab, the system drops to a dracut emergency shell at boot because the initramfs cannot unlock the disk. What is the correct fix?
options: Rebuild the initramfs so it includes crypt support: dracut --force --add crypt
Add the LUKS UUID to /etc/fstab so it mounts at boot
Run cryptsetup luksOpen manually at every boot before the mount
explain: The initramfs was built before encryption was configured, so it lacks the crypt module and crypttab handling; rebuilding it with dracut --add crypt pulls in what early boot needs to prompt for the passphrase and unlock root. Reinstalling GRUB fixes bootloader binaries, not the initramfs contents; fstab cannot unlock LUKS devices — that is crypttab's job; manually opening the volume at each boot is not a persistent fix.

q: The XFS filesystem on /data is mounted with the gquota option, and the research group must be hard-limited to 50 GB. Which command enforces this?
explain: XFS group limits are managed with xfs_quota, and the limit subcommand requires expert mode (-x); the gquota mount option enables group quota accounting. tune2fs manages ext4 features and does nothing on XFS; xfs_admin changes filesystem parameters like labels, not quotas; without -x, xfs_quota refuses the limit command because it is restricted to expert mode.

q: The root filesystem is btrfs. The admin wants /var/lib/docker to live in its own subvolume so that snapshots of / exclude container storage. Which command creates this?
explain: btrfs subvolume create makes an empty, independently snapshottable subvolume at that path. mkdir creates an ordinary directory inside the parent subvolume, so it would still be captured by / snapshots; snapshot creates a copy-on-write clone of an existing subvolume rather than an empty one; lvcreate operates at the LVM layer and knows nothing about btrfs subvolumes.

q: An admin must overcommit storage: create several logical volumes whose combined virtual size exceeds the physical disks, allocating blocks only as data is actually written. Which sequence does this with LVM?
options: Create each logical volume with lvcreate -L, relying on the filesystem to thin-provision
Create a thin pool with lvcreate --thinpool, then create thin volumes with lvcreate -V --thinpool
Create a snapshot of an empty volume for each tenant with lvcreate -s
Create a RAID0 array with mdadm and put one large ext4 filesystem on it
explain: LVM thin provisioning uses a thin pool as backing store; thin volumes (-V for virtual size) allocate extents from the pool only on write, which is exactly overcommit. Regular lvcreate -L allocates all extents up front, so there is no overcommit; snapshots are copy-on-write rollback points, not a provisioning model; RAID0 plus ext4 stripes data but still allocates every block physically.

q: Using parted non-interactively, the admin must create a primary partition covering exactly the second half of /dev/sdb. Which command does this?
options: fdisk /dev/sdb and answer the interactive prompts for the second half
explain: parted accepts percentage positions, so 50% to 100% covers exactly the second half regardless of disk size. fdisk is interactive and cannot be driven non-interactively this way; hardcoded gigabyte values assume a specific disk size and break on any other; bare numbers 50 and 100 are interpreted as megabytes, creating a tiny 50 MB partition.
