q: After re-cabling disks, the admin needs a single tree view showing every block device with its filesystem type, label, and UUID to rewrite fstab correctly. Which command produces this?
explain: lsblk -f renders the device tree and adds filesystem, label, and UUID columns — everything needed to match devices to fstab entries. blkid prints the same identifiers but as a flat list without the parent-child tree; plain lsblk shows the tree but omits filesystem details; df -T only covers filesystems that are currently mounted.

q: Before rebooting a server after heavy fstab edits, the admin wants the fstab validated against the current system state without mounting anything. Which command does this safely?
explain: findmnt --verify parses fstab and checks each entry against the running system (devices, mount points, options) without performing any mounts. mount -a actually mounts everything, which can trigger failures or mask ordering problems; plain findmnt only lists current mounts; systemd-analyze verify checks unit files, not fstab semantics.

q: Two swap devices exist: fast NVMe and slower SATA. The admin wants the kernel to prefer the NVMe device whenever both have free space. Which configuration does this?
options: Set pri=1 on the NVMe entry, since lower numbers are used first
Set pri=10 on the NVMe entry, since the kernel uses the highest-priority swap first
Set vm.swappiness=10 to prefer the faster device
List the NVMe device first in /etc/fstab, since order decides preference
explain: swapon priority works so that the available swap area with the highest pri value is used first; giving the NVMe device pri=10 makes it preferred. The trap is believing lower numbers win — they do not; vm.swappiness controls how eagerly the kernel swaps at all, not which device it picks; fstab ordering has no effect on swap preference.

q: A VM on thin-provisioned storage is not returning freed blocks to the hypervisor, so the virtual disk keeps growing. The admin wants weekly reclamation with minimal performance impact. Which is the recommended approach?
options: Add discard to every mount option in /etc/fstab for continuous TRIM
Run hdparm --trim-sectors on a monthly cron schedule
Defragment the filesystems weekly with e4defrag
Enable fstrim.timer so discarded blocks are batched weekly
explain: fstrim.timer issues batched discard requests once a week, returning freed blocks without the per-write overhead of continuous discard. The discard mount option sends TRIM on every delete, which hurts latency on many workloads; hdparm --trim-sectors is a low-level manual operation, not the filesystem-aware tool; defragmentation reorganizes file layout and reclaims nothing from thin storage — and is pointless on SSDs.

q: A vendor support engineer asks for a comprehensive snapshot of the system's configuration, logs, and package state to troubleshoot a kernel issue. Which single command generates the standard archive for this?
explain: sosreport is the standard tool vendors request: it collects configuration files, logs, hardware details, and package information into one archive. dmesg and journalctl each capture only one log stream; strace traces system calls of a process and is useless for a general system snapshot.

q: Releases live in /opt/app/v2.3, /opt/app/v2.4, and so on, and /opt/app/current must always resolve to the newest release directory — including after future releases are deployed to a different filesystem. Which command sets this up?
explain: A symbolic link stores a path, so it can point at directories and cross filesystem boundaries, and repointing it at deploy time is atomic. A hard link cannot reference a directory and cannot span filesystems; cp -al copies hard links of files rather than creating a pointer; a bind mount works but requires a mount entry and privileges on every deploy instead of a simple link swap.

q: HR renamed an employee's login from jsmith to jdoe. The UID, home directory contents, and all group memberships must remain exactly as they are. Which command renames the account correctly?
options: Edit /etc/passwd and replace jsmith with jdoe using sed -i
explain: usermod -l changes only the login name, preserving the UID, GID memberships, and file ownership. Deleting and recreating the account assigns a new UID and drops group memberships; groupmod renames a group, not a user; hand-editing /etc/passwd with sed bypasses locking and shadow-file consistency checks.

q: User ops's home directory must move from /home/ops to /data/homes/ops, including all existing files, and the account must point at the new location. Which command does this in one step?
explain: usermod -d sets the new home path and -m moves the current home's contents there, keeping the account consistent in a single operation. -d alone updates the path but leaves the files behind; mv moves the files but never updates /etc/passwd; the cp plus usermod pair works but is two steps and temporarily duplicates the data.

q: HR delivers a file with 40 lines in the format username:password:UID:GID:comment:home:shell for the new intern cohort. Which is the fastest correct way to create all 40 accounts?
options: Run adduser once per line and answer its interactive prompts
Write a for loop calling useradd for each line
vipw and paste the 40 lines into /etc/passwd
explain: newusers is purpose-built for bulk account creation from exactly this colon-delimited format, creating users and setting passwords in one pass. adduser is interactive and impractical at scale; a useradd loop works but reimplements what newusers does natively; vipw edits /etc/passwd safely but sets no passwords and expects full passwd-format lines, not this simpler format.

q: After a scripted bulk edit of /etc/passwd, the admin wants to verify the file has no syntax errors, missing fields, or orphaned entries before anyone logs in. Which command validates it?
explain: pwck checks /etc/passwd (and shadow) for malformed entries, bad field counts, and inconsistencies. grpck validates /etc/group, not passwd; getent passwd merely queries the user database through NSS without validating file integrity; id looks up a single account and reports nothing about the file as a whole.

q: Policy requires that manual edits to /etc/passwd use locking against concurrent edits and reject malformed entries on save. Which is the correct tool?
options: sed -i to apply the change directly
explain: vipw locks the password files, invokes the editor, and runs syntax checks before committing, refusing to save a broken file. Plain vi provides no locking and no validation; sed -i and shell redirection edit the live file with no locking, no syntax check, and a real chance of corrupting logins system-wide.

q: New policy: every account created from now on must have its password expire after 60 days by default, without the admin touching each account. Where is this default set?
options: chage -M 60 applied to each existing account
useradd -D to set the default shell and skeleton directory
explain: PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs defines the default maximum password age applied to newly created accounts. chage -M changes existing accounts one by one; useradd -D manages account-creation defaults like shell and skeleton directory, not password aging; passwd -x sets expiry per account, and /etc/shadow is never edited directly.

q: A monitoring script must decide in a shell conditional whether app.service is currently running, without parsing human-readable output. Which command fits best?
explain: systemctl is-active prints the state and exits 0 only when the unit is active, making it ideal for if-statements. Parsing status output is brittle; is-enabled reports whether the unit starts at boot, not whether it is running now; grepping ps output is fragile and can match unrelated processes.

q: An application fails at boot, and the admin suspects a missing ordering dependency. Which command displays the full dependency tree of app.service so the ordering can be inspected?
explain: list-dependencies renders the complete Requires, Wants, After, and Before tree for the unit. list-units shows a flat list of loaded units; cat shows the unit file text without resolving the effective dependency graph; show -p After prints one property as a flat list, not the tree.

q: A systemd timer must run a report at 06:00 on the first day of every month. Which timer setting expresses this?
explain: systemd calendar syntax *-*-01 06:00:00 means every year, every month, day 01 at 06:00. Cron-style five-field syntax is not valid in OnCalendar; the special string 'monthly' does not exist in systemd; OnBootSec schedules relative to boot time, not calendar dates.

q: Five hundred laptops all run a software-inventory timer at 09:00, and the resulting thundering herd overwhelms the collection server. Which single timer setting spreads the runs out?
explain: RandomizedDelaySec adds a random delay up to the given value before the timer elapses, spreading 500 clients across 30 minutes. AccuracySec only widens the window in which systemd may schedule the timer for efficiency, without decorrelating hosts; Persistent=true catches up missed runs, which worsens the herd; per-host drop-ins are an unmaintainable manual workaround.

q: A metrics job must run every 15 minutes around the clock. Which crontab entry is correct?
explain: */15 in the minute field steps every 15 minutes, and a valid entry needs all five time fields. '15 * * * *' fires once an hour at :15; a four-field entry is invalid and ignored; '* * * * *' would run the job every minute, hammering the system four times too often.

q: Security policy states that only members of the admins group may create personal cron jobs; everyone else must be refused. Which mechanism enforces this?
explain: When /etc/cron.allow exists, only users named in it may use cron — a whitelist. cron.deny is a blacklist and cannot express 'everyone except'; access.conf controls login access, not cron submission; removing the execute bit from crontab would block even the admins.

q: Compliance requires the journal to retain only the last 14 days of logs, and the 60-day backlog must be trimmed immediately. Which command enforces the retention window right now?
explain: journalctl --vacuum-time=14d deletes journal files older than 14 days immediately. --vacuum-size limits by disk space, not age; journald.conf settings only bound future growth and trim nothing now; deleting journal files by hand risks removing the active journal and corrupting the log store.

q: logrotate rotates nginx's access log weekly. After rotation, nginx must start writing to the fresh log file without dropping any client connections. Which postrotate action is correct for nginx?
explain: nginx reopens its log files on SIGUSR1 by design, so signaling the master process rotates logs with zero connection loss. Restarting drops in-flight connections; copytruncate works but risks losing or duplicating log lines written mid-copy; SIGHUP makes nginx reload its configuration, which is heavier than needed and not the log-reopen signal.

q: For a load test, the admin must temporarily double a running service's memory cap; the change must take effect immediately and vanish on the next reboot with no cleanup. Which command does this?
options: Add MemoryMax=4G with systemctl edit app.service and run systemctl daemon-reload
explain: systemctl set-property applies cgroup properties at runtime by default, storing them under /run so they disappear on reboot — exactly the temporary change requested. systemctl edit writes a persistent drop-in under /etc; writing the cgroup filesystem directly works momentarily but systemd can overwrite it and it bypasses unit management; --runtime=no makes the change persistent, the opposite of what is wanted.

q: Dozens of java processes run on a server, but only the ones executing ReportGen.jar have hung and must be killed; the others are production-critical. Which command targets exactly the hung ones?
explain: pkill -f matches against the full command line, so only processes whose command line contains ReportGen.jar are signaled. Plain pkill java matches the process name and would kill every JVM including production ones; killall -9 java and kill $(pgrep java) likewise target all java processes indiscriminately.

q: A nightly backup job saturates the disk array, starving the database of I/O. The backup must still run, but only using I/O bandwidth nothing else wants. Which command launches it correctly?
explain: ionice -c3 places the job in the idle I/O scheduling class, so it only gets disk time when nothing else needs it. nice and renice adjust CPU priority, not I/O; ionice -c1 is the realtime I/O class, which would make the starvation worse by prioritizing the backup above everything.

q: An admin created /etc/sudoers.d/deploy.conf.bak as a backup of a sudoers drop-in, and sudo now warns about it on every invocation. What is wrong?
options: sudo ignores (and warns about) files in sudoers.d whose names contain a dot
Drop-in files must be owned by the deploying user, not root
The .bak file needs a matching entry in /etc/sudoers
visudo must be run to re-index the sudoers.d directory
explain: sudo skips any file in sudoers.d containing a '.' or ending in '~' to avoid picking up editor backups, and it warns about them. Ownership must be root, not the deploying user; no central index entry is needed since #includedir reads the directory; visudo edits files but there is no re-index step.

q: A developer working from an untrusted network needs their browser traffic to travel encrypted through bastion.example.com as a SOCKS proxy. Which SSH invocation sets this up?
explain: ssh -D opens a dynamic SOCKS proxy on local port 1080, tunneling the browser's traffic through the bastion. -L forwards one specific local port to one fixed destination rather than acting as a proxy; -R forwards a port from the remote side back, the wrong direction; -X enables X11 forwarding for graphical apps, not a SOCKS proxy.

q: The threat-intel feed provides 200 malicious IP addresses that must be blocked at the firewall. The admin uses firewalld and wants the most efficient persistent implementation. Which approach is best?
options: Create an ipset containing the addresses and add it as a source to the drop zone with --permanent
Add 200 individual --add-rich-rule entries to the public zone
Run iptables -A INPUT -s <ip> -j DROP once per address
explain: An ipset stores the 200 addresses in a single hashed kernel structure, and attaching it as a source to the drop zone blocks them all with one rule, persistently. Two hundred rich rules work but bloat the ruleset and slow matching; hosts.deny belongs to the long-removed TCP wrappers; bare iptables -A rules vanish on reboot and append-ordering mistakes can bury them below an ACCEPT.

q: On a host using native nftables, the admin must block a list of attacker IPs and have each block entry expire automatically after one hour. Which native nftables feature does this?
options: An ipset created with the ipset command and referenced from nft
An nftables set with type ipv4_addr and the timeout flag, with elements added with a timeout
One nft add rule statement per address, re-run hourly from cron
A firewalld ipset, since nftables cannot expire entries
explain: nftables sets natively support the timeout flag, so elements added with a timeout vanish automatically — no external tool needed. ipset is the older standalone tool and mixing it with native nftables is unnecessary; individual rules cannot expire on their own; firewalld is not required, and the claim that nftables lacks timeouts is false.

q: A hardening checklist requires the host to drop packets arriving on an interface with a source address that could not legitimately arrive there (spoofed packets), and to log the events. Which persistent sysctl settings do this?
explain: Reverse-path filtering (rp_filter=1) drops packets whose source address is unreachable via the receiving interface — the standard anti-spoofing control — and log_martians=1 logs them. Disabling forwarding and redirects is good hygiene but does not filter spoofed sources; accept_source_route blocks source-routed packets, a different attack; syncookies and ignoring ping neither detect nor log spoofed ingress.

q: The security baseline forbids the host from accepting ICMP redirect messages, which an attacker could abuse to reroute traffic. Which persistent sysctl settings enforce this?
explain: accept_redirects=0 on all and default interfaces makes the kernel ignore ICMP redirects, closing the traffic-rerouting vector. accept_source_route blocks a different feature (source-routed packets); rp_filter drops spoofed sources but still honors redirects; disabling forwarding stops the host acting as a router but does not stop it accepting redirects for its own traffic.

q: During an audit, the admin must report exactly which SELinux booleans differ from the shipped policy defaults on this host. Which command lists only the locally modified booleans?
explain: semanage boolean -l -C filters the boolean list to entries with local customizations, which is precisely the audit question. getsebool -a dumps every boolean with no indication of which were changed locally; setsebool changes a boolean rather than reporting; sestatus -b lists booleans but does not flag local modifications.

q: Before restoring /srv/www/index.html from backup, the admin wants to know which SELinux context the policy expects at that exact path, so the restored file can be labeled correctly. Which command answers this?
explain: matchpathcon queries the policy for the expected context of a path without touching the file. ls -Z shows the file's current context, which may already be wrong; chcon sets a context rather than reporting the expected one; grepping the full fcontext listing works but is a manual hunt where matchpathcon gives the direct answer.

q: One in-house application's SELinux denials are flooding the audit log while its policy module is being fixed. The admin must make just that application's domain permissive without weakening enforcement for anything else. Which command does this?
explain: semanage permissive -a makes a single domain permissive while the rest of the system stays enforcing. setenforce 0 drops the entire system to permissive immediately; the config-file change does the same after a reboot; audit2allow generates a new allow policy, which is the eventual fix, not a way to quiet one noisy domain.

q: Compliance requires audit rules that cannot be altered or deleted — even by root — until the next reboot. Which audit rule flag provides this immutability?
options: Run auditctl -D to lock the rule set
explain: The -e 2 flag makes the audit configuration immutable: once loaded, no rule can be added, changed, or deleted until reboot, which is exactly the compliance demand. -e 1 merely enables auditing while leaving rules changeable; chattr +i protects the file on disk but does not stop auditctl from altering the loaded rules; auditctl -D deletes all rules, the opposite of locking them.

q: The admin must verify that the kernel audit subsystem is currently enabled, check its failure mode, and see the backlog limit — without reading any log files. Which command shows this status?
explain: auditctl -s prints the audit subsystem status: enabled flag, failure mode, backlog limit, and lost records. auditctl -l lists the loaded rules, not the subsystem status; ausearch queries logged events rather than the current configuration; systemctl only reports whether the userspace daemon is running, not the kernel audit state.

q: File watches were created with -k identity so related events can be found later. The admin must now pull every audit event tagged with that key. Which command does this?
explain: ausearch -k searches the audit logs by the key assigned at rule-creation time, returning exactly the tagged events. -f searches by filename, which misses events the key was meant to group; aureport produces summaries rather than the matching events; grepping the raw log works crudely but bypasses ausearch's parsing, time filtering, and formatting.

q: A user is locked out after too many failed logins, and faillock shows the account as blocked. The admin verified the user's identity and must clear the failure count so they can log in again. Which command does this?
options: Delete the tally file under /var/run/faillock by hand
explain: faillock --user jdoe --reset clears the recorded failures for that user, which is the supported unlock for pam_faillock lockouts. passwd -u unlocks a password locked with passwd -l, a different mechanism; chage -E -1 removes an account expiry date, unrelated to failure counts; deleting the tally file by hand works on some systems but bypasses the tool and its accounting.

q: The admin has a file listing 50 newly provisioned hosts and must collect their SSH host keys into known_hosts, fetching both RSA and ED25519 key types. Which ssh-keyscan invocation reads the host list from the file?
options: Log in to each host once manually and accept the key
explain: ssh-keyscan -f reads hostnames from a file and -t selects the key types to fetch, appending everything to known_hosts for later out-of-band verification. ssh-keygen -R removes entries rather than adding them; StrictHostKeyChecking=no accepts keys blindly with no verification record; manual logins do not scale to 50 hosts.

q: A minimal container image ships openssl but no GPG, and the admin must symmetrically encrypt a database dump with AES-256-CBC before uploading it offsite. Which command encrypts dump.sql?
explain: openssl enc performs symmetric file encryption, and -salt -pbkdf2 applies modern key derivation with the AES-256-CBC cipher. openssl passwd hashes a password string rather than encrypting file contents; gpg is explicitly unavailable in this image; chmod only restricts access and encrypts nothing.

q: Managing authorized_keys files across 300 servers has become unmanageable. The admin wants servers to trust user keys signed by a central SSH certificate authority instead. Which pieces implement this?
options: Distribute each user's public key to every server's authorized_keys via Ansible
Sign user keys with ssh-keygen -s ca_key -I key_id user_key.pub and set TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/ca.pub in sshd_config
Enable Kerberos ticket forwarding in ssh_config
Set PasswordAuthentication yes and deploy a shared password
explain: An SSH CA signs user public keys into short-lived certificates; sshd verifies them against TrustedUserCAKeys, eliminating authorized_keys management entirely. Option A is the status quo being replaced; Kerberos is a different authentication infrastructure; shared passwords are a severe security regression, not a solution.

q: Before adding a new passphrase to the encrypted data volume /dev/sdb1, the admin wants to inspect the LUKS header: cipher, key slots in use, and UUID. Which command shows this?
explain: cryptsetup luksDump prints the full LUKS header including cipher mode, UUID, and the status of each key slot. luksAddKey adds a slot rather than inspecting; blkid shows only the filesystem type and UUID; fdisk -l shows the partition table, nothing about encryption.

q: Database servers in a remote datacenter must unlock their LUKS data volumes automatically at boot, with no passphrase typed and no plaintext key stored on disk. The site runs a Tang server for network-bound encryption. Which solution fits?
options: Place a keyfile on the unencrypted /boot partition
Disable LUKS and rely on filesystem permissions
Bind the LUKS volume with clevis to the Tang server (clevis luks bind -d /dev/sdb1 tang ...)
explain: Clevis with a Tang binding seals the LUKS key so it can only be released when the Tang server is reachable at boot — automatic unlocking with no stored secret. A passphrase in crypttab is world-readable plaintext; a keyfile on unencrypted /boot is equally exposed; removing encryption abandons data-at-rest protection entirely.

q: Policy requires application allowlisting: only explicitly trusted binaries may execute, and anything else must be denied and logged. Which framework implements this on RHEL 9?
explain: fapolicyd is the file-access policy daemon that allowlists binaries by trust database and denies everything else, with logging. SELinux enforces mandatory access control on subjects and objects but is not an executable allowlist; noexec on /usr would break the system since /usr holds all binaries; AppArmor is the Ubuntu/SUSE MAC framework, not an allowlist engine.

q: Compliance requires full terminal session recordings of everything administrators do through sudo, reviewable after the fact during incident response. Which configuration provides this?
options: Run the script command before each sudo session
Set log_output in sudoers and review sessions with sudoreplay
explain: sudo's log_output captures complete input/output session logs, and sudoreplay replays them like a terminal recording — the purpose-built forensic trail. The script command depends on user cooperation; auditd logs syscalls, not an interactive replay; bash history is trivially edited or disabled by the user being monitored.

q: A playbook targeting 200 hosts takes far too long with the default parallelism. The control node can handle much more. Which setting increases how many hosts Ansible configures simultaneously?
explain: forks controls how many hosts Ansible works on in parallel; the default of 5 is conservative and raising it speeds up large fleets. serial: 1 does the opposite, forcing one host at a time; throttle limits a single task's parallelism downward; disabling fact gathering saves per-host seconds but does not change parallelism.

q: A playbook task runs a database migration that takes 45 minutes. The admin does not want the play to block on it, nor the SSH session to time out and fail the task. Which task keywords handle this?
explain: async launches the task in the background with a 45-minute (2700s) limit while poll: 60 has Ansible check back every minute, surviving long runs without blocking. wait_for waits on a condition rather than detaching a long task; no_log only hides output; ignore_errors would mask a genuine migration failure.

q: A playbook task registers a variable containing a database password, and the password must never appear in playbook output or logs. Which task keyword guarantees this?
explain: no_log: true suppresses the task's arguments and results from all output, keeping secrets out of logs. become controls privilege escalation, not output; check_mode controls dry-run behavior; diff: true would expose even more detail, the opposite of what is wanted.

q: A play includes OS-specific setup tasks, but the task file to include must be chosen at runtime from a variable, since the value is only known after facts are gathered. Which include mechanism supports this?
options: A role with a static role name
A handler notified by the setup task
explain: include_tasks is evaluated dynamically at execution time, so it can use variables set by earlier tasks or facts. import_tasks is processed statically when the playbook is parsed, before any variables exist; roles are likewise static; handlers run at the end of a play and cannot conditionally include task files.

q: Every managed host must have the deploy user's current public key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys — added if missing, never duplicated, and reported as unchanged when already present. Which module does this idempotently?
options: ansible.builtin.copy with the full key file
explain: The authorized_key module manages individual keys idempotently: it adds the key only if absent and never duplicates it. copy would overwrite the whole file and clobber other keys; ssh-copy-id via command is not idempotent and breaks check mode; a template requires the playbook to know every key that should exist.

q: A log-cleanup cron job must exist for root on all managed hosts with the exact schedule '0 3 * * 0', and repeated playbook runs must not create duplicates. Which module is the right tool?
options: ansible.builtin.command with crontab -l piped into crontab -
explain: The cron module manages individual cron entries idempotently by name, creating or updating without duplication. Shelling out to crontab is not idempotent and fails check mode; templating /etc/cron.d works but requires managing the whole file; appending to the spool file duplicates the entry on every run.

q: After 'tofu apply' creates the infrastructure, the CI pipeline needs the new load balancer's DNS name printed to stdout so later jobs can consume it. Which OpenTofu construct exposes this value?
options: A locals block computing the DNS name
A variable block with a default for the DNS name
An output block referencing the load balancer resource
Grepping the terraform.tfstate file in the pipeline
explain: Output blocks publish values after apply and print them to stdout, designed exactly for handing results to automation. locals are internal to the configuration; variables are inputs, not results; grepping the state file is fragile and bypasses OpenTofu's interface.

q: The team needs three identical web servers, plus database servers where each instance has a distinct name taken from a map of environments. Which OpenTofu constructs fit each case?
options: count for the databases and for_each for the web servers
count for the identical web servers and for_each over the map for the databases
explain: count creates N identical instances addressed by index, ideal for clones; for_each iterates over a map or set so each instance gets a meaningful key like its environment name. depends_on only orders creation; using for_each for identical clones adds needless key management; swapping them gives the databases numeric indices and the web servers map keys, backwards from the requirement.

q: Five engineers run OpenTofu against the same infrastructure, and two simultaneous applies just corrupted the shared state. Which backend configuration gives shared state with locking?
options: A backend 's3' block with a dynamodb_table for state locking
The default local backend with the state file on NFS
explain: An S3 backend stores state centrally while DynamoDB provides the lock that serializes applies, preventing concurrent corruption. A local state file on NFS has no locking and is exactly what just corrupted; tfvars holds variable values, not state; -backup only keeps a local copy of the previous state and does nothing about concurrency.

q: Every new VM must boot with a custom /etc/app/config.yaml containing environment-specific settings, written during first boot. Which cloud-init user-data feature writes arbitrary files?
options: runcmd with echo lines redirected into the file
The write_files module listing the path, content, and permissions
bootcmd running before the network is up
explain: write_files is the declarative module for creating files at first boot, with explicit content, owner, and permissions. Building files with echo in runcmd is fragile with quoting and ordering; bootcmd runs too early for most configuration; the users module manages accounts and keys, not arbitrary files.

q: A deployment script keeps a list of hostnames — some containing spaces — and must iterate over each exactly once. Which bash construct handles this safely?
explain: A bash array with "${hosts[@]}" expands to each element as a separate word, preserving spaces inside elements. Unquoted $hosts, $@, and $* all undergo word splitting, so 'web 1' becomes two iterations; the quoted array expansion is the only form that keeps each hostname intact.

q: A script must convert each filename in a directory listing to uppercase without spawning external processes in the loop. Which parameter expansion does this?
explain: ${f^^} uppercases every character in the variable using pure shell expansion with no subprocess. tr and awk work but fork an external process per file, which the requirement forbids; ${f^} uppercases only the first character, not the whole name.

q: A script must verify that $path is a regular file before reading it — a directory or device node at that path must be rejected. Which test is correct?
explain: -f is true only for regular files, rejecting directories and device nodes. -e is true for anything that exists, including directories; -d specifically matches directories, the thing being rejected; -r only checks readability, which directories also satisfy.

q: The admin must diff the sorted contents of two command outputs without creating temporary files. Which bash feature feeds both command outputs to diff as filenames?
explain: Process substitution <(...) runs each command with its output attached to a file descriptor path, so diff receives two readable filenames. Command substitution $(...) would pass the entire sorted text as arguments; a single pipeline can only feed one stream to diff's stdin; brace expansion { } just generates strings and executes nothing.

q: Team policy requires feature branches to merge into main with linear history — no merge commits. A developer's feature branch is three commits behind main. Which sequence complies?
options: git merge main into the feature branch, then merge the branch into main
git cherry-pick each feature commit onto main
git rebase main on the feature branch, then merge with --ff-only
explain: Rebasing replays the feature commits on top of the latest main, after which a fast-forward merge adds them with no merge commit — linear history. Merging main into the branch (then into main) creates merge commits; cherry-picking duplicates commits with new hashes instead of moving the branch; pull --no-rebase is a merge-based update, the opposite of linear.

q: A regression appeared somewhere in the last 50 commits, and the developer needs to find the exact commit that introduced it with the fewest test runs. Which command automates this bisection?
options: git log --oneline -50 and test each commit manually
git blame on the failing lines
git stash and rebuild at each commit
git bisect start, marking a known-good and the bad commit
explain: git bisect performs a binary search across the commit range, checking out the midpoint each time, so 50 commits need at most six test runs. Manual log walking is linear and slow; blame shows who last touched lines, not which commit introduced a behavioral regression; stashing is unrelated to historical searching.

q: A Python monitoring script must run 'systemctl is-active nginx', capture its output, and stay safe if the service name ever comes from user input. Which call is correct?
explain: Passing the command as a list with shell=False (the default) avoids shell interpretation entirely, so a malicious service name cannot inject commands, while capture_output and text return the output as a string. os.system and shell=True both invoke a shell and are injectable; eval executes arbitrary Python and is never appropriate for running commands.

q: A colleague suggests testing /dev/sdb for bad blocks with 'badblocks -w', but the disk holds the only copy of a 2 TB archive with no backup. What is the critical problem with this plan?
options: The -w flag performs a destructive write-mode test that overwrites every block, destroying the archive
badblocks cannot test disks larger than 1 TB
badblocks only works on mounted filesystems
The -w flag is read-only and therefore too slow to be useful
explain: badblocks -w writes test patterns to every block, which irrecoverably destroys existing data — the classic destructive trap; with no backup this would wipe the archive. The safe choice is the non-destructive read-only mode badblocks -sv. Size is not a limitation; badblocks must run on unmounted devices, not mounted ones; and -w is the destructive write test, not a read-only one.

q: The root filesystem shows errors in dmesg, but the system is running with / mounted read-write. The admin considers running fsck directly on the mounted root device. What is the correct course of action?
options: Run fsck -y /dev/sda1 immediately; the -y flag makes it safe on mounted filesystems
Do not fsck a mounted read-write filesystem; schedule the check for the next boot or boot rescue media
Run fsck on the mounted filesystem but omit the -y flag to stay safe
Reboot normally; the journal will repair the errors on its own
explain: Running fsck on a mounted read-write filesystem lets the checker and the live kernel modify metadata simultaneously, causing corruption far worse than the original errors. The safe paths are forcing a check at next boot or booting rescue media with the filesystem unmounted. The -y flag only auto-answers prompts and adds no safety; a plain reboot replays the journal but repairs nothing.

q: smartctl -a /dev/sdb shows Current_Pending_Sector = 48 and rising. The filesystem is currently fine. What does this indicate, and what is the correct response?
options: 48 sectors were remapped long ago; the drive is healthy and no action is needed
The filesystem has 48 bad inodes; run fsck to repair them
48 sectors cannot be read and are waiting to be remapped; back up the data and replace the drive
The drive's cache holds 48 pending writes; reboot to flush them
explain: Current_Pending_Sector counts sectors the drive failed to read that are queued for reallocation on the next write — a sign of a deteriorating surface, especially while rising. It is not the historical Reallocated_Sector_Ct; fsck repairs filesystem metadata, not unreadable hardware sectors; and these are not cached writes awaiting a flush. The correct response is an immediate backup and drive replacement before pending sectors become unrecoverable ones.

q: An admin used mv to move index.html from /tmp into /srv/www, and Apache now gets AVC denials serving it — yet files copied there with cp work fine. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: mv corrupts file contents; re-copy the file with cp
The moved file lost its DAC permissions; run chmod 644 on it
The file needs a new SELinux boolean; run setsebool -P httpd_enable_tmp 1
mv preserves the source SELinux context while cp creates the file with the destination's default context; run restorecon on the file
explain: mv keeps the original inode and its SELinux context (user_tmp_t from /tmp), which httpd cannot read; cp creates a new inode that inherits the destination directory's default context. The file contents and DAC permissions are untouched by mv, so re-copying or chmod misses the point; no boolean is needed since the policy already allows the correct context. restorecon resets the label to the policy default.

q: Before querying logs from a previous boot, the admin wants to see which boot records the journal actually retained and the negative offset number for each. Which command lists them?
explain: journalctl --list-boots shows every retained boot with its index and the negative -b offset used to query it. last reboot reads wtmp login records, not journal offsets; who -b shows only the current boot time; dmesg has no --list-boots flag at all.

q: After fixing the NTP configuration, the admin must confirm the system clock's stratum, the current offset from the selected source, and overall sync health. Which command shows this summary?
explain: chronyc tracking reports the system clock's stratum, reference ID, measured offset, and RMS — the sync-health summary requested. chronyc sources lists per-source details rather than the clock summary; timedatectl only shows whether NTP is active; ntpdate is deprecated and a one-shot query tool, not the chronyd status interface.

q: Convinced that deleted-but-open log files are pinning disk space under /var, the admin wants to list each offending process and the size it holds before restarting anything. Which command produces this list?
explain: lsof +L1 lists open files with a link count below 1 — precisely deleted-but-held-open files — along with the owning process and size. fuser shows which processes use a mount but not deleted-file details; du --inodes counts inode usage, unrelated to open unlinked files; finding large files misses the point, since the space is pinned by files that no longer have names.

q: The admin suspects the server is running out of sockets — connections pile up in TIME_WAIT and new ones are refused. Which command shows a concise summary of socket statistics by type?
explain: ss -s prints a summary of socket counts by type and TCP state, which is exactly the view for diagnosing socket exhaustion. ss -tlnp lists listening sockets with processes, not totals; netstat -i shows interface counters; counting lines in /proc/net/tcp is a crude manual hack that misses other socket families entirely.

q: A new web server at 10.0.0.9 must be tested exactly as production clients see it: the request must carry Host: shop.example.com, but DNS still points shop.example.com at the old server. Which curl invocation tests the new server without touching DNS?
options: Add 10.0.0.9 shop.example.com to /etc/hosts, test, then remove it
explain: curl --resolve overrides DNS for that single invocation, sending the correct Host header and SNI to 10.0.0.9 with no system-wide change. -k only skips certificate verification against the wrong host; editing /etc/hosts works but affects every application and risks being forgotten; -L follows redirects on the old server, testing nothing new.

q: A multi-homed server has interfaces eth0 and eth1. The admin must verify that ICMP echo requests sourced specifically from eth1 reach 8.8.8.8. Which ping invocation does this?
explain: ping -I (uppercase) sets the source interface or address. The classic trap is -i (lowercase), which sets the interval between packets; -c sets the packet count; -s sets the packet size. Only -I controls which interface the echo requests leave from.

q: After a network renumbering, a server holds a stale DHCP lease and the admin must release it and obtain a fresh one from the command line. Which sequence does this?
options: ip addr flush dev eth0 && ip addr add 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0
nmcli con down eth0 && nmcli con up eth0
explain: dhclient -r releases the current lease and a bare dhclient requests a new one — the direct DHCP client workflow. Flushing the address manually abandons DHCP management; bouncing the NetworkManager connection may renew the lease but is not the DHCP release/renew operation; restarting NetworkManager is a blunt instrument that disrupts all interfaces.

q: dmesg shows 'nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet' and new outbound connections are failing on a busy NAT gateway, though CPU and memory look fine. What is the correct fix?
options: Raise the open-files limit with ulimit -n
Reboot the gateway to clear the table
Raise net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max (and the hash size) persistently via sysctl
explain: The connection-tracking table has a fixed maximum; raising nf_conntrack_max (with the hash buckets sized accordingly) is the documented fix for a full table. File-descriptor limits govern open files, not conntrack entries; adding RAM does not resize the table; a reboot empties it temporarily but the limit that caused the failure remains.

q: The admin set a one-time saved boot entry with grub2-set-default and now wants to confirm which entry GRUB will actually boot next, by inspecting the GRUB environment block. Which command shows it?
explain: grub2-editenv list dumps the variables in the GRUB environment block, including saved_entry — the authoritative answer for what boots next. /proc/cmdline describes the currently running boot, not the next one; grepping grub.cfg shows menu order, not the saved selection; efibootmgr manages UEFI boot order, a different layer from GRUB's menu.

q: On a minimal container host with no systemd journal, the admin needs kernel messages with human-readable timestamps to correlate a crash with an application event. Which command provides this?
explain: dmesg -T converts the kernel's monotonic timestamps into human-readable wall-clock times, enabling correlation with application logs. Plain dmesg shows seconds-since-boot, which cannot be matched to wall-clock events; /var/log/dmesg (where it exists) captures only boot-time messages; uname -r prints the kernel release, not messages.

q: A server is completely hung: no SSH, no console login response. The admin is at the physical console and must sync filesystems and reboot as safely as possible. Which emergency sequence does this?
options: Hold the power button for five seconds
Use the magic SysRq sequence REISUB (raising elephants is so utterly boring)
Unplug the network cables and wait for the watchdog
explain: The magic SysRq REISUB sequence — unRaw, tErminate, kIll, Sync, Unmount, reBoot — syncs filesystems and remounts read-only before rebooting, the safest option on a hung box. A power-button hold cuts power with dirty buffers; Ctrl+Alt+Del depends on a responsive init; unplugging network cables does nothing for a local hang.

q: free -h shows nearly all RAM consumed, yet ps aux reveals no userspace process using significant memory. The admin suspects kernel slab caches are the culprit. Which tool shows live per-slab kernel memory usage?
explain: slabtop displays real-time kernel slab allocator usage sorted by cache size, revealing runaway dentry or inode caches that ps can never show. free only aggregates totals; ps sees userspace processes alone; grepping /proc/meminfo yields a single static Slab number with no per-cache breakdown.

q: Users reported a disk slowdown yesterday between 2 PM and 3 PM. The admin needs historical per-device I/O statistics for that window. Which command retrieves them?
explain: sar -d reads the sysstat archives for block-device statistics, -f selects yesterday's file, and -s/-e bound the window — the only option reaching into history. iostat and vmstat report live data only; sar -u covers CPU, not disks.

q: Before a RAM upgrade, the admin must inventory the installed memory — slot population, module sizes, and speeds — without opening the chassis. Which command provides this from the firmware tables?
explain: dmidecode -t memory decodes the SMBIOS tables, listing each DIMM slot, installed module size, speed, and manufacturer. free and /proc/meminfo report totals only, with no slot or module detail; lscpu describes CPUs, not memory.

q: A server shuts down randomly under load with no log entries, and the admin suspects overheating. Which command reads the CPU and motherboard temperature sensors?
explain: sensors (from lm_sensors) reads hardware monitoring chips for CPU, motherboard, and fan readings — the direct check for a thermal shutdown. uptime shows load averages; smartctl reports disk health and drive temperature only; free shows memory usage, nothing thermal.

q: Users report that outbound email is not being delivered. The admin must see which messages are stuck in the Postfix queue and why. Which command inspects the queue?
explain: mailq / postqueue -p lists every queued message with its sender, recipients, size, and the reason it is deferred. The journal shows log lines but not the queue state; postconf shows configuration; telnet tests SMTP connectivity, not the queue contents.

q: A monitoring check must verify that MariaDB is actually accepting connections, without authenticating or running a query. Which command performs this lightweight liveness probe?
explain: mysqladmin ping asks the server for a lightweight alive response without credentials or a query. SELECT 1 requires authentication and a working session; is-active only proves the systemd unit is up, not that the daemon answers; telnet proves the port is open but says nothing about the database itself.

q: While testing an internal HTTPS service that uses a self-signed certificate, curl fails with a certificate verification error. The admin needs a quick test-only workaround without changing system trust. Which flag does this?
options: Permanently add the certificate to the system trust store
explain: curl -k (--insecure) skips certificate verification for that single invocation, which is acceptable for testing but must never be used in production automation. --resolve overrides DNS rather than trust; -L follows redirects and does not affect verification; installing the self-signed cert into the system trust store is the permanent fix, not the quick test workaround.

q: An admin edited /usr/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service directly to add an Environment= line, but the next package update wiped the change. Which is the supported way to make the customization survive updates without maintaining a full copy of the unit?
options: Run systemctl edit nginx.service and put the setting in the drop-in snippet under /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/
Edit /usr/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service again and then run systemctl daemon-reload
Copy the entire unit to /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service and edit that full copy
Use systemctl set-property --runtime to apply the setting
explain: systemctl edit creates a drop-in snippet in /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.d/ that overrides only the specified directives; files under /etc are never touched by package updates, so the customization persists. Editing /usr/lib directly is reverted by the next update; maintaining a full copy in /etc works but must be hand-synced with upstream changes; set-property --runtime applies only until reboot and daemon-reload alone creates no persistent configuration.

q: CSV files arrive in /var/incoming via SFTP at unpredictable times, and a processing service must start each time a new file appears. Which systemd mechanism starts the service automatically on file arrival?
options: A udev rule matching the directory path
A systemd.path unit watching /var/incoming paired with a same-named .service unit
A systemd.timer unit with OnCalendar set to every minute
A cron job that polls the directory with ls every minute
explain: A systemd.path unit monitors filesystem paths and activates its same-named .service unit the moment the path condition (PathExists, PathChanged, etc.) is met — the event-driven, systemd-native answer. udev rules react to hardware device events, not regular files; a timer polls on a schedule rather than reacting to arrivals; and a cron polling loop works but is not the systemd mechanism the scenario calls for.

q: An admin ran systemctl isolate multi-user.target on a workstation that boots into the graphical desktop, but after a reboot the GUI comes back. Which command makes multi-user.target the persistent default boot target?
options: Remove the display manager package entirely
Edit /etc/inittab and change the initdefault line to 3
explain: systemctl set-default rewrites the /etc/systemd/system/default.target symlink, which is what systemd actually boots into on every startup. isolate and init 3 only switch the current runtime state and vanish at reboot; /etc/inittab is a SysV artifact systemd ignores; and removing the display manager does not change the default target, so graphical.target would still be selected.

q: After every reboot, journalctl only shows logs from the current boot and all previous boot history is gone. The admin wants journal history to survive reboots. Which configuration change makes journald store logs persistently?
options: Run journalctl --vacuum-time=7d to retain a week of logs
Install rsyslog so logs are written to /var/log/messages
Increase SystemMaxUse in journald.conf to allow more storage
Set Storage=persistent in journald.conf (creating /var/log/journal) and restart systemd-journald
explain: journald defaults to volatile storage under /run/log/journal when /var/log/journal does not exist, so history is lost at reboot; Storage=persistent makes it write to /var/log/journal on disk. --vacuum-time only prunes old entries and cannot preserve what was never stored; installing rsyslog adds a separate text log but does not fix journald's volatility; and raising SystemMaxUse only lifts the size cap without changing where journals are stored.

q: A new Fibre Channel HBA was installed and its driver module loads fine now, but the admin worries the next reboot will fail because the initramfs was built before the card existed. Which command rebuilds the initramfs to include the new driver?
options: dracut --force (optionally with --add-drivers for the specific module)
update-grub to refresh the bootloader entries
depmod -a to rebuild the module dependency map
explain: dracut is the modern initramfs builder on RHEL/Fedora-family systems; --force regenerates the image for the running kernel, and --add-drivers guarantees a specific module is included. update-grub only regenerates bootloader menu entries without touching initramfs contents; depmod -a rebuilds module dependency metadata, not the initramfs image; and mkinitrd is the obsolete RHEL 5-era tool that no longer exists on current systems.

q: An admin ran firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --zone=public, yet the web server is still unreachable from other hosts and firewall-cmd --list-services shows no http. What is wrong?
options: The --zone=public flag was misspelled so the rule went nowhere
The --permanent change was written to disk but never applied to the runtime; run firewall-cmd --reload
firewalld requires the iptables service to be restarted afterward
SELinux is blocking port 80 regardless of firewalld rules
explain: firewall-cmd --permanent writes to the on-disk configuration only; the running firewall is untouched until firewall-cmd --reload (or a restart) loads it, which is why --list-services shows nothing new. The zone flag was valid; firewalld is the active manager so restarting the legacy iptables service is irrelevant; and SELinux denials would appear in the audit log, whereas here the rule simply was never loaded into the runtime.

q: A contractor's account must stop working entirely after Friday, even if the contractor never logs in again before then. Which command enforces a hard account expiration date?
options: chage -M 7 contractor to force a password change within a week
passwd -l contractor to lock the account password
chage -E 2026-10-23 contractor to set the account expiry date
usermod -s /sbin/nologin contractor to remove the login shell
explain: chage -E sets the account expiration date in /etc/shadow, after which all authentication for the user fails regardless of login activity. -M only limits password age and never disables the account; passwd -l locks the password hash but SSH key authentication can still succeed; and /sbin/nologin blocks interactive shell logins yet the account itself remains valid for cron jobs and key-based forced commands.

q: An admin ran usermod -G docker operator to grant Docker access. The next day the operator can no longer use sudo, although nothing else changed. What happened?
options: The docker group membership takes effect only after a reboot
The operator must run newgrp docker before sudo works again
Membership in docker automatically revokes sudo privileges
usermod -G without -a replaced all supplementary groups, silently dropping wheel/sudo membership
explain: usermod -G sets the complete supplementary group list, so without -a (append) it removed every existing group — including wheel — leaving only docker. The fix is usermod -aG docker operator. A reboot is unnecessary for group changes to take effect at next login; newgrp only affects the current shell and cannot restore lost memberships; and no mechanism strips sudo rights merely for joining the docker group.

q: timedatectl shows 'NTP service: inactive' and 'System clock synchronized: no' on a server with chronyd installed. Which command enables network time synchronization through the installed service?
options: ntpdate pool.ntp.org to sync the clock once
hwclock --systohc to write the system time to hardware
Add server lines to /etc/chrony.conf and nothing else
explain: timedatectl set-ntp true enables NTP via systemd, which starts and enables the installed NTP service (chronyd on modern systems) so synchronization begins and persists. ntpdate performs a one-shot sync and is deprecated without enabling ongoing synchronization; hwclock --systohc only copies time to the hardware clock; and editing chrony.conf without starting the service leaves NTP inactive, which is exactly the reported state.

q: Every new developer account must default to /bin/bash with home directories created under /home/dev instead of /home. Which command sets these defaults for all future useradd invocations?
options: Edit /etc/passwd and change the template entry
explain: useradd -D modifies /etc/default/useradd, the file useradd consults for defaults (-s default shell, -b base home directory) on every future invocation. /etc/passwd has no template entry to edit; usermod has no -D defaults mode; and /etc/login.defs controls password aging and mail settings, not the default login shell, so setting SHELL there has no effect on useradd.

q: Security policy requires that files created by the deploy user have no group-write and no permissions at all for others (rw-r----- style). New files currently appear as 664. Which umask enforces the policy for newly created files?
options: Run chmod 640 on the existing files
Set umask 022 in the deploy user's shell profile
Set umask 027 in the deploy user's shell profile
Run setfacl -m g::--- on the deployment directory
explain: umask 027 masks the group-write bit plus all other bits, so new regular files come out 640 (rw-r-----) — exactly the policy. umask 022 yields 644, which still grants read to others and violates the policy; chmod and the non-default setfacl -m only change existing files and do nothing for files created in the future, since only the process umask (or a default ACL) governs new file modes.

q: Auditors require that root can never log in over SSH with a password, but existing key-based automation running as root must keep working. Which sshd_config setting satisfies both requirements?
explain: PermitRootLogin prohibit-password (also accepted as 'without-password') disables password and keyboard-interactive root logins while still allowing public-key authentication, matching both requirements precisely. 'no' blocks root SSH entirely including keys; PasswordAuthentication no would disable password logins for every user, which is broader than asked; and DenyUsers root refuses all root SSH connections regardless of method.

q: After downloading a Linux ISO and its published SHA256SUMS file, which command properly verifies the ISO's integrity against that file?
options: sha256sum installer.iso and visually compare the output to the website
md5sum installer.iso since MD5 is faster
gpg --verify SHA256SUMS to check the ISO
explain: sha256sum -c reads the checksum file, recomputes each listed file's hash, and reports OK/FAILED — the purpose-built verification workflow. Manually eyeballing a hash is error-prone and does not scale; md5sum computes a different, weaker digest that cannot be compared against SHA-256 values; and gpg --verify checks a cryptographic signature of the checksum file itself, not the ISO's digest.

q: Files created in /srv/shared must automatically grant the dev group read/write access, without anyone running extra commands after each file is created. Which command sets this up?
explain: A default ACL (-d) is inherited by newly created files and directories, so g:dev:rwX on the default ACL grants the group access automatically going forward. The non-default -m form sets an access ACL affecting only existing entries; chmod g+s makes new files inherit the directory's group ownership but grants no extra permissions; and chown :dev only changes ownership of the directory itself.

q: A user is locked out after too many failed SSH logins and pam_faillock is in use. The admin must unlock the account immediately rather than waiting for the timeout. Which command clears the lockout?
explain: faillock --user alice --reset is the supported tool that clears the failure tally and unlocks the account immediately. passwd -u unlocks a password-locked account, which is a different mechanism than faillock's tally; hand-deleting tally files bypasses the tooling and can leave inconsistent state across faillock's database files; and chage -E -1 removes account expiry, which is unrelated to a brute-force lockout.

q: A playbook task runs command: /opt/app/install.sh, and every playbook run reinstalls the application even when nothing changed. Which change makes the task idempotent so it runs only when needed?
options: Switch the module from command to shell
Add changed_when: false to the task
Add ignore_errors: true to the task
Add creates: /opt/app/.installed so the task is skipped once the marker file exists
explain: The creates argument makes the command module skip execution when the given file already exists, which is the idempotent pattern for one-shot installers. Switching to shell changes nothing about re-execution; changed_when: false merely lies in the report (the installer still runs every time); and ignore_errors: true hides failures instead of preventing redundant runs.

q: A playbook must ensure sshd_config contains exactly 'PermitRootLogin no', replacing any existing variant (including commented ones) without managing the whole file and without leaving duplicates. Which task does this idempotently?
options: lineinfile with path set, regexp: '^#?PermitRootLogin', and line: 'PermitRootLogin no'
lineinfile with only line: 'PermitRootLogin no' and no regexp
A shell task running sed -i to rewrite the line
blockinfile inserting a marked block with the setting
explain: With regexp matching the existing (possibly commented) directive, lineinfile replaces that line in place; on later runs the line already matches, so nothing changes and no duplicate appears. Without regexp, lineinfile appends a second line if any variant exists — and sshd honors the first occurrence, so the old value would still win; a shell/sed task is not idempotent and reports changed every run; blockinfile leaves the original directive in place, creating a conflicting duplicate.

q: A backup script kept running after a failed rsync and then deleted the source directory. Which line at the top of the script makes Bash exit on any command failure, treat unset variables as errors, and fail a pipeline if any stage fails?
explain: set -euo pipefail combines errexit (-e: exit on command failure), nounset (-u: error on unset variables), and pipefail (a pipeline fails if any stage fails) — the defensive trio that would have stopped the script after the rsync failure. set -x only enables execution tracing; bare set -e (or #!/bin/bash -e) misses unset variables and masks failures inside pipelines, which is how the destructive cleanup ran anyway.

q: A health-check script must run every 90 minutes around the clock. The admin put '*/90 * * * * /opt/bin/health.sh' in crontab, but it actually runs once per hour. Which approach correctly schedules a 90-minute interval?
options: Change the entry to '0 */90 * * *' so the hour field steps by 90
Add a second cron entry offset by 45 minutes to interleave the runs
Use a systemd timer with OnBootSec=90min and OnUnitActiveSec=90min instead of cron
Put sleep 5400 at the top of the script and keep the hourly cron entry
explain: cron's minute field only accepts values 0-59, so */90 collapses to minute 0 — once per hour; a systemd timer with OnUnitActiveSec=90min expresses the 90-minute interval natively and keeps it persistent and logged. '0 */90' is invalid in the same way since hours only step within 0-23; two interleaved cron entries drift and double-fire at overlaps; and sleep 5400 inside an hourly job stacks overlapping runs and breaks if one execution overruns.

q: A CI deployment script does a full git clone of a 2 GB repository on every run, but the deployment only ever needs the latest commit. Which clone option slashes the download while still producing a usable checkout?
options: git archive to download a tarball
git clone --depth 1 to fetch only the latest commit
explain: git clone --depth 1 creates a shallow clone containing only the newest commit, which is all a fresh deployment needs and avoids downloading gigabytes of history. git pull requires an existing clone to update; git fetch --all still retrieves the full history; and git archive depends on the server allowing archives and does not produce a git working tree the rest of the script may expect.

q: A backup process has been hung for two hours with no log output and no CPU usage. Which command shows exactly which system call the process is currently stuck in?
options: kill -9 <PID> and check the logs afterward
explain: strace -p attaches to the running process and displays the system call it is blocked in (e.g. a read on a dead NFS handle), directly revealing the hang. ltrace shows library calls, which is less direct for kernel-level waits; kill -9 destroys the evidence before diagnosis; and ps only shows the process state letter without identifying the blocking call.

q: Inside a minimal container that has no lsof or netstat installed, an admin must identify which process is listening on TCP port 443. Which command does this with the standard iproute2 toolkit?
options: cat /proc/net/tcp and decode the hex addresses
explain: ss -tlnp (TCP, listening, numeric, with process info) is part of iproute2, present on virtually every Linux system, and shows the owning PID for each listener. ps cannot display socket listeners; /proc/net/tcp works but requires manual hex decoding of addresses and ports; and netstat is deprecated and not installed in the minimal container.

q: An application was found dead at 3 AM with nothing in its own logs. dmesg | grep -i oom shows 'Out of memory: Killed process 1842 (app)'. What does this indicate?
options: The application hit a segmentation fault in its own code
An administrator manually killed the process overnight
The kernel OOM killer terminated the process because the system ran out of memory
systemd stopped the service after a stop-timeout expired
explain: The 'Out of memory: Killed process' message is the kernel OOM killer's signature: with no reclaimable memory left, it selected and terminated the app to protect the system — the fix is more RAM/swap or memory tuning, not an app patch. A segfault would leave a signal-11 trace or core dump, not an OOM line; a manual kill leaves no such kernel message; and a systemd stop timeout produces a 'stop-sigterm' style service message instead.

q: df -h reports the root filesystem 100% full, but du -sh /* accounts for only about half the disk. The admin already checked inodes. What best explains the discrepancy and how is the space reclaimed?
options: Filesystem corruption is misreporting usage; unmount and run fsck
The 5% reserved blocks are hidden from du; lower them with tune2fs -m 1
Sparse files are confusing du; copy everything with cp --sparse=never
Deleted log files are still held open by running processes; find them with lsof +L1 and restart the owning service
explain: When a process holds an open file descriptor to a deleted file, the kernel keeps its blocks allocated (visible in df) while the file has no name for du to count — lsof +L1 lists these unlinked-but-open files, and restarting the service releases them. Corruption would show I/O errors rather than a clean df/du split; reserved blocks are a fixed 5% that cannot explain a ~50% gap; and sparse files make du report less than apparent size, not a df/du usage mismatch of this kind.

q: Internal DNS resolves db.corp to the wrong IP, and the admin suspects a bad record somewhere up the delegation chain. Which command traces the resolution step by step from the root servers down?
explain: dig +trace performs iterative resolution starting at the root servers, showing each referral and the response at every delegation level — exactly how you spot which server in the chain returns the bad record. Querying a single resolver with @8.8.8.8 only shows that resolver's final answer; nslookup and host perform ordinary recursive queries and reveal nothing about the intermediate delegation steps.

q: After adding a drop-in override for nginx, an admin wants to see the final merged unit configuration exactly as systemd will apply it, including all drop-ins. Which command shows this?
explain: systemctl cat prints the main unit file concatenated with every active drop-in snippet, showing exactly what systemd parsed. Reading /usr/lib directly misses the /etc overrides; systemctl show dumps raw properties rather than the unit text; and systemctl status shows runtime state and recent logs, not the configuration.

q: An admin loaded a kernel module with modprobe, but it is gone after every reboot. Which is the correct persistent way to have the module loaded automatically at boot?
options: Add the module name to a file under /etc/modprobe.d/
Create a .conf file with the module name under /etc/modules-load.d/
Append the module name to /etc/rc.local and chmod +x it
explain: /etc/modules-load.d/*.conf is the systemd mechanism that loads listed modules at boot, making the modprobe effect permanent. /etc/modprobe.d/ only sets module options, aliases, and blacklists — it never loads anything; .bashrc runs per interactive shell, not at boot; and rc.local is a deprecated SysV leftover that systemd ignores by default.

q: The root password on a RHEL 9 server is lost and there is no external boot media available. Which GRUB-level procedure regains root access?
options: Boot normally and press Ctrl+Alt+F2 to reach a root console
Append init 1 to the kernel line; sulogin will drop to a root shell
Edit /etc/shadow from the GRUB command line before booting
Interrupt GRUB, append rd.break to the kernel line, then remount /sysroot read-write, chroot, run passwd, and touch /.autorelabel
explain: rd.break stops the boot in the initramfs before the root filesystem is mounted, allowing remount read-write, chroot into /sysroot, a password reset, and /.autorelabel so SELinux relabels on the next boot. A text console still requires login; init 1 invokes sulogin, which demands the (lost) root password on RHEL; and GRUB's command line cannot edit files inside the not-yet-mounted filesystem.

q: The fstab mounts filesystems by UUID, and the admin must confirm which physical disk carries a given filesystem UUID before replacing a failing drive. Which command lists block devices with their filesystem UUIDs?
explain: blkid reports each block device's filesystem type, LABEL, and UUID — precisely the mapping needed to match fstab entries to disks. fdisk -l shows partition tables and disk identifiers, not filesystem UUIDs; plain lsblk omits UUIDs unless -f is added; and df -h only covers mounted filesystems without showing UUIDs.

q: A database server suffers latency spikes that correlate with the default power-saving CPU behavior. Which tool applies a system-wide latency-optimized tuning profile persistently?
options: Run nice -n -20 on the database process at startup
explain: tuned-adm profile throughput-performance activates a tested bundle of kernel, scheduler, disk, and power settings optimized for latency-sensitive workloads, and the profile persists across reboots. nice only adjusts one process's priority; sysctl -w changes a single knob at runtime and forgets it on reboot; and cpupower sets just the CPU governor without the rest of the coordinated tuning.

q: An application's log file is held open by the running daemon, which cannot be signaled to reopen logs, yet logs must rotate nightly without restarting the app. Which logrotate directive handles this?
explain: copytruncate copies the log to the rotated name and then truncates the original in place, so the daemon's open file descriptor keeps writing to the same (now empty) file with no restart or signal needed. create makes a fresh file but the daemon keeps writing to the old handle; missingok merely tolerates a missing file; and compress only affects already-rotated archives.

q: A developer's systemd --user timer runs while they are logged in but stops after logout. Which command lets that user's systemd services keep running without an active session?
options: Run the timer with nohup instead of systemd
Start the timer with su - developer -c from root's crontab
explain: loginctl enable-linger creates the linger flag that keeps the user's systemd manager (and its timers/services) alive after logout — the designed solution for persistent user services. nohup abandons systemd management entirely; /etc/systemd/system holds system units, not user units; and a root cron workaround duplicates scheduling outside the user's own systemd instance.

q: A new hire's account is provisioned through SSSD/LDAP and does not appear in /etc/passwd. Which command confirms the account resolves with its login shell and home directory?
explain: getent passwd queries the full NSS stack (files, sss, ldap), so it returns the account's entry including shell and home directory regardless of the backend. grepping /etc/passwd only sees local files and misses SSSD/LDAP users; the home directory may not exist yet even for a valid account; and groups shows group memberships, not the shell or home directory.

q: A developer wants to switch their own login shell from bash to zsh without involving an administrator. Which command lets a non-root user change their own shell?
options: Edit /etc/passwd directly and change the shell field
explain: chsh is the setuid tool designed exactly for this: an unprivileged user may change their own login shell to any shell listed in /etc/shells. Editing /etc/passwd requires root and risks corrupting the file; usermod requires root privileges; and exporting SHELL only changes a variable for the current session, not the login shell recorded in the account database.

q: An admin ran systemctl disable cups, but the service still starts whenever a print job is queued. Which command prevents the service from being started by any trigger, including socket activation?
options: Remove the cups package with dnf
explain: systemctl mask symlinks the unit to /dev/null, which blocks every activation path — manual starts, dependencies, and socket/D-Bus activation — while disable only removes the [Install] symlinks. stop is runtime-only and the socket will reactivate it; disable --now still leaves the socket unit able to pull it in; and removing the package is overkill that also deletes configuration and binaries the site may want later.

q: A provisioning script must create accounts with a preset password using a single useradd call. Which form correctly supplies the credential to useradd -p?
options: useradd -m alice and let it prompt for the password
explain: useradd -p expects an already-encrypted password hash, so openssl passwd -6 generates the proper SHA-512 crypt hash to embed in the command. Passing plaintext to -p stores it verbatim in the shadow field and login always fails; useradd reads no password from stdin; and useradd never prompts interactively — that is passwd's job, which cannot be scripted this way.

q: Users keep deleting each other's files in the shared /srv/dropbox directory, which is mode 777. Which change stops users from deleting files they do not own while keeping the directory world-writable?
explain: The sticky bit (mode 1777, shown as 't') on a world-writable directory restricts deletion and renaming to the file's owner, the directory's owner, or root — the classic /tmp protection. Plain 777/0777 is the current vulnerable state; changing ownership does not affect deletion rights inside a world-writable directory; and the ACL entry merely restates the existing other permissions without adding the sticky restriction.

q: Before installing a downloaded source tarball, the admin wants to prove it was actually released by the upstream project and not tampered with in transit. The project publishes .asc signature files. Which check provides authenticity, not just integrity?
options: Comparing the file size to the website listing
Downloading over HTTPS instead of HTTP
explain: gpg --verify checks the cryptographic signature against the project's imported public key, proving both authenticity (it came from the key holder) and integrity. sha256sum only proves the file matches a checksum, which an attacker hosting a fake file could also publish; file size is trivially spoofed; and HTTPS protects the transport but says nothing about whether the file itself is the genuine release.

q: Only members of the deploy group should be allowed to establish SSH sessions; all other users must be refused at the SSH layer. Which sshd_config directive implements this?
explain: AllowGroups deploy restricts SSH logins to members of the deploy group, which is exactly the group-based gate requested. DenyUsers * would refuse everyone including deploy members; PermitEmptyPasswords no blocks only empty passwords, not users; and MaxSessions limits multiplexed sessions per connection without restricting who may log in.

q: The security team wants every write or attribute change to /etc/shadow recorded in the audit log with the tag 'shadow_watch'. Which command installs this persistent-style audit watch rule?
explain: auditctl -w places a filesystem watch that logs write and attribute-change events on /etc/shadow to the audit log under the key shadow_watch. ausearch only queries already-recorded events and creates no rule; chmod hardens permissions but logs nothing; and inotifywait is a manual monitoring tool whose output is not the audit log and which dies with the shell.

q: A playbook targets 50 web servers and includes a task that builds a combined deployment report from gathered facts. Running it on every host would produce 50 duplicate reports. Which keyword makes the task execute only once for the entire play?
options: run_once: true on the report task
delegate_to: localhost on the report task
when: inventory_hostname == groups['web'][0] on the report task
explain: run_once: true executes the task a single time on one host (optionally combined with delegate_to to choose where), which is the purpose-built mechanism for one-per-play work like aggregate reports. serial: 1 only throttles batching without reducing executions; delegate_to alone still runs the task once per host (all delegated to localhost); and hardcoding groups['web'][0] is fragile if inventory order or membership changes.

q: A script fails with '[: ==: unary operator expected' whenever $ENV is empty. The test line is: if [ $ENV == "prod" ]; then. What is the correct fix?
options: Remove the spaces around the brackets
explain: An unquoted empty variable vanishes during word splitting, leaving '[ == "prod" ]' — a syntax error; quoting ("$ENV") preserves the empty string as one argument so the test evaluates cleanly. -eq is numeric comparison and wrong for strings; the spaces around [ ] are mandatory syntax, not the bug; and (( )) performs arithmetic evaluation, not string comparison.

q: A playbook downloads an installer and must run the install task only when the download task actually fetched a new file. Which construct expresses this conditional execution?
options: Add changed_when: true to the install task
Register the download task's result and add when: dl is changed to the install task
Add failed_when: false to the download task
Use notify on the download task with the install as a handler
