explain: register captures the download task's result, and 'when: dl is changed' runs the installer only when the download reported a change — the standard conditional pattern. changed_when: true forces a changed report rather than testing one; failed_when controls failure classification, not conditional execution; and handlers run at the end of the play, which misplaces an install step that later tasks may depend on.

q: A script creates temp files in /tmp/app.$$ and must remove them even if the script is killed by SIGTERM or fails midway. Which line guarantees cleanup in all exit paths?
options: Add rm -rf /tmp/app.$$ as the last line of the script
Run the script under nohup so signals are ignored
explain: trap on EXIT fires on every shell termination path — normal exit, error exit, and caught signals like TERM and INT — so cleanup always runs. A trailing rm never executes if the script dies early; trapping only INT misses SIGTERM and error exits; and nohup merely immunizes against SIGHUP while leaving all other death paths leaking temp files.

q: A nightly sync script should commit and push only when files actually changed; an empty commit makes git exit nonzero and pages the on-call. Which check gates the commit correctly?
options: git diff --quiet --exit-code || git commit -am 'nightly sync' && git push
Parse git status output with grep for the word 'modified'
git stash push -m 'nightly sync' instead of committing
explain: git diff --quiet --exit-code exits nonzero exactly when the working tree differs, so the || chain commits and pushes only when there is something to commit — no empty commits, no pager storms. --allow-empty deliberately creates the empty commits the scenario forbids; grepping git status is fragile across locales and porcelain formats; and stash push shelves changes instead of publishing them.

q: Users report intermittent slowness reaching an application server, and the admin suspects packet loss at a specific hop along the path. Which tool continuously probes each hop and reports per-hop loss percentages over time?
options: ping the application server for an hour
Run traceroute once and note the slowest hop
explain: mtr combines ping and traceroute, sending continuous probes to every hop and reporting loss% and latency per hop over the run — exactly what identifies a flaky intermediate router. End-to-end ping cannot localize which hop drops packets; a single traceroute is one snapshot that misses intermittent loss; and ss -s summarizes local socket counters, revealing nothing about the network path.

q: After a reboot, several services did not come up and the admin needs a quick list of every unit that failed to start. Which command produces exactly that list?
explain: systemctl --failed filters the unit list to units in the failed state — the direct answer to 'what did not start'. journalctl -b shows the entire boot log, burying the failures; plain list-units shows everything including healthy units; and dmesg only covers kernel messages, missing most service-level failures.

q: An HTTPS site returns errors and the admin needs to see the TLS handshake, certificate details, and response headers in one pass. Which command provides this diagnostic output?
explain: curl -v is verbose: it prints the TLS handshake, the presented certificate chain, and the request/response headers alongside the body — the full picture in one command. curl -s silences everything including errors; wget downloads the body with minimal diagnostics; and openssl s_client shows the TLS layer but never issues the HTTP request, so header-level problems stay invisible.

q: A server feels sluggish and the admin suspects memory pressure rather than CPU. Which output most directly confirms the system is actively swapping?
options: top showing high %CPU on several processes
vmstat 1 showing consistently nonzero si and so columns
df -h showing the root filesystem 80% full
uptime showing a high load average
explain: The si (swap in) and so (swap out) columns of vmstat directly measure paging activity; sustained nonzero values prove the kernel is actively swapping, confirming memory pressure. High %CPU indicates a CPU bottleneck instead; df reports disk usage, unrelated to swap activity; and load average aggregates CPU and I/O wait without identifying memory as the cause.

q: A gigabit NIC is negotiating only 100 Mbps, slowing backups. Which command first confirms the actual negotiated link speed and duplex of eth0?
explain: ethtool eth0 reports the negotiated Speed and Duplex straight from the driver, confirming whether the link settled at 100 Mb/s half or full duplex before any fix is attempted. ifconfig is deprecated and does not reliably show negotiation results; ip link set only changes administrative state; and mii-tool is the obsolete predecessor that many modern drivers no longer support.

q: A RHEL 9 server needs the kernel parameter intel_iommu=on applied to every installed kernel persistently, surviving kernel updates. Which command adds it correctly?
explain: grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args updates the bootloader entries for all installed kernels and integrates with kernel-install so future kernels inherit the argument — the supported persistent path on RHEL. Hand-editing grub.cfg is overwritten on kernel updates; /proc/cmdline is a read-only view of the current boot parameters; and kernel-install manages UKI/initramfs layout, not arbitrary kernel arguments.

q: An application crashed overnight and the admin needs its core dump and a backtrace for the developers. The system uses systemd-coredump. Which tool lists, inspects, and debugs the captured crashes?
options: coredumpctl list, coredumpctl dump, and coredumpctl gdb
Look for core files manually under /var/crash/
Send the process SIGSEGV again to reproduce it
explain: coredumpctl is the frontend to systemd-coredump: list shows captured crashes, dump extracts a core file, and gdb launches a debugger session on it. dmesg only notes that a segfault occurred without the dump itself; /var/crash is the ABRT/kdump location, not where systemd-coredump stores cores; and re-crashing the process destroys the original evidence instead of analyzing it.

q: Before migrating a virtualization host, the admin must confirm the CPUs expose hardware virtualization flags and check the NUMA topology. Which command presents CPU architecture, flags, and topology in readable form?
explain: lscpu parses /proc/cpuinfo and sysfs into a readable summary of architecture, cores, threads, NUMA nodes, and CPU flags such as vmx/svm. free reports memory, not CPUs; dmidecode shows SMBIOS firmware tables with limited flag detail; and uname -m prints only the machine architecture string like x86_64.

q: After months of changes by several admins, nobody remembers which systemd units have drop-in overrides, masked units, or redirected symlinks. Which command summarizes all such deviations from the vendor defaults?
options: systemctl cat on each service one by one
explain: systemd-delta is purpose-built to report every unit that differs from vendor defaults — overridden, extended via drop-ins, masked, or redirected — in one concise report. list-unit-files shows enablement state, not configuration deltas; a raw recursive diff is noisy and misses symlinks semantics; and running systemctl cat per unit is impractical across hundreds of units.

q: An admin needs to shrink the XFS filesystem on /data to free space for a new partition. What is the correct approach?
options: XFS cannot be shrunk: back up the data, recreate a smaller filesystem, and restore
xfs_growfs -d /data with a smaller size argument
lvreduce the logical volume; XFS shrinks automatically
explain: XFS has no shrink support by design — only growth via xfs_growfs — so the safe procedure is backup, mkfs a smaller filesystem, and restore. xfs_growfs only grows; resize2fs works solely on ext2/3/4 and refuses XFS; and lvreducing beneath a mounted XFS filesystem truncates live data and corrupts it.

q: An admin added 'PasswordAuthentication no' at the top of sshd_config plus a 'Match User backup' block below it, but password logins still work for everyone. Why is the global setting not taking effect?
options: sshd was not restarted after the edit
AllowUsers must be used instead of a Match block
A Match block applies to everything beneath it until the next Match, so the global setting got scoped; Match blocks must go at the end of sshd_config
The Match block is indented incorrectly
explain: In sshd_config, a Match block scopes every directive below it until the next Match or end of file, so directives placed after a Match no longer apply globally — Match blocks belong at the end. A restart was presumably done and would not fix scoping; AllowUsers is a different mechanism that does not explain the scoping bug; and sshd_config ignores indentation, so formatting is never the cause.

q: Users keep setting passwords like 'password123' and 'qwerty2024'. Which mechanism actually enforces password complexity rules (length, character classes, dictionary checks) on this Linux system?
options: passwd -l on accounts with weak passwords
explain: pam_pwquality enforces complexity at password-change time using /etc/security/pwquality.conf — minimum length, required character classes, and dictionary-word rejection. chage -M only controls password aging, not content; passwd -l locks accounts instead of guiding password choice; and login.defs PASS_MIN_LEN is ignored once pam_pwquality is in the PAM stack, which is the modern default.

q: A service the admin never enabled starts on every boot, and they need to see which unit pulls it in as a dependency. Which command shows the reverse dependency chain?
explain: systemctl list-dependencies --reverse walks the dependency tree backwards, revealing exactly which targets or units require the service — the direct answer to 'what pulls this in'. is-enabled only reports whether the unit itself is enabled; grepping the config dirs is manual and misses generated and transient dependencies; and chkconfig is the obsolete SysV tool that knows nothing about systemd wants.

q: Application logs are timestamped in UTC but the operations team needs the system timezone set to America/New_York persistently. Which command does this correctly?
explain: timedatectl set-timezone updates /etc/localtime properly and notifies the system, making the zone change persistent and system-wide. Exporting TZ only affects shells that source the profile; date -s sets the clock time rather than the zone; and hwclock manages the hardware clock, not the system timezone.

q: After an emergency hand-edit of /etc/passwd with a text editor, the admin wants to verify the file's integrity — correct field counts, valid shells, and no duplicate UIDs — before anyone logs in. Which tool performs this check?
options: getent passwd to list all accounts
Reboot and watch for login errors
explain: pwck validates /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow integrity: field counts, UID/GID validity, duplicate entries, and login shell existence — the purpose-built checker after manual edits. getent only lists entries without validating them; rebooting to 'see what breaks' risks locking everyone out; and visual inspection misses subtle errors like duplicate UIDs or a mistyped shell path.

q: A file copied from /tmp into /var/www/html is served with 403 errors because it carries the wrong SELinux context. Which command restores the policy-defined default context on the web content?
explain: restorecon applies the contexts defined in the SELinux policy's file-context database, which is the persistent, correct fix for mislabeled web content. chcon sets the context manually but it is lost on the next restorecon or filesystem relabel; chmod changes discretionary permissions, not the SELinux label; and setenforce 0 disables enforcement system-wide, masking the problem while destroying the security control.

q: An internal service needs a self-signed TLS certificate and private key for testing. Which command generates a new 4096-bit key and a self-signed X.509 certificate in one step?
explain: openssl req -x509 with -newkey generates the RSA keypair and self-signs an X.509 certificate in a single invocation — exactly the TLS test artifact needed. openssl enc performs symmetric file encryption, not certificate issuance; ssh-keygen creates SSH keys, which are not X.509 certificates; and gpg generates PGP keys for signing/encryption, unusable as a TLS server certificate.

q: The firewall must rate-limit incoming SSH to 5 new connections per minute while firewalld remains the active manager. Which command adds this as a persistent rule?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule service name="ssh" limit value="5/m" accept'
explain: A firewalld rich rule with a limit element expresses the rate limit natively and --permanent keeps it across reboots, staying inside the active manager. Raw iptables rules bypass firewalld and get wiped on the next reload; hosts.deny relies on deprecated TCP wrappers most services ignore; and MaxStartups throttles concurrent unauthenticated connections with drop probabilities, not a per-minute connection rate.

q: The deploy user needs to restart nginx via sudo without a password, but must gain no other passwordless privileges. Which sudoers entry grants exactly this?
options: Add deploy to the wheel group
explain: A Cmnd_Alias-style entry naming the exact binary and arguments confines passwordless sudo to that one action — the least-privilege answer. NOPASSWD: ALL grants passwordless root for everything; wheel membership typically still requires a password and grants broad sudo; and setuid on systemctl is dangerous and does not integrate with sudo's logging and controls.

q: After a suspected intrusion, the admin wants to find system binaries that differ from what the packages originally installed. Which check compares installed files against the package database?
options: ls -la /usr/bin/ and look for recent timestamps
explain: rpm -Va verifies every installed file's size, mode, and hashes against the RPM database, flagging modified binaries regardless of forged timestamps. ls timestamps and find -mtime are trivially spoofed by an attacker touching files; and chkrootkit hunts known rootkit signatures rather than verifying package integrity.

q: A playbook repository must contain an API token, but secrets cannot live in plaintext in git. Which Ansible mechanism encrypts the secret while keeping the playbook usable?
options: ansible-vault encrypt_string to store the token as an encrypted variable
chmod 600 the playbook files in the repository
Keep the token in plaintext; the repo is private
explain: ansible-vault encrypts the value with AES, so the repository holds ciphertext that Ansible decrypts at runtime with the vault password — secrecy plus usability. Base64 is encoding, not encryption, and decodes trivially; chmod 600 protects files on one host but git still distributes plaintext to every clone; and a private repo still exposes the secret to every collaborator and backup.

q: An interactive maintenance script must present a numbered menu and branch on the operator's choice, re-prompting on invalid input. Which Bash construct is purpose-built for this?
options: A chain of if/elif tests on $REPLY
A select loop with a PS3 prompt
Installing the dialog package for menus
A single read followed by exit on bad input
explain: select automatically numbers the options, displays them, sets REPLY, and loops on invalid input with the PS3 prompt — the built-in menu construct. An if/elif chain on REPLY reimplements that machinery by hand; dialog adds an external dependency for a job the shell does natively; and a single read with no retry loop abandons the operator on the first typo.

q: A playbook managing 500 hosts is slow because fact gathering runs on every host, yet no task uses any ansible_facts. Which change removes this wasted work?
options: gather_facts: false at the play level
Run with ansible-playbook -f 50 for more forks
explain: gather_facts: false skips the setup module entirely, eliminating the per-host fact collection that nothing consumes. More forks parallelize the waste rather than removing it; serial: 5 actually slows the run further; and pipelining reduces SSH connection overhead but does not skip fact gathering.

q: A startup script must wait until the database accepts TCP connections on db:5432 before launching the app, without a fixed sleep that is either too short or wasteful. Which loop waits correctly?
options: sleep 60, then start the app unconditionally
while nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done
Add a cron job that starts the app every minute
until nc -z db 5432; do sleep 2; done
explain: until loops while the probe fails and exits the moment nc -z succeeds, so the app starts at the earliest possible instant with no guessed timeout. A fixed sleep races the database startup; the while form shown loops while the port is OPEN (inverted logic) and exits immediately when the database is down; and a cron poller starts the app outside the script's control, possibly many times.

q: A script runs under set -u and references an optional LOG_DIR variable that may legitimately be unset. Which reference keeps nounset protection while supplying a fallback?
options: Disable nounset with set +u for the whole script
${LOG_DIR} with a comment saying it may be empty
export LOG_DIR="" at the top of the script
explain: The :- expansion substitutes the default when LOG_DIR is unset or null without tripping nounset, preserving -u protection everywhere else. set +u abandons the safety net for the entire script; a bare ${LOG_DIR} aborts under set -u; and pre-exporting an empty value changes semantics, since code can no longer distinguish 'unset' from 'set empty'.

q: After a messy reboot, the admin wants to see only error-and-above messages from the current boot's journal, hiding all the informational noise. Which command does this?
explain: journalctl -p err filters to priority err and higher while -b restricts output to the current boot — the precise slice requested. Plain journalctl -b dumps everything including debug noise; dmesg shows only kernel messages, missing service errors; and grepping /var/log/messages depends on rsyslog being configured and misses the structured journal entirely.

q: On a minimal system without lsof, the admin must list every file descriptor a suspect PID currently has open, including deleted files it still holds. Which inspection works with only procfs?
explain: /proc/<pid>/fd contains a symlink per open file descriptor, so listing it reveals every open file — including ones showing as '(deleted)' that the process still holds. ps shows process attributes, not file descriptors; maps shows memory mappings rather than the fd table; and ss only covers sockets, missing regular files entirely.

q: Name resolution behaves oddly and /etc/resolv.conf only contains the 127.0.0.53 stub. The system uses systemd-resolved. Which command shows the actual upstream DNS servers and per-link configuration in effect?
explain: resolvectl status queries systemd-resolved directly, showing the real upstream servers, per-link DNS settings, and DNSSEC state that the stub resolv.conf hides. The stub file only points at the local resolver; nslookup and dig perform queries but report nothing about which upstream servers resolved is configured to use.

q: An XFS filesystem shows corruption and the admin is about to run xfs_repair. What is the critical prerequisite, and why does the common fsck.xfs shortcut fail here?
options: Run xfs_repair on the mounted filesystem for a live repair
Reboot and let the filesystem self-heal
Unmount the filesystem first, then run xfs_repair (fsck.xfs is a no-op stub that only prints a message)
explain: xfs_repair must run on an unmounted filesystem; repairing a mounted XFS can worsen corruption, and -L (log zeroing) is a last resort that discards recent transactions. fsck.xfs is literally a stub that prints a message telling you to run xfs_repair and exits — it repairs nothing; and XFS does not self-heal structural corruption across a reboot.

q: A newly installed NIC never appears in ip link output. Which step first determines whether the kernel even sees the hardware before chasing driver or config issues?
options: lspci | grep -i net to confirm the device is enumerated, then check driver and firmware
explain: lspci shows whether the kernel enumerates the PCI device at all; if it is absent, the problem is hardware/seating/BIOS, and if present, the next step is the driver and firmware. ifconfig is deprecated and cannot show a device the kernel never registered; ip link cannot bring up a nonexistent interface; and rebooting repeatedly diagnoses nothing.

q: An admin set vm.swappiness=10 in /etc/sysctl.conf and ran sysctl -p, but sysctl -a still shows 60 after reboot. A file /etc/sysctl.d/99-sysctl.conf also sets vm.swappiness=60. What explains this?
options: sysctl -p must be run twice to take effect
Files in /etc/sysctl.d/ are processed after /etc/sysctl.conf in lexical order, so the drop-in wins; move the setting to a higher-numbered drop-in or remove the conflict
The kernel ignores sysctl.conf entirely on this distribution
explain: sysctl applies configuration files in lexical order with later files overriding earlier ones, and the whole /etc/sysctl.d/ directory is processed after /etc/sysctl.conf — so the drop-in's value wins. Re-running sysctl -p or rebooting reapplies the same losing precedence; /proc writes are runtime-only; and the kernel honors sysctl.conf fine when no later file contradicts it.

q: Yesterday's automated update broke an internal application, and the admin must revert the system to the exact package set from before the update. Which dnf feature performs this rollback?
options: rpm -e each updated package one by one
Run dnf update again to get a newer fix
dnf history list to find the transaction, then dnf history rollback <id>
explain: dnf history records every transaction, and history rollback computes the inverse operations needed to return to the pre-update package set — the designed revert path. Removing packages by hand invites dependency hell; a bare downgrade picks versions heuristically rather than the exact prior set; and updating again moves forward instead of reverting.

q: The admin must confirm the exact driver version and available parameters of the loaded ixgbe network driver. Which command reports module version, author, description, and parameters?
explain: modinfo reads the module's metadata section and reports version, author, description, license, and every configurable parameter. lsmod and /proc/modules only show loaded modules with size and use counts; dmesg may contain a version line from load time but never the parameter list.

q: For filesystem repairs, the admin needs a boot target with all local filesystems mounted and a root shell, but without starting the full multi-user service set. Which systemd target fits?
options: rescue.target (via systemd.unit=rescue.target on the kernel command line)
explain: rescue.target is the single-user mode that mounts all local filesystems and starts a sulogin root shell without the full multi-user service set — exactly the repair environment requested. emergency.target is even more minimal with the root filesystem read-only and almost nothing mounted; poweroff shuts the machine down; and graphical.target starts the entire desktop stack.

q: An admin ran 'hostname db1' but the old name returns after every reboot. Which command sets the hostname persistently?
explain: hostnamectl set-hostname writes the static hostname to /etc/hostname via systemd-hostnamed, surviving reboots. The bare hostname command and --transient only change the runtime (transient) hostname; and exporting HOSTNAME sets a shell variable that does not affect the system's hostname at all.

q: A critical service must restart automatically if it crashes, but must stay stopped when an admin stops it cleanly for maintenance. Which unit setting implements exactly this policy?
options: A cron @reboot entry that starts the service
explain: Restart=on-failure restarts the service on unclean exits (nonzero status, signals, timeouts) while honoring a clean stop — the precise policy requested. Restart=always also restarts after a deliberate clean stop, fighting the admin during maintenance; Restart=no never restarts; and a cron @reboot entry only covers boot, not mid-runtime crashes.

q: The security team asks who is logged into the server right now and what each session is doing. Which command shows current logins with their activity?
explain: w (like who with activity) lists currently logged-in users, their terminals, login times, and current processes — the real-time session view requested. last reports historical login/logout records from wtmp, not the present moment; finger is often not installed and queries user info rather than sessions; and id shows only the invoking user's own identity.

q: A user's primary group must change from dev to ops so that files they create are owned by ops by default. Which command changes the primary (login) group?
explain: usermod -g sets the primary group recorded in /etc/passwd, which determines default group ownership of new files. -G (uppercase) only adjusts supplementary groups and leaves the primary untouched; groupmod -n renames the group for every member, which is far broader than asked; and chgrp fixes existing files but not the default for future ones.

q: A newly written service unit fails at startup and the admin wants its configuration validated for structural errors before digging through logs. Which tool checks the unit file?
explain: systemd-analyze verify loads the unit and reports structural problems — unknown directives, bad paths, ordering cycles — before runtime. bash -n checks shell syntax, meaningless for unit files; systemctl status and journalctl show what happened at runtime but do not validate configuration structure.

q: The helpdesk must check whether alice's account is locked, has no password, or has a usable password, without reading raw shadow fields. Which command reports the account status clearly?
options: grep alice /etc/shadow and decode the hash field manually
explain: passwd -S prints the account status line showing Password set (P), Locked (L), or No Password (NP) — the direct answer without manual shadow parsing. Decoding /etc/shadow by hand works but is error-prone; chage -l shows password aging, not lock state; and id shows UID/GID memberships, nothing about password status.

q: The shadow entry for a backup service account reads 'svc-backup:*:19700:0:99999:7:::'. What does the '*' in the password field mean for SSH access?
options: The account is completely locked; no SSH authentication method works
The password is literally the single character *
Password authentication is impossible, but SSH public-key authentication still works
The account's password expired on day 19700
explain: A '*' (or '!') in the shadow password field makes password authentication cryptographically impossible since no input hashes to it, while SSH public-key authentication bypasses the password field entirely and keeps working. The account is not locked — sshd accepts key logins; the literal character is never a usable password; and field 3 is the last-change date, not an expiry.

q: After setfacl -m u:bob:rwx project/, getfacl shows bob's entry as 'rwx' but 'effective:r--'. Which concept explains the reduction, and how is full access granted?
options: chmod g+rwx project/ to raise the group permissions
Delete and recreate the ACL from scratch
The ACL mask limits all group-class entries; inspect with getfacl and raise it via setfacl -m m::rwx project/
explain: On files with an ACL, the mask entry caps the effective permissions of all named-user and owning-group entries, so bob's rwx is masked to r--; setfacl -m m::rwx raises the mask. chmod g+rwx on an ACL file actually modifies the mask (a classic trap that confuses the group entry); re-running the same setfacl changes nothing about the mask; and recreating the ACL wastes effort when only the mask needs adjusting.

q: A typo in /etc/sudoers once broke sudo for every admin on a server. Which practice prevents a malformed sudoers file from ever being saved?
options: Always edit sudoers with visudo, which syntax-checks before saving
Edit /etc/sudoers directly with vim for full control
Keep a backup copy of sudoers in /root/
Run sudo -l after each edit to test
explain: visudo locks the file and runs a syntax check on save, refusing to install a broken sudoers — the preventive control. Editing directly with vim offers no validation; a backup only helps recovery after the breakage; and sudo -l tests the already-saved file, which is too late if the syntax error locked everyone out.

q: The admin must confirm which firewalld zone is currently applied to the eth0 interface. Which command reports the zone bound to that interface?
explain: firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface queries firewalld's runtime binding directly, reporting exactly which zone governs eth0. iptables -L bypasses the zone abstraction entirely; --list-all shows the default zone's configuration, not per-interface bindings; and firewalld.conf holds daemon settings, not interface-to-zone assignments.

q: In a shared project directory, newly created subdirectories must be accessible by the group (750) rather than owner-only (700). The current umask is 077. Which change fixes new directory modes while keeping files at 640?
options: Keep umask 077; it is the most secure choice
chmod g+rwx each new directory after it is created
Set umask 027 so new directories are 750 and new files are 640
explain: umask 027 masks write-for-group and all-for-other, yielding 750 directories and 640 files — the group-collaboration modes requested. umask 077 produces 700/600, which is the current problem; recursive 777 destroys all access control; and manually fixing each new directory does nothing for future ones, since only the umask (or a default ACL) governs creation modes.

q: A playbook deploys a new config file and restarts the service; if the restart fails, the previous config must be restored automatically before the play continues. Which construct implements this try/catch behavior?
options: ignore_errors: true on the restart task
Split the deploy and the rollback into two separate plays
A block: containing the deploy and restart tasks, with a rescue: section that restores the backup config
failed_when: false on the restart task
explain: block/rescue is Ansible's try/catch: tasks in rescue run only if a block task fails, so the backup config is restored exactly on failure. ignore_errors hides the failure without rolling anything back; two plays cannot react to the first play's failure mid-run; and failed_when: false merely reclassifies the failure as success, so no recovery ever triggers.

q: After running 'mysqldump mydb | gzip > /backup/mydb.sql.gz' in a script without pipefail, the admin must determine whether mysqldump itself failed. Which check captures the dump command's exit status?
options: Add set -e after the pipeline runs
explain: The PIPESTATUS array holds each pipeline stage's exit code in order, so index 0 is mysqldump's status regardless of what gzip did. Bare $? reports only the last stage (gzip), which can succeed while the dump failed — the classic trap; set -e after the fact cannot retroactively catch it; and PIPESTATUS[1] is gzip's status.

q: A @reboot cron job that syncs files to a NAS fails at boot because the network is not up yet. What is the most robust fix?
options: A systemd service with After=network-online.target and Wants=network-online.target
explain: A systemd unit ordered After=network-online.target starts only once the network is genuinely up, which is deterministic unlike a guessed sleep. sleep 30 races slow DHCP and wastes time on fast boots; rc.local is deprecated and unordered; and ~/.bashrc runs per interactive shell, not at boot, and never for a headless server.

q: A tarball already staged at /tmp/app.tgz on each target must be extracted to /opt/app idempotently. Which task does this correctly?
options: A copy task for the tarball plus a shell task running tar -xzf
get_url to download the tarball again, then unarchive
explain: remote_src: true tells unarchive the archive is already on the target; without it, unarchive looks for the file on the control node — the classic trap that fails or copies unexpectedly. A shell tar extraction is not idempotent and always reports changed; and re-downloading with get_url wastes bandwidth when the file is already staged.

q: Under set -u, a script must distinguish an unset CONFIG variable from one set-but-empty. Which test detects 'was never set' without triggering nounset?
explain: [[ -v CONFIG ]] tests whether the variable is set at all, returning false for unset and true for set-but-empty, without expanding it — so nounset never fires. -z on the expansion cannot distinguish unset from empty and aborts under set -u; echoing the variable also trips nounset; and grepping env misses shell-local variables that were never exported.

q: Under heavy traffic, eth0 shows rising RX drops but no errors, suggesting the NIC ring buffers are too small. Which command inspects the current ring buffer sizes?
options: ethtool -g eth0 (enlarge with ethtool -G eth0 rx 4096 if undersized)
Set a larger MTU on eth0
explain: ethtool -g displays the RX/TX ring buffer sizes, and -G resizes them — the direct diagnostic and fix for buffer-exhaustion drops. ifconfig shows drop counters but not buffer sizes; plain ethtool reports link negotiation, not rings; and MTU changes frame size rather than receive buffering.

q: An ext4 filesystem forces a full fsck every 30 mounts, delaying reboots of a production server. Which command disables the mount-count and time-interval forced checks?
options: Run fsck manually every week instead
Reformat the filesystem with different defaults
Set the fstab pass field to 2
explain: tune2fs -c 0 -i 0 clears the maximum mount count and check interval that trigger periodic forced fscks. Manual fscks do not change the counters; reformatting is destructive overkill; and the fstab pass field only controls boot-time fsck ordering, not the mount-count-triggered checks.

q: A noncritical data disk listed in fstab occasionally fails to appear, and its absence drops the whole boot into emergency mode. Which fstab option lets the boot continue when the disk is missing?
options: Add nofail to the mount's option field
Remove the entry from fstab entirely
Set the fstab pass field to 0
explain: The nofail option tells systemd not to consider the mount critical, so boot proceeds when the device is absent (usually paired with x-systemd.device-timeout). Removing the entry means the disk never mounts even when present; the pass field only affects fsck ordering; and masking the mount unit permanently disables the mount rather than tolerating its absence.

q: On a multihomed host, the admin must ping 10.0.0.1 with packets sourced from the eth1 interface. Which command does this?
explain: ping -I (uppercase i) selects the source interface or address for outgoing packets. Lowercase -i sets the interval between packets — the classic trap; -s sets packet size; and -p sets a fill pattern, neither of which chooses the interface.

q: The admin must verify that TCP port 5432 on db.example.com is reachable, but telnet is not installed. Which command tests the TCP connection directly?
explain: nc -zv opens a TCP connection to the port and reports success or failure verbosely without sending data — the purpose-built connectivity test. ping only proves ICMP reachability, not that the port accepts TCP; ssh speaks the SSH protocol to a database port; and curl attempts HTTP, which a database server does not serve.

q: After a suspected intrusion, an admin runs rpm -V httpd and sees S.5....T.  c /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf in the output. What does this result mean?
options: The httpd package is not installed, so verification cannot run
The file failed verification because its SELinux context is wrong
The package database is corrupt and rpm -V output cannot be trusted
The file's size, MD5 checksum, and modification time differ from the packaged version, but that is expected for a config file
explain: In rpm -V output, S means size differs, 5 means MD5 digest differs, T means mtime differs, and 'c' marks a configuration file — edited config files legitimately differ from the packaged originals, so this is normal. The output does not indicate a missing package (that would be an error, not a flag line), SELinux contexts are reported with a different indicator, and a corrupt database would prevent verification from running at all rather than producing per-file flags.

q: A dnf update applied 40 package updates overnight and the application now fails to start. The admin wants to revert exactly that transaction. Which command reverses the most recent dnf transaction?
options: dnf downgrade --all to roll every package back one release
rpm --rollback -t 1 to revert the last transaction
dnf reinstall $(rpm -qa) to refresh every installed package
dnf history undo last to undo the most recent transaction
explain: dnf history undo last reverses precisely the most recent transaction (installs, removals, and upgrades within it) using the recorded history. dnf downgrade --all blindly downgrades everything rather than targeting the transaction; rpm has no --rollback option; and reinstalling all packages refreshes files but does not revert version changes. The history subcommand is the transaction-aware tool for this job.

q: On an Ubuntu database server, a custom-tuned kernel must stay at its current version while all other packages keep updating. Which command pins the kernel package against upgrades?
options: apt-mark hold linux-image-generic to mark the package as held back
Add the package name to /etc/apt/sources.list to block it
Run apt autoremove linux-image-generic to exclude it from updates
explain: apt-mark hold sets a hold flag on the package so apt upgrade skips it while everything else updates normally; apt-mark showhold lists held packages. sources.list defines repositories, not per-package blocks; autoremove removes unused dependencies rather than pinning; and dpkg.cfg has no such option. The hold is the purpose-built pinning mechanism on Debian-family systems.

q: An admin creates a 4 GB swap file with fallocate, runs mkswap and swapon, but swapon fails with "swap file has holes." What is the correct fix?
options: Run chmod 600 on the file and retry swapon — the error is a permissions warning
Add the discard option to the fstab entry so holes are trimmed automatically
Recreate the file with dd instead of fallocate, then run mkswap and swapon
Format the file with mkfs.ext4 first so the holes are filled by the filesystem
explain: fallocate can create sparse (hole-punched) files, and the kernel refuses swap files with holes; dd writes every block for real, producing a fully allocated file that mkswap and swapon accept. chmod 600 is required for swap files but does not fix holes; discard is an SSD trim mount option unrelated to sparseness; and formatting the file as ext4 would destroy its use as raw swap space rather than fixing allocation.

q: The /data logical volume is full. The admin adds a new disk to the volume group and runs lvextend -L +50G /dev/vg0/data, but df still shows the old size. What was missed?
options: The volume group must be reactivated with vgchange -ay before extending
The filesystem on the LV must also be grown — rerun with lvextend -r, or run resize2fs/xfs_growfs afterward
The physical volume must be formatted with mkfs before vgextend accepts it
The LV must be deactivated with lvchange -an during any extend operation
explain: lvextend grows only the block device; the filesystem inside keeps its old size until grown separately with resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (XFS), or in one step with lvextend -r (--resizefs). The VG needs no reactivation after adding a disk; PVs are initialized with pvcreate, never formatted with mkfs; and LVs extend online — deactivation is not required and would defeat the purpose of online growth.

q: An admin writes a custom service that benefits from a cache daemon when it is running, but must start even if the cache daemon is down. Which dependency directive expresses this optional relationship?
options: BindsTo=cache.service, because it tolerates cache failures
Conflicts=cache.service so the units never run together
explain: Wants= creates a weak dependency: systemd attempts to start the cache daemon but starts the unit regardless if it fails, and After= orders the startup. Requires= is a hard dependency — the unit is stopped if the required unit fails; BindsTo= is even stronger, stopping the unit when the bound unit stops; and Conflicts= does the opposite, preventing co-existence. For an optional-but-ordered relationship, Wants plus After is correct.

q: A legacy application daemonizes itself (double-forks into the background) when started. Which Type= setting lets systemd track it correctly?
options: Type=forking with a PIDFile= pointing at the daemon's pid file
Type=simple, because systemd handles forking daemons automatically
Type=oneshot with RemainAfterExit=yes to keep the unit active
Type=notify, because the daemon notifies systemd when ready
explain: Type=forking tells systemd the start command will fork and exit, so it waits for the parent to exit and then tracks the daemon via PIDFile=. With Type=simple systemd tracks only the initial process, so a forking daemon's exit looks like a failure and the real daemon becomes untracked; oneshot is for run-to-completion tasks; and notify requires the daemon to actually send sd_notify messages, which legacy daemons do not implement.

q: A service unit reads EnvironmentFile=/etc/sysconfig/myapp, but the file is only created on some hosts. On hosts without it, the service fails to start. Which change makes the file optional?
options: Add ConditionPathExists=/etc/sysconfig/myapp so the unit is skipped cleanly
Move the variables into the [Install] section where they are always read
Change the line to EnvironmentFile=-/etc/sysconfig/myapp with a leading dash
Replace EnvironmentFile with Environment= and list every variable inline
explain: A leading dash on EnvironmentFile= (-/path) tells systemd to ignore a missing file instead of failing the unit, which is exactly the optional-file semantics needed. ConditionPathExists= would skip the entire unit on those hosts rather than starting it with defaults; the [Install] section only controls enablement symlinks, not runtime config; and inlining every variable with Environment= works but duplicates config and must be maintained in the unit itself.

q: An admin runs systemctl status nginx and sees "enabled" in the Loaded line, but the site is down. Which command distinguishes whether the service is actually running right now?
options: systemctl is-enabled nginx, which reports the runtime state
systemctl is-active nginx, which reports whether it is running now
systemctl list-unit-files nginx, which shows the current process ID
systemctl cat nginx, which prints live resource usage
explain: is-active reports the current runtime state (active, inactive, failed), while is-enabled only reports whether the unit is configured to start at boot — a service can be enabled but stopped, which is exactly this situation. list-unit-files shows enablement state of unit files, not process state; cat prints the unit file contents. Enabled describes boot behavior; active describes right now.

q: To save memory, an admin wants the backup service to start only when a client connects to TCP port 9100, using systemd socket activation. Which setup is correct?
options: Enable and start backup.service with --now so it is already running when clients arrive
Enable backup.socket (which carries ListenStream=9100); systemd starts backup.service on demand per connection
Add ListenStream=9100 to the [Service] section of backup.service and enable it
Create a backup.timer with OnActiveSec=10s to poll the port for new connections
explain: Socket activation works through the .socket unit: it holds ListenStream=9100 and, when enabled, systemd listens on the port and spawns the same-named .service per connection — the service itself stays inactive until needed. Pre-starting the service defeats on-demand activation; ListenStream belongs in the [Socket] section, not [Service]; and a polling timer is a workaround, not socket activation.

q: An admin moves Apache to listen on port 8080 and opens the firewall, but connections are still refused and AVC denials appear in the audit log. Which command permits the web server to bind that port under SELinux?
explain: SELinux confines httpd to the ports labeled http_port_t; semanage port -a adds 8080 to that type's port list persistently. There is no standard httpd_listen_any boolean; chcon on the config file changes file context, not port labeling; and the firewall was already opened — the AVC denials prove this is an SELinux port-label problem, not a firewall or file-context problem.

q: A web application on an SELinux-enforcing host cannot reach its database on another server; the audit log shows httpd_t denials for name_connect. Which fix is correct and survives reboot?
options: Run setenforce 0 to put the whole system in permissive mode
Add the database port to http_port_t with semanage port
Edit /etc/selinux/config to set SELINUX=disabled for the httpd domain
Run setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on to allow database connections
explain: The httpd_can_network_connect_db boolean exists precisely for web-to-database TCP connections, and -P writes it to the policy store so it survives reboot. setenforce 0 disables enforcement system-wide (and is runtime-only); the database port needs no http_port_t label since httpd is connecting out, not binding; and /etc/selinux/config has no per-domain disable option — SELINUX=disabled would turn off SELinux entirely.

q: An SELinux denial blocks a custom monitoring agent. The admin wants to understand WHY the denial happened before deciding on a fix. Which tool explains the AVC denial in plain language?
options: audit2allow, which prints the human-readable cause of the denial
audit2why, which translates the AVC denial into an explanation and suggests fixes
semanage boolean --explain, which decodes AVC messages
ausearch --interpret, which generates a loadable policy module
explain: audit2why reads AVC denials and explains the cause (missing boolean, mislabeled file, etc.) with suggested remedies — the diagnostic step before any fix. audit2allow generates allow-rule policy modules but does not explain; semanage has no --explain flag for AVC messages; and ausearch --interpret only renders numeric values as names. Diagnose with audit2why first, then decide between a boolean, a file-context fix, or a custom module.

q: An admin adds an SSH exception with firewall-cmd --add-service=ssh, verifies it works, but the rule is gone after a reboot. What was missed?
options: firewalld must be restarted with systemctl restart firewalld after every rule change
The rule must also be added to /etc/sysconfig/iptables or it is discarded
The command only changed the runtime configuration — rerun with --permanent, then --reload
The --zone=public option is mandatory; rules without a zone are temporary
explain: firewall-cmd without --permanent changes only the runtime configuration, which firewalld discards at reboot; --permanent writes to the zone files and --reload applies them. No restart is needed for runtime changes to take effect; /etc/sysconfig/iptables belongs to the legacy iptables service, not firewalld; and omitting --zone simply targets the default zone — it is not what made the rule temporary.

q: Before restarting sshd after hardening, an admin wants to see the effective configuration with all includes and Match blocks resolved. Which command prints it?
options: sshd -T, which dumps the effective configuration
sshd -t, which prints the merged configuration to stdout
sshd -d, which shows the configuration in debug output
cat /etc/ssh/sshd_config, which reflects all includes and Match blocks
explain: sshd -T prints the effective configuration after processing includes and Match blocks — the true runtime view. sshd -t only tests syntax and prints nothing on success; -d runs a debug server instance; and reading the raw file shows directives but not how Match blocks conditionally override them. -T is the verification step before a restart.

q: A privilege-escalation wrapper re-runs scripts as root with exec sudo "$0" "$@" when the invoking user is not root. A colleague suggests replacing "$@" with $* to simplify the line. Why must the quoted "$@" stay?
options: Unquoted $* is faster because the shell skips word-splitting entirely
"$@" keeps each original argument as a separate word, so filenames with spaces survive; $* would merge or split them
$* silently drops the last positional parameter, so scripts would lose arguments
"$@" and $* expand identically once quoted, so the suggested change is harmless
explain: "$@" expands to each positional parameter as its own protected word, so arguments containing spaces pass through sudo intact; unquoted $* word-splits and (quoted "$*") joins everything into one word, both corrupting spaced filenames. $* does not drop the last parameter, and "$@" vs "$*" differ precisely in word-splitting behavior — the quoting is what preserves argument boundaries across the re-exec.

q: A deployment script creates a temp working directory and must remove it even if the script fails partway through. Which construct guarantees cleanup?
options: trap 'rm -rf "$TMPDIR"' EXIT to run cleanup when the shell exits for any reason
Appending rm -rf "$TMPDIR" as the last line of the script
Using trap 'rm -rf "$TMPDIR"' KILL, which catches every termination
Wrapping the script in a function and calling rm in the function's return path
explain: trap ... EXIT registers a handler that runs whenever the shell exits — normal completion, error exit, or caught signals — so the temp directory is always removed. A trailing rm line never runs if the script exits early via set -e or an explicit exit; KILL (SIGKILL) cannot be trapped at all; and a function return path is skipped on the same early exits. EXIT traps are the reliable cleanup idiom.

q: A script needs a default log directory: use $LOGDIR if set, otherwise /var/log/myapp, but it must NOT modify LOGDIR itself. Which expansion is correct?
options: ${LOGDIR=/var/log/myapp}, which fills in the default only when LOGDIR is unset
${LOGDIR:-/var/log/myapp}, which substitutes the default without assigning it
explain: ${LOGDIR:-default} substitutes the default when LOGDIR is unset or empty but never assigns it — exactly the non-modifying fallback required. ${LOGDIR=...} still assigns (only when unset, but assigns); := always assigns the default into the variable; and $LOGDIR || ... is not valid shell syntax for a value fallback. The :- operator is the read-only default.

q: A script must process every .log file under /var/log/app, including filenames with spaces. Which loop handles this safely?
options: for f in $(ls /var/log/app/*.log); do ... done, which lists files cleanly
for f in /var/log/app/*.log; do ... done, which is safe only without spaces
find /var/log/app -name '*.log' -print0 | while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do ... done
ls /var/log/app/*.log | while read f; do ... done, which handles spaces via read
explain: find -print0 with while IFS= read -r -d '' is the robust idiom: null-delimited names survive spaces, newlines, and glob characters. for $(ls ...) word-splits on spaces and breaks; a plain glob for loop is actually safe for spaces too, making B's claim wrong but C still the best for recursion via find; and piping ls into read mangles unusual names. Null-delimited streaming is the defensive standard.

q: An admin sets ANSIBLE_CONFIG=/opt/ansible/ansible.cfg but Ansible seems to use different settings. A ./ansible.cfg also exists in the project directory. Which file wins?
options: The ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable takes precedence over ./ansible.cfg
./ansible.cfg always wins because it is closest to the playbook
~/.ansible.cfg wins because user config overrides environment
explain: Ansible's config precedence is: ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable first, then ./ansible.cfg in the current directory, then ~/.ansible.cfg, then /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg. If settings look wrong despite the env var, the usual culprit is running from a different directory or a typo in the variable name — but by precedence, the environment variable beats the local file.

q: After a failed boot attempt, an admin wants to see only error-and-worse messages from the current boot. Which journalctl invocation does this?
options: journalctl -b -p info, which shows info-level and more severe messages
journalctl -b -p err, selecting err and more severe priorities from this boot
journalctl -b -2 -p err to include messages from the two previous boots
explain: -p err selects err, crit, alert, and emerg (err and more severe — lower syslog numbers) and -b limits output to the current boot. There is no --errors flag; -p info would show info plus everything more severe, which is nearly the whole log; and -b -2 selects a different boot (two boots ago), not additional ones. Priority filtering with -p is the precise tool.

q: Users report the web app is unreachable. The admin suspects nothing is listening on 443. Which command lists listening TCP ports with process names?
options: netstat -tulpn, the modern replacement for ss
ss -tulpn, showing TCP/UDP listening sockets with numeric ports and PIDs
lsof -P, which lists only listening network sockets
ip addr show, which includes bound service ports
explain: ss -tulpn lists TCP (-t) and UDP (-u) listening (-l) sockets with numeric (-n) addresses and owning processes (-p) — the current standard tool. netstat is deprecated in favor of ss, not the other way around; lsof -P needs -i to show network files and lists all open files otherwise; and ip addr shows interface addresses, never ports. ss is in iproute2 and present on every modern distro.

q: df -h shows /var at 60% full, but applications fail with "No space left on device" when writing small files. Which check diagnoses this?
options: Run du -sh /var to locate which subdirectory is actually full
Run lsof +L1 /var to find deleted files still held open
Run fsck on the /var filesystem to repair the allocation tables
Run df -i /var to check whether inodes are exhausted
explain: "No space left" with free blocks but millions of tiny files points to inode exhaustion, which df -i reveals — blocks and inodes are separate pools. du measures block usage, not inodes; lsof +L1 finds unlinked-but-open files, a different cause of hidden usage; and running fsck on a mounted filesystem is dangerous and would not fix inode depletion. Small-file workloads exhaust inodes long before bytes.

q: An admin locked out of a RHEL 9 system boots with rd.break to reset the root password. After switching to the sysroot, which sequence completes the reset on an SELinux-enforcing system?
options: chroot /sysroot, passwd root, touch /.autorelabel, then exit twice to continue boot
passwd root directly at the rd.break prompt, then reboot -f
chroot /sysroot, passwd root, restorecon -R /etc, then reboot
Remount /sysroot read-write, edit /etc/shadow by hand, then exit
explain: With rd.break the real root is mounted at /sysroot (read-only, so remount -o remount,rw first); chroot /sysroot, passwd root, then touch /.autorelabel so SELinux relabels /etc/shadow at next boot — otherwise the password change is mislabeled and login fails. passwd at the initramfs prompt changes the initramfs root, not the system; restorecon on a partial tree is unreliable here; and hand-editing shadow risks syntax errors and still mislabels the file.

q: An admin runs du -sh /* to find disk usage but the totals double-count and crawl through /mnt and /proc. Which option restricts du to one filesystem?
options: du -sh -L /*, following symlinks into their target filesystems
du -c /*, which prints a grand total instead of per-directory lines
du -x -sh /*, staying on one filesystem and skipping other mounts
explain: du -x (--one-file-system) refuses to descend into directories on other filesystems, so /proc, /sys, and mounted volumes are skipped. Manually excluding each mount is fragile and easy to miss; -L follows symlinks, the opposite of containment; and -c only adds a total line while still traversing everything. For "what is filling /" questions, du -x is the right flag.

q: After replacing a failed disk in a RAID 1 array, an admin runs mdadm --add and wants to watch the rebuild progress. Which source shows the live resync status?
options: mdadm --detail /dev/md0, which streams the rebuild percentage continuously
cat /proc/mdstat, which shows the resync progress and estimated finish time
dmesg -w, which prints the RAID sync bar as it advances
lsblk -f, which displays the mirror sync state per device
explain: /proc/mdstat is the kernel's live RAID status view, showing resync/recovery percentage, speed, and ETA. mdadm --detail gives a static snapshot (one would have to re-run it); dmesg shows kernel messages but no progress bar; and lsblk shows block-device topology and filesystems, not array sync state. For a running rebuild, /proc/mdstat is the canonical watch point.

q: An encrypted data volume must unlock automatically at boot using a key file, without prompting for a passphrase. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Add the passphrase to /etc/fstab as the fourth field of the volume's entry
Store the key file on the encrypted volume itself and reference it in crypttab
Run cryptsetup luksAddKey with the --batch-mode flag to skip future prompts
Add an entry to /etc/crypttab naming the device, with the key file path as the third field
explain: /etc/crypttab maps encrypted devices to their unlock method at boot; its third field can be a key file path (or 'none' for a passphrase prompt). fstab has no passphrase field and cannot unlock LUKS; a key file stored on the very volume it unlocks is unreachable before unlocking; and luksAddKey only enrolls an additional key — it does not configure boot-time unlocking. crypttab is the boot-unlock mechanism.

q: An admin wants to require a password before anyone can edit kernel boot parameters at the GRUB menu. Which command sets this protection on a GRUB 2 system?
options: grub2-setpassword, which stores a PBKDF2-hashed password for GRUB authentication
passwd grub, creating a system user that GRUB consults at boot
grub2-mkconfig --password, which embeds a password prompt into the config
chmod 600 /boot/grub2/grub.cfg so only root can read the menu
explain: grub2-setpassword writes a hashed GRUB password (and optional superuser) into the GRUB config so editing menu entries or dropping to the GRUB shell requires authentication. There is no grub system user for this purpose; grub2-mkconfig has no --password flag; and file permissions on grub.cfg do not gate the interactive GRUB menu at boot — anyone at the console can press 'e' without GRUB-level authentication.

q: After adding a new storage controller, a RHEL 9 server drops to the dracut emergency shell because the initramfs lacks the controller's driver. Which command rebuilds all initramfs images to include current drivers?
options: update-initramfs -u -k all, the Debian-family initramfs rebuild command
grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg to regenerate the boot menu
dracut --regenerate-all --force to rebuild every initramfs image
depmod -a to rebuild module dependencies inside the initramfs
explain: dracut --regenerate-all --force rebuilds the initramfs for all installed kernels, picking up currently available drivers including the new controller's. update-initramfs is the Debian/Ubuntu tool, not RHEL's; grub2-mkconfig regenerates the boot menu but not initramfs contents; and depmod -a only rebuilds module dependency maps on the running system, not the initramfs images. On RHEL-family systems, dracut is the initramfs builder.

q: A server fails to boot fully and the admin needs a root shell with filesystems mounted to repair the damage. Which systemd target provides a root shell with filesystems mounted but minimal services?
options: emergency.target, which mounts all local filesystems before the shell
rescue.target, which gives a sulogin root shell with filesystems mounted
multi-user.target with the single option appended to the kernel line
explain: rescue.target (runlevel 1 equivalent) starts a root sulogin shell after mounting local filesystems, with almost no services — the repair environment. emergency.target is even more minimal: it provides a shell with the root filesystem mounted read-only and little else, requiring manual mounts. Appending 'single' is the SysV way to reach the same state rescue.target provides; and graphical.target runlevel 1 is a contradiction — graphical is runlevel 5.

q: An admin creates a service account with useradd svcacct but the application fails because /home/svcacct does not exist. What is the correct fix?
options: Recreate with useradd -m svcacct, since -m creates the home directory from skeleton
Run usermod --home /home/svcacct svcacct, which creates the missing directory
Add HOME=/home/svcacct to /etc/default/useradd to backfill existing users
Run pwconv to synchronize the home directory from /etc/passwd
explain: useradd without -m does not create the home directory; -m creates it (populated from /etc/skel), or CREATE_HOME in /etc/login.defs can make it default. usermod -d only updates the passwd field without creating the directory (use -m with usermod to move/create); /etc/default/useradd sets defaults for future users only; and pwconv syncs shadow passwords, not home directories. The -m flag is the direct fix.

q: A contractor's account must stop working at the end of Friday, regardless of password settings. Which command sets a hard account expiration date?
options: passwd -x 5 contractor, expiring the password five days out
usermod -L contractor, locking the password immediately
chage -M 5 contractor, setting maximum password age
chage -E 2026-10-23 contractor, setting the account expiry date
explain: chage -E sets the account expiration date, after which login is denied entirely regardless of password validity. passwd -x and chage -M control password maximum age (the user can still log in and change the password); usermod -L locks the password hash but the account itself remains valid. Only -E (also available as usermod -e) terminates the account itself on the given date.

q: Before delegating a task, an admin wants to confirm exactly which commands a junior can run with sudo. Which command lists the invoking user's sudo privileges?
options: sudo -v, which prints the user's allowed command list
sudo --show-defaults, which dumps the user's privilege set
sudo -l, which lists the commands the user may run via sudo
cat /etc/sudoers, which is readable by any user for auditing
explain: sudo -l lists the sudo privileges granted to the invoking user, including NOPASSWD tags and command arguments. sudo -v only validates/refreshes the timestamp without listing anything; there is no --show-defaults flag; and /etc/sudoers is mode 440 root-owned, not world-readable. -l is the self-audit command.

q: A sudoers.d drop-in grants deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh, but sudo still prompts for a password. A later line in /etc/sudoers grants deploy ALL=(ALL) ALL. Why does the prompt persist?
options: NOPASSWD requires the target command to be owned by root with mode 755
The last matching sudoers entry wins, so the later ALL entry (with password) overrides the earlier NOPASSWD
NOPASSWD only works in the main sudoers file, not in sudoers.d drop-ins
The deploy.sh script must be listed with its SHA256 hash for NOPASSWD to apply
explain: sudoers uses last-match-wins: when multiple entries match a user, the final one decides, so the later ALL entry requiring a password overrides the earlier NOPASSWD grant — the NOPASSWD entry must come last. Command ownership does not affect NOPASSWD; sudoers.d files are fully honored (that is their purpose); and sudoers does not hash-match commands. Ordering is the classic sudoers trap.

q: An admin creates /etc/cron.d/vacuum with the correct system-crontab format including the user field, but the job never runs. ls -l shows the file as -rw-rw-r-- owned by root. What is wrong?
options: The user field must come before the schedule in /etc/cron.d entries
Jobs in /etc/cron.d require a .cron filename extension to be picked up
The file is group-writable, and cron ignores /etc/cron.d files writable by anyone but the owner — fix with chmod 644
cron.d jobs require a MAILTO line or they are silently discarded
explain: cron refuses to trust /etc/cron.d files that are writable by group or others, silently skipping them — a security measure against tampering. The schedule-then-user field order in the entry is already correct; no filename extension is required for cron.d (that rule applies to run-parts directories); and MAILTO is optional. Mode 644 root-owned is the safe, working permission set.

q: A custom backup agent is being blocked by SELinux, but the admin must keep the rest of the system enforcing while debugging the agent's denials. Which approach isolates the debugging?
options: semanage permissive -a backup_agent_t to make only that domain permissive
setenforce 0, then re-enable with setenforce 1 after testing
Add SELINUXTYPE=permissive to /etc/selinux/config for the agent
chcon -t unconfined_t on the agent binary to exempt it permanently
explain: semanage permissive -a <domain> puts just that SELinux domain into permissive mode (denials logged, not enforced) while everything else stays enforcing — the surgical debugging tool. setenforce 0 drops the whole system to permissive; /etc/selinux/config has no per-domain setting; and labeling the binary unconfined_t is a broad, persistent exemption rather than a debugging step. Per-domain permissive is the precise instrument.

q: A web root moved to /srv/www must be labeled httpd_sys_content_t, and the label must survive a filesystem relabel. Which command sets this persistently?
options: chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/www, which writes the label into the policy store
setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on to cover the new document root
Edit /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts directly with the new path
explain: semanage fcontext -a records the label in the file-context database, which survives relabels and policy updates; restorecon then applies it to the existing files. chcon changes only the on-disk label and is wiped by the next relabel; the homedirs boolean is unrelated to /srv/www; and hand-editing the contexts files is overwritten by policy updates. The fcontext-plus-restorecon pair is the durable method.

q: Only the admin workstation at 192.0.2.10 may reach SSH on a server; all other SSH attempts must be rejected. Which firewalld construct implements this?
options: firewall-cmd --add-service=ssh --source=192.0.2.10 to bind the service to an address
A rich rule: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=192.0.2.10 service name=ssh accept'
firewall-cmd --set-target=DROP on the public zone to block everything
Creating a new zone named 192.0.2.10 and moving ssh into it
explain: Rich rules express source-specific policy: this rule accepts SSH only from 192.0.2.10 (with the zone's default target rejecting the rest). --add-service has no --source companion in that form; setting the zone target to DROP would block all traffic, not just SSH from others; and zones cannot be named after an IP to get this behavior. Rich rules are firewalld's per-source filtering language.

q: A shared project directory needs new files to default to rw for owner and group but nothing for others. Which umask produces 664 files and 775 directories?
options: umask 022, the standard default giving 644 files
umask 077, which strips all group and other permissions
umask 002, which yields 664 files and 775 directories
umask 007, which blocks other but keeps group full
explain: umask subtracts from the base 666 (files) and 777 (directories): 666-002=664 and 777-002=775, giving group read/write on new files — the collaboration-friendly setting. 022 yields 644/755; 077 yields 600/700 (private); and 007 yields 660/770, which removes group write... actually 007 gives 660 files — group keeps rw but other gets nothing. For the stated 664/775 target, 002 is the exact mask.

q: During a hardening audit, an admin must list every SUID-root binary on the system. Which find command does this?
options: find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null, matching files with the SUID bit set
find / -perm 4000 -type f, matching files with exactly mode 4000
find / -user root -executable, which implies SUID binaries
ls -laR / | grep '^-..s', the reliable recursive SUID search
explain: -perm -4000 matches files with ANY of the 4000 (SUID) bits set, regardless of other permission bits — the correct semantic. -perm 4000 (no dash) matches only files whose mode is exactly 4000, missing real binaries like 4755; -user root -executable matches all root executables, not just SUID ones; and parsing ls -laR output is fragile and slow. The dash prefix is the critical detail.

q: A script accepts optional flags (-v, -f file) followed by target hostnames. After parsing flags, it must drop them so $1 is the first hostname. Which builtin does this?
options: unset OPTIND, which clears the parsed flags from the positional parameters
shift, advancing the positional parameters past the consumed flags
set -- $@, which rebuilds the parameter list without flags
popd, which removes processed arguments from the stack
explain: shift discards $1 and renumbers the remaining positional parameters, so after parsing flags the script shifts past them and $1 becomes the first hostname. unset OPTIND only resets getopts state without touching parameters; set -- $@ reassigns the same list unchanged; and popd manipulates the directory stack, not arguments. shift (optionally shift $((OPTIND-1)) after getopts) is the argument-consuming builtin.

q: A script uses getopts "vf:" opt to parse -v and -f filename. Inside the loop, how does the script retrieve the filename passed to -f?
options: From $OPTIND, which holds the option's argument string
From $opt, which contains both the flag letter and its value
From $2, since an option's value is always the second positional parameter
From $OPTARG, which getopts sets to the current option's argument
explain: The colon after f in the optstring tells getopts that -f takes an argument, which it delivers in $OPTARG. $OPTIND is the index of the next parameter to process, not the value; $opt holds only the option letter; and $2 is whatever the second positional parameter happens to be, unrelated to where -f appears. The colon-plus-OPTARG pairing is the getopts contract.

q: A script should use $PORT if set, but default to 8080 AND remember that default for later use in the script. Which expansion both substitutes and assigns?
options: ${PORT:=8080}, which assigns 8080 to PORT when it is unset or empty
${PORT:-8080}, which assigns the default into PORT permanently
${PORT:?8080}, which sets PORT and aborts if it was already set
explain: := assigns the default to the variable when it is unset or empty, so later references see 8080 — substitution plus assignment. :- substitutes without assigning (the read-only default); ${PORT=8080} without the colon assigns only when unset (not when empty) and is easy to confuse; :? aborts with an error when the variable is unset rather than defaulting. := is the 'default and remember it' operator.

q: An admin wants to diff the process list before and after a deployment without creating temp files. Which construct feeds both command outputs to diff?
options: diff $(ps aux) $(ps aux), using command substitution for both snapshots
diff <(ps aux) <(ps aux), with process substitution presenting outputs as files
ps aux | diff | ps aux, piping both snapshots through diff
diff <<< "$(ps aux)" <<< "$(ps aux)", using here-strings as file arguments
explain: Process substitution <(cmd) runs each command with its output attached to a named pipe or /dev/fd file, giving diff two readable 'files' with no temp files — the classic use case. $(...) command substitution would word-split the output into arguments; a pipeline cannot feed two inputs to one diff invocation; and here-strings pass text on stdin, which diff reads as one stream, not two files. <(...) is the purpose-built construct.

q: Before running an Ansible playbook that edits production configs, an admin wants a dry run showing exactly what would change. Which flags provide this?
options: ansible-playbook --syntax-check, which simulates the run against inventory
ansible-playbook --check --diff, running in check mode with per-task change output
ansible-playbook --force-handlers, which runs handlers in simulation mode
explain: --check runs the playbook without making changes (check mode) and --diff shows the unified diffs of what would change — the dry-run combination. --syntax-check only validates YAML/playbook syntax; --list-tasks lists task names without executing or diffing; and --force-handlers forces handler execution on real runs, not simulations. Note check mode can mislead with command/shell tasks that cannot predict their effects.

q: An admin suspects the system clock jumped during a suspend/resume cycle and wants kernel messages with human-readable timestamps. Which command shows them?
options: journalctl -k --no-pager, which prints kernel logs with wall-clock time
dmesg, whose default output uses human-readable dates
uptime -s, which correlates boot time with kernel messages
dmesg -T, rendering kernel timestamps as human-readable dates
explain: dmesg -T converts the kernel's seconds-since-boot timestamps into human-readable dates (with the caveat that suspend/resume can skew them — relevant to this very scenario). Plain dmesg shows raw monotonic timestamps, not dates; journalctl -k shows the same kernel ring buffer with journal timestamps but the question asks about dmesg-style output; and uptime -s only prints when the system booted. -T is the human-time flag.

q: After a gateway failover, a server ARPs a stale MAC for the gateway IP and traffic blackholes. Which command clears the neighbor cache so fresh ARP resolution occurs?
options: ip neigh flush all, clearing stale neighbor entries
arp -d with no arguments, which flushes the entire ARP table
ip route flush cache, which clears the ARP neighbor entries
systemctl restart NetworkManager, the only way to refresh ARP
explain: ip neigh flush all clears the kernel neighbor (ARP/NDP) table, forcing fresh ARP resolution for the gateway's new MAC. Bare arp -d requires a hostname argument and the net-tools arp is deprecated; ip route flush cache clears the routing cache, not neighbor entries; and restarting NetworkManager is a heavy-handed side effect, not the targeted fix. Flushing the neighbor table is the precise remedy for stale ARP after failover.

q: An admin needs just the IP addresses for www.example.com, without dig's full verbose output, to feed into a script. Which invocation is best?
options: nslookup www.example.com, whose output is already script-friendly
host -v www.example.com, the verbose but parseable lookup
dig +short www.example.com, printing only the answer records
getent hosts www.example.com, which bypasses DNS for /etc/hosts only
explain: dig +short prints just the answer section (the IPs), ideal for scripting. nslookup's output includes headers and server info requiring parsing; host -v is verbose by design; and getent hosts consults nsswitch (files before DNS typically) rather than querying DNS directly, which can mask DNS-specific problems. +short is dig's machine-friendly mode.

q: A database server is slow and the admin runs iostat -x. Which pair of metrics distinguishes a saturated disk from processes merely waiting on I/O?
options: r/s and w/s throughput figures, which directly prove disk saturation
A %util near 100% combined with a growing avgqu-sz, showing the device cannot keep up
High %iowait alone, which always means the disk is saturated
A large await value by itself, which measures only device service time
explain: %util approaching 100% with a rising avgqu-sz (average queue depth) shows requests piling up because the device cannot service them fast enough — the saturation signal. High %iowait alone only means CPUs are idle waiting on I/O, which a single slow request can cause; r/s and w/s measure throughput, not saturation; and await includes queue time, so it is elevated whenever requests wait for any reason. The %util plus avgqu-sz pair is the diagnostic.

q: After a power blip, several services did not come back. Which command lists all systemd units currently in a failed state?
options: systemctl status --errors, filtering unit output down to errors
journalctl -p emerg, which lists units currently in the failed state
systemctl is-failed *, checking every unit with a shell glob
systemctl list-units --failed, showing units in the failed state
explain: systemctl list-units --failed (equivalently systemctl --failed) queries systemd for units in the failed state — the direct post-outage check. status has no --errors flag; journalctl -p emerg shows emergency-priority log messages, not unit states; and is-failed takes explicit unit names — the shell would expand * to filenames before systemctl ever sees it. list-units --failed is the precise command.

q: An application's log at /var/log/app.log grows by gigabytes daily. The admin writes /etc/logrotate.d/app with a size trigger, but after rotation the app keeps writing to the renamed old file and disk pressure continues. Which directive fixes this?
options: copytruncate, so logrotate copies the log then truncates the original in place and the app's open file handle stays valid
compress, which shrinks the renamed file so the app's writes take less space
dateext, which timestamps rotated files so the app finds the new one
create 0640 root adm, which recreates the log file after rotation
explain: The app holds an open file descriptor to the original inode, so renaming the file does not redirect its writes; copytruncate copies the contents to the rotated file and truncates the original, keeping the same inode the app is writing to. compress only shrinks the already-renamed file; dateext changes rotated filenames, not the app's handle; and create makes a fresh file that the app never opens. Alternatively a postrotate kill -HUP makes the app reopen the path.

q: An XFS filesystem on /dev/vg0/data (mounted at /data) just had its LV extended. Which command grows the XFS filesystem to fill the new space?
options: resize2fs /dev/vg0/data, the standard online grow tool
umount /data, then run xfs_growfs /dev/vg0/data on the unmounted device
xfs_growfs /data, run against the mount point while the filesystem is mounted
tune2fs -O resize_inode /dev/vg0/data to enable online growth
