explain: xfs_growfs grows XFS and must be run against the mount point while the filesystem is mounted — XFS cannot be shrunk and its grow tool takes the mount path, not the device. resize2fs is the ext2/3/4 tool and refuses XFS; unmounting is unnecessary and xfs_growfs on a device path is wrong usage; and tune2fs is the ext-family tuner with no effect on XFS. For XFS: extend the LV, then xfs_growfs on the mountpoint.

q: Before patching a database, an admin wants a point-in-time copy of the /dev/vg0/db logical volume that can be discarded after the patch. Which command creates it?
options: lvcreate -n dbsnap -L 20G vg0/db, which clones the full volume instantly
lvcreate -s -n dbsnap -L 20G vg0/db, creating a copy-on-write snapshot
dd if=/dev/vg0/db of=/dev/vg0/dbsnap bs=1M, the LVM snapshot method
vgsnapshot vg0 --name dbsnap, the volume-group snapshot command
explain: lvcreate -s creates a copy-on-write snapshot: instant to create and initially tiny, recording only changed blocks. Without -s, lvcreate makes a regular (empty) LV, not a snapshot; dd is a full block copy — slow and space-hungry; and there is no vgsnapshot command. Size the snapshot for the change rate during the patch window: if it fills, the snapshot is invalidated.

q: The root filesystem reports 100% full and even root cannot create temp files for cleanup. The admin recalls ext4 reserves a percentage of blocks for root use. Which command lowers the reservation to 1% to free emergency space?
options: dumpe2fs -m 1 /dev/sda2, writing the new reservation into the superblock
mkfs.ext4 -m 1 /dev/sda2, recreating the filesystem with a smaller reservation
explain: tune2fs -m sets the reserved-blocks percentage (default 5%); lowering it to 1% releases those blocks for immediate use — the emergency lever when root itself cannot write. dumpe2fs is read-only and has no -m write flag; resize2fs resizes filesystems, not reservations; and mkfs would destroy all data. The reservation exists so root can recover a full filesystem, and tuning it is the recovery step.

q: chronyc sources shows every NTP source stuck in the '?' (unreachable) state, though DNS resolves the pool hostnames fine. Which is the most likely cause?
options: UDP port 123 is blocked outbound by the firewall, so NTP packets never return
The system timezone is set incorrectly, preventing source selection
chronyd requires the --makestep flag at install time to reach sources
/etc/chrony.conf changes require a reboot before sources become reachable
explain: NTP communicates over UDP port 123; when DNS works but all sources show '?', the packets are being dropped — typically an outbound firewall rule. Timezone does not affect NTP reachability; makestep only corrects large clock offsets; and chronyd re-reads its config on restart, not reboot. The '?' state specifically means chronyd never got a response, pointing at the network path.

q: An employee leaves and the admin runs passwd -l jdoe. A week later, logs show jdoe authenticated via SSH. How is this possible?
options: passwd -l only locks the account for 7 days, then it unlocks automatically
passwd -l locks the password hash, but SSH key authentication bypasses password checks
The lock was applied to /etc/passwd instead of /etc/shadow due to a typo
passwd -l requires a daemon-reload before sshd honors it
explain: passwd -l prefixes the password hash with !, blocking password authentication — but SSH public-key authentication does not consult the password hash, so key-based logins still succeed. The lock is permanent until removed (no 7-day expiry); passwd operates on /etc/shadow correctly; and no daemon reload is needed since sshd reads the files per attempt. To fully disable the account, expire it (usermod -e 1) or remove the authorized_keys.

q: An admin is added to the docker group but docker commands still fail with permission denied in the current shell. Which command makes the new group effective immediately?
options: newgrp docker, starting a new shell with docker as the primary group
groups docker, which refreshes group membership for the session
id -G, which reloads the group database into the current shell
su docker, switching to the docker group context
explain: Group memberships are read at login, so the current shell does not know about the new group; newgrp docker starts a new shell with docker as the effective primary group. groups and id only report membership — they change nothing; and su switches users, not groups (sg runs a single command with a group). The alternatives are logging out and back in, or newgrp for the current session.

q: An admin scheduled a one-time job with at for 2 AM, then the maintenance window moved. Which commands list pending at jobs and remove job number 5?
options: at -l to list and at -r 5 to remove
crontab -l to list and crontab -r 5 to remove
jobs to list and kill %5 to remove
atq to list and atrm 5 to remove
explain: atq lists the pending at queue with job numbers, and atrm 5 deletes job 5 (at -d 5 is equivalent). crontab manages cron, not at; jobs/kill manage the current shell's background jobs, not the at daemon's queue. The atq/atrm pair is the at-queue management interface.

q: A nightly backup cron job never runs on a developer's laptop because the lid is closed at night. Which scheduler runs missed jobs when the machine powers on?
options: cron with the @reboot special string, which catches up missed runs
anacron, which runs overdue daily/weekly/monthly jobs at startup
atd, which replays missed cron schedules automatically
systemd timers with Persistent=false, the laptop default
explain: anacron is designed for machines that are not always on: it tracks last-run timestamps in /var/spool/anacron and executes overdue periodic jobs when the system is up. cron never runs missed jobs — @reboot runs once at boot, not the missed schedule; atd handles one-shot at jobs, not cron catch-up; and systemd timers need Persistent=true (not false) for catch-up behavior. For laptops, anacron is the classic answer.

q: An admin writes backup.timer with OnCalendar=daily but the timer never activates after a reboot, though systemctl start backup.timer works manually. What is missing?
options: The .service unit must be enabled instead; timers cannot be enabled directly
OnCalendar requires AccuracySec=0 or the timer is ignored at boot
The timer must be symlinked manually into /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/
The timer unit must be enabled: an [Install] section with WantedBy=timers.target plus systemctl enable backup.timer
explain: Like services, timers only start at boot when enabled — that requires an [Install] section (WantedBy=timers.target) and systemctl enable backup.timer (followed by daemon-reload after writing the file). Enabling the .service does not activate the timer; AccuracySec only controls scheduling jitter; and hand-symlinking duplicates what enable does. A timer that starts manually but not at boot is almost always a missing enable.

q: Before installing a downloaded RHEL ISO, an admin wants to confirm it is genuine and unmodified. The vendor publishes SHA256SUMS and SHA256SUMS.sig. Which sequence verifies authenticity?
options: Run sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.sig directly on the ISO file
Decrypt the ISO with gpg --decrypt and compare it to the published size
Run md5sum on the ISO and compare with the .sig file contents
Import the vendor's GPG public key, then gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.sig SHA256SUMS, then sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
explain: Authenticity comes from the signature chain: import the vendor's public key, gpg --verify proves SHA256SUMS was signed by the vendor, and sha256sum -c proves the ISO matches the checksums. Verifying the .sig against the ISO directly mixes up the steps; ISOs are not GPG-encrypted; and MD5 is both the wrong algorithm here and provides no authenticity without a signature. Key import first — verification fails without the signer's public key.

q: A monitoring script must report a TLS certificate's expiration date for alerting. Which openssl command prints the certificate's expiry?
options: openssl rsa -in site.crt -check, showing the key expiry
openssl s_client -connect host:443, which prints only the expiry
openssl verify -expired site.crt, returning the expiration date
openssl x509 -in site.crt -noout -enddate, printing the notAfter date
explain: openssl x509 -enddate -noout prints the certificate's notAfter date — the standard expiry check (scriptable with -checkend N for 'expires within N seconds' logic). openssl rsa inspects private keys, not certificates; s_client dumps the whole handshake including the cert but is a connectivity tool; and there is no -expired flag on verify. Parse -enddate output for alerting thresholds.

q: A team shares /srv/designs and every new file must automatically belong to the designers group regardless of the creator's primary group. Which permission setup does this?
options: chmod 777 /srv/designs, so group ownership no longer matters
chmod g+s /srv/designs, setting the SGID bit so new files inherit the directory's group
chown :designers /srv/designs, which propagates the group to future files
setfacl -d -m g::rw /srv/designs, which forces group inheritance
explain: The SGID bit on a directory makes new files and subdirectories inherit the directory's group ownership — the classic shared-workspace mechanism. 777 only widens access without touching group inheritance; chown sets the directory's own group but new files still take the creator's primary group; and a default ACL grants permissions but does not change the owning group. g+s is the inheritance flag.

q: Users share /srv/dropbox and keep deleting each other's files. The admin wants users to delete only their own files in the shared directory. Which mode fixes this?
options: chmod 700 /srv/dropbox, restricting the directory to one user
chmod g+s /srv/dropbox, so deletions require group membership
chmod +t /srv/dropbox, setting the sticky bit so only owners can delete their files
explain: The sticky bit (+t, as on /tmp) on a directory restricts deletion/renaming to the file's owner, the directory's owner, or root — exactly the shared-dropbox semantics. 700 would lock everyone else out entirely; SGID governs group inheritance, not deletion; and +i immutable would freeze the directory for everyone including new file creation. Sticky bit is the purpose-built protection.

q: An admin runs auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k shadow-watch and gets alerts, but the rule is gone after a reboot. How is the watch made permanent?
options: Run auditctl --permanent -w /etc/shadow to write it to disk
Append the rule to /etc/sysconfig/auditd for the daemon to read
Enable the auditd timer unit so rules reload every hour
Add the rule to /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules so it loads at boot
explain: auditctl manages the runtime rule set only; persistence comes from rule files under /etc/audit/rules.d/, which augenrules compiles into /etc/audit/audit.rules at boot. auditctl has no --permanent flag; /etc/sysconfig/auditd holds daemon options, not rules; and no timer unit reloads rules. Runtime testing with auditctl, then committing to rules.d, is the correct workflow.

q: A script tracks retries with the variable n and must add 1 to it each loop iteration. Which statement performs arithmetic on n?
options: n="n + 1", which the shell evaluates as arithmetic automatically
n=n+1, which increments because n was declared with declare -i
explain: (( ... )) evaluates its contents as arithmetic, so (( n++ )) increments n — no $ needed inside. n="n + 1" stores the literal string; plain n=n+1 stores the literal text unless n was declared integer (it was not, in this scenario); and $n = $n + 1 is a syntax error (spaces around = in assignments). For arithmetic, use (( )), $(( )), or declare -i.

q: An admin wants to grep a multi-line variable $REPORT for the word ERROR without writing it to a file or using echo in a pipeline. Which construct feeds the variable to grep's stdin?
options: grep ERROR < $REPORT, redirecting the variable as a filename
grep ERROR << $REPORT, the here-document variable form
grep ERROR "$REPORT", passing the variable's content as filenames
explain: The here-string <<< "$REPORT" feeds the variable's value (plus a trailing newline) to grep's stdin — no temp file, no pipeline. < $REPORT treats the value as a filename; << starts a here-document that needs a delimiter word, not a variable; and quoting "$REPORT" as an argument passes its content as filenames to search. The here-string is the variable-to-stdin idiom.

q: A script offers an interactive menu with select choice in start stop restart. Inside the loop, how does the script know which NUMBER the user typed?
options: $REPLY, which holds the number the user entered
$choice, which holds the typed number rather than the word
$OPTARG, set by select to the user's numeric input
$#, which select sets to the menu selection
explain: select stores the user's typed input in $REPLY and the corresponding menu word in the named variable ($choice) — so $REPLY gives the number. $choice holds the selected word (start/stop/restart), not the number; $OPTARG belongs to getopts; and $# is the positional parameter count, untouched by select. Test $REPLY for the number, $choice for the value.

q: An Ansible task must deploy nginx.conf containing {{ worker_connections }} tuned per host. The current task uses the copy module and the literal text {{ worker_connections }} lands on servers. Which module renders the variables?
options: unarchive, which expands Jinja2 during extraction
synchronize, which templates files during rsync
template, which renders Jinja2 variables before deploying the file
lineinfile, which substitutes variables line by line
explain: The template module renders the source through Jinja2 before copying, so {{ worker_connections }} becomes the host's value; copy transfers bytes literally, which is why the raw braces landed on servers. unarchive extracts archives without templating; synchronize wraps rsync with no Jinja processing; and lineinfile manages single lines, not whole-file rendering. Variable-bearing configs need template, with the source conventionally named .j2.

q: An Ansible lineinfile task ensures "PermitRootLogin no" is in sshd_config, but repeated runs keep appending duplicates because some hosts have "PermitRootLogin yes". Which parameter fixes idempotency?
options: state=present, which is already the default and prevents duplicates
insertafter=EOF, forcing the line to the end of the file
regexp=^PermitRootLogin, matching the existing line so it is replaced instead of duplicated
backrefs=yes, which skips the task when the line already exists
explain: lineinfile without regexp only checks for the exact line, so 'PermitRootLogin yes' does not match and the desired line is appended again; regexp=^PermitRootLogin matches any existing variant and replaces it in place — idempotent. state=present is the default and does not add matching; insertafter controls placement, not matching; and backrefs only affects how backreferences in line are expanded. regexp is the idempotency key for lineinfile.

q: An admin needs to capture HTTP traffic on any interface while troubleshooting, without DNS lookups slowing the capture. Which tcpdump invocation does this?
options: tcpdump -i eth0 port 80, which skips DNS by default
tcpdump -i any -nn port 80, capturing all interfaces with numeric output
tcpdump -p port 80, where -p disables DNS resolution
explain: -i any captures on all interfaces and -nn disables both DNS resolution and port-name lookups, keeping the capture fast and the output numeric. Plain tcpdump resolves addresses by default, which stalls output; the long options shown do not exist; and -p disables promiscuous mode, not DNS. -nn is the standard 'do not resolve' flag pair for live troubleshooting captures.

q: A server with mostly idle CPUs shows a load average of 25. ps reveals dozens of processes in D state (uninterruptible sleep) waiting on an NFS mount whose server went away. What explains the high load?
options: Load average counts uninterruptible-sleep tasks, so the stuck NFS I/O inflates it despite idle CPUs
Each D-state process consumes 100% of a CPU, overloading the scheduler
The load average is miscalculated whenever an NFS filesystem is mounted
Idle CPUs always report maximum load until they are utilized
explain: Load average counts runnable tasks plus tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D state) — typically disk/NFS I/O waits — so a hung NFS mount inflates load with zero CPU consumption. D-state processes are asleep, not burning CPU; the calculation is correct, not miscalculated; and idle CPUs contribute nothing to load. High load with idle CPUs is the signature of an I/O hang, and the fix is the stuck mount, not more CPUs.

q: free -h shows only 400 MB 'free' but 6 GB 'available' on a 16 GB server, and the admin worries memory is exhausted. What does 'available' mean here?
options: Physical RAM chips that are installed but not yet initialized
Swap space reserved for emergency allocation
Memory the kernel estimates it can reclaim (page cache, buffers) for new processes without swapping
Memory locked by the kernel that user processes can never use
explain: 'available' estimates reclaimable memory — page cache and buffers the kernel can drop instantly — so 6 GB available means new processes can allocate freely despite low 'free'. Linux deliberately keeps 'free' low by caching disk data; uninitialized RAM would be a hardware fault, not a free column; swap is listed separately; and kernel-locked memory is not counted as available. Low free plus high available is healthy, not exhaustion.

q: An application fails to open its config file with 'Permission denied' though the path looks correct. Which strace invocation pinpoints the failing syscall?
options: strace -c ./app, summarizing all syscalls by total time
lsof -p $(pidof app), listing the app's open files
strace -e trace=openat -f ./app 2>&1 | grep -i denied, filtering to file-open syscalls
ltrace ./app, tracing library calls instead of syscalls
explain: strace -e trace=openat filters the trace to file-open syscalls, revealing the exact path and the EACCES return — the pinpoint diagnostic (-f follows forks). -c gives timing summaries, not the failing call; lsof shows open files but the open is what fails; and ltrace traces library calls, missing direct syscalls. Filter by syscall class to cut the noise.

q: A system drops to the grub rescue> prompt and the admin does not know which partition holds /boot/grub. Which commands locate it?
options: boot --list, which enumerates bootable partitions automatically
fdisk -l, available at the grub rescue prompt
ls to list devices, then ls (hd0,1)/ to inspect each partition's contents
cat /boot/grub/grub.cfg, which rescue mode keeps in memory
explain: At grub rescue>, ls lists detected devices/partitions and ls (hd0,1)/ shows a partition's top-level contents — the admin walks partitions until finding /boot/grub, then sets root, prefix, insmods normal, and runs normal. There is no boot --list command; fdisk is a Linux userspace tool unavailable in GRUB; and grub.cfg cannot be read before the prefix is set — finding it is the whole problem. ls plus per-partition inspection is the rescue workflow.

q: An admin needs to reboot a test server as fast as possible, skipping firmware initialization and the bootloader. Which mechanism performs this fast reboot?
options: systemctl reboot --firmware, which skips POST and goes straight to the kernel
echo b > /proc/sysrq-trigger, the fastest possible reboot method
shutdown -r now --no-firmware, bypassing the bootloader entirely
kexec, which loads the new kernel directly and jumps into it without a full hardware reboot
explain: kexec loads a new kernel into memory and transfers control directly, skipping BIOS/UEFI initialization and the bootloader — the fast-reboot mechanism. There is no --firmware skip flag for reboot (reboot --firmware-setup enters setup); sysrq-trigger b performs a full immediate reboot including firmware; and shutdown has no --no-firmware option. kexec trades speed for skipping hardware re-initialization.

q: A database service started by systemd keeps hitting 'too many open files' even though /etc/security/limits.d/db.conf sets nofile to 65535. Which setting actually applies to the systemd-managed service?
options: The limits.d file, once the admin runs ulimit -n 65535 in the service's shell
pam_limits, which systemd reads for every service at startup
LimitNOFILE=65535 in the service unit (or its drop-in), since systemd services ignore limits.conf
explain: systemd services do not go through PAM, so /etc/security/limits.d never applies to them; the resource limit must be set with LimitNOFILE= in the unit file or a drop-in. ulimit in a shell affects only that shell; pam_limits applies to PAM login sessions, not systemd services; and file-max is the system-wide total, not a per-process cap. limits.conf versus LimitNOFILE= is the classic trap.

q: On a RHEL 9 fleet, the kernel package must stay at the current version while all other packages update normally. Which dnf mechanism pins the kernel?
options: Add exclude=kernel* to /etc/dnf/dnf.conf, which is the versionlock method
dnf versionlock add kernel, pinning the package via the versionlock plugin
dnf mask kernel, preventing the package from being upgraded
explain: dnf versionlock (from the python3-dnf-plugins-core package) pins packages to their current versions while everything else updates. exclude= in dnf.conf also works but is a blunt repo-wide filter rather than the pinning mechanism; there is no dnf mask subcommand (mask is a systemctl concept); and protected.d only prevents removal, not upgrades. versionlock is the purpose-built pinning tool.

q: After deploying a fleet of servers, an admin discovers they all use the wrong console keymap and locale. Which command sets the system locale and keymap persistently?
options: localectl set-locale LANG=en_US.UTF-8 and localectl set-keymap us
export LANG and loadkeys in /etc/profile for all future logins
locale-gen with the desired locale, which also sets the keymap
timedatectl set-locale, the systemd locale and keymap tool
explain: localectl manages /etc/locale.conf (system locale) and /etc/vconsole.conf (console keymap) — the persistent systemd interface. /etc/profile exports affect shells only, not the system locale; locale-gen generates locale data on Debian-family systems but does not configure it; and timedatectl handles time/timezone, not locale. localectl set-locale plus set-keymap is the durable fix.

q: An admin adds a database hostname to /etc/hosts, but the application still resolves the old IP. getent hosts shows the new entry. What is the most likely cause?
options: /etc/hosts entries require a systemctl restart systemd-hostnamed to take effect
nscd or sssd is caching the old lookup; the application may also cache DNS itself
The hosts file needs a trailing dot on the hostname to be valid
/etc/hosts is only consulted when the network is unreachable
explain: getent hosts proving the new entry works means the file is fine; a stale answer implies caching — nscd/sssd caches or the application's own resolver cache (common in Java/Go apps). No daemon restart is needed for /etc/hosts; trailing dots apply to DNS zone files, not hosts entries; and nsswitch consults files per its configured order regardless of network state. When the file is right but the app sees old data, suspect a cache.

q: A developer's user-level systemd service (systemctl --user) dies every time they log out, breaking overnight jobs. Which command lets their user manager persist after logout?
options: systemctl --user enable-linger, which is set per user service
loginctl enable-linger developer, allowing the user manager to survive logout
Set KillUserProcesses=no in /etc/systemd/logind.conf for that user only
explain: loginctl enable-linger <user> starts the user's systemd manager at boot and keeps it running after logout, so --user services survive. There is no --user enable-linger flag; usermod has no --linger option; and KillUserProcesses=no in logind.conf is system-wide and controls process killing, not the user manager lifecycle. Linger is the per-user persistence switch.

q: On RHEL 9, an admin hand-edits /etc/pam.d/system-auth to add a module, but the change vanishes after a reboot. What is the supported way to customize PAM on RHEL 9?
options: Edit /etc/pam.d/system-auth-ac instead, which is never regenerated
Run authselect select with a custom profile, since authselect regenerates the PAM stack
explain: On RHEL 8+, authselect owns the PAM stack and regenerates files like system-auth from profiles, wiping hand edits; the supported path is authselect select <profile> with --feature options or a custom profile. system-auth-ac is a legacy authconfig artifact; there is no PAM_CONFIG_PERSIST knob; and /usr/etc is not the PAM location. If hand edits vanish, authselect is the owner.

q: A server must lock accounts for 10 minutes after 5 consecutive failed SSH logins. Which PAM module implements this account lockout?
options: pam_faillock, configured in the auth stack to deny after consecutive failures
pam_cracklib, which locks accounts after failed attempts
pam_limits, which enforces login attempt quotas
pam_access, which blocks users after too many failures
explain: pam_faillock tracks consecutive authentication failures and temporarily locks the account (unlock_time, deny parameters) — the lockout module. pam_cracklib/pwquality checks password strength, not login failures; pam_limits enforces resource limits (nofile, nproc); and pam_access controls access by origin/host, not failure counts. faillock is the brute-force mitigation in the PAM stack.

q: An admin runs a long series of sudo commands and wants to extend the sudo timestamp so no password prompt appears for the next 15 minutes. Which command refreshes it?
options: sudo -l, which lists privileges and refreshes the timestamp
sudo -k, which extends the timestamp for 15 more minutes
sudo -s, which resets the timestamp without a password
sudo -v, which validates and extends the sudo timestamp
explain: sudo -v validates the user's credentials and (re)starts the timestamp timeout without running a command — the refresh. sudo -l lists privileges but does not extend the timeout; sudo -k kills (invalidates) the timestamp, forcing the next prompt sooner; and sudo -s spawns a root shell, unrelated to timestamp management. -v is 'validate', -k is 'kill'.

q: Company policy requires users to be warned 14 days before their password expires. Which chage option sets the warning period?
options: chage -M 14, setting the warning to 14 days
chage -W 14, warning the user 14 days before password expiry
chage -E 14, expiring the account with 14 days notice
explain: chage -W sets the warning period (days before expiry the user is notified). -M sets the maximum password age itself, not the warning; -E sets the account expiration date; and -I sets the inactivity lockout period after expiry. -W is 'warn', -M is 'max days' — the classic chage flag confusion.

q: An admin generates an SSH key pair for automation. Which key type and file permissions follow current best practice?
options: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 with ~/.ssh at 700 and the private key at 600
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 1024 with the private key at 644 for script readability
ssh-keygen -t dsa with ~/.ssh at 755 so the daemon can read it
Copying the private key to each server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file
explain: ed25519 is the modern recommended key type (small, fast, secure); ~/.ssh must be 700 and the private key 600 or sshd refuses to trust them. RSA-1024 is weak and 644 on a private key is rejected; DSA is deprecated; and authorized_keys holds PUBLIC keys — deploying a private key to servers defeats the entire model. Generate ed25519, protect the private key, distribute the .pub.

q: An admin must deploy their public key to 30 servers for key-based login. Which command installs the key into a remote account's authorized_keys correctly?
options: ssh-add user@server, forwarding the key into authorized_keys
ssh-copy-id user@server, appending the public key with correct permissions
explain: ssh-copy-id appends the public key to the remote authorized_keys, creating ~/.ssh with proper permissions if needed — the purpose-built tool. scp would overwrite (destroying existing keys); ssh-add manages the local agent, not remote files; and piping the PRIVATE key anywhere is the cardinal sin — only the .pub belongs on servers. ssh-copy-id is the safe, idempotent deployer.

q: An admin manages firewall rules with nftables directly and wants to review the entire active ruleset. Which command dumps it?
options: iptables -L -n, which reads the nftables ruleset on modern systems
cat /etc/nftables.conf, which always reflects the running ruleset
nft list ruleset, printing tables, chains, and rules
explain: nft list ruleset dumps the complete active nftables configuration — all tables, chains, sets, and rules. iptables -L shows the iptables-nft translation layer, not native nftables objects; there is no nftables --dump command; and the config file only reflects the running state if it was loaded from there and never changed at runtime. nft list ruleset is the source of truth.

q: An admin tested a firewalld rich rule in the runtime configuration and now wants to keep it permanently without retyping it. Which command preserves it?
options: firewall-cmd --save, writing the runtime config to the zone files
firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent, writing runtime rules into permanent config
systemctl reload firewalld, which persists runtime changes automatically
cp /run/firewalld /etc/firewalld, copying the runtime state over
explain: firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent copies the current runtime configuration into the permanent zone files — the 'keep what I tested' command. There is no --save flag; reload applies permanent config to runtime (the reverse direction); and hand-copying /run state is unsupported and fragile. Test in runtime, then --runtime-to-permanent to keep it.

q: A critical config file must not be modified by anyone, including root, until planned maintenance. Which command makes it immutable, and how is the flag checked?
options: chmod 000 on the file; check with ls -l for the missing permissions
chattr +a on the file; check with lsattr for the append-only flag
setfacl -m u:root:--- on the file; check with getfacl
chattr +i on the file; verify with lsattr showing the 'i' attribute
explain: chattr +i sets the immutable flag — even root cannot modify, delete, or rename the file until chattr -i removes it; lsattr displays the attribute. chmod 000 still allows root (root bypasses permission checks); +a is append-only, which still permits writes; and an ACL denying root is ineffective since root bypasses ACL checks too. Only the immutable attribute stops root.

q: A script has uncommitted changes but the admin must urgently pull upstream fixes. Which git sequence safely shelves the work, pulls, and restores it?
options: git stash push, git pull, then git stash pop to restore the work
git commit -m wip, git pull, then git reset HEAD~1 to uncommit
git checkout -- ., git pull, then git checkout stash@{0}
git diff > /tmp/wip.patch, git pull, then git apply --reverse
explain: git stash push shelves working-tree changes, git pull updates cleanly, and git stash pop restores the changes — the standard interrupt workflow. Committing a wip just to pull pollutes history; checkout -- . discards the work permanently; and the manual patch round-trip works but apply --reverse would undo rather than restore. Stash is the purpose-built shelf.

q: A team wants linear history on their shared automation repo. A developer rebased a branch that a colleague had already pulled. What is the risk?
options: Rebase is forbidden on shared repos; git blocks pushing rebased branches
The rebased commits are deleted from the remote automatically
The colleague's next pull may duplicate or conflict commits, since rebase rewrites commit hashes
git rebase on a pulled branch corrupts the local repository
explain: Rebase rewrites commit hashes, so the colleague's copy and the rebased branch diverge: their next pull sees 'the same' changes as new commits, causing duplicates or conflicts. Git does not block pushing rebased branches (it may require --force-with-lease); nothing is auto-deleted remotely; and the local repo is not corrupted. The rule: never rebase commits others have based work on — rebase local-only branches, merge shared ones.

q: An Ansible playbook needs a database password inline without committing it in plaintext. Which command encrypts just the secret value for embedding?
options: ansible-vault encrypt_string 's3cret' --name db_password, producing an inline !vault block
ansible-vault encrypt vars.yml, which encrypts a single string value
echo 's3cret' | ansible-vault hash, generating the vaulted variable
gpg --encrypt vars.yml, the Ansible-native string encryption
explain: ansible-vault encrypt_string encrypts a single value into an inline !vault block assignable to db_password — the embedded-secret workflow. ansible-vault encrypt encrypts whole files, not inline values; there is no ansible-vault hash subcommand; and raw gpg output is not in Ansible's vault format. Pair it with --vault-password-file or prompt at run time.

q: An Ansible task must ensure /opt/app/data exists with mode 0750, including any missing parents. A second run must not report changes if it already exists. Which task is idempotent?
explain: The file module with state=directory is idempotent: it creates missing parents, sets the mode, and reports ok (no change) when the state already matches. command/shell tasks always report changed and re-run blindly; copy with a directory dest behaves unexpectedly (it copies the dir's contents semantics differ). For declarative filesystem state, the file module is the idempotent choice.

q: A developer runs rootless Podman and maps container port 8080 to host port 80, but the container fails to start. What is the most likely cause?
options: Podman requires --privileged to publish any host port
Rootless containers cannot bind host ports below 1024; use a high port or run rootful
Port 80 is reserved for the Podman API and can never be published
Rootless Podman cannot use port mapping at all; only host networking works
explain: Unprivileged users cannot bind ports below 1024 (the privileged range) — a kernel restriction, not a Podman bug — so rootless port 80 fails; map to 8080+ or run rootful. --privileged affects container capabilities, not host port binding; port 80 is not Podman-reserved; and rootless Podman supports port mapping fine within the unprivileged range. The sub-1024 bind rule is the classic rootless gotcha.

q: An admin needs journal entries for the nginx service from the last 90 minutes only. Which journalctl invocation filters this precisely?
options: journalctl -u nginx --tail 90, showing the last 90 minutes
journalctl -u nginx --last 90m, the relative time filter
explain: journalctl --since accepts natural relative times like '90 minutes ago' (also --until for the end bound) — the precise time filter. There is no --tail flag (--lines/-n limits line count, not time); -b selects a boot, not a duration; and --last is not a journalctl option. Combine -u with --since/--until for surgical log windows.

q: An unprivileged helpdesk user must trace the network path to a remote host, but traceroute fails without root. Which tool works without elevated privileges?
options: ping -R, which records the route without privileges
mtr --raw, which bypasses the privilege requirement
tracepath, which uses UDP and needs no special privileges
explain: tracepath performs path discovery with UDP packets and works unprivileged — the purpose-built non-root tracer. Classic traceroute needs raw sockets (root) for its default UDP/ICMP methods; ping -R records routes but is not a hop-by-hop trace; mtr still needs privileges for most modes; and traceroute -I uses ICMP which requires raw socket privileges. tracepath is the helpdesk-friendly answer.

q: An admin cannot unmount /data because it is busy, and needs to identify the holding processes. Which command lists processes using the mountpoint?
options: lsof /etc/mtab, listing processes attached to mounts
fuser -v /data, showing which processes hold the filesystem busy
ps aux | grep data, finding processes with 'data' in the name
umount -f /data, which lists blockers before force-unmounting
explain: fuser -v /data lists the PIDs and users accessing the mountpoint — the direct 'who is holding it busy' query (fuser -k would kill them). lsof /etc/mtab inspects the wrong file; grepping ps matches names, not open files; and umount -f force-unmounts without listing blockers. fuser identifies; lsof /data would also work.

q: lsof -i :8080 shows a PID holding the port, but every kill is followed by a new PID holding the same port. What is happening, and what is the fix?
options: The process is a zombie; zombies hold ports until the parent reaps them — kill the parent PID
The port is stuck in TIME_WAIT; wait 60 seconds for the kernel to release it
A supervisor (systemd) is restarting the service; stop the owning unit with systemctl stop instead of killing PIDs
lsof caches its output; the port is actually free, so just retry the service start
explain: A respawning PID means a supervisor — usually systemd with Restart= — is bringing the service back; killing PIDs fights the supervisor forever. The fix is systemctl stop (and disable if unwanted) on the owning unit, found via systemctl status <pid> or the service name. Zombies hold no resources including ports; TIME_WAIT does not respawn PIDs; and lsof reads live kernel state, not a cache.

q: An application crashes intermittently and the admin wants to inspect its core dumps with metadata (timestamps, executable, signal). Which tool lists and examines them?
options: coredumpctl list and coredumpctl info, the systemd core-dump journal interface
dmesg | grep -i core, which archives core dump metadata
explain: systemd-coredump stores crashes centrally and coredumpctl list/info/gdb provide the metadata and inspection interface — timestamps, executable, signal, and stack traces. dmesg only logs that a segfault occurred; the raw files under /var/lib/systemd/coredump are compressed (lz4) and not directly readable; and core_pattern is a configuration knob, not an inspector. coredumpctl is the crash-triage tool.

q: An admin downloads nginx-1.24.0.rpm from a vendor site for an air-gapped server and wants to inspect its metadata and file list before installing anything. Which command shows the package info and the files it would install without touching the system?
options: rpm -qip nginx-1.24.0.rpm and rpm -qlp nginx-1.24.0.rpm — the -p flag queries the package file itself
rpm -qi nginx and rpm -ql nginx — query the installed-package database directly
dnf info nginx-1.24.0.rpm — dnf reads local package files without a repo
rpm -ivh --test nginx-1.24.0.rpm — test mode lists the files instead of installing
explain: The -p flag tells rpm to query a package FILE rather than the installed database, so -qip shows metadata and -qlp lists payload files with zero system changes. Without -p, rpm -qi/-ql only consult the RPM database and fail for uninstalled packages. dnf info on a local path is not the portable rpm-native inspection method, and rpm -ivh --test performs a transaction dependency test, not a file listing.

q: A security scan flags /usr/sbin/sshd as modified. The admin wants to know which installed package owns that binary so it can be verified next. Which command answers that?
options: rpm -ql openssh-server — lists every file the package installed
rpm -qf /usr/sbin/sshd — queries which package owns the file
rpm -qi /usr/sbin/sshd — info lookup by file path
dnf provides /usr/sbin/sshd — only works against remote repositories
explain: rpm -qf (query file) maps an installed path back to its owning package — the first step before running rpm -V on it. rpm -ql goes the other direction (package to files); rpm -qi needs a package NAME, not a path; and while dnf provides can resolve paths, it may hit the network, whereas -qf answers instantly from the local database.

q: An admin worries that anyone with console access can press 'e' at the GRUB menu and append init=/bin/bash to bypass authentication. Which command sets a password that GRUB requires before allowing menu edits?
options: passwd root — the root password also guards the GRUB menu
grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 — it generates a hash but does not install it into GRUB
grub2-setpassword — stores a PBKDF2-hashed GRUB password that locks menu editing
echo 'set superusers=root' >> /boot/grub2/grub.cfg — hand-editing the generated config persists
explain: grub2-setpassword prompts for a password, hashes it with PBKDF2, and writes it into the GRUB user config so editing boot entries requires authentication. The OS root password is unrelated to the bootloader menu; grub2-mkpasswd-pbkdf2 only PRINTS a hash for manual config use; and hand-editing the generated grub.cfg is overwritten on the next grub2-mkconfig run.

q: After a firmware update, a server boots straight into the rescue entry instead of the production RHEL entry. The admin wants to reorder UEFI boot entries persistently. Which tool does this?
options: grubby --set-default — reorders UEFI NVRAM boot entries
grub2-reboot — permanently changes the UEFI boot order
tuned-adm — boot entry priority is a tuned profile setting
efibootmgr -o 0001,0000,0003 — rewrites the UEFI BootOrder variable in NVRAM
explain: efibootmgr manipulates UEFI NVRAM variables directly, and -o sets the BootOrder list the firmware follows. grubby manages kernel boot arguments and the GRUB default entry, not firmware NVRAM order; grub2-reboot selects the next boot only (one-shot); and tuned-adm adjusts performance profiles, having nothing to do with boot entries.

q: An admin adds a kernel module to /etc/dracut.conf.d/ so it loads during early boot for LUKS decryption, then reboots — but the module is still missing at boot. What step was missed?
options: Rebuild the initramfs with dracut --force so the new configuration is baked into the early-boot image
Run grub2-mkconfig — dracut.conf changes are picked up by the bootloader automatically
Run modprobe -r first — the module must be unloaded before dracut can include it
Edit /etc/modules-load.d/ instead — dracut.conf is only read at install time
explain: The initramfs is a static cpio image built at kernel-install time; editing dracut config files changes nothing until dracut --force regenerates the image containing the module. grub2-mkconfig regenerates the boot menu, not the initramfs; modprobe -r unloads the live module, which is unrelated to early-boot inclusion; and modules-load.d handles post-boot loading, not initramfs content.

q: An admin uses systemctl edit sshd to add a drop-in override, saves, then runs systemctl restart sshd — but the new setting has no effect. What is missing?
options: systemctl edit writes to /tmp — the file must be copied into /etc/systemd/system manually
systemctl daemon-reload — systemd must re-read unit files before the restart picks up the change
systemctl enable sshd — overrides only apply to enabled services
A reboot — drop-in overrides are only parsed at boot time
explain: systemd caches parsed unit files in memory, so any edit — drop-in or full — requires systemctl daemon-reload before a restart will honor it. systemctl edit writes directly into the proper /etc/systemd/system/*.d/ directory, not /tmp; enablement controls boot-time activation, not configuration parsing; and no reboot is needed once the daemon reloads.

q: A service is running fine right now, but the admin suspects it will not survive a reboot. Which check confirms whether it starts automatically at boot?
options: systemctl is-active app.service — active means it will start at boot
systemctl status app.service — the enablement line in status output is decorative
systemctl is-enabled app.service — it reports the boot-time enablement state
ps -ef | grep app — a running process proves boot persistence
explain: is-enabled queries the boot-time state (enabled/disabled/static/masked) from the unit symlinks, which is exactly the reboot question. is-active and ps only describe this moment — a manually started service is active but not enabled; and while status does show the Loaded enablement state, is-enabled is the direct, scriptable check.

q: During boot troubleshooting, an admin wants to see everything multi-user.target pulls in, in tree form. Which command shows that dependency tree?
options: systemctl list-units --type=target — shows the tree of all targets
systemd-analyze dot multi-user.target — renders the full dependency tree as text
systemctl show multi-user.target — prints Requires= and Wants= as a tree
systemctl list-dependencies multi-user.target — prints the dependency tree
explain: list-dependencies walks Requires/Wants relationships and prints them as an indented tree. list-units shows a flat list of loaded units; systemd-analyze dot emits Graphviz DOT source meant for piping to dot, not reading as a tree; and systemctl show dumps flat key=value properties without tree formatting.

q: A server takes six minutes to boot. The admin wants to know which unit is actually blocking the boot chain rather than just slow on its own. Which analysis answers that?
options: systemd-analyze critical-chain — highlights the time-critical chain of units blocking boot
systemd-analyze blame — identifies the single unit blocking the boot
journalctl -b -p emerg — lists the boot-blocking unit by severity
systemctl list-jobs — shows which units blocked the completed boot
explain: critical-chain computes the chain of units whose delays actually serial-blocked boot completion, unlike blame which merely sorts all units by individual startup time (a slow-but-parallel unit misleads). journalctl -b -p emerg filters log severity, not timing; and list-jobs shows currently queued jobs, which is empty after boot finishes.

q: A terminated employee's processes keep respawning under their UID even after pkill -9 -u. Which command cleans up all of the user's sessions, services, and lingering processes?
options: userdel exuser — deleting the account kills all running processes
loginctl terminate-user exuser — kills all sessions and user processes tracked by logind
systemctl stop user@UID.service — stops only the user's systemd services
killall -u exuser — stronger signal delivery than pkill
explain: loginctl terminate-user tells systemd-logind to kill every session, scope, and lingering process belonging to the user — the only option reaching processes supervised outside plain sessions. userdel removes the account but leaves processes running; stopping user@UID.service misses session scopes; and killall -u is just another signal sender, which already failed via pkill.

q: An admin moves nginx to listen on TCP 8080, but SELinux blocks the bind even though the firewall is open. Which command permits the web server domain to bind that port?
options: semanage boolean -P -e httpd_can_network_connect — booleans control port binding
chcon -t http_port_t /usr/sbin/nginx — labels the binary for the new port
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 — adds the port to the SELinux policy's web-port type
setsebool -P httpd_bind_all_unreserved=1 — the standard fix for custom web ports
explain: SELinux policy maps ports to types; semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 persistently authorizes web-server processes to bind 8080. Booleans like httpd_can_network_connect govern outbound connections, not binds; chcon labels files, never ports; and there is no httpd_bind_all_unreserved boolean — port labeling is the documented mechanism.

q: AVC denials appear in the audit log for a custom application. The admin first wants to know WHY the denial happened (missing boolean? mislabeled file?) before writing any policy. Which tool explains the denial?
options: audit2allow -a — it explains the root cause of each denial
semanage permissive -a app_t — diagnosing requires permissive mode first
ausearch -m AVC --raw | setenforce 0 — raw output self-explains with enforcing off
audit2why -a — it translates AVC denials into human-readable causes and suggested fixes
explain: audit2why parses AVC denials and reports the cause — e.g., a boolean to flip or a file needing restorecon — which is the diagnostic step. audit2allow generates allow-rule policy modules (the fix, not the explanation); making the domain permissive skips diagnosis entirely; and piping raw denials into setenforce 0 is nonsense — setenforce takes no stdin and toggling enforcing masks the symptom.

q: An admin runs setenforce 0 to troubleshoot, fixes the issue, and reboots — SELinux is enforcing again. How should the admin have made a lasting mode change instead?
options: Set SELINUX=permissive in /etc/selinux/config — setenforce only changes the runtime mode
Run setenforce -P 0 — the -P flag makes the mode change permanent
Edit /etc/sysconfig/selinux — setenforce reads its persistent state from there
Run semanage permissive -a unconfined_t — setenforce 0 only affects unconfined domains
explain: setenforce toggles the current kernel mode only; the /etc/selinux/config SELINUX= line is what the init process reads at boot, so persistence requires editing it. There is no -P flag on setenforce; /etc/sysconfig/selinux is merely a symlink to /etc/selinux/config on RHEL, not a separate source; and semanage permissive makes one domain permissive — a narrower tool than the system-wide mode.

q: On Ubuntu, an application keeps getting killed and the admin suspects its AppArmor profile. They want the profile to LOG violations instead of enforcing while they investigate. Which command does that?
options: aa-disable /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.app — disabling is the only way to stop enforcement
aa-complain /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.app — switches the profile to complain (log-only) mode
apparmor_parser -R /etc/apparmor.d/usr.bin.app — reloads the profile in debug mode
setenforce 0 — AppArmor follows the SELinux enforcing flag
explain: aa-complain flips a profile into complain mode, where violations are logged but permitted — the safe diagnostic posture. aa-disable removes enforcement AND logging entirely; apparmor_parser -R unloads (removes) the profile rather than debugging it; and setenforce is an SELinux command with no effect on AppArmor.

q: An admin sets chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf to stop NetworkManager overwriting it, but later even root gets 'Operation not permitted' editing the file. What is happening?
options: The filesystem is mounted read-only — remount it read-write first
SELinux is denying root — check for AVC denials before editing
The immutable flag is set — root included, nobody can modify the file until chattr -i clears it
The file's ACL mask was zeroed by chattr — restore it with setfacl
explain: chattr +i sets the immutable attribute, which the kernel enforces against all users including root; only chattr -i removes it. A read-only mount would block writes to every file, not one; SELinux denials log to the audit log and would not follow a chattr +i change; and chattr does not touch ACLs — the mask theory confuses two unrelated mechanisms.

q: Before a Friday change window, an admin wants an Ansible playbook run that reports exactly what WOULD change on the fleet without changing anything. Which flags do that?
options: ansible-playbook site.yml --syntax-check — validates syntax and reports changes
ansible-playbook site.yml --step — prompts before each change, which is the dry-run mode
ansible-playbook site.yml --force — forces a report-only run
ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff — check mode predicts changes, diff shows them
explain: --check runs the play in dry-run mode where modules report would-be changes, and --diff renders the file/template differences that would be applied. --syntax-check only parses YAML without contacting hosts; --step is interactive confirmation per task but still applies changes; and there is no --force report-only flag.

q: An Ansible project behaves differently on two machines. The admin suspects conflicting ansible.cfg files. Which location wins when several exist?
options: ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable, then ./ansible.cfg in the project dir, then ~/.ansible.cfg, then /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg
/etc/ansible/ansible.cfg always wins — system config overrides user config
The first ansible.cfg found by searching upward from the playbook directory
explain: Ansible's documented precedence is the ANSIBLE_CONFIG env var first, then ansible.cfg in the current working directory, then ~/.ansible.cfg, then /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg last. System config is the weakest, not the strongest; home config loses to the project-local file; and Ansible does not search upward through parent directories.

q: A playbook connects as the deploy user but one task must run as the postgres OS user to run psql. How should the task escalate?
options: Set remote_user: postgres on the task — the task reconnects over SSH as the postgres user
Set become: true and become_user: postgres on the task — privilege escalation to the named user
Use ansible_user: postgres in the task vars — per-task connection users switch the OS user
Prefix the command with sudo -u postgres — privilege escalation belongs in the shell command
explain: become: true with become_user: postgres is Ansible's privilege-escalation mechanism, applying sudo/su to that task as the postgres user within the existing connection. remote_user would open a NEW SSH connection as postgres (needing its keys and host access) rather than escalating; ansible_user likewise sets the connection user, not a mid-task switch; and embedding sudo in shell commands breaks idempotency reporting and --check mode.

q: A playbook manages 50 config files for nginx. The admin wants nginx restarted once, and only if at least one file actually changed. Which pattern does this?
options: Add a restart task after every file task with when: changed — handlers are deprecated
Use notify: restart nginx on each task and define the handler with listen: always_run
notify: restart nginx from the file tasks and define a handler — handlers run once at the end, only if notified by a changed task
Register each task result and add a final task with when: results is changed
explain: Handlers notified by tasks run once at the end of the play and only when a notifying task reported changed — exactly the desired semantics. when: changed on restart tasks would restart per-file (multiple restarts); a listen: always_run handler would restart unconditionally; and hand-rolling registered-result logic duplicates what notify already does idempotently.

q: A command task runs a legacy check script that exits 1 even on success, printing 'OK' to stdout. The admin wants the task to fail only when the output does NOT contain OK. How?
options: ignore_errors: yes — then grep the registered output in a later task
Set check_mode: no — check mode overrides the script's exit code
Use shell: with set -e — the shell normalizes the exit code
Register the result and set failed_when: "'OK' not in result.stdout" — custom failure logic on the output
explain: failed_when lets the task define failure from any Jinja2 expression, here keying off stdout content instead of the lying exit code. ignore_errors: yes would mask real failures and needs extra tasks; check_mode: no only forces execution in check mode, unrelated to exit codes; and set -e makes the shell exit on the script's nonzero status, which still fails the task.

q: A BIOS-booted server fails with 'error: file /grub/i386-pc/normal.mod not found' and drops to a grub rescue prompt — the GRUB core image no longer matches its module directory. After booting rescue media and chrooting into the system, which command reinstalls GRUB consistently?
options: grub2-install /dev/sda — rewrites the boot-sector core image and the module directory together
grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg — regenerates the missing module files
dracut --force — rebuilds the GRUB modules into the initramfs
efibootmgr -c -d /dev/sda — recreates the BIOS boot entry in NVRAM
explain: grub2-install writes a fresh core image to the disk's boot sector/MBR gap AND installs the matching module tree, fixing the version mismatch that caused normal.mod not found. grub2-mkconfig only regenerates the menu config, never modules; dracut builds the initramfs, not the bootloader; and efibootmgr manages UEFI NVRAM entries — meaningless on a BIOS-booted disk.

q: On an Ubuntu server, the admin boots into recovery mode (root shell) to reset a lost password, but passwd fails with 'Authentication token manipulation error'. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The root account is locked — run passwd -u root first
The filesystem is mounted read-only in recovery mode — run mount -o remount,rw / then passwd
Recovery mode requires the old password — use sudo passwd instead
AppArmor blocks the change — run aa-complain on the passwd profile first
explain: Recovery mode mounts the root filesystem read-only, so passwd cannot write /etc/shadow — 'Authentication token manipulation error' is the telltale; remounting read-write fixes it. The account is not locked; sudo is pointless in a root shell; and AppArmor is not the cause — the read-only mount is.

q: After an unclean shutdown the root filesystem mounted read-only, and nothing can be written. The admin wants to remount it read-write without rebooting. Which command does it?
options: mount -a — re-reads /etc/fstab and remounts everything read-write
fsck -y / — repairs the filesystem while it is mounted read-only
mount -o remount,rw / — remounts the live root filesystem read-write
tune2fs -o rw /dev/sda1 — flips the filesystem's mount mode flag
explain: mount -o remount,rw / changes the live mount's options in place with no reboot. mount -a only mounts entries not yet mounted and will not flip an existing ro mount; fsck on a mounted filesystem risks corruption and does not remount; and tune2fs edits filesystem superblock features, not the current mount state.

q: An admin deleted a 50 GB log file, but df still shows the space as used because the application holds the file open — and the service cannot be restarted right now. How can they reclaim the space immediately?
options: Run sync — sync flushes deleted file data back to the free pool
Run fstrim -av — trim reclaims deleted-but-open space
Recreate the filename with touch — a new name frees the old data
: > /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> — truncating the open file descriptor releases the blocks while the process keeps running
explain: The blocks stay allocated while any file descriptor references them; truncating via /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> empties the file in place, freeing the space without killing the process. sync only flushes pending writes; fstrim discards unused SSD blocks, not open-file data; and recreating the name creates a NEW file — the orphaned data stays allocated.

q: Large file transfers stall over a VPN while small packets flow fine. The admin suspects an MTU black hole. Which test probes the path MTU?
options: ping -i 0.2 target — faster pings reveal MTU issues
ping -M do -s 1472 target — sets Don't-Fragment with a large payload to test MTU
ping -I eth0 target — binding the interface measures its MTU
traceroute --mtu target — traceroute auto-discovers MTU by default
explain: -M do sets the Don't-Fragment bit and -s 1472 sends a full-size payload; if an intermediate link has a smaller MTU and cannot fragment, the ping fails — bisecting the size finds the path MTU. -i only changes the interval; -I selects the source interface (the classic -i/-I trap in reverse); and traceroute has no --mtu option and does not discover MTU.

q: A RHEL VM runs latency-sensitive workloads and the admin wants the OS to apply a canned, tested set of kernel and device tunings favoring throughput. Which tool applies such a predefined performance profile?
options: tuned-adm profile throughput-performance — activates a predefined tuning profile
cpupower frequency-set -g powersave — the powersave governor maximizes throughput
sysctl -w kernel.tuned=throughput — enables the throughput sysctl
nice -n -20 workload — nice values apply system-wide tuning profiles
explain: tuned ships tested profiles (throughput-performance, latency-performance, virtual-guest, etc.), and tuned-adm profile applies one, adjusting sysctl, disk, and CPU settings coherently. cpupower powersave throttles CPUs — the opposite of throughput; there is no kernel.tuned sysctl; and nice only adjusts one process's CPU priority, not system tuning.

q: A compute node should never drop CPU frequency, even at idle. Which setting pins the scaling governor to maximum performance?
options: cpupower frequency-info — info mode locks the current frequency
cpupower frequency-set -g performance — selects the performance governor
echo performance > /proc/cpuinfo — the kernel reads the governor from cpuinfo
tuned-adm off — disabling tuned forces maximum frequency
explain: cpupower frequency-set -g performance selects the performance governor, which keeps CPUs at top frequency. frequency-info only reports; /proc/cpuinfo is read-only kernel output, not a control knob; and disabling tuned merely stops profile management without pinning any governor.

q: After dnf update upgraded glibc and openssl on a production server, the admin wants to know whether a reboot is required and which services need restarts. Which command answers both?
options: systemctl daemon-reload — reloads daemons after library updates
lsof | grep DEL — lists libraries needing a reboot
needs-restarting -r and needs-restarting -s — reboot check plus services using outdated libraries
dnf check-update — shows which updates require a reboot
explain: needs-restarting -r reports whether core libraries changed enough to warrant a reboot, and -s lists services still running against deleted (updated) library files. daemon-reload only re-reads unit files; grepping lsof for DEL is a manual approximation, not the supported tool; and dnf check-update lists pending updates, not post-update restart requirements.

q: An admin blacklists the nouveau driver in /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist.conf, rebuilds nothing, and reboots — nouveau still loads. Why?
options: Blacklist entries require a matching alias line to take effect
modprobe.d is only read by lsmod — use /etc/modules-load.d/ instead
The blacklist syntax changed — modern systems use denylist= instead of blacklist
The driver is baked into the initramfs — rebuild it with dracut --force so the blacklist applies at early boot
explain: Drivers needed at early boot live inside the initramfs, which is built once; a blacklist added afterward has no effect until dracut --force regenerates the image. blacklist lines need no alias companion; modprobe.d is read by modprobe itself (lsmod just lists); and while 'denylist' is a newer alias, 'blacklist' still works — the stale initramfs is the real cause.

q: A database server swaps aggressively under load. The admin wants the kernel to avoid swap unless memory is nearly exhausted, persistently. Which change does this?
options: Add vm.swappiness=10 to /etc/sysctl.d/99-db.conf and run sysctl --system — lowers swap tendency persistently
Run sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10 — the -w flag writes through to the config file
Add vm.swappiness=10 to /etc/fstab — fstab stores kernel tunables
echo 10 > /proc/sys/vm/swappiness and add it to /etc/rc.local — proc writes persist via rc.local
explain: A /etc/sysctl.d/ drop-in plus sysctl --system applies and persists the tunable across reboots; 10 makes the kernel strongly prefer reclaiming file cache over swapping. sysctl -w is runtime-only despite the name; fstab configures mounts, not kernel tunables; and /proc writes vanish at reboot while rc.local is obsolete on systemd systems.

q: A user is locked out after too many bad passwords and insists they now remember the right one. The admin wants to clear the lockout immediately. Which command does it?
options: passwd -u username — unlocks the password after faillock trips
faillock --user username --reset — clears the recorded failures and the lock
chage -E -1 username — removes the faillock expiry
pam_faillock --clear username — faillock is managed through the PAM module binary
explain: faillock --user <name> --reset clears the failure tally that pam_faillock recorded, immediately ending the lockout. passwd -u unlocks a manually locked password (passwd -l), a different mechanism; chage -E manages account expiry dates, not failure counts; and there is no pam_faillock user-facing binary — faillock is the admin tool.

q: Company policy requires new passwords to be at least 14 characters with at least one digit. Where should the admin enforce this for all local users?
options: /etc/security/pwquality.conf — minlen=14 and dcredit=-1 via the pam_pwquality module
/etc/pam.d/common-password — complexity is hardcoded in the PAM service file
explain: pam_pwquality enforces complexity and reads its rules from /etc/security/pwquality.conf, where minlen=14 sets length and dcredit=-1 requires at least one digit. login.defs PASS_MIN_LEN only affects some tools and has no digit-credit concept; chage manages aging/expiry, not complexity; and /etc/pam.d files reference the module — the tunable values live in pwquality.conf.

q: A RHEL 9 fleet must authenticate against FreeIPA with home directories auto-created on first login. Which command configures the auth stack for this?
options: authconfig --enableldap --enablemkhomedir — the classic auth configuration tool
Edit /etc/pam.d/system-auth by hand — authselect is read-only reporting
realm permit --all — realm handles both SSSD config and home directory creation
authselect select sssd with-mkhomedir — applies the SSSD profile with automatic home directory creation
explain: authselect select sssd with-mkhomedir writes the consistent PAM/nsswitch stack for SSSD and enables the mkhomedir feature. authconfig was removed after RHEL 7; hand-editing system-auth fights authselect, which regenerates those files; and realm joins domains and can permit users, but profile selection with the mkhomedir feature is authselect's job.

q: An admin removes a departed contractor with userdel contractor, but a later audit finds /home/contractor and their mail spool still on disk. What should have been used?
options: userdel -r contractor — the -r flag also removes the home directory and mail spool
userdel -f contractor — force mode cleans up home directories
deluser --system contractor — the system flag removes home directories
usermod -L contractor — locking the account purges its files
explain: Plain userdel removes only the account entries; -r additionally deletes the user's home directory and mail spool. -f forces removal despite a logged-in user but does not touch the home dir; deluser is Debian-family and --system is for system accounts; and usermod -L merely locks the password, leaving all files in place.

q: A vendor needs SSH access for exactly 30 days. The admin wants the account itself to stop working after that date, not just the password. Which enforces an account expiration date?
options: chage -M 30 vendor — password aging disables the account after 30 days
chage -E $(date -d '+30 days' +%F) vendor — sets the date the account itself expires
passwd -x 30 vendor — password max days locks the whole account
usermod -e never vendor — the -e flag with 'never' expires the account
explain: chage -E sets the account expiration date in /etc/shadow, after which no login is possible regardless of password validity. chage -M and passwd -x only age the PASSWORD (forcing a change, not disabling the account); and usermod -e takes a date — 'never' is not valid input for expiring an account.

q: Users report certificate warnings on the company webmail. The admin wants to check the presented certificate's expiry and chain from the command line. Which command does it?
options: curl -I https://webmail --cert-info — curl prints the full chain by default
openssl x509 -in /etc/ssl/cert.pem — reads the server's live certificate
openssl s_client -connect webmail:443 -servername webmail < /dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer — fetches the live cert and shows dates and issuer
explain: openssl s_client performs a real TLS handshake against the live service (with -servername for SNI), and piping the cert to openssl x509 -noout shows its dates and issuer — verifying what clients actually see. curl -I shows headers, not cert details; openssl x509 -in reads a local file that may not match what is served; and ssh-keygen -L inspects SSH certificates, not X.509 TLS certs.

q: SSH to a host is using an unexpected key, and the admin suspects overlapping Host blocks in ~/.ssh/config and /etc/ssh/ssh_config. How can they see the final merged configuration ssh will use?
options: sshd -T — dumps the effective client configuration
cat ~/.ssh/config — the user config overrides everything, so the system file can be ignored
ssh -v host — verbose output prints the merged config file contents
ssh -G host — prints the effective configuration after merging all config sources
explain: ssh -G resolves a hostname through every config source (system ssh_config, user config, command line) and prints the resulting effective options — the authoritative answer for 'which IdentityFile wins'. sshd -T dumps the SERVER daemon config, not the client; the user file does not override everything (first-obtained value wins per option); and ssh -v shows negotiation debug, not the merged config.

q: SSH brute-force attempts are hammering a server. The admin installed fail2ban and wants to confirm the sshd jail is active and see currently banned IPs. Which command shows this?
options: fail2ban-client status sshd — shows the jail's status and banned IP list
systemctl status fail2ban — lists banned IPs in the unit status
iptables -L -n — fail2ban bans appear as ACCEPT rules
lastb | grep sshd — lastb is fail2ban's ban database
explain: fail2ban-client status <jail> queries the running daemon for that jail's filter, action, and currently banned IPs. systemctl status shows daemon state, not jail data; fail2ban inserts DROP/reject rules (not ACCEPT), and reading raw iptables is indirect; and lastb reports failed logins from btmp — the INPUT fail2ban watches, not its ban list.

q: An admin downloads a kernel tarball plus its .sig signature file from kernel.org. Before building, they want to verify the tarball is authentic. Which command does this?
options: gpg --verify tarball.tar.xz.sig tarball.tar.xz — verifies the detached OpenPGP signature
openssl dgst -sha256 tarball.tar.xz — digests authenticate the publisher
gpg --decrypt tarball.tar.xz.sig — decrypting the signature reveals the tarball
explain: gpg --verify checks the detached .sig against the tarball using the publisher's public key, proving both integrity AND origin. Checksums and openssl dgst only prove the file matches a hash — an attacker can ship a matching hash file; and --decrypt is for encrypted data, while a .sig is a signature to be verified, not decrypted.

q: An admin wants firewalld to rate-limit SSH: accept new connections but drop bursts above 5 per minute from one source. Which rule expresses this?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=ssh-limit — firewalld ships a rate-limited ssh service
firewall-cmd --permanent --direct --add-rule ipv4 filter INPUT 0 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT — direct rules support limits
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=0.0.0.0/0 port port=22 protocol=tcp limit value="5/m" accept' — a rich rule with a rate limit
explain: Rich rules support a limit element (value="5/m") that caps matching packets per time unit — the native firewalld way to throttle SSH. There is no ssh-limit service; --direct rules bypass firewalld's abstractions and the example has no limit match; and --timeout makes a runtime rule temporary, unrelated to rate limiting.

q: Before running a playbook against a new inventory, an admin wants a fast sanity check that Ansible can reach every host and that facts gather cleanly. Which ad-hoc commands do this?
options: ansible all -m shell -a uptime — shell is the fastest connectivity check
ansible-playbook --list-hosts — lists hosts and tests connectivity
ansible all -a 'echo ok' — the raw echo module tests SSH
ansible all -m ping, then ansible all -m setup --tree /tmp/facts — ping module verifies the Python/SSH path, setup gathers facts
explain: The ping module (which sends no ICMP — it runs a Python echo over the connection) verifies Ansible's full connection path, and the setup module exercises fact gathering; --tree saves facts per host for inspection. shell -a uptime works but skips module-subsystem validation; --list-hosts only prints inventory without connecting; and -a 'echo ok' uses the command module implicitly — fine for SSH but not for Ansible's Python bootstrap.

q: A developer committed to the wrong branch and wants to move the branch pointer back one commit but KEEP the changes staged for recommitting elsewhere. Which command does this?
options: git reset --soft HEAD~1 — moves the branch pointer, keeping index and working tree intact
git reset --hard HEAD~1 — the standard undo that preserves staged changes
git revert HEAD — revert keeps the changes staged
git checkout HEAD~1 — detaches the branch with changes preserved
explain: --soft moves only the branch pointer, leaving the index and working tree untouched so the changes stay staged for the correct branch. --hard also wipes the working tree and index — destroying the work; revert creates a NEW inverse commit rather than removing one; and checkout HEAD~1 detaches HEAD without moving any branch pointer.

q: A regression appeared somewhere in the last 200 commits. The developer wants Git to binary-search the history, testing each midpoint. Which workflow does this?
options: git log --oneline | head -100 — manual bisection through the log
git bisect start, then git bisect bad, git bisect good <known-good>, testing each checkout and marking good/bad — Git binary-searches to the culprit commit
git blame file — blame binary-searches commit ranges automatically
git reflog --bisect — reflog has a built-in bisect mode
explain: git bisect automates the binary search: given a known-bad and known-good commit it checks out midpoints and narrows to the first bad commit from good/bad verdicts. Manually paging git log is the laborious alternative; git blame attributes LINES, not regressions across ranges; and there is no reflog --bisect flag.

q: A developer must urgently fix a production bug on main while their feature branch has uncommitted changes they don't want to stash. How can they work on main simultaneously?
options: git stash push --keep-index — stashing is required before switching branches
git checkout -b hotfix — a new branch shares the working tree, so uncommitted changes carry over safely
git worktree add ../hotfix main — creates a second working tree on main alongside the current one
git clone . ../hotfix — cloning the repo directory is the supported method
explain: git worktree add creates an additional working tree checked out to another branch, so the feature branch's uncommitted changes stay untouched while the hotfix proceeds in parallel. Stashing is not mandatory — just one option; checkout -b carries the dirty tree into the new branch, mixing the changes; and re-cloning duplicates the object store wastefully when worktree is built for this.

q: A backup script occasionally hangs on a stale NFS mount. The admin wants any single rsync invocation to be killed if it runs longer than 30 minutes. Which wrapper does this?
options: nice -n 10 rsync ... — lowering priority prevents hangs
nohup rsync ... & — backgrounding adds an implicit 30-minute limit
ulimit -t 1800; rsync ... — CPU-time limits kill wall-clock hangs
timeout 1800 rsync ... — sends TERM (then KILL) when the duration elapses
explain: timeout runs a command with a wall-clock deadline, delivering SIGTERM (and SIGKILL with -k) when it expires — the direct fix for hung invocations. nice only affects scheduling priority; nohup merely immunizes against hangup with no time limit; and ulimit -t caps CPU seconds, which a process blocked on I/O may never consume.

q: A server shows corrupt packets and TCP retransmits on a new NIC, but the switch and cables test clean. The admin suspects a buggy TCP segmentation offload. How can they test by disabling it?
options: ethtool -K eth0 tso off gso off — disables segmentation offloads at the driver level
ethtool -s eth0 speed 100 duplex full — forcing link speed fixes offload bugs
ip link set eth0 tx off — ip link controls hardware offloads
sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tso=0 — offloads are kernel sysctls
explain: ethtool -K toggles NIC hardware offload features; disabling tso/gso moves segmentation back to the CPU, isolating driver-offload bugs. -s sets link speed/duplex — unrelated to offloads; ip link has no tx-offload knob (that is ethtool's domain); and there is no net.ipv4.tcp_tso sysctl — offloads live in the driver, not the IP stack.

q: During a suspected connection flood, an admin wants a quick summary count of TCP states (how many SYN-RECV, TIME-WAIT, etc.) rather than a full socket list. Which command gives that?
options: ss -tlnp — the -s flag is implied when listing listening sockets
ss -s — prints summary statistics including TCP state counters
netstat -s — netstat is the only tool with socket summaries
ss --summary=full — summaries require the long option
explain: ss -s prints a compact summary: total sockets plus per-state TCP counters — ideal for flood triage. ss -tlnp lists listening sockets with processes (verbose, not summarized); netstat -s shows protocol statistics but is deprecated and not socket-state counts; and --summary=full is not a real ss option.

q: Internal name resolution fails for one zone while others work. The admin wants to trace the full delegation chain from the root servers down to see where it breaks. Which command does this?
options: dig zone.internal — a normal query shows the delegation chain
nslookup -debug zone.internal — nslookup traces delegations by default
dig +trace zone.internal — iteratively queries root, TLD, and authoritative servers, showing each delegation
getent hosts zone.internal — getent follows the delegation chain
explain: dig +trace performs iterative resolution starting at the roots, printing every referral — exposing exactly which delegation is broken. A plain dig asks the configured recursive resolver (hiding the chain); nslookup lacks iterative tracing; and getent consults local nsswitch sources, never the DNS delegation hierarchy.

q: A monitoring script must record only the HTTP status code from a web app's health endpoint, with no body output. Which curl invocation does this?
options: curl -I https://app/health — -I suppresses the body and prints only the code
curl -s https://app/health | head -1 — the status line is always the first body line
curl --fail https://app/health — --fail prints just the numeric code
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://app/health — discards the body and prints only the status code
