explain: -o /dev/null discards the body while -w '%{http_code}' prints exactly the numeric status — the scriptable pattern. curl -I issues a HEAD request and prints all headers (not just the code, and HEAD may behave differently); the body never contains the status line; and --fail makes curl exit nonzero on errors while printing nothing.

q: traceroute to a web server returns only asterisks after the third hop — the network filters ICMP and UDP probes. The admin needs a hop-by-hop path using TCP instead. Which approach works?
options: traceroute -T -p 443 target — TCP SYN probes to the open HTTPS port trace the path
traceroute -I target — ICMP mode bypasses the UDP filtering
ping -M do -s 1500 target — large pings map each intermediate hop
tracepath -n target — tracepath uses TCP by default
explain: traceroute -T sends TCP SYN segments with increasing TTLs; targeting an open port (443) gets past filters that drop ICMP/UDP, revealing each hop. -I still uses ICMP, which is filtered here; ping measures end-to-end MTU, never per-hop paths; and tracepath uses UDP, not TCP.

q: An admin adds a partition with fdisk on a running system, but /dev/sda3 does not appear. They want the kernel to re-read the partition table without rebooting. Which command does this?
options: partprobe /dev/sda — asks the kernel to re-read the partition table
fdisk -l /dev/sda — listing forces the kernel to rescan
blkid /dev/sda3 — probing the device creates the node
udevadm trigger — triggers partition table re-reads directly
explain: partprobe informs the kernel of partition-table changes so new device nodes appear without a reboot. fdisk -l only reads and displays; blkid cannot probe a node that does not exist; and udevadm trigger replays device events but does not make the kernel re-read the table — partprobe is the purpose-built tool.

q: A disk previously used in an LVM volume group confuses the installer, which still detects the old VG. The admin wants to erase all filesystem, RAID, and LVM signatures before reusing the disk. Which command does this?
options: dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdb bs=1M count=1 — zeroing the first megabyte removes all signatures
wipefs -a /dev/sdb — erases all detected signatures from the device
fdisk /dev/sdb then 'o' — a new DOS label wipes LVM metadata
pvremove /dev/sdb — removes every signature type, not just LVM
explain: wipefs -a detects and erases every signature (filesystem, RAID, LVM, partition-table magic) on the device — the comprehensive cleanup. dd zeroing the first megabyte can miss signatures stored elsewhere (e.g., at the end of the disk); a fresh DOS label only rewrites the label area, leaving PV metadata; and pvremove only clears LVM metadata, not filesystem or RAID signatures.

q: An admin writing a provisioning script needs the UUID and filesystem TYPE of every block device in a parseable format. Which command is built for exactly that?
options: lsblk -f — topology-focused; UUIDs require extra -o flags
fdisk -l — lists UUIDs and filesystem types per partition
blkid — prints each block device's UUID, TYPE, and LABEL attributes
df -T — shows UUIDs for all mounted filesystems
explain: blkid queries block-device metadata and prints NAME=value pairs (UUID, TYPE, LABEL, PARTUUID) — ideal for scripts. lsblk -f is topology-oriented; fdisk -l shows partition layout without UUIDs or filesystem types; and df -T only covers mounted filesystems and omits UUIDs.

q: A server's interface negotiated 100Mb half-duplex against a gigabit switch, causing collisions and slowness. The admin wants to confirm the negotiated link parameters. Which command shows them?
options: ip addr show eth0 — displays negotiated speed and duplex
ss -i — socket info includes link negotiation state
nmcli dev show eth0 — NetworkManager reports PHY negotiation
ethtool eth0 — reports speed, duplex, and link status from the NIC
explain: ethtool queries the NIC/PHY directly for speed, duplex, auto-negotiation, and link detection. ip addr shows addressing, not link parameters; ss -i shows TCP socket internals; and nmcli reports connection profiles, not PHY-level negotiation — ethtool is the link-layer diagnostic.

q: An admin must switch eth0 from DHCP to static address 192.168.10.50/24 with gateway 192.168.10.1 via NetworkManager, effective immediately. Which sequence works?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.10.50/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.10.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.10.1 && nmcli con up eth0 — modifies the profile and reactivates it
nmcli dev set eth0 managed no && ip addr add 192.168.10.50/24 dev eth0 — unmanaged devices keep static config
echo the address into /etc/hosts — hosts entries configure interfaces
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual — the method change alone assigns the previous DHCP address statically
explain: nmcli con mod writes the static parameters into the connection profile, and nmcli con up reactivates it so the change takes effect immediately. Unmanaging the device abandons NetworkManager control (fragile); /etc/hosts maps names to IPs, never configures interfaces; and switching to manual without addresses leaves the interface address-less.

q: sshd behaves oddly and the admin suspects a drop-in override is changing its config. They want to see the base unit plus all applied drop-ins in one view. Which command shows the merged result?
options: systemctl show sshd — shows the merged unit file text
systemctl cat sshd — concatenates the unit file and its drop-ins
cat /usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service — the vendor file includes drop-ins
systemd-delta sshd — prints the merged configuration
explain: systemctl cat prints the unit file followed by each drop-in fragment, revealing exactly what systemd merged. systemctl show dumps property key=value pairs, not file text; the vendor file alone omits /etc overrides; and systemd-delta is not the standard merged-view tool — cat is.

q: cups.service shows inactive (dead), yet print jobs still process whenever one is submitted. What explains this?
options: The service crashed — dead units continue processing queued jobs
systemd restarted it invisibly — status output lags behind reality
Socket activation — cups.socket listens and systemd starts the service on demand per connection
The jobs run via cron — the service unit is unrelated to printing
explain: With socket activation, the .socket unit holds the listening socket while the .service stays inactive until traffic arrives — then systemd spawns it on demand. A dead unit processes nothing; status reflects live state, not lag; and while cron can schedule tasks, on-demand per-job startup is the textbook socket-activation pattern.

q: A custom backup service should only run when /mnt/backup is mounted. The admin wants systemd to skip the service cleanly (not fail) when the mount is absent. Which directive does this?
options: Requires=mnt-backup.mount — the service fails if the mount is missing
After=mnt-backup.mount — ordering alone skips the service when the mount is absent
Conflicts=umount.target — conflicts prevent startup without the mount
ConditionPathExists=/mnt/backup — the service is skipped (not failed) when the path is missing
explain: ConditionPathExists= is evaluated before startup; if the path is absent the unit is skipped cleanly without entering failed state. Requires= creates a hard dependency that FAILS the unit when unmet; After= only orders startup, never gates it; and Conflicts= stops the unit when the conflicting unit starts — the wrong semantics entirely.

q: A script running as root must execute a command as the postgres user without a password prompt and without full login-session semantics. Which is the cleanest way?
options: runuser -u postgres -- psql -c 'SELECT 1' — runs the command as postgres with no PAM session overhead
su postgres -c "psql -c 'SELECT 1'" — su is identical to runuser for scripts
sudo -u postgres psql — sudo requires no configuration for root
su - postgres — the login shell is required for any command as another user
explain: runuser is designed for root-run scripts: it switches UID directly without PAM authentication prompts or login-session side effects. su works but goes through PAM and can prompt or pull in session semantics; sudo -u works yet consults sudoers policy unnecessarily; and su - spawns a full login shell — heavyweight and wrong for a single command.

q: The deploy user needs to run only /usr/bin/systemctl restart app as root without a password. Which grants exactly that, verifiably?
options: Add 'deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL' to /etc/sudoers — least privilege for one command
Create /etc/sudoers.d/deploy with 'deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart app' and verify with sudo -l -U deploy — scoped grant, verified
Run chmod u+s /usr/bin/systemctl — setuid gives deploy the needed right
Add deploy to the wheel group — wheel membership grants passwordless systemctl
explain: A sudoers.d drop-in scoping NOPASSWD to the single exact command is least privilege, and sudo -l -U deploy verifies the effective rule. NOPASSWD: ALL grants unlimited root — the opposite of scoped; setuid on systemctl would give EVERY user root via systemctl — catastrophic; and wheel membership typically still requires a password and grants broad rights, not one command.

q: A server uses nftables, but the admin keeps checking iptables -L and seeing empty chains. How should they view the actual active packet-filter rules?
options: iptables -L -n -v — iptables shows nftables rules in compatibility mode
firewall-cmd --list-all — firewalld always reflects nftables state
nft list ruleset — dumps the active nftables ruleset
cat /etc/sysconfig/iptables — the saved file is the active ruleset
explain: nft list ruleset prints the live nftables configuration — tables, chains, and rules. iptables -L reads the legacy xtables backend, empty when nftables is native; firewalld only reflects rules if it is the manager in use; and /etc/sysconfig/iptables is a saved file, not proof of what is loaded in the kernel.

q: A Linux box is the gateway for a private LAN (net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 set, FORWARD policy ACCEPT). Internal hosts can ping the gateway but cannot reach the internet — their private source addresses go out unchanged. Which iptables rule fixes this?
options: iptables -A INPUT -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE — masquerade on the INPUT chain
iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE — source NAT on outbound traffic
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i eth0 -j DNAT --to-destination 203.0.113.5 — destination NAT on inbound traffic
iptables -P POSTROUTING ACCEPT — the nat table needs an ACCEPT default policy
explain: POSTROUTING in the nat table is where outbound source addresses are rewritten; MASQUERADE dynamically NATs them to the gateway's public IP — the missing piece for LAN-to-internet access. INPUT filters packets destined FOR the gateway, not forwarded ones; PREROUTING DNAT handles inbound port-forwarding (the reverse direction); and nat chains default to ACCEPT anyway — the policy was never the problem.

q: An admin wants root to be able to log in via SSH ONLY with key authentication — password login for root must be impossible, while other users keep password login. Which sshd_config line does this?
options: PermitRootLogin prohibit-password — root may authenticate, but not with a password
PermitRootLogin no — equivalent to key-only root access
PasswordAuthentication no — disables root password login specifically
PubkeyAuthentication yes — enabling keys automatically disables root passwords
explain: PermitRootLogin prohibit-password allows root login while forbidding password/keyboard-interactive auth for root — keys still work, and other users are unaffected. 'no' blocks root entirely (stronger than asked); PasswordAuthentication no disables passwords for EVERYONE; and merely enabling PubkeyAuthentication does not turn password auth off for root.

q: SSH key login fails with 'bad ownership or modes for directory /home/alice/.ssh'. The directory is currently 755. What is the correct fix?
options: chmod 644 ~/.ssh — key files must be world-readable
chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys — strict ownership/modes that sshd requires
chown root:root ~/.ssh — root must own the .ssh directory
chmod 777 ~/.ssh — permissive modes let sshd read the keys
explain: sshd's StrictModes requires ~/.ssh be 700 (owner-only) and authorized_keys 600, both owned by the user — otherwise it refuses key auth as a tampering safeguard. 644/777 are far too permissive and fail the check; and the directory must be owned by alice herself, not root.

q: An admin wants a second passphrase for an existing LUKS-encrypted volume without destroying the data or the original passphrase. Which command adds it?
options: cryptsetup luksFormat /dev/sdb1 — reformatting adds a key slot cleanly
cryptsetup luksOpen --add-key /dev/sdb1 — open accepts a second passphrase directly
cryptsetup luksAddKey /dev/sdb1 — adds a passphrase to a new key slot
echo newpass | cryptsetup luksUUID /dev/sdb1 — the UUID command manages keys
explain: luksAddKey writes an additional passphrase into a free LUKS key slot, leaving data and existing keys intact. luksFormat destroys the LUKS header and all data; luksOpen merely unlocks with an existing key (there is no --add-key option); and luksUUID prints the volume UUID — it manages no keys.

q: An admin must gzip 2,000 log files and wants 4 compression jobs running in parallel, one file per invocation. Which command does this?
options: ls *.log | xargs gzip — xargs parallelizes automatically
find . -name '*.log' -exec gzip {} + — -exec runs jobs in parallel
for f in *.log; do gzip $f & done — backgrounding equals xargs parallelism
printf '%s\0' *.log | xargs -0 -P 4 -n 1 gzip — null-delimited input, 4 parallel jobs, one file each
explain: xargs -0 -P 4 -n 1 reads null-delimited names (safe for odd filenames), runs 4 gzip processes concurrently, one file per process. Plain xargs runs sequentially; find -exec + batches but does not parallelize; and a manual & loop with no wait/job control is fragile and unbounded — xargs -P is the controlled tool.

q: Two scripts must communicate: a producer writes records and a consumer reads them in order, without intermediate files piling up on disk. Which IPC mechanism fits?
options: mkfifo /tmp/pipe; producer > /tmp/pipe & consumer < /tmp/pipe — a named pipe streams data with kernel buffering
producer > /tmp/out; consumer < /tmp/out — regular files are the standard streaming IPC
export PIPE_DATA=$(producer) — environment variables stream between processes
ln -s /tmp/pipe /dev/stdin — symlinks create pipes between scripts
explain: mkfifo creates a named pipe (FIFO): the writer blocks when the kernel buffer fills and the reader consumes in order — true streaming with no disk accumulation. Regular files grow unboundedly and need polling; environment variables are copied per-process, not streams; and a symlink to /dev/stdin creates no pipe.

q: Before deploying a 400-line Bash script to production, an admin wants a fast syntax check that parses the whole file without executing anything. Which does this?
options: bash -x script.sh — trace mode parses without executing
bash -n script.sh — no-execution mode: parses for syntax errors only
shellcheck --execute script.sh — shellcheck runs the script safely
bash --dry-run script.sh — dry-run is the syntax-check flag
explain: bash -n reads and parses the script, reporting syntax errors, and never executes a line. bash -x EXECUTES with tracing — dangerous for an untested script; shellcheck is a static linter (excellent, but --execute is not its syntax-check flag and it never runs code); and there is no --dry-run flag on bash.

q: An admin wants a simple numbered menu in Bash: '1) start 2) stop 3) status', looping until the user quits. Which builtin builds this menu?
options: read -p with a case statement — read renders numbered menus natively
select choice in start stop status quit; do case $choice in ...; esac; done — select generates the numbered menu and loops
while read with PS3 unset — while loops print menus automatically
explain: select is Bash's menu builtin: it prints numbered options, prompts with PS3, and loops until break. read only reads input (no menu rendering); getopts parses OPTION FLAGS like -v, not menus; and while read iterates input lines — it generates no menu.

q: A script receives f=/var/backups/db-2026-10-18.tar.gz and needs just the filename (db-2026-10-18.tar.gz) without the directory, using only shell builtins. Which expansion strips the leading path?
options: ${f#*/} — strips through the first slash, leaving var/backups/db-2026-10-18.tar.gz
basename "$f" — works but forks an external process
${f%.tar.gz} — strips the suffix instead of the directory
${f##*/} — greedy-removes everything through the last slash
explain: ${f##*/} uses the greedy ## to delete the longest leading match of */ — everything through the final slash — leaving the bare filename with no subprocess. ${f#*/} is non-greedy and stops after the FIRST slash (wrong for absolute paths); ${f%.tar.gz} trims the trailing suffix (the other end); and basename is correct but external, while the question asks for a pure-shell expansion.

q: An admin needs nightly incremental backups: a full backup Sunday, then only changed files each following night, using tar. Which mechanism does this?
options: tar --listed-incremental=/var/backups/snap.file -czf nightly.tar.gz /data — the snapshot file tracks state between runs
tar -czf nightly.tar.gz --newer=yesterday /data — --newer alone makes true incrementals
tar --diff -czf nightly.tar.gz /data — --diff mode writes incremental archives
rsync --link-dest — tar cannot do incrementals; use rsync
explain: --listed-incremental maintains a snapshot file recording directory state, so each run archives only files changed since the last snapshot — genuine incrementals. --newer filters by mtime but cannot detect renames/deletions reliably and is not a true incremental scheme; --diff COMPARES an archive to disk rather than creating one; and tar absolutely supports incrementals via the snapshot mechanism.

q: An admin suspects XFS corruption on an unmounted data volume and wants a NON-DESTRUCTIVE assessment before attempting any repair. Which command does this?
options: fsck.xfs /dev/sdb1 — the fsck wrapper checks XFS filesystems
xfs_repair -n /dev/sdb1 — no-modify mode reports what repair would do
mount -o ro /dev/sdb1 /mnt && dmesg — read-only mounts repair XFS automatically
explain: xfs_repair -n runs the full repair logic in no-modify mode, reporting corruption without writing — the safe first look. fsck.xfs is a stub that exits 0 doing nothing; xfs_growfs only extends healthy filesystems; and a read-only mount may replay the journal but performs no structural assessment.

q: mdadm --detail /dev/md0 shows one drive as faulty/removed in a RAID 1 mirror. The replacement disk is installed as /dev/sdc. What is the correct recovery sequence?
options: mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sda /dev/sdc — recreate the array on the new disk
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdc && mount it — the mirror rebuilds from any mounted disk
mdadm /dev/md0 --remove /dev/sdb --add /dev/sdc (or --manage --add) — evict the failed member and add the replacement; the mirror resyncs
mdadm --assemble --scan — assembly alone resyncs onto the new disk
explain: The failed member is removed and the new disk added to the EXISTING array, triggering a resync that rebuilds the mirror. --create would destroy the array and its data; formatting/mounting /dev/sdc does nothing for the array; and --assemble only activates already-complete arrays — it cannot adopt a blank disk.

q: A server's disk occasionally throws I/O errors. The admin wants a quick verdict on whether the drive's own firmware considers itself failing. Which command gives that?
options: hdparm -I /dev/sda — hdparm reports the SMART health verdict
dmesg | grep -i error — kernel errors are the drive's self-assessment
fsck -y /dev/sda1 — filesystem checks reveal drive health
smartctl -H /dev/sda — prints the drive's overall SMART health self-assessment
explain: smartctl -H queries the drive's SMART subsystem for its PASSED/FAILED self-assessment — the firmware's own verdict. hdparm -I shows drive identity/capabilities, not health; dmesg shows OS-observed errors, not the drive's assessment; and fsck checks filesystem structures, which can be fine on a dying disk.

q: A critical database keeps getting killed at peak load with no crash logs. dmesg shows 'Out of memory: Killed process 1832 (postgres)'. How can the admin make the OOM killer prefer killing a less important batch worker instead?
options: nice -n 19 batchworker — nice values steer the OOM killer
Raise /proc/<batchpid>/oom_score_adj (up to 1000) and lower postgres's — the OOM killer targets the highest score
sysctl -w vm.oom-kill=postgres — the OOM victim is a sysctl
ulimit -m unlimited on postgres — memory limits exempt processes from OOM
explain: The OOM killer selects victims by oom_score (adjusted by oom_score_adj, -1000..1000); raising the batch worker's score and lowering postgres's steers kills toward the worker. nice affects CPU scheduling only; there is no vm.oom-kill sysctl naming victims; and ulimit -m is largely unenforced on modern kernels and does not exempt anyone from OOM.

q: An air-gapped server needs the htop package, but the connected workstation must fetch the RPM (and its dependencies) without installing anything locally. Which command downloads them?
options: dnf download --resolve htop --downloaddir=/tmp/rpms — downloads the package plus dependencies, no install
dnf install --downloadonly htop — the download-only flag exists on install
rpm -ivh --fetch htop — rpm fetches from configured repos
dnf repoquery htop > /tmp/rpms — repoquery saves the RPM files
explain: dnf download fetches RPMs into a directory without installing, and --resolve pulls in dependencies too. There is no --downloadonly flag on dnf install; rpm cannot fetch from repos (--fetch is not an rpm option); and dnf repoquery only prints metadata — it does not save package files.

q: An admin must install a new kernel RPM while KEEPING the currently running kernel as a fallback. Which rpm invocation is safe?
options: rpm -Uvh kernel-*.rpm — upgrade replaces the old kernel, which is the safe method
rpm -Fvh kernel-*.rpm — freshen installs kernels in parallel
rpm -e kernel-old && rpm -ivh kernel-*.rpm — erase first, then install
rpm -ivh kernel-*.rpm — install (not upgrade) keeps both kernels side by side
explain: rpm -i installs alongside existing packages, so the old kernel remains bootable as a fallback; rpm -U would REMOVE the old kernel first. -F (freshen) only upgrades already-installed packages — same removal problem; and erasing the running kernel before installing the new one risks an unbootable system if the install fails.

q: A server moved from the Chicago office to New York and still reports Central time. The admin wants the system timezone changed persistently. Which command does this?
options: export TZ=America/New_York — the environment variable sets the system timezone
explain: timedatectl set-timezone rewrites the /etc/localtime symlink — the system-wide persistent timezone. TZ only affects the current shell's processes; date -s sets the CLOCK, not the zone; and on systemd systems the canonical path is /etc/localtime (/etc/timezone is a Debian convention that systemd ignores).

q: An admin suspects the system clock is drifting and wants to see the NTP stratum, root dispersion, and whether the clock is synchronized — not the peer list. Which command shows that?
options: chronyc sources -v — the verbose peer list includes stratum and sync state
timedatectl status — shows NTP stratum and dispersion
ntpq -p — the standard chrony status command
chronyc tracking — reports stratum, leap status, RMS offset, and synchronization state
explain: chronyc tracking summarizes the LOCAL clock's discipline state: stratum, leap status, last offset, RMS offset, and sync status. chronyc sources lists PEERS (the reverse trap); timedatectl shows only a yes/no NTP-active line; and ntpq is the legacy ntpd tool, not chrony's.

q: /var/log/journal is consuming 4 GB and the admin wants to cap retained journals at 500 MB going forward AND trim existing logs now. Which does both?
options: Set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and run journalctl --vacuum-size=500M — config caps future use, vacuum trims now
Run journalctl --vacuum-size=500M — vacuuming also writes the persistent cap
Set Storage=volatile — volatile mode deletes old journals automatically
rm -rf /var/log/journal/* — deleting files sets the 500M cap
explain: SystemMaxUse= in journald.conf sets the ongoing ceiling (applied when journald restarts), while journalctl --vacuum-size= immediately deletes oldest journals down to the target. Vacuuming alone does not persist the cap; Storage=volatile moves journals to /run (lost at reboot), not a size cap; and rm-ing files frees space once but leaves no limit — and risks racing the running journald.

q: A server boots into the graphical login, wasting RAM on a headless machine. The admin wants it to boot to a text console by default. Which change does this?
options: systemctl isolate multi-user.target — changes the default boot target
systemctl set-default multi-user.target — sets the persistent default boot target
systemctl disable gdm — disabling the display manager changes the default target
Edit /etc/inittab — the default runlevel lives in inittab
explain: systemctl set-default rewrites the default.target symlink to multi-user.target, making text-mode boot persistent. isolate only switches the CURRENT boot's target; disabling gdm stops that service but leaves graphical.target default (which may pull in other GUI services); and /etc/inittab is SysV legacy, ignored by systemd.

q: The admin notices lastb output full of failed root login attempts from a foreign IP. What does this indicate and what is the right first response?
options: Normal background noise — lastb always shows foreign root attempts
The root password is compromised — immediately reinstall the server
An SSH brute-force attack against root — block the IP and consider key-only auth / fail2ban
A misconfigured monitoring agent — whitelist the IP in /etc/hosts.allow
explain: lastb reads /var/log/btmp (failed logins); a flood of foreign root attempts is a brute-force attack in progress. It is not harmless noise to ignore; there is no evidence of actual compromise warranting a reinstall; and assuming a monitoring agent without verification is dangerous — block first, then harden SSH.

q: passwd -S alice shows 'alice LK 2026-01-10 0 99999 7 -1'. What does LK mean and how did the account get this way?
options: Locked by faillock — too many failed logins; clear with faillock --reset
Locked because the password expired — the user must change it at next login
Locked kernel account — system accounts show LK permanently
Password locked (passwd -l or usermod -L) — the hash was prefixed with !, blocking password login
explain: LK means the password field is locked — passwd -l / usermod -L prepends ! to the hash so password authentication fails (SSH keys may still work). faillock lockouts do not change the passwd -S status field; expiry shows different flags and forces a change rather than LK; and LK is not a system-account marker.

q: Alice belongs to groups dev and ops, with dev as her primary. She needs files she creates this afternoon to be owned by group ops without changing her default primary group. Which command does this for her shell session?
options: newgrp ops — switches her current primary group to ops for the session
usermod -g ops alice — required before any file can be group-owned by ops
chgrp ops on each file afterward — group ownership cannot be set at creation
sg ops -c 'touch file' — sg only works for a single command, not a session
explain: newgrp ops spawns a shell with ops as the effective primary group, so files created during the session inherit it — no permanent change. usermod -g would permanently change her default; chgrp afterward works but is the tedious alternative, not a requirement; and while sg CAN run a single command, newgrp is the session-wide answer.

q: An admin adds /etc/tmpfiles.d/app.conf to create /run/app with specific ownership at boot, but the directory does not exist right now. How can they apply the config immediately without rebooting?
options: systemctl restart systemd-tmpfiles — tmpfiles are applied by restarting the service
systemd-tmpfiles --create — processes tmpfiles.d configs and creates the entries now
touch /run/app — manual creation registers the tmpfiles entry
explain: systemd-tmpfiles --create reads all tmpfiles.d configuration and creates the declared files/directories immediately. There is no systemd-tmpfiles service to restart (it runs via systemd-tmpfiles-setup.service at boot); manual touch does not apply ownership/mode rules; and udevadm handles device events, not tmpfiles.

q: After a suspected compromise, the admin wants to check whether system binaries differ from a known-good baseline recorded at install time. Which tool is built for this?
options: rpm -V on every package — the RPM database is the integrity baseline
sha256sum /usr/bin/* — manual hashing is the standard baseline method
aide --check — compares current files against the AIDE database baseline
git status /usr — version control tracks system binary changes
explain: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) maintains a database of file hashes and permissions from a trusted baseline; aide --check reports deviations. rpm -V only covers packaged files and the RPM database itself may be compromised; manual sha256sum has no stored baseline to compare against; and /usr is not a git repo.

q: A shared server needs new files to default to rw-r----- (640) and new directories to rwxr-x--- (750). Which umask achieves this, and where should it be set for all users?
options: umask 077 in ~/.bashrc — home-directory bashrc covers all users
umask 002 in /etc/login.defs — login.defs sets the shell umask
umask 027 set system-wide (e.g., /etc/bashrc or /etc/profile) — 027 masks write for group and all for others
explain: umask 027 subtracts write-for-group and rwx-for-others: 666 becomes 640 for files, 777 becomes 750 for directories. 022 yields 644/755 (world-readable — wrong); 077 yields 600/700 (too restrictive); and ~/.bashrc is per-user while login.defs UMASK is inconsistently applied — the shell startup files are the reliable system-wide spot.

q: After a breach, the admin wants a list of every setuid-root binary on the system to spot planted privilege-escalation backdoors. Which command lists them?
options: ls -l /usr/bin | grep rws — covers the only directory that can hold setuid binaries
find / -type f -perm 4755 — exact-mode match finds all setuid binaries
find / -xdev -type f -perm -4000 -ls — matches any file with the setuid bit set, staying on the root filesystem
getfacl -R / | grep -i suid — ACLs record the setuid bit
explain: -perm -4000 matches files with the setuid bit set (the '-' prefix means 'these bits set', extra bits allowed), -xdev avoids descending into /proc and other mounts, and -ls details them. Grepping /usr/bin misses /sbin, /usr/sbin, and /opt; -perm 4755 matches ONLY exactly rwsr-xr-x, missing e.g. 4750 or 6755 binaries; and getfacl does not report the setuid bit.

q: A script runs fine as alice but fails under sudo with 'command not found' for /usr/local/bin/tool. The tool exists and is executable. What is the most likely cause?
options: sudo strips the PATH entirely — commands must use absolute paths under sudo
The tool needs setuid root — sudo does not grant file-execution rights
alice's shell is sh — sudo only works with bash
sudo's secure_path doesn't include /usr/local/bin — sudo resets PATH to the compiled secure_path
explain: sudo replaces the user's PATH with secure_path (commonly /sbin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin, excluding /usr/local/bin), so the tool is not found despite existing. sudo does not strip PATH entirely — it substitutes the configured one; setuid is irrelevant when sudo already elevates; and the user's shell does not affect sudo's PATH handling.

q: A hardening scan flags kernel pointer addresses visible in /proc/kallsyms to any local user, aiding kernel-exploit development. Which persistent setting hides them?
options: kernel.dmesg_restrict=1 — restricts kallsyms output to root
chmod 600 /proc/kallsyms — file permissions hide the pointers
kernel.kptr_restrict=2 in /etc/sysctl.d/10-hardening.conf — replaces kernel pointers with zeros for all users
kernel.kexec_load_disabled=1 — disables pointer exposure in kallsyms
explain: kernel.kptr_restrict=2 makes the kernel print zeros instead of real addresses in kallsyms and similar interfaces for everyone, including root; the sysctl.d drop-in persists it. dmesg_restrict only gates the dmesg buffer, not kallsyms; chmod on proc pseudo-files does not control this exposure; and kexec_load_disabled toggles kexec loading, unrelated to pointer visibility.

q: A playbook task registers a database password and the value appears in the Ansible log output. How should the task prevent secrets from being logged?
options: Use vault: true on the task — vault encrypts task output automatically
Set check_mode: no — check mode is what leaks registered variables
Pipe the output through ansible-vault encrypt_string at runtime
Add no_log: true to the task — suppresses the task's arguments and results from output
explain: no_log: true tells Ansible to censor that task's parameters and results in all output — the standard secret-hygiene flag. There is no vault: true task attribute; check_mode does not cause logging leaks; and encrypt_string is for authoring encrypted VARIABLES, not for suppressing runtime task output.

q: A playbook configures web servers, but one task must call the load balancer's API from the Ansible controller itself rather than from each web node. How?
options: delegate_to: localhost on the task — runs that task on the controller
connection: local on the play — runs the whole play on the controller
run_once: true — runs the task on the first web node instead of the controller
delegate_to: 127.0.0.1 with remote_user — localhost delegation needs explicit credentials
explain: delegate_to: localhost redirects that single task to execute on the control node — the pattern for API calls and local tooling. connection: local would move the ENTIRE play; run_once still executes on a managed host (the first), not the controller; and localhost delegation uses the local connection implicitly — no SSH credentials needed.

q: A repo's build left hundreds of untracked .o files and the developer wants them gone, but modified tracked files must be kept. Which command removes only the untracked files?
options: git reset --hard — removes untracked build artifacts
git clean -fd — deletes untracked files (-f) and directories (-d), leaving tracked modifications alone
rm -rf $(git status --porcelain | cut -c4-) — the manual equivalent, equally safe
explain: git clean -fd removes untracked files and directories while never touching tracked modifications — exactly the scoped cleanup. git reset --hard and git checkout -- . only affect TRACKED files (the opposite of needed); and the rm pipeline is fragile (whitespace in names, includes staged entries) where git clean is purpose-built.

q: A script creates temp files in /tmp and must delete them even if it exits early on error or via Ctrl-C. Which pattern guarantees cleanup?
options: rm -f /tmp/myapp.* at the end of the script — the final line always runs
set -e — errexit automatically removes temp files
tmp=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT — the EXIT trap runs on any shell exit
Run the script under timeout — timeout cleans up temp files
explain: trap ... EXIT registers a handler that runs when the shell exits for ANY reason — normal end, error, or signal — making cleanup reliable. A trailing rm never runs after an early exit; set -e only changes exit behavior, deleting nothing; and timeout kills the process without any file cleanup.

q: An admin runs a Podman container that must start at boot and restart on failure, managed like a normal service. What is the modern supported approach?
options: Add podman run to /etc/rc.local — rc.local starts containers at boot
Use docker-compose with restart: always — compose handles boot startup natively
nohup podman run -d — nohup containers survive reboots
podman generate systemd --new --name web, install the unit, systemctl enable it — a systemd unit manages the container's lifecycle
explain: podman generate systemd creates a native systemd unit (Restart= included) so the container starts at boot and restarts on failure like any service. rc.local is obsolete on systemd systems; compose's restart: always only helps if the compose project itself is started at boot; and nohup does nothing across a reboot.

q: After a host reboot, a KVM guest is down. virsh list --all shows it as 'shut off'. The admin wants it to start automatically with the host from now on. Which command enables that?
options: virsh autostart webvm — marks the domain to start with the libvirt daemon
systemctl enable webvm — guests are enabled as systemd units
virsh start webvm --persistent — the --persistent flag enables autostart
Add the VM to /etc/rc.local — rc.local starts defined guests
explain: virsh autostart sets the domain's autostart flag so libvirtd starts it when the host boots. Guests are not systemd units to enable; virsh start has no --persistent flag (the domain definition is already persistent); and rc.local is obsolete.

q: An admin must confirm whether a VM disk image is qcow2 or raw and whether it has a backing file before migrating it. Which command reports the image format and metadata?
options: file disk.img — file detects qcow2 backing chains reliably
qemu-img info disk.img — reports format, virtual size, and backing file
fdisk -l disk.img — lists the image format in the header
ls -lh disk.img — sparse size reveals qcow2 vs raw
explain: qemu-img info reads the image header and reports format (qcow2/raw), virtual vs disk size, and any backing file — the authoritative pre-migration check. file gives only a generic guess; fdisk reads PARTITIONS inside the image, not its container format; and ls sizes cannot distinguish formats or reveal backing files.

q: Users report missing emails and the admin suspects the local Postfix queue is backed up. Which command shows the queued messages and the reason they are deferred?
options: mailq --flush — mailq prints the queue and flushes it
postfix check — validates the queue contents
postqueue -p (or mailq) — lists queued messages with their deferral reasons
journalctl -u postfix --vacuum — journald shows the mail queue
explain: postqueue -p (mailq is its alias) lists every queued message with its status and the SMTP error deferring it. mailq has no --flush flag (flushing is postfix flush / postqueue -f); postfix check validates config/permissions, not queue contents; and journalctl --vacuum deletes journals — it does not display any queue.

q: df hangs indefinitely because an NFS server died, and umount /mnt/data also hangs. The admin needs the mount detached from the hierarchy immediately without waiting for the dead server. Which option does this?
options: umount -a — unmounts all filesystems, clearing the hung mount
fuser -km /mnt/data — killing processes detaches the mount
mount -o remount,ro /mnt/data — remounting read-only releases the hang
umount -l /mnt/data — lazy unmount detaches now, cleans up when no longer busy
explain: umount -l (lazy) detaches the filesystem from the namespace immediately and finishes cleanup once it is no longer busy — the standard escape from a dead-server hang. umount -a would try to unmount EVERYTHING (dangerous and equally hung); fuser -km kills processes but leaves the dead mount attached; and remounting still requires talking to the dead server.

q: A server crashed overnight and booted cleanly this morning. The admin wants to see only errors from the PREVIOUS boot to find what led to the crash. Which command shows exactly that?
options: journalctl -b -1 -p err — previous boot's journal, priority err and above
journalctl -b -p err — the -b flag defaults to the previous boot
dmesg -T | grep -i error — dmesg persists across reboots
journalctl --since yesterday -p warning — since-yesterday covers the crashed boot
explain: -b -1 selects the previous boot's journal and -p err filters to errors and more severe priorities — the precise crash-triage view. Plain -b means the CURRENT boot; the dmesg ring buffer does NOT survive reboot (only persistent journald does); and --since yesterday spans multiple boots with the wrong priority cutoff (warning, not err).
